Body:
We will resolve a person’s nomsNumber on demand during requests to the custody endpoint rather than persisting or pre-synchronizing it. The custody service will call an external authoritative source via a dedicated adapter to fetch the latest nomsNumber at request time, using known identifiers for correlation. The API contract remains unchanged: nomsNumber stays optional; absence indicates “unknown/unavailable.” The endpoint will not fail solely due to a lookup failure unless a client explicitly opts in via a requireNoms=true query flag, in which case a 424 Failed Dependency will be returned on lookup failure.

To mitigate latency and load, we will introduce an in-memory read-through cache (e.g., Caffeine) with a short TTL (e.g., 15 minutes) and a brief negative-cache TTL (e.g., 1 minute). The adapter will implement resilience patterns: bounded timeouts (e.g., 500–800 ms), limited retries with jitter on transient failures, and a circuit breaker. If the breaker is open or the lookup times out, the custody response is returned without nomsNumber unless requireNoms is set.

All calls will use service-to-service authentication with least-privilege scopes; sensitive error details will be suppressed from client responses and captured in logs/metrics. We will emit metrics for cache hit ratio, latency, error rates, and fallback counts, and add structured logs for traceability. A feature flag will control rollout and allow quick disablement.

Any existing background synchronization of nomsNumber will be deprecated and removed after rollout stability is confirmed. No data storage changes are required. This approach ensures freshness, reduces drift, and limits operational coupling while preserving API compatibility and predictable behavior under failure.

## Decision

Adopt a modular monolith as the initial deployment model, with clear bounded-context modules that map 1:1 to service candidates. Each module owns its data, exposes a narrow internal API, and communicates with others via domain events. External consumers access functionality through a single API gateway. We will split modules into independent services only when operational or scaling needs justify it.

Initial module/service scope:
- Identity & Access: authentication, authorization, user/org/role management.
- Accounts & Billing: subscriptions, plans, invoicing, payments.
- Core Domain (Product): primary business entities, workflows, and state.
- Catalog/Configuration: reference data, feature flags, templates.
- Search & Indexing: indexing pipelines and query endpoints.
- Notifications: email/SMS/push/webhook dispatch and templates.
- Audit & Compliance: audit log, data retention, PII redaction.
- Reporting & Export: aggregate views and data exports.
- Integration Gateway: connectors to approved third-party systems.

Ownership and interfaces:
- Each module owns its schema (separate schema namespaces in a shared database initially), migrations, and domain models.
- Inter-module calls prefer asynchronous events; synchronous calls only for read/query use cases with strict SLAs.
- Public API contracts are versioned; breaking changes require an API deprecation policy.

Out of scope for initial release:
- Real-time ML/recommendation services.
- Ad hoc BI/warehouse and ELT pipelines beyond minimal exports.
- Custom integrations beyond the Integration Gateway catalog.

Exit criteria for service extraction:
- Independent scaling needs, distinct runtime constraints, or change cadence requiring isolated deployment.
- Clear operational boundaries (SLOs, on-call ownership, observability) and automated CI/CD in place.

## Decision
We will remove support for defining or using a custom, bindable JNDI “lookup-name” across the platform. All components must resolve resources via:
- Standardized, container-managed JNDI names (java:/, java:comp/, java:module/, java:app/ as applicable), and/or
- Framework-native dependency injection and configuration mechanisms.

The JNDI registry will be treated as read-only at runtime; dynamic rebinds and aliasing through custom lookup-name entries are disallowed. Any remaining references to custom lookup-name will be deprecated immediately and hard-removed in the next major release.

Migration path:
- Provide a mapping layer that resolves legacy lookup-name values to the canonical, fully qualified JNDI names during the deprecation window and logs structured WARN diagnostics with remediation hints.
- Ship a static analysis rule and a build-time check that fail the build on new usages of lookup-name and suggest the canonical name or DI alternative.
- Update samples, docs, and templates to reference canonical names or DI.

Failure behavior post-removal:
- If a legacy lookup-name is encountered, startup will fail fast with a clear error message including the computed canonical name (if derivable).

Acceptance criteria:
- No runtime writes to JNDI.
- Zero occurrences of lookup-name in codebase and configuration.
- All consumers successfully use canonical names or DI with green integration tests.

We will run the backend in Docker for all local development to maximize environment parity, simplify onboarding, and standardize tooling across OSes.

- Use Docker Desktop with Docker Compose as the primary entrypoint: docker compose up starts the backend and all dependent services.
- Build from a single Dockerfile with multi-stage targets (dev and prod). Local uses the dev target with hot-reload, debugging, and test tooling enabled.
- Source code is bind-mounted for hot reload. Build artifacts/cache directories are volume-mounted to improve performance. File change polling is enabled where required.
- Dependent services (e.g., databases, cache, message broker) run as containers in the same Compose project; data services can use named volumes for persistence.
- Expose well-known ports; internal service discovery uses the Compose network and service names. No host service installs are required beyond Docker/Compose.
- Configuration is injected via .env files referenced by Compose; secrets are excluded from VCS and may be loaded via Docker secrets on supported hosts.
- Provide Make/NPM scripts (or equivalent) that wrap common tasks (build, up, down, logs, test, lint, migrate) to hide Docker verbosity.
- Enforce resource limits for services to avoid host contention. Prefer multi-arch images (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) to support Apple Silicon and Intel.
- CI uses the same Dockerfile and Compose definitions to ensure parity; native local runs are supported as a best-effort fallback but not the default path.
- Documentation will treat Docker-based local execution as the canonical workflow; native-only instructions may be deprecated over time.

We will package and run all application services as OCI-compliant containers and deploy them across multiple virtual machines (“boxes”) for isolation, scalability, and resilience.

- Containerization: Each service runs in its own container, one main process per container. Base images are minimal and pinned; images are built via CI, signed, scanned, and stored in a private registry.
- Orchestration: Production and staging run on a Kubernetes cluster with at least two node pools spread across availability zones. Resource requests/limits are defined per container; autoscaling is enabled where applicable.
- Multi-box topology: Workloads are distributed across multiple VMs/nodes to isolate failure domains and enforce blast-radius limits. Public-facing gateways are separated from internal workloads. Stateful data stores are provided by managed services and not containerized where a managed alternative exists.
- Networking and security: In-cluster communication is restricted by namespace and NetworkPolicies; secrets are mounted from a centralized secrets manager (e.g., Vault/KMS). Image pull policies, admission controls, and runtime policies (e.g., seccomp/AppArmor, read-only root FS, non-root) are enforced.
- Deployments: Use rolling or blue/green deployments with health checks and readiness/liveness probes. Canary releases are supported for high-risk changes.
- Environments: Local development uses Dev Containers/Docker Compose; ephemeral review environments are provisioned per PR. Test parity is maintained with production via the same container images.
- Observability: Standardized logging, metrics, and tracing are sidecar/agent collected; per-container dashboards and alerts are defined.
- Data and storage: Persistent volumes are provisioned via CSI where needed; backups and disaster recovery are managed at the storage/service level with cross-zone replication.

This decision standardizes packaging, deployment, and runtime isolation, and mandates distribution across multiple machines to meet availability, security, and scaling requirements.

## Decision

Persist new tide projections in Google Cloud Firestore (Native mode) as the system of record, with Google Cloud Storage used for bulk artifacts, and Firebase Hosting/Functions for controlled ingestion and access.

- Data model:
  - Collection: tideProjections
    - Document: {stationId}
      - Subcollection: runs
        - Document: {runId} (idempotent key = sourceVersion+ingestTimestamp hash)
          - Fields: sourceMeta, modelVersion, generatedAt, validFrom, validTo, checksum
          - Subcollection: points
            - Document: {tsISO} with fields: ts, height, units, quality, tideType
  - Denormalized index collection for queries:
    - tideIndex: documents keyed {stationId}_{yyyymm} with array/map of daily summaries and min/max to accelerate range queries.
- Write path:
  - Ingestion via Cloud Function/Cloud Run, authenticated service account. Upsert semantics per {stationId, runId}; points written in batches (commit size <= 500) with parallelism capped to avoid hotspotting.
  - Idempotency enforced by runId and checksum; stale runs soft-deprecated with status=obsolete.
- Reads:
  - Primary queries by stationId and time range use tideIndex; detailed time-series fetched from points if needed. Composite indexes created for station/time shards as required.
- Retention:
  - Points retained 24 months via Firestore TTL on points; runs retained 36 months; monthly tideIndex retained 36 months.
- Security:
  - Firestore Security Rules: read public for tideIndex and points (optional: read-scope per project stage); writes restricted to ingestion service accounts. Validation on field types/ranges.
- Performance:
  - Use batched writes, distributed timestamps to avoid single-key hotspots, and document size < 1 MB. Cache monthly tideIndex via CDN.
- Observability:
  - Structured logging, metrics on ingest latency/error rate, and checksums to verify completeness.

## Decision

Adopt ECMAScript Modules (ESM) as the standard module system for all new code. Prefer named exports and disallow default exports to improve discoverability, enable reliable tree-shaking, and avoid import ambiguities. Avoid CommonJS module.exports in new code; retain it only in legacy modules that are not yet migrated.

Implementation details:
- Node.js runtime: configure package.json with "type": "module" for ESM .js files. For TypeScript, use "module": "NodeNext" and "moduleResolution": "NodeNext"; prefer .ts with .mts/.cts only when necessary for dual-mode interop.
- Linting: enforce "no default exports" (e.g., eslint rule import/no-default-export) and prefer-module usage.
- Build/bundle: ensure bundlers are configured for ESM entry points to leverage tree-shaking. Avoid transpiling ESM down to CJS for application bundles.
- Interop:
  - From ESM to CommonJS: use node:create-require (createRequire) or dynamic import and access default appropriately. Wrap legacy CJS only as needed.
  - From CommonJS to ESM: when consuming ESM in CJS, use dynamic import; avoid relying on Babel-style synthetic default interop.
- Publishing (libraries only): expose ESM as the primary entry via package.json exports with "import" condition; optionally provide a CJS fallback with "require" if consumer ecosystems require it. Do not mix default and named export shapes across formats.

Migration strategy: migrate existing module.exports to ESM with named exports incrementally; add compatibility shims where integration points are sensitive. New modules must not use module.exports or export default.

We will standardize all ECS EC2 launch-type capacity on the ECS-Optimized Amazon Linux 2 (AL2) AMI (including GPU and ARM variants where required). All existing clusters using Amazon Linux 1 or generic Linux AMIs will be migrated via rolling replacement of Auto Scaling Group (ASG) instances.

Key actions:
- Adopt the AWS-recommended AL2 ECS-optimized AMI via SSM Parameter Store (/aws/service/ecs/optimized-ami/amazon-linux-2/recommended/image_id) in Launch Templates.
- Maintain separate Launch Templates per workload class (x86_64, arm64, GPU) pinned to the corresponding recommended AMI parameters.
- Enforce IMDSv2-only, gp3 EBS volumes, encrypted-by-default, and instance profile with least privilege.
- Enable containerd runtime, CloudWatch/FireLens logging, and SSM Agent; retain cgroup v1 initially to avoid regressions, with a plan to evaluate cgroup v2 later.
- Implement rolling refresh: increase ASG desired capacity by one batch, drain ECS tasks before termination, and complete replacement with zero downtime. Blue/green will be used for latency-sensitive services.
- Establish AMI refresh cadence: automatic minor refresh monthly; security hotfixes ad hoc; change approval via infrastructure pipeline.
- Decommission AL1/generic AMIs and associated bake pipelines; converge on a single hardened user data bootstrap.
- Rollback by reverting the Launch Template AMI reference to the prior version and initiating an ASG instance refresh.

Acceptance criteria: all services schedule and run on AL2 nodes with no functional regressions, equal or improved cost/performance, successful observability/agent operation, and passing security benchmarks.

- Prefer composition over inheritance for code reuse and variability. Use inheritance only when there is a strict “is-a” relationship, a stable abstraction, and a clear behavioral contract that cannot be achieved cleanly via composition.
- Limit hierarchy depth to one level (abstract base → concrete subtype). Deep or wide hierarchies are prohibited.
- Provide polymorphism via interfaces/traits/protocols. Use abstract base classes only to define minimal, cohesive contracts and shared invariants; avoid sharing state via inheritance.
- Mark classes final by default. Explicitly mark extension points as open/sealed only when necessary and document supported customization hooks.
- No multiple inheritance of implementation. Where the language allows, use interfaces plus composition or lightweight mixins without shared state. Avoid diamond patterns.
- Disallow protected state/methods. Use private members and explicit extension mechanisms (composition, delegation, strategy, decorator).
- Enforce Liskov Substitution Principle: subtypes must not weaken preconditions or strengthen postconditions; behavioral compatibility is mandatory.
- Backwards compatibility: changing base-class contracts or method signatures is a breaking change and follows major-version bumps. Prefer additive interfaces.
- Testing: provide contract tests for base abstractions; all subtypes must pass the shared test suite. Include mutation/static analysis to detect hierarchy violations and depth limits.
- Performance and observability: avoid inheritance-based proxies; prefer decorators/composition for cross-cutting concerns with explicit telemetry.
- Code review gates and linters will reject new inheritance unless it meets the above criteria and includes rationale and contract documentation.

We will provide downloadable search results via an export capability that mirrors the current search filters, permissions, and result ordering.

- Export flow: small result sets (≤5,000 rows) are delivered as an immediate, streaming response; larger exports run as asynchronous background jobs with progress, retry (exponential backoff, max 3), and failure reporting.
- Formats: CSV (UTF-8, RFC 4180) and JSON Lines. Optional ZIP compression for files >10 MB. Dates are ISO‑8601 UTC; numbers unlocalized; booleans true/false. CSV includes a header row with stable field keys.
- Scope and schema: only fields visible in the active search view are exported, in the same order; hidden/masked fields remain masked. A companion metadata JSON (for async jobs) includes query parameters, column definitions, schema version, export timestamp, and user id.
- Limits and quotas: default row cap 50,000; hard cap 200,000 per export. Per‑user concurrency limit of 2 active exports and daily quota of 10. Server‑side pagination uses keyset/streaming to avoid memory spikes.
- Delivery: async exports are stored in encrypted object storage and exposed via time‑limited pre‑signed URLs (15 minutes). Artifacts auto‑expire and are deleted after 7 days. UI provides “Export” with format, compression, and row limit options, plus job status and download link when ready. Webhooks and email notifications are available for completion.
- Security and compliance: exports enforce RBAC and row‑level security at query time; PII masking policies apply. All export requests and downloads are audited (user, time, filter hash, counts, IP). Data at rest is encrypted; in transit uses HTTPS/TLS. Admins can revoke and purge pending/finished exports.
- Performance: heavy exports are offloaded to a dedicated worker queue; queries use read replicas. Index hints and snapshot isolation are used to ensure consistency at export start time.
- Observability: metrics (counts, durations, sizes), structured logs, and alerts on failure rates and quota breaches.
- Backward compatibility: field keys are stable; deprecations are versioned via schema version in metadata.

We will introduce a distinct “In‑Depth Katas” track, separate from the existing “Normal Katas,” to better serve advanced, exploratory learning objectives without degrading approachability for general users.

- Create a dedicated category/namespace (“In‑Depth”) with its own landing page, navigation entry, and API endpoints/filters so users can explicitly browse, search, and subscribe to this track.
- Apply clear labeling and visual differentiation (badges, color, icon) across lists, detail pages, and progress views; in-depth items do not appear in default “Normal” recommendations unless explicitly opted in.
- Establish entry prerequisites and guidance: recommended skill levels, estimated time (multi‑session), and prerequisite topics; provide structured outlines, references, and expected outcomes.
- Adopt a different pacing and evaluation model: multi-step checkpoints, richer rubrics, optional peer review, and artifact submissions; completion is tracked per checkpoint with resumable progress.
- Govern content separately: contribution templates, review criteria, and publication workflows tailored for longer-form, research-oriented exercises; maintain versioning and changelogs.
- Analytics and success metrics are partitioned to avoid skewing engagement KPIs for Normal Katas and to assess depth-specific outcomes (retention across sessions, checkpoint completion rates).
- Migration: existing long-form katas will be audited and moved to the In‑Depth track with redirects and preserved progress; normal katas remain concise and time-bounded.
- Opt-in discovery: surfaces (home, emails) include an “Explore In‑Depth” prompt for qualified users; default learning paths remain “Normal” unless user preference or skill profile indicates readiness.

We will standardize on Docker to containerize all application services, supporting components, and operational tooling. All deployable units must provide a Dockerfile using multi-stage builds, minimal/OCI-compliant base images, non-root users, and explicit healthchecks. Local development will use Docker Compose for multi-service orchestration, consistent environment parity, and reproducible setups.

Container images will be built exclusively via CI pipelines, not locally for release, with deterministic builds, reproducible tags, and content-addressable digests. We will adopt semantic versioning plus immutable digests (e.g., vX.Y.Z and sha256) and disallow mutable latest in production. Images must be vulnerability scanned, include SBOMs, and be signed (e.g., cosign) with provenance attestations. Approved base images (distroless, Alpine, or distro LTS) are centrally curated and regularly refreshed.

A private OCI registry will host all images with role-based access, retention policies, and automated cleanup of stale tags. Build caching is enabled to optimize CI performance. Secrets are injected via runtime configuration, not baked into images. Resource limits and read-only filesystems are required where feasible. Rootless execution is preferred; where not possible, justification is required.

This decision deprecates bespoke VM-based deployment artifacts. Non-containerized workflows are allowed only for exceptional cases (e.g., hardware-bound dependencies) with an approved exemption and a mitigation plan.

Orchestration choices (e.g., Kubernetes, ECS) are out of scope for this decision; however, images must remain portable across OCI-compliant runtimes. Developer tooling (Make targets, linting, hadolint) will enforce conventions, and pre-commit checks will validate Dockerfile best practices.

## Decision
Adopt a unified Design Guideline to ensure consistency, maintainability, and product quality across all services and clients:

- Architectural principles: favor simplicity, high cohesion/low coupling, explicit boundaries, and evolutionary architecture; apply Clean Architecture for core domains and 12-Factor for services.
- Patterns and modularity: domain-driven design for bounded contexts; hexagonal ports/adapters for integrations; prefer composition over inheritance; use feature modules and shared libraries with strict dependency rules.
- API standards: RESTful JSON APIs with consistent resource naming, HATEOAS optional; versioned via URI (vN) and semantic changes documented; OpenAPI-first contracts; idempotency for unsafe operations; consistent pagination, filtering, and error schema (RFC 7807).
- UI/UX: design tokens and system-driven components; accessibility WCAG 2.1 AA; responsive first; dark mode and i18n-ready.
- Coding standards: language-specific style guides enforced via linters/formatters; SOLID and defensive programming; public APIs documented; no cyclic dependencies.
- Data: immutable events, soft deletes where appropriate, migration scripts versioned; PII handling per data-classification policy.
- Security: least privilege, secure defaults, OWASP Top 10 controls, secrets via vault, input validation and output encoding, mTLS/service auth, OAuth2/OIDC for users.
- Reliability and performance: SLOs per service, performance budgets, backpressure and circuit breakers; zero-downtime deploys and rollbacks.
- Testing: pyramid-aligned (unit > contract > integration > e2e); deterministic CI; test data builders; mutation testing for critical modules.
- Observability: structured logs, distributed tracing, RED/USE metrics, health/liveness/readiness probes.
- Documentation and governance: ADRs per change; living style guide; code reviews mandatory; automated checks as gates; deviations require approved RFC with sunset plan.

## Decision
Adopt Axon Framework (v4.x) to implement CQRS and Event Sourcing in bounded contexts that require strong auditability, temporal reasoning, and long‑lived process coordination (initially: Orders and Inventory). Use aggregates for command handling and event‑sourced state; expose queries via dedicated read models with Spring Data projections. Coordinate cross‑aggregate workflows with Sagas.

Run Axon Framework with:
- Event Store: PostgreSQL (Axon JDBC) for portability and operational simplicity; enable snapshots after ~100 events per aggregate (tunable).
- Messaging: Use Axon’s local bus within the service boundary; publish domain events to Kafka for cross‑service integration and replayable downstream consumption. Do not adopt Axon Server at this stage to avoid additional operational surface; reassess if routing/scalability needs exceed current scope.
- Serialization: Jackson JSON with explicit event versioning and upcasters; forbid breaking changes to event schemas.
- Concurrency and delivery: Optimistic concurrency on aggregates with retry policies; tracking event processors with token store in PostgreSQL; enable back‑off and batch processing.
- Read models: Separate schemas; eventual consistency with compensating updates; rebuild capability from the event store is mandatory.
- Sagas: Timeouts via scheduler; persist saga state in PostgreSQL; ensure idempotent command dispatch and event handling.
- Testing and tooling: Axon test fixtures for aggregates and sagas; contract tests for integration events; operational dashboards for processor lag and token positions.

Scope this decision to the identified bounded contexts; other services remain CRUD-first. Revisit after the first two releases to evaluate operational overhead, performance, and team proficiency.

## Decision
Adopt Terraform (v1.x) as the authoritative Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) tool for provisioning, changing, and documenting all cloud infrastructure across environments. We will:

- Standardize on a modular architecture: a central “platform-modules” repository (reusable, versioned modules) and per-system “stacks” repositories (environment compositions). Modules and providers are pinned with semantic versions.
- Use a remote state backend with locking (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB or Terraform Cloud) per workspace/environment; no local state is permitted. State access is controlled via IAM/RBAC; state is encrypted at rest and in transit.
- Manage environments via Terraform workspaces or distinct folders/states (dev, staging, prod) with strict separation and promotion workflows.
- Enforce a CI-driven workflow: fmt/validate/tflint/checkov → terraform plan (artifact) → manual/PR approval → apply to target environment. Plans are immutable artifacts; applies occur only from CI with least-privilege service principals.
- Implement policy-as-code (Sentinel/OPA) for guardrails (naming, tagging, regions, costs, security baselines) and merge gates.
- Handle secrets via a dedicated secrets manager (Vault/Cloud provider) referenced as data sources; no secrets in code, state, or plans.
- Document modules and stacks with autogenerated READMEs (terraform-docs), examples, inputs/outputs, and architecture diagrams; changes require ADR updates.
- Establish tagging/naming conventions and mandatory metadata (owner, cost center, environment, data classification).
- Perform drift detection via scheduled plans and alerts; adopt import workflows for existing resources; define deprecation and migration procedures for modules.
- Provide onboarding, code review standards, and a break-glass emergency apply protocol with audit logging.

This decision makes Terraform the single source of truth for infrastructure, enabling reproducibility, compliance, and auditable change management.

Adopt a continuous, mixed-method usability testing program integrated into the delivery lifecycle to ensure the product meets user goals, accessibility needs, and business outcomes.

- Methods: Use a blend of moderated remote sessions for deep qualitative insights, unmoderated task-based tests for scale, in-product analytics and session replay for behavioral evidence, and A/B tests for causal validation. Conduct heuristic evaluations between cycles.
- Cadence: Run formative tests during discovery and before major design commits; conduct per-release summative benchmarks on core flows; perform monthly accessibility spot checks and quarterly comprehensive audits.
- Participants: Recruit representative users across key personas, platforms, assistive technologies, and locales. Maintain a research panel and inclusive screening practices.
- Metrics and thresholds: Track task success rate (>90% on critical tasks), time-on-task (baseline hold or improvement), error rate (<5% critical), System Usability Scale (SUS ≥ 80), qualitative severity ratings, and conversion/retention impacts. Issues rated “critical” must be resolved before release.
- Process integration: Make “passes usability thresholds” part of Definition of Done for core flows. Log findings in a centralized research repository, link to backlog items, and prioritize by severity and impact. Product and Design own remediation; Engineering allocates capacity each sprint for fixes.
- Tooling and compliance: Standardize on approved tools for recruiting, testing, analytics, and session replay with data minimization, consent capture, and privacy-by-design. Store artifacts securely with retention policies.
- Governance: Establish a UX Research Ops practice to manage protocols, templates, and participant welfare; review results in a recurring cross-functional forum to drive decisions and track trends.

We will adopt “directory as input” as the primary interface. The system will accept a folder path and process its contents recursively, discovering supported files by extension and/or an optional manifest file (manifest.yaml/json) at the root. Ordering and grouping will be determined by the manifest when present; otherwise, a deterministic sort (by relative path, case-insensitive) will be applied. Include/exclude patterns (glob/regex) will be configurable via CLI flags and API options and can also be specified in the manifest. Symlinks will be ignored by default for security but may be enabled via an explicit flag.

Backward compatibility will be maintained: providing a single file path remains supported and is treated as a degenerate folder with one item. Existing APIs will add overloads/parameters that accept a directory; the previous single-file entry points will be kept but marked as deprecated and will internally wrap the directory-based pipeline. The CLI will accept either a file or directory; if both are given, directory takes precedence with a warning.

Validation will enforce: directory exists and is readable; contents do not exceed configured limits (file count, total size, max depth); unsupported or malformed files are skipped with warnings; fatal errors cause a non-zero exit. Processing will be parallelized per file where safe, with bounded concurrency. Outputs remain identical in format; multi-file inputs will aggregate results in a deterministic combined artifact.

Security constraints include path traversal prevention, extension allowlists, size limits, and refusal of executable/binary types unless explicitly enabled. We will provide a migration period with deprecation notices in logs and release notes for two minor versions before removing legacy single-file-only code paths.

We will adopt AWS Lambda as the default compute for event-driven, bursty, and asynchronous workloads, and for lightweight synchronous APIs. Long-running jobs, persistent connections/websockets, sustained high-throughput workloads, and specialized OS/runtime needs will use containerized or EC2-based services instead.

Standardize on Node.js 20 and Python 3.11; use Java/.NET only when necessary. Synchronous HTTP access will be fronted by Amazon API Gateway (HTTP APIs). Asynchronous integrations will use Amazon EventBridge for event routing, SQS for durable retries and back-pressure, and SNS for fan-out. Business workflows will be orchestrated with AWS Step Functions.

Packaging will default to ZIP; container images will be used when dependencies exceed ZIP limits or require native system libs. Functions will not run in a VPC unless required (DB access, private endpoints). When VPC is required, place functions in private subnets, provide egress via NAT, and use VPC endpoints for AWS services.

Set timeouts tightly (≤30s for synchronous paths; up to 15 minutes for async), and tune memory/CPU for latency and cost. Apply reserved/provisioned concurrency for latency-critical paths; enforce concurrency limits per function to protect downstreams.

Manage everything via Infrastructure as Code (Terraform), with per-environment accounts and per-function least-privilege IAM. Enable AWS X-Ray tracing and structured JSON logging; adopt Lambda Powertools for logging, metrics, and tracing. Configure retries, DLQs (SQS), and alarms on errors, throttles, latency, and DLQ age.

Use versioning and aliases with canary deployments (e.g., 10/90) for safe rollouts. Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager/SSM with KMS encryption; prohibit secrets in code or environment variables. Implement budgets and cost monitors for concurrency, duration, and invocations.

Adopt a layered brute-force protection strategy combining edge, gateway, and application controls. At the edge (CDN/WAF), enable bot management, IP reputation filtering, geo/rule-based blocking, and baseline rate limits per IP/ASN, returning 403 for known bad actors. At the API gateway, enforce per-endpoint token-bucket/sliding-window rate limits with bursting (e.g., 60 req/min per IP per auth-sensitive endpoint; stricter for login/password-reset/token issuance), return 429 with Retry-After, and maintain separate limits for authenticated vs. anonymous traffic. In the application, implement adaptive throttling keyed by multiple dimensions (IP, user/account, device fingerprint, tenant, and credential tuple) stored in Redis. For authentication endpoints, apply exponential backoff and require step-up challenges (e.g., CAPTCHA or WebAuthn/MFA prompt) after N failed attempts (default N=5 within 10 minutes). Temporarily suspend the specific account for authentication (soft lock) after repeated failures (e.g., 10 failures in 30 minutes → 15-minute cooldown), without disclosing which field was incorrect. Protect enumeration vectors by returning uniform error messages and response times. For credential-stuffing resistance, detect high cardinality of failed usernames/passwords per source and block at gateway/edge. Exempt health checks and allowlist internal service IPs with separate limits; apply stricter caps to high-cost endpoints. Provide admin-configurable, per-tenant overrides and dynamic tuning via feature flags. Log all throttling, challenges, and lockouts with correlation IDs and export to SIEM for alerting and anomaly detection. Regularly pen-test and tune thresholds; include blue/green rollout and kill-switch. Ensure privacy by hashing identifiers used for counters and comply with applicable rate-limit headers.

We will standardize testability and accessibility by introducing a UITestablePage interface and requiring all new and refactored screens/components to implement it.

- Define a UITestablePage interface in the presentation layer with:
  - property testIdPrefix: String (e.g., "Login")
  - function applyTestIds() invoked during view lifecycle (e.g., viewDidLoad/onViewCreated) to set accessibilityIdentifier/testTag on key UI elements
- Provide a companion UITestableComponent for reusable widgets to ensure consistent behavior outside full-page contexts.
- Centralize identifiers per page/component in a static/companion object (e.g., enum/object TestIds) and reference them inside applyTestIds() to avoid inlined strings and keep IDs stable.
- Adopt a naming convention: <PageName>.<ElementPurpose>[.<Variant>], human-readable and stable over time (e.g., "Checkout.PlaceOrderButton").
- Always include identifiers in all build types (debug/release); they are non-sensitive and safe for production, improving assistive technology support and enabling black-box UI tests.
- Scope: Applies to all platform UIs (iOS accessibilityIdentifier, Android testTag/view tag, Web data-testid/aria attributes) via platform-specific adapters behind the same interface contract.
- Gradual adoption: mandatory for new screens; migrate existing screens opportunistically during touchpoints or refactors.
- Testing and governance: add lightweight lint/checks to flag missing applyTestIds() calls; include in PR checklist; UI tests must use these canonical IDs.
- Documentation: provide a short guide and examples; maintain a registry of reserved prefixes to avoid collisions.
- Backward compatibility: do not rename existing public IDs unless necessary; deprecate old IDs with a transition window and dual-tagging where required.

## Decision

We will adopt an inclusive language policy across all user-facing and developer-facing artifacts to avoid offensive, exclusionary, or derogatory vocabulary. This applies to UI text, documentation, logs, error messages, APIs (endpoints, parameters, payloads), data schemas, metrics, code identifiers, test data, commit messages, and issue titles.

Key elements:
- Establish a vetted glossary of approved inclusive terms (e.g., allowlist/denylist, primary/replica, blocker, parent/child) and disallowed terms with suggested replacements.
- Enforce automated checks: linters for prose and code (e.g., alex, inclusive-lint), pre-commit hooks, and CI gates that flag or fail offending terms.
- Integrate review checklists into code and docs review; violations must be resolved or explicitly exempted.
- Implement a deprecation and migration strategy for existing public surfaces:
  - Introduce inclusive replacements with backward-compatible aliases and clear deprecation notices.
  - Version and document breaking changes; provide migration guides and changelogs.
  - Plan data and schema migrations with scripts and rollback paths.
- Handle localization with locale-specific guidance and translator notes to avoid culturally offensive phrasing.
- Define an exception process for unavoidable uses (e.g., legal citations) requiring approval from the editorial board and annotated justification.
- Assign ownership to an Inclusive Language Working Group responsible for glossary maintenance, tooling configuration, audits, and training.
- Provide education and quick-reference materials; measure compliance via periodic audits and CI metrics.

This decision is effective immediately for new work; legacy remediation will proceed incrementally per product roadmap and risk prioritization.

An “environment” is a named, isolated execution and configuration boundary that encapsulates infrastructure, platform/runtime services, application deployments, configuration, secrets, data stores, access controls, and observability for a specific stage, tenant, or purpose.

Key decisions:
- Scope and identity: Each environment is uniquely identified by an env slug (lowercase, [a-z0-9-], ≤20 chars), tier (e.g., dev, test, staging, prod), region(s), and optional tenant. Examples: dev, staging, prod, pr-123.
- Isolation: Production runs in a separate cloud account/subscription/project from non-production. Non-prod environments may share accounts but must be isolated by VPC/VNet, clusters/namespaces, IAM principals, and data boundaries to limit blast radius.
- Mapping: An environment maps 1:1 to the following labels and constructs: cloud account/subscription/project, network boundary (VPC/VNet), K8s cluster/namespace, CI/CD context, secrets path, artifact repository scope, and observability labels (env=<slug>).
- Lifecycle: Environments are provisioned and modified only via Infrastructure as Code and pipelines; manual changes are prohibited. Long-lived environments: dev, staging, prod. Ephemeral environments may be created per PR/feature and auto-destroyed on merge/close.
- Deployment policy: Artifacts are promoted between environments; rebuilds are not allowed during promotion. Environment-specific configuration overlays are applied deterministically; defaults → env overrides. Drift detection is enforced.
- Access and compliance: RBAC is scoped per environment; production changes require approvals. Data classification and retention policies are enforced per environment. Backups, RPO/RTO, and monitoring/SLOs are defined per environment.
- Secrets/config: Stored per environment in a managed secret store with distinct paths and keys; no cross-environment secret reuse.
- Observability: All logs, metrics, and traces must include environment labels; dashboards and alerts are environment-scoped.

Environment variables do not constitute an environment; they are per-environment configuration inputs.

We will isolate each architectural layer into its own Git repository and consume them in the root application repository as Git submodules. The root repository will remain the composition locus (app wiring, configuration, deployment manifests), while layers (e.g., domain, application/services, adapters/infrastructure, UI components, shared libraries) are versioned and released independently.

Implementation details:
- Structure: layers/<layer-name> as submodule paths; no nested submodules within layers.
- Versioning: layers use semantic versioning with annotated tags; the root repo pins submodules to immutable tag commits (not branches) to ensure reproducible builds.
- Update policy: layer changes are released in their repos, then introduced into the root via a “submodule bump” pull request that updates the pinned commit. Each bump includes changelog notes and impact assessment.
- Ownership: each layer has explicit codeowners; cross-layer changes require coordinated PRs and sequential releases.
- Tooling: CI uses git submodule update --init --recursive and fails builds on dirty or detached submodule states. A pre-commit hook prevents unintended submodule pointer changes. Renovation bots may propose submodule bumps when new tags are available.
- Compatibility: breaking changes require major version increments; the root may track multiple layer major versions across branches when necessary.
- Security and compliance: only approved repositories are allowed as submodules; commit SHAs are verified in CI. No external writable submodules.
- Migration: extract current layer directories into standalone repos preserving history (git filter-repo), add them back as submodules at layers/<name>, and create initial semver tags.

This decision standardizes modular boundaries, enables independent release cadences, and ensures deterministic, auditable integration via pinned submodule commits.

We will implement Translations 2.0 with a key-based, ICU MessageFormat-driven internationalization system backed by a Translation Management System (TMS) integrated into CI/CD. English remains the source language; all user-facing strings are externalized into locale-scoped namespaces (e.g., app.home.title) stored as versioned JSON/resource bundles. We will support pluralization, gender, select, and interpolation via ICU; number/date/time formatting will use CLDR data. Runtime translations are lazy-loaded per locale with code-splitting and HTTP caching; server-rendered paths preload critical bundles. Fallbacks use a deterministic chain (locale-region → base locale → en) and missing keys fail loudly in non-production.

We will introduce a v2 namespace alongside v1, freeze v1 except for critical fixes, and migrate modules incrementally. A feature flag will control runtime fallback from v1 to v2 during rollout. Keys are immutable once published; changes require new keys and automated deprecation tracking. No PII or dynamic values appear in keys; interpolation variables are validated and escaped by the i18n layer.

Tooling includes: extraction linters to prevent hardcoded text, pseudolocalization for early UI fit/bidi checks, screenshot diffing for layout regressions, and a CLI to validate ICU syntax and missing translations in CI. RTL, bidi isolation, and font/line-height constraints will be first-class. Mobile and web share message catalogs where feasible; platform-specific resources are generated from the canonical catalogs.

Operationally, the TMS syncs via API/PRs with review workflows, glossary and style guides, and locale completeness gates for release. Telemetry tracks missing/unused keys and bundle sizes. This decision standardizes i18n across platforms, improves translator velocity and quality, and enables safe, incremental migration from the legacy system.

## Decision

Adopt a four-layered architecture for each service: Presentation, Application, Domain, and Infrastructure.

- Presentation layer (e.g., HTTP controllers, CLI, messaging endpoints) handles I/O, authentication handoff, request validation, and maps to/from DTOs. No business logic.
- Application layer coordinates use cases, transactions, and orchestration. It depends on Domain abstractions and Infrastructure interfaces. No persistence or transport concerns.
- Domain layer contains entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events, and domain services. Pure business rules; no external dependencies. Persistence ignorance is mandatory.
- Infrastructure layer provides technical implementations (ORM repositories, messaging, file/storage, external API clients, email, caching), conforming to interfaces defined in Domain/Application.

Rules:
- Dependencies point inward only. No layer skipping. Presentation → Application → Domain; Infrastructure → Domain/Application via interfaces.
- Communication across layers uses interfaces and DTOs; mapping is explicit. No exposing Domain types externally.
- Transactions and unit-of-work live in Application; domain raises events; outbox or equivalent is implemented in Infrastructure.
- Cross-cutting concerns (logging, metrics, tracing, feature flags, security policies) are applied via middleware/aspects without leaking into Domain.
- Validation: structural in Presentation; invariants in Domain.
- Enforce boundaries via module/package separation, visibility controls, and static analysis rules.
- Testing: unit tests for Domain, application service tests with fakes, integration tests for Infrastructure, and end-to-end for critical flows.

This decision applies per service and is technology-agnostic.

We will implement Kubernetes health probing across all long-running workloads using three distinct probes with standardized, configurable behavior:

- HTTP/1.1 health endpoints exposed on an internal-only port (or path) per service:
  - /health/startup returns 200 only after the application has fully initialized (migrations, cache warm-up, config loaded).
  - /health/ready returns 200 when the service can accept traffic; it may verify essential dependencies (e.g., DB connectivity) but must be fast and non-blocking.
  - /health/live returns 200 if the process is healthy; it must not depend on external systems to avoid kill loops on transient outages.
  For gRPC services, we will use grpc_health_probe with the standard gRPC Health Checking protocol.

- Probe policies (defaults, overridable via Helm/values):
  - startupProbe: periodSeconds=10, timeoutSeconds=2, failureThreshold=30 (up to ~5 minutes for slow boots). While startupProbe is failing, liveness/readiness are ignored.
  - readinessProbe: periodSeconds=5, timeoutSeconds=1, failureThreshold=1 to minimize serving unready pods. Readiness will return non-200 immediately on SIGTERM to drain traffic.
  - livenessProbe: periodSeconds=10, timeoutSeconds=2, failureThreshold=3 to avoid flapping and only restart on persistent faults.

- Scope and exclusions:
  - Apply to Deployments/StatefulSets; Jobs/CronJobs are excluded.
  - Components with sidecars (e.g., proxies) expose independent probes per container where applicable.

- Operational considerations:
  - Health endpoints are unauthenticated but bound to localhost or a dedicated health port not exposed externally.
  - Probe outcomes are instrumented via metrics and logs for observability and SLO analysis.
  - Each service team may refine thresholds to match startup profiles and dependency criticality, but must adhere to endpoint contracts and non-blocking behavior.

Adopt hapi.js (@hapi/hapi) as the standard HTTP server framework for all new Node.js backend services and for incremental migration of existing HTTP endpoints. This decision establishes hapi.js as the default for routing, request/response lifecycle management, input validation, authentication/authorization strategies, and plugin-based extensibility.

Scope:
- Applies to all internal/external HTTP APIs, webhooks, and service-to-service HTTP interfaces within Node.js runtimes (LTS versions supported by hapi).
- New services must use hapi.js. Existing Express/Koa services may remain as-is but should migrate opportunistically during significant feature work or refactors.

Key directives:
- Use @hapi/hapi (current LTS-compatible major) and official ecosystem packages: @hapi/joi for validation, @hapi/boom for errors, @hapi/catbox for caching (with approved adapters), and @hapi/crumb for CSRF where applicable.
- Enforce schema-first request/response validation via Joi at route level. Reject invalid input early.
- Standardize error handling with Boom and consistent problem details mapping.
- Implement authentication/authorization via hapi auth strategies (JWT/OAuth2/session) with centralized plugins.
- Adopt hapi plugin architecture for modular features (observability, rate limiting, security headers, CORS).
- Centralize server configuration (TLS, timeouts, payload limits) via config management and environment overlays.
- Provide OpenAPI integration via approved hapi plugins; auto-generate API docs and contract tests.
- Establish baseline observability: structured logging, request metrics, tracing hooks via plugins.
- Security hardening: enable CORS policies, helmet-equivalent headers, input sanitization, and payload constraints.

Exceptions:
- Non-Node runtimes or serverless platforms that mandate alternative handlers are exempt.
- High-performance streaming/edge cases may justify specialized stacks with architecture review approval.

Review this decision annually or upon major hapi.js releases.

We will adopt a Security-by-Design, Zero Trust, and Defense-in-Depth posture across the stack, integrating security controls into architecture, processes, and tooling.

- Identity and access: Enforce single sign-on with MFA; apply least privilege via role/attribute-based access control; use short-lived credentials; centralize authorization; isolate tenants by design.
- Data protection: Classify data; encrypt in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest with managed KMS; segregate keys and data; rotate keys and secrets; minimize data retention; apply privacy-by-design and regional residency as required.
- Network and platform: Segment networks; default-deny policies; secure service-to-service communication (mTLS); egress controls; WAF/API gateway with rate limiting and threat protection; hardened base images and CIS benchmarks.
- Application security: Mandate secure coding standards (OWASP ASVS/Top 10); perform threat modeling per feature; protect against injection, authZ bypass, SSRF, and deserialization; secure configuration with immutable infrastructure and policy-as-code.
- Supply chain: Enforce dependency allowlists and SCA; generate SBOMs; sign artifacts; verify provenance (SLSA); pin versions; scan container images.
- SDLC and CI/CD: Integrate SAST, DAST, IAST, and secrets scanning; block on critical findings; run IaC scanning; protect pipelines with least privilege; require code review; enforce branch protections.
- Monitoring and response: Centralize logs with tamper evidence; enable audit trails; implement anomaly detection; establish incident response runbooks, playbooks, and post-incident reviews.
- Vulnerability and patching: Continuously scan infrastructure and apps; patch within defined SLAs; track with risk-based prioritization.
- Resilience: Regular backups with encryption and restore testing; define RPO/RTO; chaos and recovery drills.
- Compliance: Map controls to ISO 27001/SOC 2 and applicable regulations (e.g., GDPR); document exceptions with risk acceptance.

These principles are mandatory, versioned, and measured via automated policy checks and security KPIs.

Adopt a layered, auto-generated, versioned SDK documentation structure with a single authoritative docs site per SDK. Structure content as: Overview (purpose, supported platforms), Getting Started (installation, authentication, quickstart), Core Concepts (architecture, data models, error handling, threading/async), Guides (task-oriented how-tos), API Reference (auto-generated from source annotations), Examples (copy-pasteable snippets in all supported languages), Tutorials (end-to-end flows), Troubleshooting/FAQ, Configuration/Environment, Security/Privacy, Performance/Best Practices, Versioning/Migration, Changelog/Release notes, and Contributing.

Generate API reference from the source using language-appropriate tools (e.g., Typedoc/Javadoc/DocC/Sphinx) and stitch into the docs site build. Maintain multi-language parity using tabs and a content matrix; any guide must include examples for each GA language or explicitly note limitations. Version docs per SDK major version, with latest as default and archived versions accessible. Enforce doc updates in PRs via CI checks; on release, auto-publish docs with release tags. Provide deep links and stable anchors for all public APIs. Include code samples as tested, runnable snippets within the repo to prevent drift. Establish a deprecation policy with clear callouts and migration steps. Provide offline bundles and OpenAPI/JSON schema where applicable. Use full-text search, clear left-nav IA mirroring the structure, and breadcrumbs. All content follows a shared style guide and templates to ensure consistency and discoverability.

## Decision
- Adopt semantic versioning tags with a leading "v": vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., v1.4.2). Tags are immutable, annotated, and GPG-signed.
- For v0 and v1: keep the module path unchanged (no suffix), tag releases as v0.x.y or v1.x.y at the module root.
- For v2 and above: use major version suffix in the module path (e.g., module/path/v2) and tag releases as v2.x.y that resolve to that module’s directory. Do not use the v2+ suffix for v0/v1.
- For repositories containing multiple modules: place a go.mod in each module directory and tag each module independently using path-based tags (e.g., sub/module/v1.3.0 or sub/module/v2.1.0). Each tag must reference the commit where that module’s go.mod and code reflect the released version.
- Pre-releases use standard semver prerelease labels (e.g., v2.0.0-rc.1). Avoid build metadata in release tags. Do not publish +incompatible versions; instead, adopt proper module paths for v2+.
- Tags are created only after CI passes, tests are green, and the module is go mod tidy-clean. No local replace directives remain in released go.mod files.
- Breaking changes trigger a MAJOR bump and, for v2+, an updated module path suffix. Features and fixes increment MINOR and PATCH respectively.
- Retagging or moving existing tags is prohibited; corrections require a new version.
- Release automation will enforce tagging format, signing, changelog generation, and module validation (including path/version consistency and reproducible builds).

Adopt Red Hat OpenShift as the primary Kubernetes-based application platform across all environments. Use managed offerings where available (ROSA on AWS, ARO on Azure, OpenShift Dedicated) to reduce operational overhead; deploy self-managed OpenShift on-premises or in unsupported regions as needed for regulatory or latency requirements. Standardize on OpenShift-native capabilities and Kubernetes-first abstractions to maintain portability and minimize lock-in.

Scope:
- Provision clusters via Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) and configure them declaratively with GitOps (Argo CD/OpenShift GitOps).
- Implement multi-tenancy with Projects/Namespaces, ResourceQuotas, and LimitRanges; isolate workloads with NetworkPolicies.
- Use OpenShift Routes/Ingress with mandatory TLS; integrate enterprise SSO via OAuth.
- Manage CI/CD with OpenShift Pipelines (Tekton); container build via source-to-image or Tekton/Buildah, storing images in OpenShift Image Registry or an approved external registry.
- Employ Operators for platform services; prefer vendor-supported Operators; evaluate OpenShift Service Mesh for east-west traffic when required.
- Standardize observability with OpenShift Monitoring (Prometheus/Alertmanager) and cluster logging/forwarding to the enterprise log platform.
- Manage secrets with Kubernetes Secrets encrypted at rest; integrate External Secrets Operator with the enterprise secret manager (e.g., HashiCorp Vault) for high-sensitivity data.
- Enforce policy/compliance using OpenShift Gatekeeper/Kyverno and Compliance Operator; enable audit logging.
- Enable autoscaling (HPA/VPA/Cluster Autoscaler) and node pools; use spot/low-priority nodes for cost efficiency where appropriate.
- Define backup/restore and DR across clusters/regions (e.g., Velero and application-level replication); implement regular failover tests.

Success is measured by reduced time-to-deploy, platform reliability, security/compliance adherence, and cost transparency. Revisit this decision if managed OpenShift availability, total cost of ownership, or organizational constraints materially change.

## Decision
Adopt TOML as the single, authoritative configuration file format for the application across all environments.

- File format and naming:
  - Primary file: config.toml at the application root or platform-standard config directory.
  - Environment-specific overrides: config.<env>.toml (e.g., config.prod.toml).
  - Local developer overrides: config.local.toml (git-ignored).

- Loading and precedence (lowest to highest):
  1) Built-in defaults
  2) config.toml
  3) config.<env>.toml
  4) config.local.toml
  5) Environment variables
  6) CLI flags
  Last writer wins at the key level.

- Parsing and validation:
  - Use a mature, spec-compliant TOML parser in each runtime.
  - Provide a machine-readable configuration schema (e.g., JSON Schema-equivalent) for validation and documentation.
  - Validate at startup; fail fast on unknown keys, type mismatches, or missing required fields.
  - Support comments and multi-file composition via an explicit includes array of file paths (resolved relative to the including file).

- Secrets and dynamic values:
  - Do not store secrets in TOML. Load secrets from environment variables or a secret manager.
  - Allow ${ENV_VAR} interpolation for specific keys marked as interpolated.

- Backward compatibility and migration:
  - Deprecate non-TOML formats (e.g., YAML/INI). Provide a one-time migration utility and sample mappings.
  - Maintain read-only compatibility with legacy formats for two minor releases, emitting deprecation warnings.

- Tooling:
  - Provide canonical example config.toml and a schema-driven linter.
  - Enforce consistent key naming and documentation via CI checks.

Adopt modern JavaScript (ES2022+) as the primary implementation language for all application and library code in this project, foregoing TypeScript source files. We will prioritize a minimal build/tooling surface and faster iteration, while retaining developer ergonomics and safety through the following practices:

- Use JSDoc annotations for function signatures, data models, and public APIs; enable TypeScript’s checkJs in CI and local development for static analysis of JS via JSDoc.
- Enforce code quality with ESLint (including jsdoc rules) and Prettier; adopt strict lint rules that catch common type and nullability pitfalls.
- Apply runtime validation at system boundaries (e.g., API I/O, config, env) using schema validators (e.g., zod/yup/ajv) to ensure correctness beyond static checks.
- Prefer libraries with maintained type declarations; include @types packages to improve editor IntelliSense and JS static analysis.
- Maintain modular, typed-friendly interfaces (explicit exports, clear DTOs) to preserve an easy migration path to TypeScript if needed.
- Build with native ESM/bundler (e.g., Vite/Rollup/webpack) without a TypeScript compile step; no .ts/.tsx in this codebase by default.

Exceptions and re-evaluation:
- Isolated packages that are low-level, widely reused, or require advanced type modeling may be implemented in TypeScript behind stable JS interfaces, pending architecture review.
- We will revisit this decision if codebase size, defect patterns, contributor profile, or domain complexity indicate insufficient safety/maintainability with JS+JSDoc. Migration is facilitated by existing JSDoc types and schema-validated boundaries.

We will standardize on Shrine as the application’s image upload and storage library for all services handling user- and system-generated images. Shrine is adopted over Active Storage and CarrierWave due to its composable plugin architecture, strong processing pipeline, direct-to-cloud upload support, multi-storage strategies, and clear control over data flows and URLs.

Implementation scope:
- Ruby/Rails services that persist images (avatars, product media, content assets).
- Storage: Amazon S3 in production and staging (private buckets, presigned/signed URLs, CDN via CloudFront); local filesystem in development/test.
- Processing: image_processing gem with libvips for efficient resizing, format conversion, and metadata stripping; derivatives generated via shrine-derivatives.
- Upload flows: direct browser/mobile uploads to S3 with presigned POST; background promotion and deletion via Sidekiq; integrity checksums, size/type validations, and optional antivirus scanning.
- Access control: originals stored privately; derivatives public via CDN when needed; signed expiring URLs for private access; immutable originals with lifecycle rules for cost control.

Operational decisions:
- Define Uploader classes per domain with explicit validations and limits.
- Centralize storage configuration and credentials via environment variables; encryption at rest (SSE-S3/KMS) and in transit (TLS).
- Observability: structured logs for uploads, promotions, and failures; metrics on throughput, error rates, and processing times.
- Disaster recovery: rely on S3 durability, versioning, and backups; documented runbooks for reprocessing derivatives.

Migration (if applicable): implement data migration from existing attachment system, dual-write during cutover, and verify referential integrity and URL parity. This decision is binding for new image features and retrofits legacy paths as capacity allows.

We will not introduce a direct compile-time dependency from org.jabref.model to org.jabref.logic. Instead, we will enable model to “access” required logic functionality via inversion of control and shared primitives:

- Create a shared module org.jabref.base (or org.jabref.common) to host cross-cutting value types, small utilities, and pure functions currently living in logic but needed by model.
- Define narrow, domain-oriented SPI interfaces in org.jabref.model (e.g., ResolvedFieldProvider, IdentifierValidator, CitationStyleResolver) for behaviors that inherently require logic. org.jabref.logic will provide the concrete implementations.
- Bindings are supplied by the application composition root, using constructor injection or Java ServiceLoader. Model code must only depend on the SPI abstractions and must remain instantiable without logic (tests provide fakes).
- For internal model usage, services must be passed explicitly (no static singletons). Optional behavior must degrade gracefully when no implementation is present.
- Enforce architecture with ArchUnit: model → base only; logic → model, base; no imports from logic in model.
- Migrate by:
  1) Extracting shared pure code from logic to base.
  2) Introducing SPI in model for the remaining behaviors.
  3) Implementing SPIs in logic and wiring in the app layer.

This preserves a clean dependency direction, avoids cycles, and still enables model to leverage logic capabilities through stable, testable contracts.

## Decision

We will implement explicit, centralized default values across the stack, favoring secure, least-privilege, and backward-compatible behavior.

- Defaults are defined in a version-controlled, typed configuration schema. A single defaulting layer merges, in order of precedence: built-in defaults → environment-specific config → secrets → per-tenant overrides → runtime flags. Null/absent values are not interpreted as “use defaults” unless explicitly defined in the schema.
- Database-level defaults are declared in the schema/migrations for durability and parity with the application layer; the application mirrors these defaults to validate and prevent surprises. Changing a persisted default is treated as a data migration.
- Public APIs specify defaults explicitly in the contract (OpenAPI/GraphQL schema) and never rely on undocumented behavior. Requests omitting an optional field receive the documented default; responses are explicit and may echo effective values.
- Defaults related to security, privacy, and access remain conservative (deny-by-default). Defaults must not widen access, log sensitive data, or enable risky features.
- Global operational defaults: timezone UTC, locale en-US, boolean feature flags off unless specified. Client-side defaults improve UX but the server is the source of truth.
- Changes to defaults are backward-incompatible unless proven otherwise; they require versioning or a controlled rollout behind feature flags, deprecation notices, and migration guidance. Observability records when defaults are applied to aid debugging.

We will update the running database using a staging-and-merge pattern that applies idempotent, incremental changes from ETL outputs without requiring downtime.

- ETL jobs produce partitioned, versioned outputs (e.g., Parquet/CSV + manifest) per table with monotonic run_id and source_version. Files are landed to an object store and loaded into a staging schema with strict typing, constraints, and basic data quality checks.
- Each target table is updated via deterministic MERGE/UPSERT statements keyed by the business/primary key, applying inserts, updates, and soft deletes (via tombstone flag) based on source_version/updated_at watermarks. Only deltas are processed; unchanged rows are skipped.
- Operations run in bounded batches to minimize lock contention, using row-level locking and short transactions. For large rewrites, we use shadow tables and metadata swap to avoid long-running locks.
- Exactly-once semantics are enforced through a manifest, run_id idempotency keys, and deduplication in staging (primary key + source_version). Concurrency is serialized per table using advisory locks.
- Schema evolution follows a backward-compatible contract; migrations are applied before data merges. Invalid records are quarantined and do not block the pipeline.
- Rollback is supported by transactional boundaries; for non-atomic swaps, we retain pre-swap snapshots for fast revert. All changes are audited with per-batch checksums and row counts.
- Scheduling targets low-traffic windows but supports near-real-time cadence; observability includes lag, success/failure, DQ metrics, and alerting. Access uses least-privilege service accounts.

## Decision

Adopt a distributed architecture for TaskManager to enable horizontal scalability, resilience, and high throughput. TaskManager will be decomposed into:
- Stateless API/service nodes for task submission and orchestration, horizontally scalable behind a load balancer.
- A durable message broker (e.g., Kafka or SQS) as the work queue, enabling backpressure, retries, and partitioned consumption.
- A persistent store (e.g., Postgres with advisory locks or Cassandra) for authoritative task state, configured with optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys.
- A pool of stateless worker nodes that pull tasks, execute them, and update state atomically.

Processing semantics:
- Default at-least-once delivery with idempotent handlers and deduplication via idempotency keys; enable exactly-once effects where required using the outbox/inbox pattern and transactional writes.
- Retries with exponential backoff; poison messages routed to a dead-letter queue for diagnosis.

Coordination and scheduling:
- Partition tasks via consistent hashing or broker partitions; workers consume assigned partitions to minimize contention.
- Leader election (e.g., via etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper or managed coordinator) for time-based or cron scheduling; leaders schedule, workers execute.
- Long-running tasks use heartbeats and leasing; leases are renewed by active workers and reassigned on expiration.

Operational concerns:
- Rolling upgrades and blue/green deployments; workers are drainable.
- Strong observability: structured logs, distributed tracing, metrics (queue depth, lag, success/failure rate, retries, lease expirations).
- Multi-tenant isolation via partitioning and quotas; per-tenant rate limits at API and consumer levels.
- Security: per-tenant authZ, encrypted transport and at-rest storage, least-privilege credentials for workers.

Migration will be phased: introduce idempotency and state store, place a broker in front of existing workers, then scale out stateless workers and enable leader-based scheduling. The external API remains backward compatible throughout.

## Decision

We will standardize on Composer (v2) as the sole dependency and package manager for all PHP code in this project.

- Dependencies will be declared in composer.json with caret/tilde constraints aligned to upstream semantic versioning; the exact resolution will be pinned via composer.lock, which must be committed to VCS to ensure reproducible builds across all environments.
- Autoloading will follow PSR-4/PSR-0 as configured in composer.json. No manual class loading will be maintained outside Composer’s autoloader.
- The project will target a defined PHP platform (php/config.platform in composer.json) to avoid environment-specific drift; CI will enforce this version matrix.
- We will use prefer-stable: true with minimal-stability not set lower than stable. Pre-releases are allowed only by explicit constraint.
- Private dependencies will be served via our internal Composer repository (e.g., Private Packagist/Satis) with authenticated access; VCS repositories are permitted only when mirrored and tagged.
- Composer plugins are disabled by default; any plugin requires explicit approval and pinning.
- Security: composer audit will run in CI; known-vulnerable versions will block merges. We will enable the FriendsOfPHP/security-advisories source.
- Updates: routine dependency updates will be automated via Renovate/Dependabot with human review; production updates follow our release cadence and change management.
- Installation: composer install —no-dev —prefer-dist —no-interaction will be used in production; CI caches vendor/ and Composer cache to speed builds.
- No global Composer dependencies will be relied upon; all tooling is project-scoped via require-dev and composer scripts.

We will introduce “Release” as a first-class concept in sfpowerscripts to govern coherent, repeatable deployments across environments.

Key decisions:
- Define a Release Manifest (release.yaml) committed to the repo capturing release id/version, target packages and exact versions, dependency graph, environment gates, metadata (notes, owner, time windows), and checksums of artifacts.
- Establish a release lifecycle: plan → assemble → validate → publish → promote (dev → test → staging → prod) → close. All stages are idempotent and auditable.
- Make release artifacts immutable: package versions are pinned; artifacts are stored with provenance (commit SHA, pipeline run) and checksums in the configured artifact store (e.g., GitHub Releases/Container Registry/Artifactory).
- Adopt semantic versioning for releases (e.g., RYYYY.MM.DD[-n] or SemVer), with Git tags release/<version> and signed tags for traceability.
- Provide new CLI commands: release:plan, release:create, release:validate, release:publish, release:promote, release:notes (auto-changelog from commits/PRs since last release), release:status, release:rollback (re-promote prior known-good release or revert manifest).
- Enforce environment promotion policies via configurable gates (approvals, quality checks, test coverage, security scans) and maintain an audit trail/telemetry for each transition.
- Backward compatible and opt-in: existing pipelines continue to work; enabling releases adds manifest-driven orchestration without altering package build semantics.
- Store minimal server-side state; the manifest and tags are the source of truth. Pipeline annotations persist execution metadata.

Success is defined by deterministic deployments, traceable changes, simplified rollback, and clearer governance across environments.

## Decision
We will not support loading or reading event streams within the same database transaction that performs writes (appends) to streams. Write operations will use short-lived, append-only transactions; any read requirements must be satisfied either before the write transaction starts or via in-memory knowledge of newly appended events within the same process. Immediate read-after-write verification will rely on optimistic concurrency (expected version) and domain-level validation rather than re-querying the stream.

Concretely:
- Write transactions will only append to streams (and outbox) and will not execute SELECTs against event streams.
- Reads will execute in separate transactions/connections with appropriate isolation (READ COMMITTED/SNAPSHOT), decoupled from the writer to avoid lock escalation, deadlocks, and anomalies.
- For command handling that needs current state, load required aggregates/streams before opening the write transaction; during the write, use the preloaded state plus the events being appended.
- Background projectors and read models will operate in independent transactions and must not share the writer’s transaction context.
- The Event Store API will enforce this separation by exposing distinct write and read contexts; attempting to read from streams within an active write context will be blocked at the API level.
- For rare cases that require cross-stream coordination, use aggregate preloading and expected-version checks, or a dedicated coordination stream, rather than mixed read/write transactions.

This decision prioritizes correctness, reduces contention, and improves throughput by keeping write transactions minimal and avoiding mixed read/write patterns against the streams.

We will adopt a pull-based Continuous Delivery model using Argo CD as the standard GitOps controller for all Kubernetes workloads across environments. Git repositories are the single source of truth for desired state; Argo CD continuously reconciles clusters by pulling manifests (Helm charts/Kustomize) from approved repositories and correcting drift. We will standardize on:

- Argo CD per cluster (high-availability in shared/platform clusters), managed via declarative AppProjects and Applications.
- App-of-Apps pattern for hierarchical composition of platform and application stacks.
- Environment segregation via distinct repositories or directories with clear promotion flows (dev → stage → prod) driven by Git commits and protected branch policies.
- Secrets management via SOPS with KMS/CloudKMS or Sealed Secrets; no plaintext secrets in Git.
- Image promotion via Argo CD Image Updater for tag automation where applicable; otherwise, promotion PRs update manifests.
- Progressive delivery using Argo Rollouts (canary/blue-green) where needed.
- Policy guardrails with OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno; Argo CD Enforce to block out-of-policy changes.
- Access control via SSO-backed RBAC; only Argo CD service accounts apply changes to clusters.
- Reconciliation every 3 minutes (default) with drift detection, health checks, and auto-sync for non-prod; prod uses manual sync or auto-sync with PR-based approvals per risk profile.
- Observability through Argo CD Notifications to Slack/Teams and metrics/logs exported to the central monitoring stack.
- Disaster recovery via Git as the recovery source; rollbacks occur by reverting Git commits; pinned chart/image versions ensure reproducibility.

Push-based CD to clusters is deprecated. All delivery pipelines produce Git changes; no direct kubectl/helm applies in CI. Exceptions require architecture approval and time-bound mitigations.

- We will adopt Elasticsearch as the dedicated full-text search engine for user-facing search and internal discovery, replacing SQL-based LIKE/ILIKE queries and any ad-hoc text search mechanisms.
- Scope: product, content, and log/event search features requiring stemming, relevance scoring, faceting/aggregation, autocomplete, and typo tolerance. Transactional reads/writes remain in the primary relational database.
- Deployment: use a managed Elasticsearch service (e.g., AWS OpenSearch Service/Elastic Cloud) for production; Docker-based cluster for development/testing. Start with 3 data nodes (replication factor 1), 1 hot tier; revisit tiers as volume grows.
- Version and API: target Elasticsearch 8.x with the official REST APIs and client SDKs for our languages. No proprietary plugins beyond managed offering defaults.
- Indexing: implement an async indexing pipeline fed by CDC/events; eventual consistency SLA ≤ 5 seconds. Support idempotent upserts, soft deletes, and full reindexing via versioned, alias-based blue/green indices.
- Mapping/analyzers: language-specific analyzers, edge n-grams for autocomplete, keyword fields for exact match, and normalizers for case/diacritics. Use minimal field data; avoid dynamic mappings by default.
- Relevance: maintain tunable BM25 parameters, field boosts, and synonym sets; A/B test ranking changes.
- Security/compliance: TLS in transit, IAM/OIDC auth, role-based index permissions, field/document-level security for multi-tenant isolation, encrypted snapshots to managed storage.
- Observability and reliability: export metrics/logs, alert on shard health and indexing latency; daily automated snapshots and tested restore runbooks.
- Cost/scale: shard counts sized to 12–24 month growth; lifecycle policies to move/expire cold data.
- Decommission prior search endpoints after feature parity and a 2-week shadow testing period.

## Decision
We will minimize and curate the exported/public API surface to only those identifiers required for external consumption and long-term support. Concretely:

- Default to non-exported/private identifiers; export only when:
  - The functionality must be used by code outside the module/package.
  - The identifier is stable per our versioning policy and covered by tests and documentation.
- Public API shape:
  - Prefer exporting small, purpose-built interfaces over concrete types to preserve flexibility.
  - Avoid exporting mutable global state, struct fields, or error variables; expose constructors, accessors, and sentinel errors via functions where needed.
  - Use explicit constructors/factories; avoid exposing zero-value–invalid types unless clearly documented as safe.
  - Do not export transitive/internal implementation details (helpers, DTOs not meant for cross-boundary use).
- Naming and organization:
  - Follow language conventions for export visibility (e.g., Go: capitalized identifiers; use internal/ for non-exportable packages).
  - Keep package/module boundaries cohesive; avoid “utility” exports. Group exports by domain, not by layer/transport.
  - Avoid stutter and leaking transport/protocol concerns in exported names.
- Stability and lifecycle:
  - Treat exported API as a contract: semver governs breaking changes. Deprecations require @deprecated annotations, CHANGELOG notes, and a minimum two minor versions grace period before removal.
  - Public APIs must include godoc/docs, examples, and contract tests.
- Governance:
  - API review is mandatory for new/modified exports (architectural gate).
  - Linting and CI checks will fail on unauthorized exports or undocumented public identifiers.
