  - Generate and track API diffs per release to detect accidental export changes.

Adopt Spring Boot 3.x (on Java 21 LTS) as the primary web framework for all backend services. Use Spring MVC (servlet stack) with the embedded Tomcat server as the default for synchronous RESTful APIs, reserving Spring WebFlux for services with clear reactive/streaming or high-concurrency nonblocking I/O requirements, approved case-by-case.

Standardize on Spring Boot starter dependencies and auto-configuration to accelerate development and enforce consistency. Enable Spring Boot Actuator in all services for health, liveness/readiness, metrics, and info endpoints. Use Micrometer with OpenTelemetry exporters for metrics and tracing; expose Prometheus-compatible metrics by default.

Apply Spring Security with OAuth2 Resource Server for JWT-based authentication and method/endpoint authorization. Use Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation) for request/response validation and consistent error handling (RFC 7807 Problem Details).

Manage configuration via environment variables and profiles; externalize secrets through the platform secret store. Prefer convention-over-configuration; disallow custom servlet containers unless justified. Package services as container images using Spring Boot Buildpacks; run as non-root, with minimal base layers.

Adopt REST-first APIs with consistent naming, pagination, and filtering conventions; JSON as the default media type. Support graceful shutdown and startup probes. Tune Tomcat thread pools and timeouts with ops-owned defaults; document any deviations.

Testing baseline: Spring Boot Test, MockMvc/WebTestClient, and Testcontainers for integration with external dependencies. Monitor dependencies via Spring’s BOM; patch to latest compatible 3.x release proactively.

This decision establishes Spring Boot as the default framework to optimize developer productivity, observability, security, and operational consistency across services.

We will enforce optimistic concurrency across all mutable REST resources via HTTP entity tags (ETags) and the If-Match header.

- Scope: All PUT, PATCH, and DELETE operations on versioned resources must include a valid If-Match header. POST (create) is exempt. Collection-level mutations and bulk operations must provide per-entity If-Match or will be rejected.
- ETag type: Use strong ETags. ETag values are opaque, stable per version, and derived from a monotonic version token (e.g., integer version or updated_at + id salt), not from hashing the full payload.
- Generation: On every successful mutation, increment the version token atomically at the write source and emit the new ETag in the response’s ETag header. GET/HEAD always return the current ETag.
- Validation: Server compares If-Match against the current ETag; mismatch yields 412 Precondition Failed. Absence of If-Match on mutating requests yields 428 Precondition Required.
- Deletes: DELETE requires If-Match; 412 if the target ETag differs; 404 if already deleted and If-Match matches no current resource.
- Conditional reads: We also support If-None-Match for GET to enable caching, but it is optional and independent of this locking policy.
- Error contract: On 412, return a problem+json body with type, title, detail, resource identifier, and the current ETag in a response header (not in the body) to avoid accidental client overwrite logic.
- Idempotency and retries: Clients must re-fetch to obtain the latest ETag before retrying failed mutations. Server-side retries must not bypass ETag checks.
- Backward compatibility: Introduce enforcement behind a feature flag per endpoint; log missing/invalid If-Match for one release, then switch to 428/412 enforcement. Document client migration.
- Distributed systems: Ensure a single source of truth for version increments; replicas must not synthesize ETags. Propagate ETag via events for read replicas. Avoid clock-based versions without monotonic guarantees.
- Security: ETags must not encode sensitive fields and must be unguessable beyond correlation to a single resource version.

Adopt 1Password Business as the organization’s standard for creating, storing, and sharing human-accessed secrets (e.g., admin credentials, API tokens for manual use, SSH keys, recovery codes). All person-to-person and team-to-team secret sharing must occur via 1Password vaults; ad‑hoc channels (chat, email, tickets, docs) are prohibited.

Scope:
- In scope: Credentials and secrets accessed by humans, break-glass credentials, shared environment credentials for support/ops, license keys, recovery materials.
- Out of scope: Runtime application secrets managed by infrastructure secret managers (e.g., cloud KMS/Secret Manager, Vault) unless explicitly exempted. CI/CD use may leverage 1Password Secrets Automation where cloud secret managers are unavailable.

Access and organization:
- Enforce SSO + MFA, SCIM provisioning, and device approvals.
- Use least-privilege RBAC via team- and environment-scoped vaults (e.g., Eng/App/<env>, SRE/Infra, Security/Break‑Glass).
- Separate production from non‑production vaults; enforce approval workflows for production access.
- Grant time-bounded access for elevated/temporary needs.

Operational policy:
- All new secrets must be created directly in 1Password; rotate upon onboarding to the platform.
- Prohibit plaintext export/sharing; use item-level sharing with expiry when cross‑team sharing is required.
- Maintain ownership and recovery via designated Security admins and break-glass accounts stored in a restricted vault.
- Enable auditing and reporting; review access and secret hygiene quarterly.
- Define incident process for suspected secret exposure (revoke/rotate, attest, and report).

Migration:
- Migrate existing shared secrets from legacy locations to 1Password within a defined window; delete originals after verification.
- Document vault taxonomy, naming, and rotation standards in the runbook.

## Decision
Allow each item to have multiple labels, modeled as a normalized many-to-many relationship.

- Data model:
  - labels(id, name, slug, created_at, updated_at) with unique(slug), case-insensitive uniqueness on name.
  - item_labels(item_id, label_id) with composite unique(item_id, label_id) and FKs to items and labels; cascade delete on item removal; restrict label deletion if referenced (or soft-delete labels).
- API:
  - Items expose labels as an ordered array of slugs (stable order by name ASC).
  - Mutations accept a full-replacement array of slugs; operation is idempotent and upserts unknown slugs subject to governance rules.
  - Validation: max N labels per item (configurable), max label length, allowed characters; normalize to lowercase slug with display name preserved.
- Behavior:
  - Labels are first-class entities reusable across items.
  - Duplicate labels on an item are disallowed.
  - Renaming a label updates its name; slug changes trigger a migration path (aliasing or redirects).
- Querying:
  - Support filtering by labels with AND/OR semantics; provide stable, documented query parameters (e.g., labels=foo,bar for AND; any_labels=... for OR).
  - Add indexes on item_labels(item_id), item_labels(label_id), and (label_id, item_id) to optimize lookups.
- Migration:
  - For systems with a prior single-label field, backfill item_labels and deprecate the old column after verification.
- UI/UX:
  - Display labels as chips; provide autocomplete over existing labels; prevent accidental creation of near-duplicates via case/whitespace normalization.

## Decision
We will introduce a shared, versioned Defect Abstraction as a first-class domain construct used across all services that create, manage, analyze, or display defects. This abstraction will be defined by a canonical schema and a small set of core behaviors, exposed via:

- A language-agnostic schema (OpenAPI + JSON Schema; Protobuf for events) that defines the canonical Defect entity, identifiers, lifecycle states, severity, source, ownership, timestamps, links, and an extensible attributes map for domain-specific metadata.
- A shared client SDK per tier (backend: Java/Kotlin/Node/Python; frontend: TypeScript) that provides typed models, validation, mappers, and backward-compatible helpers.
- A normalized event model (DefectCreated/Updated/StateChanged/Merged/Dismissed) published on the event bus with strict versioning and compatibility guarantees.
- A façade service (Defect Registry) responsible for ID minting, deduplication, merge/unmerge operations, and cross-tool correlation; other services integrate via this façade or the shared SDK.
- Persistence guidance: services may store projections, but the canonical record remains in the Registry; projections must be derived via subscribed events.
- Evolution policy: additive-first changes, versioned fields, deprecations with sunset dates, migration playbooks, and contract tests in CI to prevent breaking changes.
- Governance: the Platform Domain team owns the schema, SDKs, and Registry; changes require RFC review and consumer sign-off; linters enforce schema compliance at boundaries.
- Interop: importers map external tool defects into the canonical model; exporters provide adapters back to tool-native formats.
- Privacy and multitenancy: all artifacts carry tenant and data-classification fields; PII is disallowed in free-form attributes by default and validated by SDK policies.
- Observability: all events and API calls carry correlation IDs; golden dashboards track volume, latency, dedup efficiency, and schema version adoption.

All new defect-related features must adopt the shared abstraction; existing services will migrate via adapters over two release cycles, after which legacy defect representations are deprecated and removed.

- We will support bi-directional bindings between clients and the platform for real-time state synchronization and command/ack flows, while retaining REST as the baseline for request/response interactions.
- The canonical bi-directional transport is WebSocket over TLS with a single multiplexed channel per principal/session. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is offered as receive-only fallback; webhooks are supported for server-to-server push where persistent connections are not feasible.
- Message model: JSON-encoded, schema-versioned envelopes with typed events, commands, acks/nacks, correlation IDs, and monotonic sequence numbers for ordering and de-duplication. Commands are idempotent and retriable; side effects must be idempotency-key guarded.
- Subscriptions use explicit resource/topic filters with server-enforced authorization. Default delivery is at-least-once with client-managed de-dupe; optional exactly-once semantics may be enabled per stream where supported.
- Backpressure is mandatory: clients declare receive window; server enforces rate limits and drops to slow-mode with resumable cursors on overload. Heartbeats and ping/pong detect liveness.
- Security: mTLS or OAuth2/OIDC bearer tokens on connect and periodic re-auth; per-message auth context evaluation; payload signing optional for high-assurance domains. Tenancy and data scoping enforced at the stream level.
- Reliability: durable event logs with retention for replay; resumable sessions via last-seen offsets; bounded retries with exponential backoff; dead-letter queues for poison messages.
- Compatibility: REST remains the source of truth for create/update; bi-directional channels emit change events and accept side-effect-free commands or intent-based mutations that map to REST semantics.
- Observability: structured logs, per-message metrics, end-to-end trace IDs; admin introspection for stream health and consumer lag.
- Rollout is opt-in per API surface via capability flags; SDKs will encapsulate protocol details and expose a uniform reactive API.

Adopt structured, centralized, JSON logging across all services, emitting to stdout/stderr with RFC3339 UTC timestamps and using OpenTelemetry semantic conventions. Instrument all services with OpenTelemetry for logs, traces, and metrics; propagate W3C Trace-Context headers and include correlation fields in every log entry: trace_id, span_id, request_id, service_name, service_version, environment, region, and tenant_id where applicable.

Route logs to an OpenTelemetry Collector sidecar/agent per node/cluster. The Collector performs enrichment (k8s metadata, host info), redaction, sampling, and routing. Exporters are environment-configurable to support multiple backends (e.g., Elastic, Datadog, Splunk, or S3/Glacier for archive) without code changes.

Define log levels and policies:
- ERROR: Failures impacting outcomes; include concise stack traces. Always collected.
- WARN: Degraded behavior; collected with rate limiting.
- INFO: High-level state changes and audit events; collected with modest sampling in high-volume paths.
- DEBUG/TRACE: Disabled in production by default; enabled via dynamic, time-bound sampling/feature flags per service or tenant.

Privacy and security:
- Prohibit logging of secrets/credentials/PII; apply server-side redaction/anonymization (hash user identifiers; mask tokens). Enforce schema validation in CI and runtime drop of nonconformant fields.
- Comply with data residency and retention: 30 days hot searchable, 90 days warm, optional 12-month cold archive; purge per regulatory requirements (e.g., GDPR).

Operational considerations:
- Structured keys are schema-versioned to allow evolution without breaking queries.
- Log volume budgets per service with backpressure and drop policies favoring INFO over DEBUG.
- Health/heartbeat logs suppressed; use metrics for high-frequency signals.
- Local dev: human-readable console format; staging/prod: JSON only.

This decision ensures observability, vendor portability, cost control, and compliance while enabling efficient incident response and forensics.

## Decision
Adopt styled-jsx as the default styling mechanism for React/Next.js UI components to achieve co-located, component-scoped CSS with first-class SSR support and zero runtime dependency beyond what Next.js already provides.

- Scope: All new UI components must use styled-jsx with <style jsx>. Use <style jsx global> sparingly for framework-level resets and layout primitives in app-wide entry points (e.g., _app, root layout).
- Co-location and encapsulation: Each component should define its styles within the same file to ensure encapsulation and ease of maintenance. Prefer component scope; avoid globals unless overriding third-party styles or defining resets.
- Theming and tokens: Define design tokens as CSS variables in a central variables.css imported globally. Theme switching (e.g., dark mode) is handled via data attributes or prefers-color-scheme that toggle variable values. Components reference only variables, not raw values.
- Dynamic styling: Prefer CSS variables for dynamic values over interpolated expressions in styled-jsx templates. Use inline style for one-off computed values when variables are insufficient. Avoid heavy runtime computations in style blocks.
- Shared patterns: Create shared utility classes (global) only for cross-cutting concerns (e.g., visually-hidden). Otherwise, favor component-local styles or small, composable components.
- Animations: Define keyframes within component-scoped styles when local; use global only if shared across multiple components.
- Linting and consistency: Enforce usage via ESLint rules and a style guide (naming, ordering, one primary <style jsx> block per component, BEM-like semantics optional but consistent).
- Performance and SSR: Leverage Next.js’ built-in styled-jsx SSR. No additional CSS-in-JS runtime or critical CSS tooling is required.
- Interop: Keep existing third-party styles; override via global styles only as needed. New components follow styled-jsx; legacy styling approaches may remain until touched, then migrated opportunistically.

We will centralize all non-secret application configuration exclusively in a versioned configuration file (e.g., YAML/TOML/JSON) loaded at startup. The application must not infer configuration from hardcoded constants, command-line flags, or database records. Environment variables are reserved only for: (a) selecting the active configuration profile or file path, and (b) injecting secrets/credentials via the platform’s secret manager. No other configuration may be supplied via environment variables.

All configurable parameters must be explicitly declared in the config schema with defaults present in the base config file. The application will expose a single, typed configuration access layer to consumers; modules must not read files or environment variables directly. Configuration is validated against a schema at startup; the application fails fast on unknown keys, missing required values, or invalid types. Layered config is allowed via file-based overlays (e.g., base + environment-specific file), with deterministic precedence; ad-hoc runtime overrides are not supported.

We will document the config file structure, allowed keys, and precedence rules. CI will validate configuration files and enforce schema drift detection. Secrets are never stored in the config file; placeholders and references to the secret manager are used instead. Migration of existing settings will move all non-secrets into the config file and remove deprecated code paths and env var reads.

We will establish a canonical actor model and registry as the single source of truth for all human and machine principals interacting with the system. The decision mandates:

- A standardized actor taxonomy: Anonymous, EndUser, OrganizationAdmin, SupportAgent, Auditor, ServiceAccount (internal), ExternalIntegration (partner), and BatchJob.
- Globally unique, stable actor IDs issued by the Identity Provider (IdP) and mirrored in an Actor Registry. No ad-hoc role strings in code.
- RBAC as the baseline authorization model, augmented with ABAC constraints (e.g., org_id, environment, data region) evaluated at the policy layer.
- Mandatory actor propagation: actor_id, actor_type, org_id, and auth_context embedded in JWT/OIDC tokens and propagated across services, events, and audit logs; for non-user calls, mTLS + service JWTs with actor_type=ServiceAccount.
- Least-privilege defaults, with permission bundles versioned and managed centrally. Temporary elevation via time-bound policies.
- Auditability: immutable, structured audit trails keyed by actor_id for all security-sensitive actions; correlation IDs preserved across requests.
- Backward compatibility: existing role checks will be migrated to policy-driven checks via a dedicated authorization service; legacy role literals are deprecated and will be removed on a defined schedule.
- Privacy and compliance: actor attributes are minimized to what policies require; PII resides only in IdP and is referenced, not replicated.

This decision ensures consistent identity semantics across UI, APIs, background jobs, and third-party integrations, enabling reliable authorization, observability, compliance, and maintainability.

We will implement RootMail (RML) as a modular, event-driven system with a service-per-capability architecture to isolate concerns, improve scalability, and enable independent deployment.

- Architecture: Event-driven microservices connected via a durable message broker (e.g., Kafka). Core services: Ingestion (SMTP/HTTP), Routing & Policy, Delivery, Bounce/Feedback Processing, Analytics/Reporting, Templates, User/Org Management, Billing, and Web/App Gateway.
- Data: PostgreSQL for relational/transactional data (tenancy, users, policies, campaigns), Redis for low-latency caching/rate limiting, and object storage for large artifacts (templates, attachments, logs requiring cold storage). Idempotency keys and exactly-once semantics at the application level.
- Protocols: Standards-compliant SMTP with STARTTLS, SPF/DKIM/DMARC support; HTTP APIs for programmatic send, webhooks for events; gRPC for internal service-to-service calls.
- Deliverability: Dedicated queueing, exponential backoff with jitter, per-provider throttling, warmup strategies, feedback loop integration, and adaptive reputation scoring.
- Security and Compliance: Multi-tenant isolation, KMS-backed envelope encryption for sensitive data at rest, mTLS between services, secret rotation, audit logging, GDPR/CCPA-ready data retention policies, and per-tenant domains/keys management.
- Observability: OpenTelemetry for tracing/metrics/logs; SLOs on acceptance latency, delivery success, event pipeline lag; circuit breakers and health probes.
- Extensibility: Plugin points via event topics and webhooks; schema versioning with backward compatibility; feature flags for progressive delivery.
- Deployment: Containerized services orchestrated by Kubernetes with HPA; blue/green or canary releases; regional isolation with active-active routing for high availability.
- Cost and Operability: Right-size storage tiers, lifecycle policies for logs, autoscaling on CPU/QPS/lag, and operational runbooks.

This decision prioritizes scalability, deliverability, and compliance, while enabling rapid iteration and clear ownership across capabilities.

We will route all traffic for bundle-related endpoints to the new Bundle Service via edge-level rules, favoring simple HTTP redirects where safe and preserving method semantics:

- For read-only, idempotent endpoints (GET/HEAD) and public assets, issue 308 Permanent Redirect when the mapping is stable; otherwise 307 Temporary Redirect during rollout. This preserves the method and request body semantics while enabling client-side cache warming and future-proofing.
- For non-idempotent or authenticated flows (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE or requests requiring Authorization headers that would not survive a browser redirect), we will not use client redirects. Instead, we will configure an edge reverse-proxy pass-through (ingress/gateway/Nginx) to forward requests to the Bundle Service, preserving headers and timeouts.

Implementation details:
- Preserve full path and query string 1:1; do not rewrite parameters. Normalize trailing slashes.
- Maintain a deterministic mapping table per endpoint; version via config to allow rapid rollback.
- Apply feature flags to enable per-environment and percentage rollout.
- Enforce timeouts, circuit breakers, and retry policies at the edge; no retries on non-idempotent methods.
- Return CORS headers from the Bundle Service; the edge will not inject CORS for redirected origins.
- Health checks and synthetic probes will follow the final target to ensure availability.
- Log original request ID and correlation headers at both edge and service; emit redirect metrics (rate, latency, error).
- For SEO-sensitive public routes, promote from 307 to 308 only after validation and cache TTL alignment.

This decision minimizes application code changes while enabling safe, observable migration and straightforward rollback.

## Decision
Adopt Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for all APIs, with the following rules:

- Public REST APIs expose the MAJOR version in the URL path (e.g., /api/v1/...). MINOR and PATCH are not encoded in the path and must remain backward-compatible. Any breaking change requires a new MAJOR path (e.g., /api/v2).
- The server returns an API-Version response header with MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH for traceability.
- At most two MAJOR versions are supported concurrently. The previous MAJOR enters maintenance (security and critical fixes only) upon release of a new MAJOR.
- Deprecation policy: announce deprecations in release notes and docs; mark endpoints as deprecated in OpenAPI; return Deprecation and Sunset headers with an explicit sunset date; maintain deprecated endpoints for a minimum of 12 months before removal. After sunset, calls return 410 Gone; unknown versions return 404.
- OpenAPI/Swagger documentation is published per MAJOR at /docs/v{major} and frozen except for backward-compatible updates. SDKs and client libraries follow SemVer and align their MAJOR with the API MAJOR they target.
- Webhooks are versioned; subscriptions specify a target MAJOR, and deliveries include X-Webhook-Version.
- Internal service-to-service contracts prefer compatibility without URL versioning; use additive schema evolution. If a breaking change is unavoidable, publish a new versioned endpoint alongside the old and migrate consumers incrementally.

Adopt a Kubernetes-native service mesh to provide end-to-end, zero-code distributed traceability across services. We will deploy Istio (current LTS) using the sidecar data plane model for broad ecosystem support and mature traffic policies, with a path to evaluate Istio Ambient for sidecarless operation once GA and feature parity are sufficient.

Scope:
- All stateless HTTP/gRPC workloads in production and staging namespaces; exclude stateful sets and high-throughput data planes initially.
- North-south ingress via Istio IngressGateway; east-west via sidecars.

Tracing and telemetry:
- Standardize on W3C TraceContext and Baggage headers; enforce propagation at gateways and via SDK linters.
- Instrument apps with OpenTelemetry SDK/auto-instrumentation where feasible; rely on mesh-generated spans for network hops.
- Export traces to Tempo/Jaeger via OpenTelemetry Collector (agent + gateway pattern); 10–20% adaptive sampling at mesh, with tail-based sampling at Collector for high-value spans.
- Metrics to Prometheus via Istio telemetry; logs unchanged.

Security and policy:
- Enable mTLS STRICT mesh-wide; use PeerAuthentication/AuthorizationPolicy to phase in per-namespace.
- Use ServiceEntry/VirtualService/DestinationRule for identity-aware routing; require SPIFFE identities for service-to-service auth.

Operations:
- Blue/green rollout by namespace: dev → staging → prod; start with a pilot service set.
- Sidecar injection set to opt-in initially, moving to opt-out after validation.
- Provide golden signals SLO dashboards and tracing exemplars; alert on trace ingestion failures.
- Define SLOs: trace end-to-end coverage ≥ 90% of sampled requests; ingestion latency p95 < 10s.

Governance and ownership:
- Platform team owns mesh control plane, upgrades, and default policies; service teams own application-level instrumentation/propagation.
- Establish a deprecation plan for bespoke tracing libraries once coverage targets are met.

Fallback/Exit:
- If Istio introduces unacceptable latency or overhead (>5% p95), reduce sampling, exclude hotspots, or revert namespaces to baseline until mitigated.

## Decision
Implement a dedicated background job, FetchRepositoryWorker, to asynchronously fetch repository metadata and (when required) source content from supported VCS providers. The worker is triggered by:
- Event-driven signals (webhooks for push/tag/release/permissions changes)
- Scheduled backfills and periodic refresh (for missed events and drift)
- On-demand user actions (manual re-sync)

Processing will use a resilient message queue with at-least-once delivery; the worker is idempotent via a stable key (provider, repo ID, ref/commit) and conditional requests (ETag/If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since) to avoid redundant work. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter; poison messages are routed to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

Concurrency is bounded globally and per provider with token-bucket rate limiting to respect API quotas. Timeouts, circuit breakers, and request budgets are enforced per call. Large repositories are processed incrementally (pagination/chunking); content fetches prefer metadata APIs and shallow clones (depth=1) only when necessary.

Secrets are obtained at runtime via the platform secret manager, using short-lived tokens and least-privilege scopes. Network egress is allowlisted; the worker runs in a sandboxed container with read-only filesystems where feasible.

Outputs:
- Normalized metadata persisted in the application database
- Large artifacts (archives, clone caches) stored in object storage with content-addressable keys and TTLs
- A provenance record (source, ref, digest) for traceability

Observability includes structured logs with correlation IDs, metrics (latency, success rate, API quota), and distributed tracing. The worker supports versioned payload contracts for backward compatibility, feature flags for provider-specific behavior, and a dry-run mode. Data minimization is enforced; deletions and access revocations trigger purge workflows.

Adopt Yarn Workspaces to manage our monorepo. We will standardize on Yarn Berry (v4) with a single lockfile at the repository root and workspace-scoped packages under predefined folders (e.g., packages/*, services/*). Intra-repo dependencies will use the workspace: protocol (e.g., "workspace:^", "workspace:*") to ensure strict linking and coherent versioning. We will use nodeLinker: node-modules initially to minimize ecosystem friction, with an option to evaluate Plug’n’Play (PnP) later for stronger determinism.

Key operational decisions:
- No node_modules committed; we will commit .yarn/releases and .yarn/cache to enable fast, reproducible installs (Zero-Install-lite) while keeping repository size reasonable.
- CI will use yarn workspaces focus for selective installs and caching, with immutable installs enforced (—immutable) to guard the lockfile.
- Dependency governance will be enforced via constraints.pro and resolution policies to prevent duplicate or conflicting versions across workspaces.
- Publishing and versioning will be handled via Changesets integrated with Yarn (yarn changeset version/release), producing coordinated releases per workspace.
- Each workspace maintains its own package.json; build/test/lint scripts are standardized and can be executed via yarn workspaces run and yarn workspaces foreach for parallelization.
- Node and Yarn versions are pinned (engines, .yarnrc.yml, and .nvmrc/.node-version) to ensure environment consistency across local and CI.

This decision centralizes dependency management, accelerates installs, improves build isolation and reproducibility, and simplifies cross-package development and releases while leaving a clear path to adopt PnP in the future if/when ecosystem compatibility is confirmed.

We will adopt GNU Make as the single, canonical task runner to centralize all developer, CI, and operational tasks.

- A Makefile will live at the repository root as the entry point; modular includes will reside under make/*.mk per domain (build, test, lint, docker, release, docs).
- The default target will be help, providing self-documenting output. All common targets will be standardized: bootstrap, deps, build, test, lint, fmt, run, watch, clean, dist, docker-build, docker-run, release, ci.
- All user-facing targets will be .PHONY, idempotent where practical, and safe to run repeatedly.
- SHELL will be set to bash with strict mode for robustness: SHELL := /usr/bin/env bash; .SHELLFLAGS := -euo pipefail -c.
- Variables will be overridable via environment; sane defaults will be defined in Makefile.defaults and included when present. Optional .env and .env.local files may be loaded for developer convenience.
- Tool discovery and version checks will be encoded in dedicated targets with helpful error messages. Missing tools will have install/bootstrapping targets where feasible.
- CI pipelines will invoke only make targets; bespoke script entry points will be deprecated or wrapped by make to ensure a single source of truth.
- Cross-platform support: GNU Make ≥ 4.3 is required. Developers on Windows will use WSL2 or Git Bash/MSYS2. Non-GNU make implementations are unsupported.
- Caching and incremental work will be enabled using stamp files and artifact directories (e.g., .cache/, build/). Targets should avoid unnecessary work by checking inputs/outputs and using pattern rules where appropriate.
- Namespacing will be applied for clarity (e.g., db-*, docker-*, infra-*). Targets should be composable and orthogonal.
- Safety conventions: no silent failures; verbose echoing of critical commands; dry-run previews via make -n; destructive targets (e.g., clean, reset) require explicit confirmation flags or echo warnings.
- Documentation will reference make targets as the authoritative commands. Editor/IDE tasks and devcontainer definitions will call make under the hood.
- Repository templates and new services will include a minimal Makefile scaffolding aligned with these conventions.

This decision standardizes execution paths, improves discoverability, and ensures reproducible, automatable workflows across environments by consolidating all tasks under GNU Make.

Adopt a managed, cloud-native identity platform with standards-based federation, selecting Auth0 as the primary customer (B2C/B2B) identity provider and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) for workforce SSO, federated via OIDC/SAML. Centralize authentication and authorization in Auth0 for all external applications and APIs, implementing OIDC/OAuth2 for app auth, SCIM for provisioning, and SAML as needed for partner SSO. Enforce MFA with WebAuthn/Passkeys by default, support social/enterprise logins for tenants, and implement adaptive/risk-based policies. Use Auth0 Actions/Rules for custom flows (progressive profiling, consent, Just-In-Time provisioning), organization/tenant features for B2B, and RBAC with fine-grained API scopes. Synchronize workforce identities via federation to Entra ID; delegate internal app SSO to Entra with conditional access and device posture, maintaining a single source of truth for employees.

Ensure regional data residency and compliance (SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR), configure log streaming to SIEM, and rotate secrets via managed vault. Migrate existing users with hashed-password import and transparent rehash, deprecating legacy auth services. Roll out in phases (dev → staging → prod) with blue/green client configurations and canary traffic. Establish SLAs, tenant isolation, rate limiting, and runbooks; monitor auth KPIs and set quarterly reviews to reassess build-vs-buy and cost.

We will implement a resilient, observable error-handling strategy for the notification service that classifies errors and responds accordingly:

- Error classification: transient (timeouts, 5xx, rate limits, network issues) vs. permanent (4xx like invalid address, blocked, policy violations) vs. unrecoverable (malformed payload, schema mismatch). Classification is provider-specific and centrally mapped.

- Retry policy: transient failures are retried with exponential backoff and full jitter, per-channel/provider caps (e.g., 6 attempts over ~12 hours), and per-tenant limits. Permanent and unrecoverable errors are not retried.

- Dead-letter handling: messages that exceed retry caps or are marked permanent/unrecoverable are moved to a dead-letter queue with rich context (payload, idempotency key, provider response, attempt history). A scheduled reconciliation job supports bulk reprocessing after configuration fixes.

- Idempotency and deduplication: all send requests carry an idempotency key; downstream calls include provider-specific dedupe features where available. We store send attempt state to prevent duplicate deliveries across retries and failover.

- Circuit breaking and failover: per-provider circuit breakers trip on consecutive transient failures; traffic shifts to secondary providers when available. Rate limiting and adaptive backoff respect provider quotas.

- Timeouts and validation: strict request timeouts and input validation prevent stuck or invalid messages from entering retry loops.

- Observability and alerts: structured logging with correlation IDs, metrics (success/failure by class, latency, retry counts, DLQ rate), and alerting on anomalies.

- User impact: status is surfaced as pending/retrying/failed with actionable reasons; optional fallback channels can be configured per template.

Adopt Transformer-based architectures as the standard for all sequence modeling and generative NLP tasks. Use encoder-only models (e.g., BERT/DeBERTa) for classification and retrieval, encoder-decoder models (e.g., T5/FLAN) for sequence-to-sequence tasks, and decoder-only LLMs (e.g., Llama/Mistral) for generation and tool use. Standardize on PyTorch with the Hugging Face ecosystem (Transformers, Datasets, Tokenizers) for training and fine-tuning, with ONNX Runtime or TensorRT for optimized inference. Employ SentencePiece/BPE tokenization. Use LoRA/QLoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, mixed precision (bf16/fp16) for training, and quantization (INT8/4) for serving where accuracy allows. Host models via a model registry with semantic versioning, reproducible training metadata, and gated promotion from staging to production. Serve through Triton or vLLM for high-throughput batch/streaming, with A/B and canary deployment supported by feature flags. Implement prompt/adapter isolation and safety filters, including PII redaction and content moderation. Log embeddings and key metrics (latency, tokens, throughput, cost, quality) with drift detection and rollback. Prefer open-weight models for self-hosting; use managed APIs only when SLAs, compliance, or latency requirements warrant. Provide fallbacks (smaller distilled/quantized variants) for edge and offline scenarios. This decision unifies architecture, tooling, and operations to ensure scalability, portability, and cost-effective performance.

Adopt the Redux architecture pattern as the application’s primary state management approach using Redux Toolkit (RTK) and TypeScript. State will be centralized in a single store composed of feature “slices,” each owning its domain state, actions, and reducers. RTK will be used for immutable updates, action creators, and slice co-location to reduce boilerplate and ensure consistency. Asynchronous workflows and side effects will be handled via RTK Thunk for simple cases and RTK Query for server cache management, data fetching, normalization, and request lifecycle. All state must remain serializable; non-serializable values are prohibited in store, actions, and selectors. Global cross-cutting behaviors (e.g., logging, error reporting, analytics) will be implemented via Redux middleware. Feature modules will expose selectors as the public query interface and avoid selectors reaching across slice boundaries directly to preserve encapsulation.

The store will be configured once at the app shell, with dynamic slice injection allowed for code-split features. Strict typing will be enforced for state, actions, thunks, and selectors. Performance will be addressed by co-locating slices, normalizing entities using RTK EntityAdapter, memoized selectors (Reselect), and component-level subscription via hooks (useSelector/useStore) with careful selector granularity. Only state requiring cross-component or cross-route consistency will live in Redux; ephemeral UI state remains local to components.

Testing will cover reducers as pure functions, selectors as deterministic mappers, and thunks/RTK Query endpoints via mocked services. Existing local or ad-hoc global state will be migrated incrementally to slices per feature. This decision standardizes state management, improves predictability, debuggability, and scalability across the codebase.

Adopt a rule-driven, deterministic simplification layer for function evaluation that performs eager constant folding and algebraic normalization only for whitelisted pure, total functions and for expressions whose operands are side‑effect‑free and fully known at evaluation time. All simplifications will be expressed as versioned rewrite rules operating on a canonical intermediate representation that encodes commutativity/associativity, numeric types, and null/NaN semantics. We will:

- Canonicalize expressions (e.g., sort commutative operands, flatten associative groups) before applying rules.
- Apply safe algebraic identities (e.g., x+0→x, x*1→x, 0*x→0) and short‑circuit rules (e.g., false AND x→false) with strict guarding on domain constraints (division by zero, overflow, NaN propagation).
- Evaluate literals and pure calls at compile/plan time; defer evaluation for impure/partial functions, non-deterministic calls, or expressions marked volatile.
- Enforce precise numeric behavior: no cross‑type coercion without explicit rules; preserve integer vs floating semantics; propagate null/NaN consistently; avoid reordering that changes rounding unless explicitly allowed.
- Support configuration flags to toggle aggressive vs conservative simplification levels and to disable specific rules for debugging or compliance needs.
- Record provenance on each transformation for explainability and enable round‑trip testing.
- Provide a monotonic, termination‑guaranteed rule application strategy (normalized form target, no oscillating rewrites) with exhaustive tests and property checks.

This decision centralizes simplification policy, improves performance predictably, and preserves correctness across runtimes.

## Decision
We will model all reusable UI elements as components and manage them within a shared design system library. Each visual or interactive element that appears more than once, or is anticipated to, must be implemented as a self-contained, composable component with a stable, documented API.

- Component taxonomy: adopt atomic design hierarchy (foundations/tokens → atoms → molecules → organisms → templates). Prefer composition over inheritance; no deep prop drilling beyond two levels—use context only for cross-cutting concerns (theme, i18n, RTL).
- Contracts: components are typed, forward refs where applicable, and expose minimal, stable props. Breaking changes require versioning and migration notes.
- Styling: exclusively via design tokens and theme variables; no ad-hoc inline styles except dynamic calculations. Dark mode and accessibility states are first-class.
- Accessibility: all interactive components ship with ARIA roles, keyboard semantics, and contrast compliance by default.
- State: default to controlled, stateless components; provide optional internal state via consistent onChange/value patterns. Side effects are prohibited inside pure visual components.
- Performance: memoize pure components; lazy-load complex organisms; avoid re-renders via stable keys and context partitioning.
- Packaging: publish as a versioned package with tree-shakeable ESM exports and per-component entry points.
- Documentation and QA: every component requires Storybook stories, usage docs, and tests (unit, a11y, visual regression).
- Adoption: new UI must use components; legacy inline elements will be refactored opportunistically or when touched. Exceptions require an approved ADR addendum.

We will externalize and standardize DLXS configuration using a declarative, version-controlled model with strict separation of non-secret settings and secrets.

- Non-secret configuration will be defined in YAML files organized by component and environment (base defaults plus environment overlays: dev, test, stage, prod) within a dedicated dlxs-config repository. A JSON Schema will validate all configuration at commit time and in CI.
- Secrets (e.g., credentials, keys) will not reside in the repository. They will be managed in a centralized secret manager (e.g., HashiCorp Vault or cloud-native equivalent) and injected at deploy time. Local development will use a .env.local pattern ignored by VCS.
- DLXS services will read configuration only from environment variables at runtime. YAML files are rendered to environment variables via a templating step (e.g., Helm/Ansible/Jinja) during deployment. This ensures immutability of images and environment-specific configuration without code changes.
- Deployments will use:
  - Kubernetes: ConfigMaps for non-secrets and Secrets for secrets, rendered from the dlxs-config repo via Helm.
  - VM/bare metal: Ansible to template and place config, with systemd-managed environment files.
- All changes follow Git-based change control with mandatory review, automated validation, and provenance through release tagging. Rollbacks are supported by reverting config repo tags.

## Decision
Adopt workspace protocol dependencies for all intra-repo package references in package.json to ensure reliable local linking, coherent builds, and consistent releases across the monorepo.

- Use workspace:^ as the default for internal library dependencies (e.g., "pkg-a": "workspace:^"), so that:
  - During local development, packages are symlinked and resolved from the workspace.
  - On publish, the range is replaced with a semver-compatible caret range to the published version, preserving consumer compatibility.
- Use workspace:* for internal app/shell packages that are not published (e.g., example apps, integration test apps) to always resolve to the exact workspace version and avoid semver drift.
- Do not use workspace: in peerDependencies; declare explicit semver ranges aligned with our public API guarantees.
- External (third-party) packages must use standard semver ranges (prefer ^ for libs, ~ where tighter pinning is required); never use workspace: for external deps.
- Enforce the above via tooling:
  - Lint rule or script validating dependency fields for correct workspace usage.
  - CI installs with frozen/locked lockfile and builds in topological order using the workspace graph.
- Release and publishing:
  - Use our release tooling (e.g., Changesets) to version internal packages; workspace ranges are transformed on publish.
  - Ensure publishConfig and access settings remain consistent across packages.
- Scope:
  - Applies to dependencies and devDependencies within the monorepo.
  - Not applicable to standalone repos or packages intentionally published independently.

This decision standardizes dependency management across the monorepo, enabling atomic refactors, faster local workflows, deterministic builds, and safer publishes without manual version wiring.

We will standardize on JUnit 5 (Jupiter) as the primary testing framework for all new unit and integration tests. The project will use the JUnit Platform with the Jupiter engine; the Vintage engine may be included temporarily to run legacy JUnit 4 tests during migration but will be removed once migration completes. New tests must be written using JUnit 5 annotations and features (e.g., parameterized tests, dynamic tests, nested tests, @TempDir, and extensions).

Build integration will be through the JUnit Platform with Maven Surefire/Failsafe (or Gradle Test) configured to discover and run Jupiter tests. Test execution will be split by tags: “unit” runs on every commit; “integration” (including Testcontainers-based tests) runs in PRs and scheduled pipelines. Parallel test execution may be enabled via JUnit Platform configuration where deterministic and thread-safe.

For mocking and assertions, we will use Mockito 5+ and AssertJ (or equivalent fluent assertions) alongside JUnit 5; Spring-based tests will use the SpringExtension where applicable. Code coverage will be enforced via JaCoCo with agreed thresholds.

Conventions: test classes colocated under src/test/java mirroring production packages; naming as ClassNameTest or ClassNameIT; use @DisplayName for readability; prefer constructor/parameter injection for test fixtures; use @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) only when necessary.

Migration policy: no new JUnit 4 tests; existing JUnit 4 tests migrate opportunistically or when touched; CI will fail on new JUnit 4 usage after a grace period; the Vintage engine will be removed after migration completes.

Minimum runtime: Java 11+ (prefer 17+) to align with JUnit 5 capabilities and ecosystem support. IDEs and CI pipelines will be updated to run on the JUnit Platform.

We will persist temporal and actor provenance for all business records and domain events.

- For mutable records, add metadata columns:
  - created_at (UTC, ISO‑8601/RFC3339 with millisecond precision), created_by_id, created_by_type
  - updated_at, updated_by_id, updated_by_type
  - deleted_at, deleted_by_id (for soft deletes)
  - Optional validity: effective_from, effective_to for temporal models
- For event-sourced streams, every event includes occurred_at and caused_by_id/caused_by_type in event metadata.

Conventions:
- Store timestamps in UTC only (TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE where supported; otherwise epoch micros + conversion). External JSON uses RFC3339 UTC.
- Actor captured as opaque principal_id plus principal_type ∈ {user, service, system}. Do not persist PII; resolve display names at read time via directory. Optionally cache a non-authoritative principal_display_name snapshot for historical readability.
- Tenant and data lineage: include tenant_id and source_system where applicable to support multi-tenant auditing.

Integrity:
- Backend derives actor from authenticated principal (token/MTLS/service identity). Client-supplied values are ignored.
- created_* are immutable; updated_* are set on mutation; deleted_* set on soft delete only.
- Enforce via application layer and DB triggers/defaults to prevent omission/spoofing.

Indexing and access:
- Index (tenant_id, updated_at) and (tenant_id, created_at) for audit and incremental ETL.
- Expose read-only provenance in APIs; exclude from write DTOs.

Migration and backfill:
- For legacy rows lacking provenance, backfill created_at from earliest known time; set actors to “system” with principal_id = system:<migration>. Record migration_id in source_system.

Compliance:
- Retain provenance per data retention policies; include in exports; redact actor PII where required by privacy rules.

We revoke and supersede ADR-0002. Effective immediately, all new request/response interceptors will be produced via CodeGen and not hand-written. Interceptor definitions will be expressed declaratively (e.g., annotations/IDL/schema), from which the CodeGen plugin will generate type-safe, centrally standardized interceptor implementations for supported stacks (HTTP, gRPC, messaging).

Scope:
- Applies to client- and server-side interceptors across services in this repository.
- Covers cross-cutting concerns such as auth, tracing, metrics, idempotency, retries, circuit breaking, request shaping, and redaction.

Implementation directives:
- Integrate the CodeGen plugin into the build pipeline and CI; generation runs deterministically during build. Generated sources are not hand-edited.
- Provide a common configuration module and templates for interceptor policies and ordering.
- Block new manual interceptors via lint/CI rules; allow explicit, reviewed exceptions only for unsupported edge cases.
- Migrate existing manual interceptors incrementally to generated equivalents; deprecate and remove manual implementations once parity is reached.
- Version CodeGen specifications alongside service code to ensure reproducible builds.

Acceptance criteria:
- All new interceptors originate from CodeGen specs.
- Uniform telemetry and policy enforcement across services.
- Zero manual interceptor boilerplate in new code paths.

We will standardize on a mature, feature-rich command-line processing library rather than implementing bespoke argument parsing. The CLI must support subcommands, nested command trees, GNU/POSIX-compliant short/long flags, default values, required flags, validation, auto-generated help/usage, shell completion, colorized output, environment-variable binding, configuration file loading, and structured error handling with clear exit codes.

Command conventions:
- Verb-first subcommands (e.g., tool init, tool build, tool deploy).
- Global flags: --version, --help, --verbose/-v (repeatable), --quiet, --config, --no-color.
- Consistent short/long options and predictable precedence: CLI args > env vars > config > defaults.
- Stable, explicit exit codes (0 success; 2 usage error; 3 config error; >10 runtime categories).
- Built-in --completion to emit shell completion scripts.

Implementation approach:
- Do not hand-roll parsing; wrap the chosen library with a thin internal module to enforce conventions, shared flag definitions, logging/telemetry setup, and uniform error/reporting behavior.
- Provide test helpers to simulate argv/env/config and capture output/exit codes.
- Backward-compatibility policy: additive changes only by default; deprecate flags/subcommands with warnings before removal; follow semver.

Default library selection by runtime:
- Go: Cobra (+ pflag) with Viper for config/env binding.
- Python: Click or Typer (Click-based) with Dynaconf for config.
- Node.js: yargs with cosmiconfig.
- .NET: System.CommandLine with Spectre.Console for UX.

If a runtime is not listed, choose a library that meets the must-haves and is actively maintained (≥1 release/year, wide adoption, permissive license). All new CLI surfaces must use this stack; existing CLIs will be incrementally migrated behind the wrapper.

We will use react-app-rewired to customize Create React App (CRA) configuration without ejecting, enabling targeted overrides to Webpack, Babel, Jest, and dev server settings while retaining CRA’s upgrade path. All configuration changes must be implemented exclusively in config-overrides.js (and optional overrides files), be minimal, reversible, and documented inline. We will pin react-app-rewired and related loader/plugin versions to known-compatible releases for CRA v5, and changes to overrides require code review by a designated frontend maintainer.

Scope:
- Allowed: aliasing, path resolution, Babel plugin/preset additions, Webpack plugin/loader configuration, CSS module/scoped styles tuning, Jest transform/jest-resolver adjustments, dev server proxy tweaks.
- Disallowed: ejecting, replacing CRA scripts, modifying TypeScript compilation outside tsconfig, introducing breaking changes to build outputs without RFC.

Operational policies:
- CI will include a “vanilla CRA” smoke test build quarterly to detect drift.
- Overrides must be guarded by environment checks and feature flags when risky.
- Dependabot/renovate updates to CRA/react-scripts are blocked until overrides compatibility is verified in a branch.

Migration/Exit:
- If CRA upgrades break overrides, we will first attempt minimal fixes; failing that, we will evaluate migration to Vite or CRA eject as a last resort. We will maintain a playbook to revert to stock CRA scripts within one working day.

Effective immediately for all CRA-based frontends; to be deprecated when the app platform migrates off CRA.

Adopt a Virtual Platform (VP) as a Mediator pattern to decouple producers/consumers from the core domain and from each other. The VP will provide capability-centric APIs and event channels, normalize contracts to a canonical data model, and mediate interactions via routing, orchestration, protocol translation, policy enforcement, and observability.

Scope:
- All third-party, partner, and internal integrations connect through the VP using adapters.
- The VP exposes synchronous REST/gRPC endpoints and asynchronous topics/queues (AsyncAPI), with contracts versioned and backward compatible.
- Orchestration supports sagas for cross-service workflows; choreography is supported via event routing.

Key decisions:
- Implement a canonical message schema and mapping layer per adapter.
- Use a managed message broker for at-least-once delivery with idempotency keys, dead-letter queues, and retry/backoff; enable optional exactly-once where supported.
- Enforce zero-trust: mutual TLS, OAuth2/OIDC, fine-grained authorization, data masking, and multi-tenant isolation.
- Provide an extension SDK for adapters/mediations with governance, linting, and conformance tests.
- Centralize rate limiting, backpressure, schema validation, PII redaction, and feature flags.
- Operate the VP as stateless, horizontally scalable services; persist orchestration state and outbox/inbox in a replicated store.

Non-goals:
- The VP does not own business logic of domain services.
- It will not provide long-term data storage beyond mediation state.

Success metrics include integration lead time, change failure rate, throughput/latency SLOs, and contract compliance. Migration proceeds incrementally via façade and strangler patterns with deprecation windows.

Adopt the IIIF Presentation API 3.0 for all digital objects, exposing a canonical, stable manifest per intellectual object at https://{host}/iiif/{objectId}/manifest with content negotiation (application/ld+json; profile="http://iiif.io/api/presentation/3/context.json"). Generate manifests on demand from the source repository metadata and derivative inventories, with CDN caching and an optional short-lived server-side cache; do not persist manifests as primary records. Structure manifests with one Canvas per page/frame; use Ranges for logical structure (e.g., chapters), and Collections to group objects (e.g., holdings, exhibitions). Reference images via the IIIF Image API 3.0 endpoints; serve tiles from the image server and include thumbnails. For time-based media, model Canvases with duration and media fragments.

Embed descriptive metadata using language maps; include required properties (id, type, label, items) and recommended fields (summary, requiredStatement, rights, provider, homepage, logo, navDate). Link technical/auxiliary data via seeAlso and rendering (e.g., METS, ALTO, PDF). Publish OCR/transcription as AnnotationPages targeting Canvases; enable full-text search via the IIIF Search API 1.0 when textual annotations exist.

Apply access control at the resource level: public manifests for open items; restricted manifests reference protected images/media using IIIF Auth API 1.0 patterns. Manifests remain resolvable and minimally informative even when media is restricted, exposing authorization services where required. Rights are expressed with standardized rights statements/Creative Commons URIs.

Ensure persistent, dereferenceable IDs; changes that affect client rendering are backward compatible where possible. Provide manifest versioning via metadata and immutable snapshot URLs when needed. Validate manifests in CI/CD using the official IIIF validators; monitor in production with schema checks and synthetic viewers. Document and guarantee SLA for availability and cache TTLs. This decision standardizes interoperability with IIIF-compliant viewers and external consumers while minimizing duplication and maximizing performance.

## Decision
Adopt globally unique, stable, and dereferenceable HTTPS URIs as the canonical identifiers for all first-class entities in the Pattern/QC Atlas (e.g., patterns, quality criteria, categories, relationships, references, authors).

- URI scheme and patterns:
  - Base: https://atlas.example.org/
  - Canonical entity: /{entity-type}/{opaque-id}
  - Human-friendly alias (optional): /{entity-type}/{slug} → 301 to canonical
  - Versioning: /{entity-type}/{opaque-id}/v/{semver|sequence}
  - “Latest” pointer: /{entity-type}/{opaque-id} → 302/307 to current version

- Identifier policy:
  - Opaque, non-semantic IDs for stability (e.g., ULIDs/UUIDv7).
  - Slugs are non-canonical and may change; permanent redirects ensure link longevity.
  - IDs never recycled; deprecated entities remain resolvable with deprecation metadata.

- Dereferencing and representations:
  - Content negotiation: text/html (human), application/json (API), application/ld+json (RDF/JSON-LD).
  - Minimal JSON includes id (URI), type, version, timestamps; HTML presents the same content for humans.
  - Provide Link headers (rel=self, canonical, alternate, describedby) and JSON-LD contexts for interoperability.

- Linking and relations:
  - All cross-entity references use canonical URIs.
  - Outbound bibliographic links prefer persistent IDs (DOI, ORCID) with resolver URIs.
  - Maintain backlinks and typed relations to support graph traversal.

- Persistence and governance:
  - Persistence commitment: URIs are intended to be permanent; changes require redirects.
  - Migration policy provides 301/308 redirects for any structural changes.
  - Deletions are avoided; when required, return 410 Gone with a tombstone document describing rationale and replacements.
  - Publishing workflow validates uniqueness, referential integrity, and generates redirects for slug changes.

- Performance and ops:
  - Edge caching of representations with appropriate ETag/Last-Modified.
  - Rate limits and pagination for API representations.
  - Availability SLOs documented; monitoring for 4xx/5xx spikes on dereferencing.

This decision standardizes identification, enables deep linking, supports evolution via versioned URIs, and ensures long-term resolvability and interoperability of the Atlas.

We will support partial resource updates via the HTTP PATCH method using JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) with Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json as the single, standardized format for request bodies. Full replacements remain via PUT, and creation via POST. PATCH will be enabled only for resources where partial updates are safe and well-defined; unsupported resources will return 405 with Allow headers.

Key rules:
- PATCH requests must be idempotent from the client’s perspective when the same patch is reapplied to the same resource state guarded by concurrency controls.
- Optimistic concurrency is required: clients must send If-Match with the latest ETag; servers will return 412 on mismatch.
- Only fields explicitly provided are updated; null explicitly clears a field where allowed. Absent fields remain unchanged.
- Server-side validation applies to the resulting resource after patch application; invalid patches return 400 with machine-readable error details. Forbidden field updates return 403.
- Partial updates to computed, read-only, or server-managed fields are rejected.
- Atomicity is per-resource: a single PATCH modifies either all targeted fields or none.
- Request and response bodies follow the canonical resource schema; server returns 200 with the updated representation or 204 No Content when representation is omitted.
- Auditing will record field-level changes derived from the patch.
- For complex structural edits not expressible via merge semantics, clients must use application-specific endpoints or full PUT; we explicitly do not support JSON Patch (RFC 6902) to reduce client/server complexity and ambiguity.

## Decision

Adopt a first-class Supervisor abstraction for all light clients, prioritizing operator ergonomics, safety, and observability:

- Model each light client as a supervised unit with declarative policy: restart strategy (one-for-one), bounded retries, exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, rate limits, and quorum requirements for verification/peering.
- Use structured concurrency for lifecycle (start, stop, drain, teardown), guaranteeing no orphaned tasks and deterministic shutdown.
- Provide a minimal, consistent control surface: create/update/delete client, attach/detach peer sets, trigger snapshot sync, subscribe to events, fetch state/health, and apply policy presets.
- Configuration is declarative (YAML/TOML/JSON) with sane defaults, environment overrides, and optional hot-reload; each reload is versioned and safely rolled back on validation failure.
- Standardize observability: per-client metrics (latency, height, divergence, error budget, restart count), structured logs with correlation IDs, and tracing spans; expose a health/readiness endpoint with granular reasons.
- Enforce backpressure and resource budgets (CPU/mem/network) per client; deny or queue work when limits are reached to protect global stability.
- Surface typed failure semantics and human-readable diagnostics; emit actionable events for threshold breaches and policy escalations.
- Design for extensibility: pluggable verification engines and transports; policy-as-code presets; compatible CLI and simple web dashboard for common workflows.

Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as the standard mechanism to capture, communicate, and govern significant technical and architectural decisions.

- Format: Markdown ADRs following the “context—decision—consequences” structure (MADR/Nygard style), one decision per file.
- Location: docs/adr/ in each service/repository; security-sensitive ADRs may reside in a private repo with a public summary when feasible.
- Naming/numbering: Sequential numeric prefix (e.g., 0001-meaningful-title.md). Titles are stable; numbers never change.
- Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded. Accepted ADRs are immutable except for typos/links; changes require a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
- Scope: Required for decisions that impact architecture, cross-cutting concerns, external contracts, significant cost/risk, or reversibility > 2 sprints. Minor implementation choices are excluded.
- Workflow: Authors create ADRs via a template; decisions are reviewed via pull request; acceptance requires approval from the designated architecture owner(s) and relevant stakeholders.
- Cross-references: ADRs must link related/superseded decisions and reference supporting evaluations (RFCs, spike results).
- Tooling: Template provided; adr-tools or equivalent script allowed. CI publishes ADRs to the documentation site and validates metadata (status, links, format).
- Discoverability: docs/adr/README indexes ADRs; repo README links the index. Release notes reference newly Accepted ADRs.
- Ownership: Architecture group curates consistency and taxonomy; all teams can propose ADRs.
- Cadence: Periodic (quarterly) review to deprecate outdated ADRs and ensure alignment with current architecture.

Adopt shared, multi-tenant ingress controllers as the default for all Kubernetes clusters and environments, managed by the platform team. A small, standardized set of controllers will be deployed per cluster, segmented by IngressClass (e.g., public, internal, partner) and environment tier, rather than per-team instances. Teams publish Ingress and HTTPRoute resources bound to an approved IngressClass; admission policies, RBAC, and namespace-scoped quotas enforce safe, self-service configuration.

The controllers will be N replicas per class for HA, with horizontal autoscaling, canary upgrades, and controlled config rollouts via GitOps. Common cross-cutting concerns (TLS via cert-manager, DNS via external-dns, WAF/OWASP rules, mTLS where required, rate limiting, IP allow/deny, DDoS protections, request/connection limits, header and body size limits) are centrally managed with per-tenant override guardrails. Network isolation is enforced using dedicated load balancers per class, distinct external IPs, and NetworkPolicies; hard multi-tenancy boundaries (e.g., strict perf isolation) are addressed via per-tenant rate limits and fair-queuing.

SLOs: availability ≥99.95% per class; p50/p95 latency budgets defined and monitored per route. Observability is standardized: per-tenant metrics, logs, and traces labeled by team via namespace and annotations, with per-team dashboards and alerts.

Exceptions: teams may request dedicated ingress only for substantiated isolation, compliance, or bespoke protocol needs; approval requires capacity review and cost attribution. We will progressively adopt Gateway API where supported, maintaining Ingress compatibility during transition.

## Decision
Adopt a hierarchical, locale-scoped user preferences model with deterministic fallback to ensure culturally appropriate behavior without duplicating unrelated settings.

- Scope and precedence:
  1) Locale-specific user preferences (user+locale)
  2) User global preferences (user-wide)
  3) Organization defaults (optional)
  4) Application defaults
  Parent-locale fallback applies (e.g., fr-CA → fr → defaults).

- Storage and schema:
  - Persist user global and per-locale preferences as JSON blobs with whitelisted keys and strict types.
  - Primary key: (user_id, locale) for locale-scoped rows; (user_id, “global”) for global.
  - Only keys explicitly marked “localizable” may vary by locale; non-localizable keys remain global.

- API and semantics:
  - GET /preferences?locale=… returns the effective merged view plus version/ETag.
  - PUT/PATCH /preferences?locale=… apply partial, schema-validated updates; null removes a key at that scope.
  - Server computes effective preferences via merge; clients remain thin and stateless.
  - 409 on concurrent updates unless If-Match matches; version increments on change.

- Resolution and merge:
  - Shallow, key-wise merge; last-writer at highest-precedence scope wins.
  - No cross-scope writes; updates only affect the addressed scope.

- Caching and propagation:
  - Server-side cache of effective preferences per (user_id, locale); cache key includes version.
  - CDN/client caching via ETag/Cache-Control; cache invalidation on write via pub/sub event.

- Access pattern:
  - Central PreferencesProvider(userId, locale) for all services; locale passed explicitly per request.

- Governance and safety:
  - Validation pipeline enforces allowed keys, types, and size limits.
  - Audited changes (who/when/what) with export/delete to honor privacy/compliance.
  - Backfill migration: initialize per-locale rows on first write; no-op for users without localizable overrides.

- We will deprecate and remove the va_profile model and consolidate its responsibilities into the canonical User domain (User + Profile aggregate).
- All required va_profile fields will be migrated to the Profile entity (or User table where appropriate), with canonicalized naming and types; non-essential or redundant fields will be dropped.
- A database migration will:
  - Create new columns/indexes on Profile/User.
  - Backfill data from va_profile to Profile/User with idempotent scripts.
  - Add foreign keys and constraints equivalent to current guarantees.
  - Remove va_profile table and related constraints after verification.
- Application code will:
  - Replace all va_profile references with Profile/User accessors.
  - Provide mapping adapters for legacy services during a grace period.
  - Remove model, serializers, DTOs, repository, and caches tied to va_profile.
- API and events:
  - Public APIs exposing va_profile will be marked deprecated immediately and removed in the next major version.
  - New/updated endpoints will expose Profile fields directly; event schemas will be revised accordingly with versioned topics.
- Authorization and privacy:
  - Migrate guards, policies, and PII handling to Profile/User; re-run privacy impact checks.
- Observability:
  - Add metrics to track legacy vs. new access paths; create alerts for migration anomalies.
- Backward compatibility:
  - Feature flags will gate read/write paths; reads will dual-source during backfill; writes will dual-write until cutover.
  - A read-only shadow of va_profile will be retained for one release for rollback only.
- Timeline:
  - Phase 1: introduce new schema/dual-write.
  - Phase 2: backfill and switch reads.
  - Phase 3: remove dual-write and delete va_profile.
- Acceptance:
  - Zero data loss, parity on contract tests, and performance within ±10% on impacted endpoints.

We will use stable, dereferenceable HTTPS URIs as the primary identifiers for domain data resources. A URI identifies the resource (the data concept), not any specific representation, storage location, or server implementation.

- Each resource has one canonical URI that is globally unique and persistent. Canonical URIs do not embed file extensions, representations, or transient attributes.
- Dereferencing a resource URI yields one of its representations via standard HTTP content negotiation (JSON as default), with alternates available per Accept headers. Alternate or legacy URIs must 301/308 redirect to the canonical URI.
- URIs are opaque identifiers; where feasible, we prefer non-semantic, immutable IDs (e.g., UUIDs). Human-readable slugs may exist as secondary aliases but are not canonical.
- Resource URIs do not encode actions; operations are performed via HTTP methods. Query parameters shape result sets or views and do not change the identity of a singular resource.
- Relationships between resources are expressed with URIs; systems may store and exchange URIs as foreign keys.
- Resource URIs are never reassigned. Deletions return 410 Gone; temporary unavailability returns 503; moved resources return 301/308.
- Versioning applies to representations (media types, headers) or API routes, not to the identity of an individual resource. Resource URIs remain stable across representation version changes.
- URI patterns are documented and validated; any necessary changes follow a deprecation schedule with redirects and telemetry to measure impact.

This decision ensures long-lived, interoperable identifiers, decouples identity from representation and deployment, and enables caching, linking, and evolution without breaking resource identity.

Adopt Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) v2 for stateless, horizontally scalable services to automatically adjust replica counts based on resource and business metrics. Use CPU utilization (target 70%) as the default signal; enable memory-based scaling (target 80%) for memory-bound workloads identified during profiling. Integrate Prometheus Adapter to expose custom/external metrics (e.g., requests-per-second, queue depth, consumer lag) for services where CPU/memory are not predictive; these services will scale primarily on the most correlated business metric with CPU as a safeguard.

Set minReplicas: 2 (production), 1 (non-production). Set service-specific maxReplicas based on capacity plans and SLO error budgets. Configure HPA behavior: scaleUp stabilizationWindowSeconds=60 with policies allowing up to +100%/60s capped at +4 pods; scaleDown stabilizationWindowSeconds=300 with policies allowing up to -50%/5m and never below minReplicas. Apply per-service cooldowns and metric aggregation windows (1–5 minutes) to dampen jitter. Require accurate resource requests/limits and readiness/liveness probes for predictable scheduling and safe scale events; enforce PodDisruptionBudgets and maxUnavailable to avoid thundering herds.

Exclude stateful databases and single-writer components from HPA; handle batch/cron workloads with fixed replicas or VPA if needed. Rely on Cluster Autoscaler to back HPA-induced demand. Roll out HPA per service behind feature flags, validated via load testing and chaos drills, with alerting on saturation and autoscaling failures. Configuration lives as code and is reviewed with performance baselines.

We will standardize metadata across the platform via a Canonical Metadata Model (CMM) represented as JSON documents validated by versioned JSON Schemas (SemVer). Each metadata entity will have a stable ULID, type, schemaVersion, timestamps, owner, classification/tags (including PII sensitivity), lineage, retention, and provenance fields. Metadata will be stored in PostgreSQL using JSONB with GIN indexes on key attributes; changes will be append-only to preserve history, with soft-deletes and deprecation flags rather than destructive updates.

A dedicated Metadata Service will be the system of record and single access point, exposing REST and GraphQL APIs and emitting change events (create/update/delete/deprecate) on the event bus (e.g., Kafka) for downstream consumers. Write operations require schema validation and authorization; read operations support projection and time-travel queries. SDKs will be provided for common languages.

Governance policies will enforce required fields (owner, classification, data domain), schema compatibility rules (backward-compatible changes only by default), and review workflows for schema evolution. Access control will use RBAC with attribute-based checks on classifications; audit logs will capture all mutations. Metadata at runtime (service/resource attributes) will leverage OpenTelemetry conventions where applicable; ingestion connectors will normalize external catalogs/sources to the CMM.

Operationally, the service will ensure high availability, encryption at rest and in transit, payload size limits, and SLOs for latency. Migrations will include backfilling existing assets into the CMM and mapping legacy keys to ULIDs. We will not adopt a third-party catalog as the source of truth; external catalogs may mirror from our events and reconcile via APIs.

## Decision
Adopt an event-driven, microservices architecture for Imo Messaging to support low-latency real-time messaging at scale with strong security and multi-device consistency.

- Communication: Use gRPC for service-to-service RPC and WebSocket (HTTP/2 where supported) for client real-time channels, with fallback to long-polling for constrained networks. Use APNs/FCM for background wake and notifications.
- Security: Implement end-to-end encryption using the Signal Protocol (libsignal) with double ratchet, prekeys, and sealed sender where possible. Store only encrypted message payloads; servers never hold plaintext or long-term private keys. Enforce TLS 1.2+ everywhere and hardware-backed key storage on devices.
- Data and state: 
  - PostgreSQL for accounts, device registrations, contacts, and policy.
  - Cassandra (or DynamoDB equivalent) for ordered, high-write message history and per-conversation streams.
  - Redis Cluster for ephemeral presence/typing state and fan-out caching.
  - Object storage (S3/GCS) + CDN for media; encrypt at rest with per-object keys wrapped by a KMS.
- Messaging guarantees: At-least-once delivery with client-generated, time-sortable ULIDs for idempotency and de-duplication. Use Kafka as the backbone event bus for fan-out, delivery retries, and audit trails. Implement per-device read-state and server-side catch-up queues with TTL.
- Multi-device sync: Device-scoped sessions with per-device encryption keys; converge using version vectors and last-writer-wins for non-critical metadata (e.g., read receipts), while messages remain append-only.
- Operability: Deploy on Kubernetes with horizontal autoscaling, regional sharding, and active-active replication. Apply zero-downtime deploys, circuit breakers, rate limits, and backpressure. Full observability with structured logs, traces, SLOs, and chaos testing.
- Compliance: Privacy by design; minimal data retention with configurable retention policies and GDPR/CCPA controls.

We will implement the frontend as a TypeScript-based React application using Next.js for hybrid SSR/SSG and Vite for local development where applicable (via next-vite or standard Next dev server if conflicts arise). UI will be built with a headless component approach using Radix UI primitives and Tailwind CSS for styling, complemented by CSS Modules for component-scoped styles where utility classes are insufficient. State management will prioritize server state with React Query and cache-first patterns; minimal global client state will use Zustand, avoiding Redux unless future complexity demands it. Routing, code-splitting, and image optimization will be handled by Next.js conventions. API integration will use a generated client from the backend’s OpenAPI/GraphQL schema with strict TypeScript types and Zod runtime validation at boundaries. Form handling will use React Hook Form with Zod schemas. Internationalization will use next-i18next; accessibility will adhere to WCAG 2.2 AA with automated checks (axe) and semantic HTML. Testing will include unit tests with Vitest/Jest and React Testing Library, integration/e2e with Playwright, and visual regression via Playwright snapshots. Linting/formatting will use ESLint (airbnb+react+tsx) and Prettier, with Husky and lint-staged enforcing CI parity locally. The project will live in a pnpm monorepo with shared UI and utility packages, adopt a feature-sliced folder structure, and use Storybook for component documentation.
