- Validator mode for validator nodes: consensus and mempool enabled; P2P restricted to sentry-only connectivity; block indexing enabled; state sync enabled for recovery but disabled during steady-state; run out-of-process ABCI over Unix domain sockets.
- Full mode for sentry and archival nodes: full consensus disabled (no proposing/voting); mempool enabled for relaying; block indexing set to “kv” on archival, “null” on transient sentries; state sync enabled by default for bootstrap; pruning tuned per role (archival=everything, sentry=recent).
- Seed mode for public seed/discovery nodes: consensus and mempool disabled; PEX enabled; no block indexing; aggressive connection limits and peer filtering.

Operational policy:
- Default mode is full; mode is selectable via a single configuration flag (e.g., TENDERMINT_MODE={validator|full|seed}) with role-specific presets applied at startup.
- Validators must be deployed behind at least two sentry full nodes; no inbound public connections to validators.
- State sync snapshots are produced by designated full/archival nodes; snapshot scheduling and retention are centralized via ops config.
- Telemetry, Prometheus metrics, and structured logging are enabled in all modes; ABCI timeouts and mempool parameters are mode-scoped.
- Mode changes require node restart; hot-switching is not supported.
- Backward compatibility is maintained with CometBFT defaults; deviations are captured in configuration templates and CI conformance tests.

We will open Kibana access to all service teams to enable self-serve observability (logs, metrics, APM, uptime, dashboards, alerts) while enforcing least-privilege, data segregation, and compliance.

- Identity and access: Enforce SSO (SAML/OIDC) and SCIM-provisioned groups. Default role is read-only. Each team gets a dedicated Kibana Space with “manage own saved objects” and “manage own alerts/actions.” Platform team retains global admin.
- Data scoping: Elasticsearch roles restrict index access by team- and env-prefixed naming conventions (e.g., logs-{team}-{env}-*). Common infrastructure indices are read-only to all. Cross-team access is opt-in via shared Spaces or explicitly granted roles.
- Write controls: No direct index write from Kibana for non-platform users. Teams may create/modify dashboards, visualizations, alerts, and index patterns only within their Space.
- Security and compliance: Ingest pipelines redact PII/secrets. Field- and document-level security applied to sensitive fields/indices. Spaces and roles prevent lateral data exposure. IP allowlists/VPN required. Audit logging enabled for Kibana and Elasticsearch (auth, role mappings, saved object changes, alert lifecycle).
- Environments: Separate Kibana/ES clusters or logical isolation per env (prod/stage/dev). Production access is read-mostly; elevated privileges require break-glass workflow with time-bound approval.
- Governance and hygiene: Quotas and rate limits on saved objects, alert executions, and API keys per team. Data retention and ILM policies are centrally managed. Exports are logged; snapshots are encrypted and region-compliant.
- Operations and support: Platform team provides SLOs for Kibana availability and upgrades; teams own their content and alerts. Onboarding/offboarding automated (Spaces, roles, API keys). Incident response playbooks include access revocation.
- Rollout: Phased enablement starting with pilot teams, then org-wide. Success metrics: reduced observability tickets, time-to-dashboard, and MTTR; monitored for performance and cost.

We will containerize all production services with Docker using multi-stage builds and BuildKit for small, reproducible images. Base images will be minimal (distroless preferred; Alpine when shell/tools are required), run as a non-root USER, drop Linux capabilities, enable read-only root filesystem with writable tmpfs only where needed, and exclude package managers, compilers, and SSH.

Images will embed a VERSION file and labels (org.opencontainers.image.*) and be tagged with immutable CI-generated tags: <semver>-<gitsha>, plus a major/minor convenience tag. latest will not be used in production. Builds will be deterministic with lockfiles and pinned base image digests. CI will produce an SBOM and provenance attestation, scan images for vulnerabilities, and push to the private registry with retention and signature verification enabled.

Configuration will be injected at runtime via environment variables and mounted secrets; secrets will never be baked into images. Certificates, keys, and tokens will come from the secrets manager or orchestrator secret store. Healthchecks will be defined in Dockerfiles and deployment manifests.

Logging will go to stdout/stderr in JSON; metrics/tracing will be enabled via environment/config and exported through sidecars or node agents. Resource requests/limits will be set per service. Only necessary ports will be exposed; services will be isolated on private bridge networks, with TLS termination handled by the ingress/reverse proxy.

Orchestration: Kubernetes for multi-node environments; Docker Compose v2 only for single-host or ephemeral deployments. Deployments will use rolling updates with readiness/liveness probes and zero-downtime settings.

Operational hygiene: weekly base-image refresh and rebuilds; automated rebuilds on CVE advisories; periodic image pruning; registry access via least-privilege tokens. Continuous compliance will block promotion on critical vulnerabilities.

## Decision
We standardize the documentation structure for all architectural and design patterns to ensure consistency, discoverability, and reuse. All pattern documents must follow the template below, in the given order, with Required and Optional sections as indicated.

Required:
- Name: Canonical, imperative form; unique within repository.
- Intent: One-sentence purpose of the pattern.
- Context: When/where the pattern applies.
- Problem: The core problem the pattern addresses.
- Forces: Key trade-offs and constraints shaping the solution.
- Solution: The essence of the pattern; how it resolves the forces.
- Structure: High-level components and relationships (diagram encouraged).
- Participants & Responsibilities: Each role/component and its duties.
- Dynamics: Typical interactions/sequence flows.
- Consequences: Benefits, liabilities, and trade-offs.
- Applicability: Clear criteria for when to use/avoid.
- Implementation Notes: Key steps, pitfalls, variations in implementation.
- Example: Minimal, concrete example (code or architecture).
- Known Uses: References to real systems/projects.
- Related Patterns: Synergies, alternatives, and incompatibilities.
- References: Sources and further reading.
- Status & Version: Draft/Proposed/Accepted/Deprecated and semantic version.

Optional:
- Variants: Recognized subtypes with distinctions.
- Security/Privacy Considerations.
- Performance Considerations.
- Operational Concerns: Observability, deployment, rollback.
- Compliance/Regulatory Considerations.

Formatting and governance:
- Use consistent headings; keep sections concise.
- Embed diagrams as text-linked assets under docs/patterns/<name>/.
- Cross-link related patterns via stable IDs.
- PR review requires all Required sections completed and consequences balanced (at least one liability).

## Decision
Adopt Vega-Lite as the standard visualization language for the product and internal analytics, with the following conventions and scope:

- Primary grammar: Vega-Lite (v5+) for all declarative charts, dashboards, and report visuals.
- Language bindings:
  - Web: vega-lite + vega-embed.
  - Python: Altair (pinned to versions compatible with selected Vega-Lite).
  - R: vegawidget (matching Vega-Lite version).
- Theming and consistency: A shared JSON theme (colors, typography, gridlines, number/date formats, accessibility contrast) will be versioned in the design system and applied across all bindings.
- Interactivity: Use Vega-Lite built-in interactions (selection, tooltip, zoom/pan) for standard needs. For advanced interactions not expressible in Vega-Lite, escalate to Vega specifications; custom D3 is allowed only by exception.
- 3D and heavy WebGL: Not in scope for Vega-Lite. When 3D or high-frequency streaming requires it, use Plotly or deck.gl by approved exception; document deviations and provide a Vega-Lite fallback where feasible.
- Export/embedding: All visuals must support PNG/SVG export and JSON spec persistence. Dashboards will embed specs via vega-embed with runtime data bindings.
- Data model: Input data must be tidy/tabular. Data transformations should prefer Vega-Lite transforms; heavy ETL belongs upstream.
- Accessibility and i18n: Enable ARIA annotations, provide descriptive titles, and respect locale-aware formats via the shared theme.
- Governance: Version-lock Vega-Lite and bindings per release; changes require review by the Visualization Guild and migration notes.
- Deprecations: New work should not use raw D3, Matplotlib-only, or ad-hoc charting libraries unless approved; existing legacy charts migrate opportunistically.

We will locate the mymove repository outside of the standard GOPATH and standardize on Go Modules for dependency management and builds.

- Require Go 1.18+ with modules enabled (GO111MODULE=on or default behavior).
- Retain the canonical module path github.com/transcom/mymove; imports remain unchanged.
- Use go mod (go.mod/go.sum) as the single source of dependency versions; prohibit GOPATH-based resolution.
- Update local dev workflow to clone mymove into any directory outside GOPATH; no GOPATH configuration is required for builds or tests.
- Update Makefiles, scripts, and CI to use module-aware commands:
  - go build ./...
  - go test ./...
  - go run ./cmd/...
  - go install ./cmd/...
- Pin toolchain and tools via:
  - go toolchain directive (if applicable) and/or asdf/Volta-like pinning in CI.
  - go install with versioned module paths for developer tools.
- Enable reproducible builds by relying on go.sum; optionally vendor with go mod vendor if CI or deployment environments require vendoring.
- Remove any GOPATH-specific assumptions from code generation, linters, and packaging; update paths in codegen and scripts to be module-relative.
- Block merges that reintroduce GOPATH dependencies via CI checks (e.g., verify go.mod/go.sum tidy, module mode).
- Update onboarding and docs to reflect module-based setup and non-GOPATH project location.

## Decision

We adopt a pragmatic testing philosophy centered on the Testing Pyramid to maximize feedback speed, reliability, and maintainability.

- Emphasis and distribution:
  - Unit tests (~70%): very fast, deterministic, isolated from external systems; validate behavior and edge cases.
  - Integration/contract tests (~20%): exercise module boundaries and real adapters (DB, message bus, HTTP) using ephemeral, containerized dependencies; include consumer/provider contract tests for inter-service APIs.
  - End-to-end tests (~10%): minimal, critical user journeys only; smoke-level in CI on each PR, fuller suites nightly; synthetic monitoring for prod-critical paths.

- Practices:
  - Prefer TDD for core logic; otherwise, tests are required with each change.
  - Tests must be hermetic, parallelizable, and order-independent; failures block merges.
  - Use dependency injection and test doubles for units; avoid over-mocking external libraries’ internals.
  - Property-based tests for pure domain logic and complex invariants; golden files only when outputs are stable and reviewed.

- Quality gates:
  - Code coverage targets: module unit tests ≥80%, overall ≥60%; coverage informs but does not replace review.
  - Mutation testing for core domain modules with a baseline score ≥60% (raised over time).
  - Flaky tests: quarantine within 24 hours with an issue opened; fix or delete within one sprint.

- Test data and environments:
  - Use factories/builders; prohibit shared mutable fixtures.
  - Ephemeral test environments via containers; no reliance on external shared services.
  - For realistic datasets, use anonymized snapshots with schema/versioned migrations.

- Non-functional testing:
  - Baseline performance tests on critical flows with thresholds enforced in CI.
  - Security: SAST on each PR, DAST and dependency scanning nightly.

- Ownership and conventions:
  - Tests live with the code and are part of the definition of done.
  - Clear naming and Given-When-Then structure; failures must be actionable and fast to diagnose.

## Decision

Adopt a consistent, resource-oriented URI design for all public HTTP APIs with the following conventions:
- Scheme and authority: HTTPS is mandatory; no mixed content or protocol-relative URIs.
- Versioning: Use a major version segment as the first path element (e.g., /v1). Breaking changes require incrementing the version. Minor, backward-compatible changes do not change the version.
- Resource modeling: Use plural, lowercase, kebab-case nouns (e.g., /v1/user-accounts). Standard patterns: /v1/{resources}, /v1/{resources}/{id}, and shallow sub-resources when necessary (e.g., /v1/orders/{id}/items). Avoid verbs in paths; actions map to HTTP methods or, when unavoidable, to /v1/{resources}/{id}:action.
- Identifiers: Use opaque, stable IDs (UUIDs or server-assigned IDs). Optional human-readable slugs may be appended but must not be required for lookup.
- Trailing slashes and extensions: No trailing slash in canonical URIs; redirect 301 from variants. Do not use file extensions for content negotiation.
- Query parameters: Use query for filtering, pagination, and sorting only.
  - Filtering: filter[field]=value (repeatable), with exact semantics documented per field.
  - Sorting: sort=field or sort=-field for descending; multiple fields comma-separated.
  - Pagination: cursor-based by default: page[after]=token, page[limit]=n. Offset pagination may be supported for small datasets: page[offset], page[limit].
- Relationships: Prefer linking via ids and provide discoverable links where appropriate; avoid deep nesting beyond one level.
- Encoding and casing: URIs are lowercase; words separated by hyphens. Percent-encode reserved characters per RFC 3986. Normalize Unicode to NFC.
- Stability and deprecation: URIs are stable once published. Deprecated endpoints return Deprecation headers and Sunset timelines before removal; removed endpoints return 410 Gone.
- Documentation: Publish URI templates (RFC 6570) and examples in OpenAPI, including all query parameters and constraints.

Adopt Flyway as the standard database migration tool, executed exclusively via a pinned Docker image to ensure consistent, reproducible migrations across all environments. All schema changes will be captured as immutable, forward-only Flyway migrations stored in the repository under db/migrations, using versioned (Vxxx__description.sql) and repeatable (R__description.sql) scripts. Flyway configuration (URL, user, schema, locations, placeholders) will be supplied via environment variables and .env files, never hard-coded; secrets will be sourced from the CI/CD secret store.

We will enable baseline-on-migrate for existing databases, require transactional migrations where supported, and rely on Flyway’s checksum validation to detect drift. No down/undo migrations will be supported; rollbacks will be handled through new forward migrations. Migrations must be idempotent where applicable and tested locally against a disposable containerized database before merge.

CI/CD will run flyway validate and flyway migrate on every deployment, using the same Docker image tag as local development. Each environment maintains a dedicated schema history table; per-environment configuration will control placeholders and target versions. Release pipelines will lock migrations (single runner) to avoid concurrency conflicts. Database permissions will be least-privilege: a migration role with DDL rights; applications use separate limited roles.

Image versions will be semver-pinned and updated via dependabot/renovate. Migration ordering is strictly by version, and code changes that depend on schema changes must be coordinated to ensure safe, incremental deploys (expand/contract pattern). Documentation and templates for new migrations will be included with linting and pre-commit validation to enforce naming and style conventions.

We will adopt a serverless-first backend on AWS for Farmacy Food to maximize elasticity, reduce operational overhead, and align costs with demand. The primary runtime will use AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway (HTTP APIs) for all external APIs and internal service endpoints. Core data will use Amazon DynamoDB as the default datastore; Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 will be used selectively for strongly relational workloads and transactions. Object storage and static content will reside in Amazon S3, with Amazon CloudFront for CDN. Authentication and authorization will use Amazon Cognito with JWT validation at API Gateway; fine-grained access will be enforced via IAM and application-level checks.

Asynchronous and event-driven processing will be implemented using Amazon EventBridge, SQS, and SNS; workflows and long-running orchestrations will use AWS Step Functions. For tasks exceeding Lambda limits or requiring sustained CPU/memory, we will use AWS Fargate on ECS as an adjunct pattern. Secrets and encryption will use AWS Secrets Manager and KMS. Observability will leverage CloudWatch Logs/Metrics, AWS X-Ray tracing, and structured logging; error budgets and SLOs will be defined per critical API. Infrastructure will be provisioned via Terraform, with CI/CD through AWS CodePipeline/CodeBuild or GitHub Actions; environments will be isolated per account and VPC. Cold starts will be mitigated via Provisioned Concurrency on latency-sensitive paths.

Compliance and data protection will be enforced through least-privilege IAM, VPC endpoints, private subnets, field-level encryption, and data retention policies. Multi-AZ is mandatory; multi-region active-passive will be adopted for critical services with defined RTO/RPO. Local development will use AWS SAM for parity.

We will represent and encode all audio positions and durations as integer milliseconds.

- Scope: Applies to all APIs, events, persisted records, messaging, and configuration that reference audio offsets, cue points, segment bounds, and durations.
- Type: 64-bit signed integer (int64). Durations must be ≥ 0; positions are ≥ 0 relative to media start (no wall-clock time). No floating-point types.
- Units and naming: Fields must be in milliseconds and use the suffix “Ms” (e.g., startMs, endMs, durationMs, positionMs).
- Serialization:
  - JSON/REST: integers (no decimals). Query params accept integer ms only.
  - Binary: little-endian int64.
  - DB: BIGINT columns; indexes maintain integer ordering.
- Conversion rules:
  - From seconds or floats: round to nearest millisecond, ties to even.
  - From samples: ms = roundToEven(samples / sampleRate * 1000).
  - From micro/nanoseconds: divide and round to nearest millisecond, ties to even.
  - UI may display finer precision, but persisted/API values remain integer ms.
- Rounding policy: When truncation is required for bounds, prefer floor for startMs and ceil for endMs to avoid data loss in ranges; otherwise use nearest, ties to even.
- Validation: Reject non-integer or sub-millisecond inputs; reject negative durations; ensure endMs ≥ startMs.
- Backward compatibility: Existing second-based fields are deprecated and will be maintained via adapters that convert to ms; new fields use ms and suffix conventions.
- Testing: Add property-based tests to ensure monotonicity of ranges after conversions and idempotence across encode/decode cycles.

## Decision
Adopt active, synthetic uptime measurement for internal Kubernetes services using an in-cluster probe service. Deploy a standardized probe (HTTP/HTTPS/TCP/GRPC) per environment that executes periodic health checks against Service DNS names (ClusterIP) and, where needed, synthetic workflows against well-defined health endpoints. Publish probe results as Prometheus metrics; visualize and report in Grafana; alert via Alertmanager against defined SLIs/SLOs.

Define uptime as the percentage of successful probe checks over rolling windows (e.g., 99.9% monthly), with success criteria per service (status codes, latency thresholds, response payload guards). Run probes from multiple nodes/zones to reduce single-point bias; record location labels for aggregation. Configure check frequency, timeouts, and retries centrally; version and manage probe configs as code. Tag all probes with service, team, environment, and compliance labels to enable ownership and auditability.

Enforce security and compliance by:
- Restricting probe namespaces and RBAC to read-only networking needs.
- Using mTLS/TLS for probe-to-service traffic where applicable; no credentials or PII in probes.
- Applying NetworkPolicies to limit egress to target services only.
- Logging and retaining probe results per compliance retention policies.

Do not rely solely on pod readiness/liveness or mesh telemetry for uptime; keep those as internal health signals. Roll out incrementally, starting with Tier-1 services, and integrate SLO reporting into the standard operational dashboards and on-call alerting.

We will adopt “GADR” as the canonical acronym for our decision record format, expanded as “Generalized Architectural Decision Record.” The plural form will be “GADRs.” This naming will be used consistently across documentation, repositories, templates, schemas, code, CLI tools, and communications.

- Canonical term and expansion: “GADR — Generalized Architectural Decision Record”; plural “GADRs.”
- File naming: gadr-<sequence>-<slug>.md (e.g., gadr-0001-naming.md).
- Repository structure: docs/gadrs/ as the default directory; legacy adr/ or adrs/ directories will be maintained as symlinks or pointers until migration completes.
- Front matter/metadata: type: gadr; id: <sequence>; status: <status>; supersedes/superseded_by; tags: [gadr].
- Template filename: gadr-template.md; snippet keys prefixed with gadr_.
- CLI/tooling: commands and flags use gadr (e.g., gadr new, --gadr-dir). Provide aliases for adr for one release cycle with deprecation warnings.
- Schema: JSON/YAML schema renamed to gadr.schema.[json|yaml]; versioned with semver, starting at 1.0.0 for the renamed schema.
- Links and references: update internal links, badges, and status dashboards to use “GADR/GADRs.”
- Communications: use GADR in commit messages, PR titles, and release notes.
- Capitalization: all-caps acronym “GADR” in prose; lowercase in filenames.
- Timeline: implement immediately for new records; migrate existing ADRs to GADRs within two sprints; maintain redirects and aliases for one minor release.
- Backward compatibility: preserve reading of existing ADR filenames/metadata; emit warnings guiding migration.

We will introduce dedicated, denormalized rollup summary tables to serve dashboard workloads, replacing on-the-fly aggregations against raw/normalized fact tables. Each dashboard’s core metrics will be materialized as purpose-built rollups at agreed grain(s) (e.g., daily, hourly) keyed by the dimensions actually used in filters and breakdowns. These rollups will live in the analytics schema of the data warehouse and be the sole data source for production dashboards.

Implementation details:
- Materialization: physical tables (not views) for predictable latency and cost, built with dbt incremental models (or equivalent) that produce idempotent upserts.
- Refresh policy: scheduled every 15 minutes (configurable per dataset) with a sliding-window reaggregation for late-arriving data (e.g., last 3 days). Full backfills run on demand via parameterized jobs.
- Partitioning and clustering: partition by event_date (or metric date) and cluster by high-cardinality filter dimensions to optimize scan efficiency.
- Naming and contracts: standardized naming (dash_<domain>_<metric>_rollup_<grain>), with documented column contracts and metric definitions versioned alongside the transformation code.
- Governance and access: read-only access for BI tools and analysts; write restricted to ETL service accounts. PII is excluded or tokenized at the rollup layer as required.
- Quality and monitoring: data tests on row counts, freshness, and metric reconciliation to source facts; observability includes SLAs/SLOs for freshness and alerting on drift or load failures.
- Change management: backward-compatible changes favored; breaking schema changes require versioned tables and deprecation windows.
- Cost controls: pruning unused columns/dimensions, retention policy aligned to dashboard time horizons (e.g., 18 months), and periodic compaction.
- Scope: initial rollout covers top dashboards with stable definitions; subsequent metrics onboarded via a documented template.

This decision prioritizes dashboard performance, consistency of metric definitions, and operational reliability while containing warehouse costs.

We will migrate the existing Angular application to the current Angular LTS in an incremental, low-risk manner using a strangler-fig approach. The target architecture adopts Angular’s standalone APIs (no NgModules), the new built-in control flow, and Signals for component state while retaining RxJS in data/services layers. We will standardize on strict TypeScript, ESLint, and Angular CLI with the Vite-based builder; Jest and Cypress remain for unit and E2E tests. SSR with hydration (Angular Universal) will be enabled for SEO-critical/public routes; internal-only routes remain CSR initially. We will keep zone.js during migration and evaluate zoneless change detection after feature parity is achieved.

Migration will be done in-place in the monorepo with feature-flagged, route-by-route replacement and route-level code-splitting. New and migrated features are built as standalone components and lazy-loaded routes. A compatibility layer (adapters/facades) will isolate legacy utilities, UI libraries, and APIs, allowing piecemeal replacement without breaking consumers. State management continues with NgRx where already used; new features favor lighter patterns (Signals + component stores), with a medium-term plan to consolidate on a single approach once migration stabilizes.

Build and runtime baselines: Node 20+, TS 5+, Angular latest LTS, RxJS per Angular compatibility, SCSS for styles, CSS variables for theming, and stricter ESLint/TS configs. CI/CD will enforce dual-builds (legacy + migrated) until the cutover milestone, with contract tests on shared APIs and visual regression for critical flows. Third-party libraries without Angular LTS support will be replaced or wrapped.

Success criteria: zero regression on top user journeys, performance parity or better (TTI/LCP), and deprecation of legacy Angular patterns (NgModules-first, ViewEngine-era APIs). A final hard cutover removes compatibility layers and zone-dependent shims after all critical routes are migrated.

We will adopt Ruby on Rails (Rails 7.x, Ruby 3.x) as the primary web application framework to build a monolithic application delivering both server-rendered HTML and JSON APIs. We will leverage Rails’ conventions, Active Record with PostgreSQL, Hotwire (Turbo/Stimulus) for interactive UX without a SPA, and Sidekiq with Redis for background processing. Caching (fragment, Russian-doll, Redis), Action Mailer, and Active Storage will be used where applicable.

Scope:
- Backend: Rails monolith exposing REST/JSON endpoints and server-rendered views.
- Frontend: Server-side rendering with progressive enhancement via Hotwire; defer SPA frameworks unless requirements change.
- Data: PostgreSQL as primary datastore; read replicas introduced as needed.
- Ops: Containerized deployment; environments standardized (12-factor), with CI/CD and observability baked in.

Rationale:
- Maximize delivery speed and maintainability via convention-over-configuration and a mature ecosystem.
- Align with current team expertise and hiring market.
- Provide a cohesive platform with batteries-included security, i18n, and admin tooling.

Trade-offs and mitigations:
- Ruby performance concerns mitigated by caching, background jobs, and database/index tuning; revisit hotspots in native extensions or services if needed.
- Real-time and streaming handled via Action Cable/AnyCable; escalate to specialized services if load requires.
- Avoid premature microservices; plan clean modular boundaries to enable later extraction.

Revisit if: sustained high throughput exceeds scaling targets, complex client-side interactivity mandates a SPA, or organizational needs favor service decomposition.

We will use GOV.UK Verify as the primary mechanism for claimant identity assurance. The service will integrate with the Verify Hub using SAML 2.0 and the Matching Service Adapter to obtain IAL2/LOA2-equivalent assurance from certified identity providers. We will not build or operate our own identity proofing; instead we will consume verified attributes (name, DOB, address, evidence confidence) and perform local matching against our claimant records. We will store only the minimum attributes required for matching and audit, never retaining source evidence or copies of identity documents.

User journeys will default to Verify for eligible users, with clear guidance and retry support. A mandated fallback path will be provided for users who cannot complete Verify (e.g., no suitable documents, failed proofing), consisting of assisted digital and manual verification operated by our caseworkers under documented controls. High-risk events (e.g., change of bank details) will trigger step-up re-verification using Verify where feasible.

We will enforce one account per verified identity, maintain audit trails of assertions and decisions, and implement monitoring for assertion validity and expiry. The integration will be abstracted behind an identity assurance adapter to allow future replacement if Verify changes or is withdrawn, with a defined migration plan to an alternative government-backed identity service.

Adopt configurable, secure command echoing for the CLI/REPL and batch modes.

- Default behavior:
  - Interactive TTY: do not echo entered commands to stdout to avoid clutter; show prompts only.
  - Non-interactive (pipelines, scripts, CI, when stdin is not a TTY, or when executing script files): echo each command prior to execution to stdout and to the application log for auditability.
- Controls and precedence:
  - Immediate flags: --echo / --no-echo and --verbose (enables echo) / --quiet (disables echo).
  - Environment variable: CLI_ECHO=1|0.
  - Config: cli.echo=true|false.
  - Precedence: flag > env > config > default.
- Format:
  - Prefix echoed commands with a stable marker (e.g., “+ ”) to aid parsing; optional timestamps enabled by --timestamps or log config.
  - Echo exactly the command as received after expansion/resolution, with normalized whitespace; do not localize.
- Security:
  - Never echo interactive secret prompts (password/passphrase).
  - Redact sensitive values in echoed commands and logs using parameter metadata (secret=true), known secret key patterns (e.g., token, password, secret, key), and env var allow/block lists; replace values with [REDACTED].
- Logging:
  - Emit at INFO level to logs; respect --quiet to suppress console echo while still logging if log level permits.
- Implementation:
  - Middleware layer before execution; zero functional side effects; comprehensive tests for TTY detection, precedence, and redaction.

- Adopt PostgreSQL as the system of record.
- Model core domain in a normalized relational schema (3NF); use JSONB columns only for well-scoped, schematized extensions and sparse attributes, never for core relationships.
- Use ULID primary keys (text) for global uniqueness and time-sortability; expose only opaque IDs externally.
- Enforce referential integrity with foreign keys; use ON UPDATE RESTRICT, ON DELETE RESTRICT by default; explicit cascading only where denormalization safety is proven.
- Implement soft deletes via deleted_at (timestamptz) and status fields; hard deletes are disallowed except for retention/SAR workflows with audit.
- Include created_at, updated_at (timestamptz, UTC) on all mutable tables; update timestamps in the database, not the application.
- Multi-tenancy via single database, tenant_id on all domain tables, and PostgreSQL Row-Level Security; all unique constraints are composite with tenant_id unless globally unique by design.
- PII/secret fields use column-level encryption (pgcrypto or extension) with keys managed via KMS; apply strict data classification and mask in non-prod.
- Constrain enumerations via lookup tables or PostgreSQL ENUMs only when change frequency is low; prefer lookup tables for flexibility.
- Define stable, semantic column and table naming (snake_case, singular nouns); avoid abbreviations; use CHECK constraints for domain invariants.
- Index by primary, foreign keys, and high-selectivity filters; maintain covering/partial indexes per query patterns; review with EXPLAIN.
- Provide CDC via outbox pattern and logical replication; no event sourcing for primary state.
- Reads are optimized with materialized views for reporting; refresh policies are explicit.
- Database migrations are forward-only, reversible scripts via a migration tool; changes must be backward compatible across one deployment window.
- Access layer uses a type-safe ORM/query builder; all writes pass through a domain service layer enforcing invariants.

We will manage project versioning natively in CMake using Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).

- The single source of truth for the version is set in the top-level CMakeLists.txt via project(<name> VERSION X.Y.Z). The version may be overridden in automated builds via -DPROJECT_VERSION=X.Y.Z, but not mutated during configure/generate.
- A generated header (e.g., <project>/version.hpp) is produced with configure_file and contains string and numeric macros for MAJOR, MINOR, PATCH, and the full version.
- Shared libraries will set VERSION to X.Y.Z and SOVERSION to MAJOR to align ABI expectations.
- Package discovery support will be versioned: we generate and install <Project>Config.cmake and <Project>ConfigVersion.cmake using CMakePackageConfigHelpers with exact/same-major compatibility.
- Packaging (CPack) will consume the CMake project version by setting CPACK_PACKAGE_VERSION[_MAJOR|_MINOR|_PATCH], ensuring consistent artifact naming.
- CLI binaries expose --version using the generated header. The version is embedded in about/help output and manifests where applicable.
- Git metadata is not a build-time dependency. Optionally, a separate release script can synchronize project(VERSION) with annotated Git tags; CI enforces that project(VERSION) matches the release tag.
- Pre-release/build metadata may be appended via an optional PROJECT_VERSION_SUFFIX cache variable that affects strings and packaging names but does not change numeric MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH or SOVERSION.
- Any module or plugin versions derive from the root project version unless explicitly set.

Adopt PostgreSQL as the primary relational database for the application, provisioned as a managed cloud service with automated backups, point-in-time recovery, encryption at rest and in transit, and built-in monitoring. Operate a single writable primary with at least one read replica to offload read-heavy workflows and support zero-downtime maintenance; use a managed connection pooler for efficient utilization. Standardize on UTC for all timestamps, UUIDv4 for primary keys, and strict foreign-key constraints; use soft deletes where business recovery is needed, otherwise hard deletes. Manage schema changes via versioned, idempotent migrations executed through CI/CD before application rollout, with backward-compatible changes favored to enable rolling deployments.

Adopt a schema-per-bounded-context approach within a single cluster to balance isolation and operational simplicity; cross-context access occurs only via application/service layers, not cross-schema joins in business logic. For multi-tenancy, use tenant_id scoping at the table level with row-level security for strong isolation; reserve the option to move strategic tenants to dedicated schemas or instances if required.

Set performance baselines with appropriate indexes, query timeouts, and statement-level logging for slow queries; require query plans for high-risk queries. Enforce size quotas and archival strategies for large tables via partitioning on time-based keys where applicable. Secrets (credentials, rotation) are managed via the platform’s secret manager; credentials are rotated at least quarterly and on personnel changes.

Backups run daily full with continuous WAL archiving; verify restores monthly in a non-production environment with documented runbooks. Establish RPO ≤ 15 minutes and RTO ≤ 1 hour for critical data. Enable audit logging for schema changes and privileged access; retain logs per compliance requirements. Non-relational needs (e.g., caching, search, analytics) will use dedicated services (Redis, OpenSearch/warehouse) to avoid overloading the OLTP store.

## Decision
We will prioritize integration tests over command-level (unit) tests to validate system behavior at the application boundary. Integration tests will exercise command execution through the application’s public interfaces against real infrastructure where feasible (e.g., database via Testcontainers or embedded engine), mocking only truly external third-party services. Command-level tests will be added selectively for complex, algorithmic domain logic that benefits from isolated, fast feedback and for branches that are hard or impractical to trigger via integration.

Practically:
- Integration tests will cover all commands’ happy paths, key failure modes, and contract/serialization concerns. Every new or modified command requires corresponding integration coverage.
- Command tests are optional and targeted; avoid duplicating scenarios already covered by integration tests. Prefer pure-domain testing without infrastructure.
- Aim for a test distribution of approximately 60–80% integration and 20–40% command by count, with coverage gates applied to domain/application layers (not infrastructure glue). We will not pursue 100% unit coverage if integration tests already assert observable behavior.
- Keep integration suites reliable and parallelizable using isolated data fixtures/builders, transactional rollbacks, and deterministic seeds. Flaky tests are treated as defects.
- CI enforces: (a) passing integration suite as the primary quality gate, (b) minimum coverage threshold focused on domain/application code, and (c) requirement that behavior changes are accompanied by updated integration tests.
- Periodically remove or refactor brittle command tests that merely mirror integration scenarios to reduce maintenance noise and encourage behavior-first testing.

Adopt ephemeral, reproducible Kubernetes end-to-end testing using KinD for default execution in CI and local development, with optional nightly runs on a managed cluster (e.g., GKE Autopilot) for scale and CNI variance. Each CI job provisions an isolated KinD cluster, installs the system under test via Helm (preferred) or Kustomize, and executes tests, then tears down the cluster.

Implement tests primarily in Go using Ginkgo/Gomega and kubetest2 as the runner to orchestrate cluster lifecycle, image loading, and parallelization. Complement behavioral tests with KUTTL for declarative manifest validation and conformance checks. Build images in CI, push to a local registry, and load into KinD; pin Kubernetes minor versions and run a matrix against n-2 versions.

Standardize readiness and stability via kubectl wait, PodDisruptionBudgets, and health probes; enforce per-spec timeouts and bounded retries to mitigate flakes. Isolate with unique test namespaces and service accounts; grant minimal RBAC scoped to the namespace. Collect and publish diagnostics (pod logs, events, describe output, node logs) on failure as CI artifacts.

Make the KinD-based e2e workflow a required pre-merge gate; schedule nightly managed-cluster suites for scale, upgrade, and network policy scenarios. Ensure deterministic cleanup (namespace finalizer removal if needed) and full cluster teardown. Version the test harness alongside application code and run it on every PR and main branch build.

## Decision

We will discontinue shipping monolithic “Wikibase Bundle” tarballs and move to officially supported, versioned, container-based distributions. The project will provide:

- Maintained Docker images for core components (Wikibase Repo, Wikibase Client, MediaWiki, Job runners, Search, and Query Service), built from a unified release pipeline with signed, SBOM-attested artifacts.
- Two deployment profiles:
  - QuickStart (Docker Compose) for local evaluation and minimal setups.
  - Production (Helm chart) for Kubernetes-based deployments with configurable persistence, scaling, and observability.
- A clearly defined versioning and compatibility policy:
  - Semantic versioning for images and charts.
  - A published compatibility matrix across MediaWiki, Wikibase, database/search/query backends, and extensions.
  - Coordinated “bundle” releases as immutable manifests (Compose file and Helm chart versions) referencing exact image digests.
- Automated integration test suites validating each coordinated release across both profiles, including upgrade paths.
- A deprecation plan for legacy bundles:
  - No new tarball releases effective immediately.
  - Security fixes for the last supported tarball release for 6 months.
  - Migration guides and tooling to move from tarballs to containers, covering data, configuration, and operational practices.
- Opinionated defaults for production (TLS termination, backups, metrics/log shipping, resource requests/limits) while retaining escape hatches for advanced operators.
- Long-term support cadence: one LTS “bundle manifest” per year with 18 months of support; regular releases every 6–8 weeks.

This decision standardizes distribution, improves security and reproducibility, simplifies upgrades, and aligns with community deployment practices while preserving an easy on-ramp via QuickStart.

Adopt an idempotent, chunked batch-loading pattern that stages immutable, partitioned files in object storage and performs atomic, set-based upserts into the target store. Source data will be written as columnar files (Parquet) partitioned by load_date/source and bundled via manifests to guarantee completeness. The orchestrator will execute time-boxed batches (e.g., hourly), with configurable chunk sizes (~100MB files; ≤1M rows per chunk) to balance throughput and memory.

Loading will use database-native bulk mechanisms (e.g., COPY) into a transient staging schema, followed by a single MERGE/UPSERT into target tables to ensure atomicity and minimize locks. Idempotency is enforced via deterministic deduplication keys (business key + load_window_id) and optimistic upserts; duplicate detection and late arrivals are handled in staging before the MERGE. Partial failures trigger retry at the file/chunk level; non-recoverable records are shunted to a dead-letter area with per-record error context.

Schema evolution is constrained to additive changes; compatibility checks run pre-load, with automatic column backfilling for nullable additions. Data quality gates (row counts, checksums, referential checks) run pre/post-load; thresholds block promotion when violated. Backfills run through the same pathway with throttling and partition pruning to avoid contention with incremental loads.

Operationally, the loader enforces concurrency limits and backpressure, prefers off-peak windows, and supports exactly-once semantics through manifest commits and transactional MERGE. Observability includes end-to-end lineage, per-batch metrics (latency, throughput, error rate), and alerting. Configuration (chunking, schedules, quality thresholds) is externalized for environment-specific tuning.

We will adopt a schema-first, versioned Entity Metadata model that is authoritative across services.

- Representation: JSON Schema (YAML-authorable) for each entity type, with a constrained profile (naming, types, required, enums, references) and extension fields for platform concerns (PII flags, retention, indexing, search, ownership, lifecycle).
- Source of truth: Schemas live in a dedicated git repo with mandatory review, semantic versioning, and changelog. Changes are proposed via PRs and validated by CI (linting, compatibility checks, documentation generation).
- Publication and discovery: A Metadata Registry service exposes read-only APIs (REST + GraphQL) for schema retrieval, querying, and diffing; schemas are also packaged and version-pinned in application builds.
- Generation and validation: Tooling generates language-specific types, serializers, DB mappings, and API contracts from schemas. Runtime validators enforce metadata constraints at boundaries (ingress/egress, ETL, CDC). Build-time validation gates deployments.
- Evolution rules: Only additive, backward-compatible changes allowed in minor versions; breaking changes require major version and migration plan with dual-read/write or transformers. Deprecation windows are encoded in schema extensions.
- Relationships: Cross-entity references are explicit via typed foreign keys/URIs with cardinality; referential integrity policies (required/optional, cascade) are declared in metadata and enforced where supported.
- Storage/indexing: Index and partition hints in metadata drive physical schema and search indexing (RDBMS/NoSQL/Elastic), but do not leak storage-specific details into domain models.
- Security and governance: Sensitivity classification, access scopes, and retention policies are encoded in metadata and enforced by policy engines and data pipelines.
- Performance: Clients cache schemas with ETags and TTL; the registry is horizontally scalable and replicated.
- Ownership: Every entity schema must declare an owning team and on-call rotation; changes require owner approval.

We will introduce a first-class “BeforeActionVariables” construct that is computed deterministically during the planning phase and finalized immediately prior to action execution. These variables form an immutable, namespaced snapshot available read-only to the action and all pre-execution hooks. Resolution sources and precedence are: (1) system defaults, (2) environment/config, (3) request inputs, (4) derived/computed values, and (5) approved overrides. Variables must conform to a declared JSON schema per action; values are validated, normalized, and redacted according to sensitivity classifications before being persisted or logged. Resolution supports templating with explicit dependency ordering; cycles cause a hard failure. Secrets are fetched via registered secret providers at resolution time and injected as handles/tokens, not raw values, unless the action explicitly requires materialization. The snapshot is versioned and recorded for observability and reproducibility; it is included in audit logs with sensitive fields masked. At runtime, mutation is disallowed; attempts to change before-action variables yield errors and must use an explicit “working context” for ephemeral computation. Concurrency is supported via copy-on-write snapshots per action instance. Backward compatibility is maintained by providing default schemas and a migration path for legacy ad-hoc parameter passing. Errors in resolution fail fast and surface with actionable diagnostics.

- Implement a dedicated Key Pair Utility as a shared library and CLI that standardizes asymmetric key lifecycle: generate, import, export (public only), rotate, retire, sign/verify, encrypt/decrypt (where applicable), fingerprint, and metadata management.
- Adopt modern algorithms by default: Ed25519 for digital signatures and X25519 for key agreement; permit RSA-2048/3072 only for backward compatibility and ECDSA P-256 where required by external integrations. Weak/legacy algorithms (e.g., RSA < 2048) are disallowed.
- Enforce centralized, secure key storage: production private keys are generated and stored in cloud KMS/HSM with non-exportable protections; staging uses KMS export-disabled where possible; local/dev allows exportable software keys gated by explicit non-prod flags.
- Provide uniform serialization formats: PKCS#8/PEM for private keys (non-prod only), SubjectPublicKeyInfo/PEM, SSH public key, and JWK for web/JWT use cases. All keys include stable key IDs (kid) with SHA-256 fingerprint (base64url).
- Define API surface: createKey(alg, usage, expiresAt), getPublicKey(kid, format), sign/verify, encrypt/decrypt/derive (as applicable), rotateKey(kid), retireKey(kid), importPublicKey, listKeys(filter), and resolveByFingerprint. All operations are idempotent and thread-safe.
- Establish rotation policy: default validity 12 months; rolling rotation with dual-publish/dual-verify during a configurable overlap window; automatic deprecation and scheduled retirement; emergency revocation supported.
- Implement strict access control and auditing: least-privilege IAM roles; every key operation is auditable with tamper-evident logs and correlation IDs. No plaintext private keys are logged or exported in prod.
- Ensure determinism only in non-prod: optional seed-based deterministic keys for tests; ephemeral keys for CI. No deterministic generation in prod.
- Provide migration utilities to import existing RSA/ECDSA keys into KMS (where allowed) and to publish corresponding public keys in required registries (e.g., JWKS endpoints).
- Enforce policy via configuration: allowed algorithms per environment, export rules, rotation intervals, and deprecation windows are centrally configured and validated at startup.

Adopt a canonical, read-only integration of EasyVista’s location_path as the single hierarchical location attribute for all downstream services. The authoritative source of truth remains EasyVista; our system will maintain a denormalized cache of location_path along with stable location IDs to ensure referential integrity and performant queries.

Key decisions:
- Representation: store location_path as a slash-delimited, UTF-8 string of decoded names (e.g., Country/Region/City/Site/Building/Floor/Room). Preserve original EasyVista casing and spacing; escape only embedded slashes using percent-encoding. Enforce a max length of 1024 chars.
- Identity: pair every location_path with EasyVista’s immutable location ID where available; when absent, generate a deterministic UUIDv5 from the full path. Use the ID as the primary key; location_path is an indexed attribute used for queries and display.
- Synchronization: implement an idempotent, incremental sync (hourly) that upserts locations, detects path changes (moves/renames), and propagates updates to dependent records via the stable ID. Maintain a change log for audit and rollbacks. Hard deletes in EasyVista are soft-deleted locally with tombstones for 90 days.
- Validation: reject malformed paths (empty segments, leading/trailing delimiters, unescaped slashes). Normalize duplicate whitespace. Enforce uniqueness on the tuple (tenant, location ID).
- Access and edit: location_path is read-only in our UI and APIs; edits must occur in EasyVista. Provide a resolver API to translate path↔ID and to list children/ancestors.
- Performance: create B-tree index on location_path and a materialized ancestors array for fast prefix/ancestor queries. Cache hot lookups with 15-minute TTL.
- Backward compatibility: maintain legacy location fields for one release with deprecation warnings; provide migration scripts and mapping reports.

Adopt GitHub as the identity provider using OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE. Register a GitHub OAuth App (not a GitHub App) with whitelisted redirect URIs per environment. The browser initiates the flow; the backend exchanges the code for tokens, validates state and PKCE verifier, and establishes an application session. Use minimal scopes: read:user and user:email; add read:org only when org/team gating is enabled. Do not request write scopes.

On first successful login, create or link a local account keyed by the immutable GitHub user ID; email is secondary and may change. Enforce one-to-one linking per local account. Store GitHub access tokens server-side only, encrypted at rest; never expose them to the client. Issue short-lived application JWTs (or server sessions) and refresh via secure HTTP-only cookies. Logout terminates the app session; we do not attempt to revoke GitHub tokens unless explicitly required.

Support both github.com and GitHub Enterprise Server via configuration of the authorize/token/userinfo endpoints. Validate email verification status when required by policy. Optional org/team access control is implemented by querying membership via the GitHub API using the granted scopes.

Implement CSRF protection (state), nonce, strict redirect URI matching, and error handling for denied/expired codes. Rate limit token exchanges and userinfo calls; implement retries with backoff. Log authentication events without sensitive data. Provide a break-glass local admin account for recovery. Regularly review scopes and rotate client secrets; rotate and revoke stored tokens on unlink.

Adopt AWS SQS as the durable, decoupled task queue and Apache Airflow as the scheduler/orchestrator for task execution. Producers will publish tasks to SQS; Airflow DAGs will consume from SQS via an SQS Sensor/Operator and dispatch work to task-specific operators. We will default to SQS Standard queues for high throughput; use SQS FIFO (with content-based deduplication) only where strict per-entity ordering is required. Each queue will be paired with a DLQ; redrive policy and maxReceiveCount will be tuned per task type.

Airflow will manage retries/backoff and idempotent task logic will ensure at-least-once delivery semantics are safe. Messages will include a stable idempotency key and a versioned payload schema. SQS visibility timeouts will exceed the worst-case task runtime with heartbeat/extension support to prevent premature re-delivery. Message retention will cover upstream outage scenarios.

Execution will scale by adjusting Airflow worker/executor capacity and parallelism; queue depth will drive autoscaling signals. Monitoring will include SQS metrics (ApproximateNumberOfMessages, AgeOfOldestMessage, DLQ inflow), Airflow DAG/task SLAs, and alerting on backlog growth or DLQ thresholds. Security will be enforced via IAM least-privilege policies, SSE-SQS encryption, KMS CMKs, and VPC endpoints for private access.

Failure handling: malformed or permanently failing messages route to DLQ with structured failure metadata and optional automated triage/replay tooling. Operational runbooks will cover replay from DLQ, message schema evolution, and capacity tuning. This design provides resilient, cost-effective, and observable asynchronous task execution with clear separation of concerns between queuing and orchestration.

## Decision

Adopt a two-tier testing strategy standardized on:
- Unit/integration tests: Vitest as the default test runner for all TypeScript/JavaScript packages, with the Testing Library family for UI/component tests. Vitest is selected for performance, Vite-native integration, TypeScript support, and Jest compatibility (expect/mocking APIs), enabling incremental migration from any existing Jest tests.
- End-to-end (E2E) and cross-browser tests: Playwright Test for browser automation, visual verification where appropriate, and API smoke checks. Playwright is selected for its reliability, parallelization, automatic waits, rich diagnostics (traces, videos), and first-class CI support.

Supporting policies and tooling:
- Network mocking: MSW (Mock Service Worker) for unit/integration/component tests to simulate HTTP/GraphQL consistently across browser and Node environments; avoid brittle global mocks.
- Test organization: Co-locate tests alongside source files (filename.spec.ts/tsx) for unit/component; place E2E under e2e/ with clear suite boundaries. Follow a test pyramid emphasizing unit > integration > E2E.
- Coverage: Enforce minimum thresholds (global: lines 80%, branches 70%, functions 80%) with per-package reporting; E2E excluded from coverage metrics.
- Determinism: Prohibit snapshot tests for dynamic content; allow targeted snapshots with review. Prefer explicit assertions. Disallow time- and locale-dependent flakiness via fixed clocks and test data.
- CI: Shard and parallelize Vitest and Playwright; enable retries for E2E (max 2) with trace-on-retry; publish HTML reports, videos, and traces as artifacts; fail builds on coverage regressions and flaky test quarantines.
- Developer workflow: Provide npm scripts (test, test:unit, test:watch, test:e2e, test:ci), pre-commit hooks for fast unit tests and lint, and templates for new tests.

This decision standardizes tooling, improves feedback speed, and supports maintainable, reliable tests across the codebase.

Adopt a two-layer read path composed of (1) transport/interface (API/Controller/GraphQL resolver) and (2) query layer (read services + repositories/projections) for all read-only use cases. The read path will bypass the domain/application layers to optimize latency, reduce complexity, and enable view-centric data retrieval, while the write path retains the full layered/domain-centric architecture.

Key implications and guardrails:
- Scope: Applies only to idempotent, side-effect-free operations. All writes, state transitions, and business invariants stay in the existing layered/domain path.
- Responsibilities: The read query layer may perform data composition, mapping to DTOs/view models, filtering, paging, sorting, authorization checks, input validation, and caching. It must not implement domain/business rules.
- Data sources: Prefer denormalized read models (projections/materialized views) where beneficial; fallback to read-optimized queries (no-tracking ORM or SQL) against replicas when feasible.
- Caching: Allow per-endpoint and per-query caching (HTTP, CDN, in-memory, Redis) with explicit TTLs and cache-invalidation strategies aligned with read model update cadence.
- Consistency: Accept eventual consistency between write and read models; document SLAs and staleness bounds per endpoint.
- Cross-cutting: Preserve security, rate limits, telemetry, and error handling in the transport layer; maintain observability with structured logs, tracing, and query timings.
- Contracts: Read endpoints return DTOs tailored to client needs; no leakage of domain entities.
- Migration: Introduce incrementally per endpoint; provide fallbacks to domain reads if specific rules require them.

We will access NOMIS data exclusively via the Elite2 API and will not connect directly to the NOMIS database or any legacy interfaces. Elite2 will be treated as the single system-of-record integration for offender, booking, movement, and location data used by this service.

Authentication and authorization will use HMPPS OAuth2/JWT service-to-service credentials with least-privilege scopes. Network access will be restricted to approved environments and IPs. Only documented, versioned Elite2 endpoints will be consumed; we will pin to a specific API version and adopt new versions via planned upgrades.

Operationally, we will:
- Implement resilient HTTP clients with timeouts, exponential backoff, circuit breakers, and idempotency where applicable.
- Enforce provider rate limits and pagination; cache short-lived read responses to reduce load and improve latency.
- Validate and map Elite2 schemas to our domain models; treat Elite2 fields as authoritative and immutable except where enrichment is needed.
- Log request/response metadata (excluding PII) and instrument metrics (latency, error rates, saturation) with alerts on SLO breaches.
- Provide graceful degradation: if Elite2 is unavailable, read-only features may serve cached data with staleness indicators; write-through operations will fail fast with user-facing guidance.

Data handling will comply with MoJ security policies: minimize PII in transit and at rest, encrypt all channels (TLS 1.2+), and apply data retention limits aligned to business needs. Test environments will use Elite2 sandbox/stubs; contract tests will detect breaking API changes early.

This decision centralizes integration risk with the supported HMPPS interface, simplifies compliance, and aligns with platform guidance. It constrains us to Elite2 data availability, model, and performance characteristics; any additional NOMIS data needs will be requested via Elite2 change processes.

We will implement aggregates and long-running processes as stateless components. Aggregates will not retain in-memory state between requests; instead, each command handler will reconstruct the required state on demand from a durable source (e.g., event stream or snapshot + tail events) and persist resulting changes atomically. Processes/sagas will likewise be stateless and persist all progress explicitly (e.g., via process state events) so that each message handling is independent, re-entrant, and idempotent.

Key implications:
- State ownership: All authoritative state resides in persistence (event store or database). Any in-memory state is per-request and disposable.
- Invocation model: Command handlers load state, validate invariants, decide, and emit events. Query handlers use read models/materialized views. No shared mutable memory or session-scoped objects.
- Processes: Orchestration is message-driven with persisted checkpoints. Correlation IDs and deterministic transitions are required. Timeouts and reminders use durable timers. No in-memory workflow engines.
- Reliability: Outbox/inbox patterns ensure exactly-once effects across message boundaries. Handlers are idempotent (dedupe keys, version checks) and safe to retry.
- Concurrency: Optimistic concurrency via aggregate version checks. Conflict detection/resolution is at write time.
- Scalability: Components are stateless and horizontally scalable; instances can be added/removed without coordination. Compatible with serverless and containerized deployments.
- Performance: Snapshots and caching may be used as optional accelerators but are non-authoritative and may be evicted anytime.
- Observability: Every decision and transition is captured as events for auditability and debugging.

This decision standardizes the domain layer as pure, side-effect-free computation over reconstructed state with side effects occurring only after durable writes, enabling resilience, simplicity, and scalability.

Adopt a single, cluster-wide ingress controller for all north-south HTTP/HTTPS traffic in the Kubernetes cluster. Standardize on one IngressClass (name: standard) implemented by the NGINX Ingress Controller, exposed via a single cloud LoadBalancer and integrated with ExternalDNS. All teams must publish services via Kubernetes Ingress resources targeting IngressClass=standard; deploying additional ingress controllers is not permitted without explicit architecture approval.

TLS will terminate at the ingress controller using cert-manager for certificate issuance/renewal (Let’s Encrypt by default; private CA supported for internal zones). Default security features (mTLS to backends optional, OWASP ModSecurity CRS/WAF where required) will be enabled per namespace via policy. Rate limiting, request size, and timeout defaults will be centrally managed with per-namespace overrides governed by admission policy.

The controller will be deployed in a dedicated namespace with:
- HPA for autoscaling on CPU/RPS,
- PodDisruptionBudget and topology spread constraints for HA across zones,
- Rolling upgrades with canarying,
- Centralized access/error logging and metrics (Prometheus/Grafana),
- SLOs: 99.95% availability and <50ms p99 added latency under baseline load.

Blue/green and canary releases will use NGINX canary annotations; path/host-based routing is the default. gRPC, WebSocket, and HTTP/2 are supported. TCP/UDP passthrough is out of scope and requires a separate gateway.

Migration will consolidate any existing ingress controllers into this single implementation with coordinated cutovers per namespace. Ownership resides with the Platform/SRE team, which will manage capacity, configuration baselines, and security posture. Future evaluation of Gateway API may replace or augment this controller; until then, the single IngressClass is mandatory.

## Decision
We will split the architecture diagrams into multiple, focused DOT files organized by domain and viewpoint to simplify contributions and reduce merge conflicts. A top-level build process will compose these files into coherent, rendered artifacts.

- Structure
  - diagrams/
    - contexts/<bounded-context>/*.dot
    - components/<service-or-app>/*.dot
    - flows/<process-or-sequence>/*.dot
    - shared/palette.dot (colors, shapes, styles)
    - shared/conventions.dot (node/edge attrs, legend)
    - index.dot.tpl (composition entrypoint template)
  - Each DOT file represents a single concern and is self-contained except for shared includes.

- Composition
  - We will use a lightweight preprocessor (e.g., m4 or gpp) to support include and macro expansion, enabling shared styles and node reuse.
  - A build script (Makefile + scripts/render.sh) will:
    - Expand templates/includes.
    - Validate with graphviz (dot -Tsvg) to catch syntax errors.
    - Emit SVG and PNG to docs/diagrams for publication.
  - The top-level index is generated by concatenating or templating subgraphs to produce overview diagrams without manual editing.

- Conventions
  - Naming: kebab-case, stable IDs for nodes to maintain layout consistency.
  - One logical diagram per file; use subgraphs for clusters.
  - Shared styles and legend come only from shared/*.dot to ensure consistency.
  - Cross-file references use agreed IDs listed in shared/conventions.dot.

- Governance and DX
  - CODEOWNERS per folder for clear review paths.
  - CI renders and diffs SVGs to surface visual changes; PRs must include updated rendered artifacts.
  - Lint/check: CI validates Graphviz version and fails on unresolved includes or orphaned references.
  - Provide templates and examples for quick starts.

- Scope
  - Replace the monolithic DOT with the multi-file approach; keep a read-only generated overview for consumers.
  - No change to the rendering backend (Graphviz) beyond preprocessing and automation.

Adopt a standardized Architectural Decision Record (ADR) practice across the codebase to capture all significant architectural choices. All ADRs will be stored in-repo under docs/adr using sequential numbering and Markdown, following a common template with sections: Title, Status, Date, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives, References. The status lifecycle will be Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded. Accepted ADRs are immutable except for status changes and append-only amendments (Errata) that do not alter the original decision.

Creation and change control will occur via pull requests. Authors are accountable for drafting; reviewers include at least one senior engineer and an architecture representative. Acceptance requires architectural review approval. Any material deviation from an Accepted ADR requires a new ADR that supersedes the prior one; no silent reversals.

ADRs must be referenced in relevant PRs, design docs, runbooks, and service READMEs. Code comments should link to ADR IDs at decision hotspots. A lightweight tool (adr-tools or equivalent script) will scaffold new ADRs, enforce naming, and check cross-links; CI will lint for template compliance and broken references.

This practice applies to all services, libraries, and infrastructure repositories. Quarterly governance reviews will identify candidates for deprecation/supersession and ensure discoverability via an index and tags (domain, component, concern).

- Default: Use the DAL for all application data access. The DAL remains the single entry point for transactions, connection management, security/tenancy enforcement, auditing, validation, soft-deletes, caching, retries/timeouts, observability, and portability.
- Exceptions (allowed plain SQL):
  - Performance-critical paths with demonstrated bottlenecks that the DAL cannot optimize (e.g., avoiding N+1, large aggregations, window functions, complex joins).
  - Bulk operations (batch insert/update/delete), data loads, and set-based maintenance where the DAL would be inefficient.
  - Read-only reporting/analytics queries, projections, and materialized views that require vendor-specific features or advanced SQL not represented in the DAL.
  - One-off migrations/maintenance scripts and data backfills (executed outside the request path).
- Constraints for plain SQL:
  - Must be parameterized (no string concatenation), pre-reviewed, and accompanied by an EXPLAIN/benchmark demonstrating necessity.
  - Lives within the data access module as a Query Object/Repository method; no ad-hoc inline SQL in services/controllers.
  - Uses the DAL’s connection/transaction, tenancy scoping, timeouts, and retry policies; honors row-level security and soft-delete conventions.
  - Read-only by default; write operations require explicit transaction boundaries and idempotency strategy.
  - Returns DTOs/read models; does not leak ORM entities or internal DB artifacts beyond the data layer.
  - Fully covered by tests (unit + integration) and observable (metrics, tracing tags).
- Upstreaming:
  - If the same plain-SQL logic is reused or becomes stable, promote it into the DAL API.
  - Reassess plain SQL periodically; prefer extending the DAL over long-term bespoke queries.

We will model Elasticsearch documents as denormalized, aggregate-centric records optimized for search and analytics, with upstream systems remaining the system of record.

- Document shape: One document per aggregate (e.g., Order, Customer, Product), embedding related data needed for common queries. Avoid parent–child joins; use nested fields only when intra-document array queries are required. Cross-aggregate relationships are materialized into the document at index time.

- Mappings: Use explicit, versioned mappings via index templates; disable dynamic fields. Apply appropriate types (keyword for exact match/aggregations/joins-by-id, text with language analyzers for full-text, numeric/date/boolean as needed). Use multi-fields (text + keyword) where applicable. Disable _all; store only _source.

- IDs and versioning: Deterministic IDs derived from business identifiers to support idempotent upserts. Use optimistic concurrency control (if_seq_no/if_primary_term) on updates. Include a domain version field in documents to facilitate reindexing and consumers’ compatibility checks.

- Updates: Prefer full upserts; allow partial updates for hot fields. Use ingest pipelines to compute denormalized projections and normalize data. Treat deletions as soft deletes via a tombstone flag; schedule hard deletes via lifecycle policies.

- Indices and aliases: Use index-per-domain with optional time-based rollover for high-churn/event data. Manage read/write via aliases (e.g., domain-read, domain-write) to enable zero-downtime reindexing and blue/green swaps. Apply ILM for rollover, shrink, and retention.

- Search and analytics: Design fields to support required filters, sort, and aggregations; precompute sortable keywords; avoid scripts in queries where possible. Paginate with search_after for deep paging.

- Reindexing and schema evolution: Additive-only changes by default; breaking changes handled by creating a new index version and reindexing behind aliases. Backfill jobs ensure denormalized consistency.

We adopt a schema-first, automated code generation pipeline in which machine-readable contracts are the single source of truth. Service APIs use OpenAPI/AsyncAPI; internal RPCs use Protocol Buffers; GraphQL schemas use SDL. From these contracts we deterministically generate server stubs, client SDKs, DTOs/types, request/response validators, and basic documentation.

Tools are pinned and containerized for reproducibility: OpenAPI Generator/Swagger Codegen for REST, Buf/protoc for Protobuf, and GraphQL Code Generator for GraphQL. Templates and generator configurations live in a dedicated repo and are versioned alongside services. Generation is invoked via make codegen (or equivalent) and enforced in CI; specification changes must include regenerated artifacts, and CI fails on drift.

Generated code is isolated under a dedicated directory with “DO NOT EDIT” headers and is never modified manually. Extension points are provided via partial classes, interfaces, and composition; customization occurs only in hand-written layers that wrap or extend generated artifacts. We do not commit generated code to source control except for explicitly published SDKs/libraries where consumers rely on the generated output; in those cases artifacts are versioned and released with semantic versioning.

All generators are pinned to exact versions, with lockfiles and container images to ensure deterministic output. Backward compatibility is enforced at the contract level (linting and breaking-change detection via buf/openapi-diff), with a deprecation policy for removals. Security, performance, and compliance rules are encoded as lint checks and CI gates. This decision standardizes interfaces, reduces boilerplate, and ensures consistent, reproducible builds across the organization.

## Decision
Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as the canonical mechanism to capture, communicate, and govern all significant technical and architectural decisions.

- Scope: Any decision with meaningful impact on architecture, quality attributes, security, costs, operations, cross-team interfaces, or long-lived constraints must have an ADR.
- Location: Store ADRs in-repo at docs/adr. For multi-repo programs, maintain a central architecture/adr repository for cross-cutting decisions and per-repo docs/adr for local ones; cross-reference where relevant.
- Format: Use the MADR template (v3.x). Each ADR includes Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Options Considered, and References.
- Naming: Sequential numbering with slug, e.g., 0001-use-architecture-decision-records.md. One decision per file. Maintain an index.md listing all ADRs.
- Status lifecycle: proposed → accepted/rejected → superseded/deprecated. Accepted ADRs are immutable except for minor corrections; changes require a new ADR that supersedes prior ones.
- Process: Create ADRs via pull request. Require at least two approvals, including the architecture owner (or delegate). Link related tickets and design docs. Record dissent and trade-offs.
- Traceability: Reference ADR IDs in code, deployment manifests, runbooks, and design docs. Link ADRs in epics/user stories that implement them.
- Tooling: Prefer adr-tools or equivalent for scaffolding and indexing; enforce checks in CI to validate ADR presence for tagged changes.
- Cadence: Review ADRs quarterly for relevance; mark obsolete items deprecated or superseded.
- Ownership and visibility: The architecture owner curates ADR quality and index. ADRs are readable by all project members and included in release notes when decisions impact external behavior.

We will use Go Modules as the sole dependency management mechanism (minimum Go 1.21). All projects must include and commit go.mod and go.sum; GOPATH-based dependency management is prohibited.

- Versioning and pinning: Dependencies are pinned to exact semantic versions (no “latest” or floating constraints). Semantic Import Versioning is required (module paths include major version ≥ v2). Upgrades occur via automated PRs (Renovate/Dependabot) on a scheduled cadence with human review.
- Resolution and integrity: CI and local builds will use GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct and the public checksum database for integrity. go.sum is authoritative and must not be edited manually. Reproducible builds are verified in CI with -mod=readonly.
- Private modules: Private dependencies are allowed only under configured GOPRIVATE (our org domains). For private modules, checksums are not uploaded; access uses SSH/HTTPS tokens via CI secrets. Optionally set GONOSUMDB to mirror GOPRIVATE.
- Replace directives: use only for local development or temporary hotfixes; they must not be merged to main unless pointing to a tagged fork with clear issue reference. Any long-lived fork must use a distinct module path.
- Vendoring: We do not vendor by default. Vendoring (go mod vendor, -mod=vendor) is permitted for air-gapped or long-term support branches and must be automated in release pipelines if enabled.
- Multi-module: Where multiple modules exist in a repo, use go work to coordinate builds and tests; it must not be required for consumers.
- Enforcement: CI validates tidy state (go mod tidy -diff), denies unexpected changes to go.sum, and runs vulnerability scans (govulncheck) on every change.

We will not introduce or enforce any automated linter (e.g., ESLint, Pylint, RuboCop, golangci-lint, StyleCop, ktlint) in local development, pre-commit hooks, or CI/CD pipelines for this project. This applies to all repositories within the program unless explicitly exempted.

Instead, we will:
- Rely on language-native formatters and opinionated formatters only (e.g., gofmt, Black, Prettier, clang-format) for code formatting.
- Depend on compiler/type-checker warnings-as-errors, unit/integration tests, and runtime checks for correctness.
- Enforce a lightweight, documented style guide and a code review checklist focused on clarity, readability, and maintainability.
- Use security and compliance scanners (SAST/DAST/Dependency auditing/secret scanning) as separate, non-linting gates in CI.
- Permit optional, developer-local linting for personal productivity, but outputs will not gate merges or builds.

Implementation steps:
- Remove existing lint configurations and CI steps that fail builds on lint issues.
- Add/standardize formatter configs and ensure “format on save” is available in editor setups.
- Update CONTRIBUTING.md with review checklist and style expectations.

Revisit triggers:
- Measurable degradation in code quality or maintainability traceable to issues linting would have prevented.
- Onboarding friction due to inconsistent patterns.
- Security or regulatory requirements that necessitate lint-like checks.
- Team consensus to pilot a narrowly scoped linter rule set with strict ROI criteria.

Any exception requires an ADR addendum specifying repository, rules scope, and CI impact.

Adopt arrays as the default representation for ordered, homogeneous collections across the codebase. Arrays will be zero-based, contiguous in memory, and row-major for multidimensional data. Public APIs will expose immutable arrays or read-only views to ensure safety and thread-friendliness; internal modules may use dynamic array wrappers for mutation (e.g., growth, in-place updates).

Provide a standard array utility layer offering allocation, bounds-checked access, slicing, mapping, reduction, and conversion to/from common collection types. Slices are views over the same backing storage and must carry length/offset metadata; functions that materialize copies must be explicitly named to avoid ambiguity. Bounds checks are enabled by default and may be elided in profiled hot paths with documented preconditions.

Use typed arrays for numeric and binary data to maximize performance and interoperability with native/accelerated code.
