All APIs must document ownership and lifetime; passing arrays across threads requires immutable snapshots or explicit synchronization. Serialization preserves order and uses JSON arrays for external protocols; binary formats include length prefixes and element type identifiers.

This decision standardizes performance characteristics, memory predictability, and cross-language interop, while constraining mutation to well-defined layers and clarifying concurrency and API contracts.

## Decision
Adopt Ports and Adapters (Hexagonal Architecture) as the primary architectural style for TCH-RES to isolate the domain core from external technologies and enable replaceable infrastructure.

- Structure:
  - Domain Core: domain model and application services (use cases) with no framework dependencies.
  - Ports: domain-owned interfaces defining inbound (driving) and outbound (driven) interactions.
  - Adapters: technology-specific implementations for web/API, messaging, CLI (inbound) and database, external services, cache, file/object storage, email, and observability (outbound).
  - Composition: dependency injection to wire adapters to ports; no adapter-to-adapter coupling.

- Boundaries and contracts:
  - One application service per use case exposed via inbound ports.
  - Outbound ports defined by the domain; adapters implement them.
  - DTOs at edges; prevent leaking domain entities across adapters.
  - Bounded contexts mapped to modules with explicit dependencies; shared kernel limited to stable abstractions.

- Cross-cutting concerns:
  - Implement via decorators/middleware around ports/adapters for logging, metrics, tracing, retries, circuit breakers, and validation.
  - Transactions initiated in application services; idempotency at inbound ports for externally triggered operations.
  - Security: validate/authenticate/authorize at inbound adapters; enforce least privilege on outbound adapters.

- Testing:
  - Unit tests for domain and application services.
  - Contract tests for ports (provider/consumer) to ensure adapter compatibility.
  - Test doubles for outbound ports; end-to-end tests per adapter.

- Evolution and migration:
  - Introduce anti-corruption layers and strangler adapters to integrate/replace legacy systems.
  - Backward compatibility via dual adapters during transitions; defined deprecation policy.

- Operational considerations:
  - Support sync/async ports; prefer asynchronous/outbox patterns where appropriate.
  - Performance via batching and pagination in adapters; caching behind outbound ports.

- Governance:
  - Repository/package layout, code templates, and lint rules to enforce boundaries.
  - ADRs required for new ports/adapters and cross-boundary changes.

We will provide a dedicated, cross-platform Light Client CLI as a standalone binary focused on verifiable, script-friendly operations. The CLI will be implemented in Rust using clap for argument parsing and tokio for async I/O, compiled as statically linked binaries where feasible. It will expose stable, composable subcommands: init, sync, verify, query, proof, status, config, keys (optional), and version. Default output will be human-readable; a --json flag will return a stable JSON schema suitable for automation. All commands will be non-interactive by default and deterministic given inputs.

Configuration will be resolved in this order: explicit CLI flags > environment variables > config file (~/.lightclient/config.toml) > built-in defaults. Network endpoints, chain IDs, trust parameters (e.g., --trusted-height/--trusted-hash, --trust-level), and data directories are all configurable. Safe defaults include TLS-enabled endpoints, minimal permissions, explicit trust anchors, and no implicit key material. If key management is enabled, it will integrate with the OS keyring when available; otherwise, keys remain out of scope.

Telemetry and update checks are opt-in. Logging supports --verbose/--quiet and structured logs via --log-format=json. Exit codes are precise and documented for robust scripting. Backward compatibility will be maintained via semantic versioning and deprecation windows; breaking changes require a major version bump.

Distribution targets include signed releases (Sigstore + checksums), Homebrew, Scoop, apt, and container images. The CLI will avoid long-running daemons, relying on ephemeral execution with clear, bounded side effects and reproducible builds.

## Decision

We will provision and consume databases exclusively as explicitly versioned services across all environments (local, CI, staging, production). Every database engine must be pinned to a specific major.minor version (e.g., PostgreSQL 15.4), never “latest,” with versions declared in infrastructure-as-code and application configuration. Driver/ORM dependencies must be pinned to compatible versions.

We will maintain a supported-version window (current stable + previous minor; maximum two active majors where required) and follow a planned upgrade cadence (e.g., quarterly for minors, annually for majors), subject to security advisories. Each upgrade requires:
- Compatibility assessment and release notes review
- Representative test coverage in CI against target version(s)
- Repeatable schema/data migrations (forward-only), with preflight checks
- Verified backup/restore and rollback plan

Upgrades will use safe rollout patterns (blue/green or replica-based switchover) to minimize downtime. Managed DB services must be configured to freeze engine version and automatic minor patching only when validated. Local development and CI will use container images that match the declared versions.

We will deprecate unsupported versions via a documented policy with notice periods, telemetry-based impact assessment, and tracked remediation tasks. Monitoring will include engine version drift alerts and driver/engine compatibility signals. Any new service introduction must specify its engine and version, support window, and migration path.

Success criteria: no unpinned database versions in any environment; reproducible builds/tests targeting declared versions; predictable, low-risk upgrades with validated backups and rollbacks.

We will define the WikibaseManifest format using OpenAPI Specification (OAS) 3.1 as the single source of truth.

- Specification: Author and maintain a canonical openapi.yaml (OAS 3.1) using the 2020-12 JSON Schema dialect for components/schemas; all fields, enums, formats, and constraints must be expressed in schema, with descriptive examples.
- Extensibility: Allow vendor-specific extensions via x-wikibase-* fields; unknown x-* extensions must be ignored by consumers.
- Versioning: Version the manifest schema with Semantic Versioning. Backward-compatible additions are minor; breaking changes require a major release. Mark fields as deprecated before removal with sunset timelines.
- Artifacts: Generate and publish:
  - JSON Schema extract for validation
  - Typed bindings (e.g., TypeScript, Java, PHP) via openapi-generator
  - Static documentation (e.g., Redoc) and an interactive Swagger UI
- Validation: Enforce schema validation in CI for examples and fixtures; use Spectral rules for style and consistency; require JSON examples to round-trip validate against the schema.
- Compatibility: Maintain a compatibility matrix for producer/consumer versions; provide migration notes per release.
- Repository layout: /spec/openapi.yaml (canonical), /schemas/jsonschema.json (generated), /docs (rendered docs), /examples (valid sample manifests), /tools (generation scripts).
- Publishing: Host the canonical spec and docs at a stable URL; publish versioned artifacts with immutable tags; latest points to the most recent stable minor.
- Conformance: Implementations must treat unspecified properties as invalid unless explicitly allowed via additionalProperties; must ignore unknown x-*; must not rely on example values as normative.
- Governance: Changes require review by the architecture group; all changes must include updated examples, generated artifacts, and a changelog entry.

Adopt Jenkins (LTS) as the organization’s Continuous Integration service, implemented as Pipeline-as-Code using declarative Jenkinsfiles stored with application repositories. Use multibranch pipelines to auto-discover and build branches/PRs; enable shared Jenkins Library for common steps and compliance controls.

Run Jenkins controller as a hardened, backed-up service with role-based access control, SSO integration, and least-privilege credentials from a centralized secrets manager. Execute builds on ephemeral agents provisioned via Kubernetes and/or Docker to ensure isolation, scalability, and reproducibility. Containerize build tools; avoid tool installation on the controller.

Standardize CI stages: checkout, build, test, security scans (SAST/Dependency), artifact packaging, and publishing to the artifact repository; integrate quality gates (e.g., test coverage, static analysis) as merge prerequisites. Enable parallelization where feasible and use remote caching where supported to reduce build times.

Integrate Jenkins with the VCS (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket) for webhooks, status checks, and required checks on protected branches. Enforce code review for Jenkinsfile changes. Maintain a curated plugin set with explicit version pinning, update cadence, and security review; prefer native features and shared libraries over new plugins. Monitor system health and pipeline metrics via centralized logging and observability.

Provide per-team folders with controlled permissions and seeded jobs via Configuration as Code (JCasC) for reproducible environments. Establish backup/restore and disaster recovery procedures; implement high availability for critical workloads as needed. Document templates and onboarding guides to accelerate adoption.

This decision remains in effect until CI requirements exceed Jenkins’ operational envelope or a managed CI offering demonstrably reduces total cost and risk. A pilot migration path to an alternative CI may be explored in parallel without disrupting current pipelines.

## Decision
Standardize on Yarn as the package manager for all JavaScript/TypeScript projects in this repository. We will use Yarn Berry (v3+) with the nodeLinker set to node-modules to maximize compatibility with existing tooling, while retaining Berry features (workspaces, constraints, and modern plug-in ecosystem).

Key points:
- Pin Yarn version per repo via yarnPath and commit .yarn/releases to ensure reproducible environments across machines and CI.
- Commit yarn.lock and treat it as the source of truth; prohibit direct npm usage and lockfile drift. Use yarn install --immutable in CI.
- Adopt Yarn Workspaces for multi-package management in the monorepo, leveraging hoisting defaults to reduce duplication and speed installs.
- Configure .yarnrc.yml with: nodeLinker: node-modules, enable globalCache, checksum integrity, and offline mirror as needed. Consider Zero-Install selectively for libraries, not applications with large artifacts.
- Use yarn constraints and yarn dedupe to enforce dependency hygiene; use resolutions for targeted overrides.
- Use yarn set version; do not mix with npm/pnpm. Scripts and lifecycle tasks must be executed via yarn.
- CI/CD will cache Yarn’s global cache and .yarn directory to accelerate builds; installs run with immutable and no-clipanion-confirm.
- Security: run yarn npm audit in CI and apply vetted resolutions; integrate Dependabot/Renovate for automated updates aligned with Yarn.
- Upgrades: minor updates monthly; major Yarn or workspace changes require a dedicated ADR and migration plan.

## Decision

We will copy the application source code and test suites into a dedicated build/test stage of our Docker image to enable deterministic, containerized builds and test execution. The final runtime image will not contain tests or development tooling.

- Adopt a multi-stage Dockerfile:
  - builder/test stage: copies dependency manifests first, installs build and test dependencies, then copies application source and test directories, and runs linters and tests.
  - runtime stage: copies only built artifacts (or application runtime files) from the builder stage, excluding tests and dev dependencies.

- Use cache-friendly layering:
  - COPY only dependency manifests (e.g., package.json/pnpm-lock.yaml, requirements.txt/poetry.lock, go.mod/go.sum, etc.) first and install dependencies to maximize cache reuse.
  - COPY src/ and tests/ (or equivalent) afterward to trigger cache invalidation only when source or tests change.

- Exclude nonessential files with .dockerignore (e.g., .git, local build artifacts, coverage outputs, node_modules/vendor when not needed) to minimize context size and improve build performance.

- In CI:
  - Build the image and run tests inside the builder/test stage to ensure parity with production-like environments.
  - Publish only the final runtime image.

- In local development:
  - Prefer bind mounts for rapid iteration; for reproducible runs and CI parity, developers may optionally build and test via the builder stage.

- Security and size:
  - The final image is minimal and free of test code and dev tools.
  - Use non-root users in both stages where feasible.

This approach standardizes test execution, improves cache efficiency, reduces runtime image size, and preserves a clean separation between build/test and production concerns.

## Decision
We will adopt JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) as the single source of truth for all structured data specifications (APIs, events, configs, persisted documents).

- Scope: Every external-facing payload and internal contract must be defined by a JSON Schema. Schemas will be versioned, reviewed, and stored under /schemas with one file per root type.
- Identification and reuse: Each schema will declare a stable $id (HTTPS URI) and use $ref for modular reuse. Common components live under /schemas/common and are referenced across domain schemas.
- Validation: All produced/consumed payloads must be validated against their schema at service boundaries. CI will run schema validation against example fixtures and contract tests; builds fail on violations.
- Compatibility policy: Additive changes (new optional fields, widened enums with defaults) are backward-compatible; removals, requiredness changes, semantic changes, and format tightening are breaking. Breaking changes require a new major version and coexistence period; deprecations must be annotated in schema descriptions.
- Documentation: Schemas must include description, examples, and enums with human-readable titles. Docs are generated from schemas and published with each release.
- Formats and conventions: We prefer standard formats (date-time, uri). Custom formats require explicit validators and documentation. Field names use snake_case; nullability is explicit via type unions including "null".
- Tooling: ajv (JS) and python-jsonschema (Py) are the reference validators in CI. Code generation and typings may be produced from schemas where useful but do not replace validation at runtime.
- Publication: Schemas are published with immutable $id URLs and changelog entries per version.

Adopt GitHub (GitHub Enterprise Cloud) as the organization’s primary source control platform for all software projects. All repositories will be hosted under a centralized organization with enforced SSO and mandatory 2FA. Git will remain the VCS; GitHub provides the hosting, collaboration, governance, and automation capabilities.

Scope and usage:
- Default to private repositories; open-source projects require explicit approval and separate org or teams.
- Standardize on trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches; main branch is protected.
- Enforce branch protection: required status checks, linear history (no merge commits), required reviews (min. 1–2), code owners for critical paths, signed commits, and restricted force-push/delete.
- Use GitHub Actions for CI/CD where feasible; secrets managed via GitHub Environments/Organization Secrets with least privilege and required approvals.
- Use GitHub Issues/Projects for lightweight tracking; integrate with Jira/Azure Boards where needed via official apps.
- Require CODEOWNERS, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, LICENSE (as applicable), and pull request templates in all repos.
- Use Dependabot for dependency updates and security alerts; enable Advanced Security (Code Scanning/Secret Scanning) where licensed.
- Enforce review workflows for protected environments (production) with deployment approvals and audit trail.

Governance and compliance:
- Apply repository templates and organization policies via GitHub App/Actions; periodic policy checks.
- Maintain audit logs; enable branch/tag protection policies org-wide.
- Establish backup and business continuity via scheduled mirroring to read-only secondary remote (e.g., AWS CodeCommit or on-prem Git) for critical repos.
- Access managed through teams with least privilege; service accounts use fine-grained PATs or GitHub Apps.

Migration and interoperability:
- Migrate existing repos preserving history; archive deprecated repositories.
- Support monorepo or multi-repo per domain needs; shared libraries published via internal package registries (GitHub Packages) with versioning.

Success criteria:
- Measurable reduction in lead time for changes, improved review coverage, zero unauthorized pushes to protected branches, compliant audit trails, and reduced security incidents via automated scanning.

This decision centralizes source control on GitHub to standardize workflows, increase developer velocity, and meet security/compliance requirements while enabling automation at scale.

We will structure the system as a set of independently ownable components aligned to bounded contexts, with clear interfaces and strict data ownership. The initial component map is:

- Client Applications: Web UI and Mobile App consuming public APIs.
- API Gateway/Edge: Single ingress, request routing, rate limiting, TLS termination, and API versioning.
- Identity and Access Management: Authentication, authorization (RBAC/ABAC), session/token services, and user/tenant provisioning.
- Core Domain Components: A set of services/modules each owning a subdomain (as defined in the domain model), including their own data stores and business rules. Interactions are API-first and event-enabled.
- Integration/Messaging: Asynchronous communication via a message broker (publish/subscribe, event bus) for domain events and workflows; outbox pattern for reliability.
- Data Access and Persistence: Per-component databases (polyglot allowed), no shared DB schemas. Read models/materialized views where needed.
- Reporting and Analytics: Read-only warehouse/lake fed by CDC/ETL, separated from operational stores.
- File/Object Storage: Managed object store for large/binary assets with signed URL access patterns.
- Observability: Centralized logging, metrics, tracing, and alerting with service-level objectives (SLOs).
- Configuration and Secrets: Centralized configuration service and secret management with environment scoping.
- Admin/Backoffice: Operational UI and APIs for support, configuration, and compliance tasks.
- Compliance and Audit: Cross-cutting audit trail, PII handling, and data retention controls.

Communication patterns:
- Synchronous: REST/gRPC with explicit contracts and semantic versioning.
- Asynchronous: Event-driven integration for decoupling and eventual consistency.

Governance:
- Shared libraries only for cross-cutting concerns; no shared domain code.
- Backward-compatible API evolution; contract testing between components.
- Clear ownership per component and independent deployment within a modular monolith or microservices topology based on operational needs.

We will record architecturally significant decisions using lightweight Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) maintained in the repository to ensure shared context, traceability, and auditable change history.

- Repository location: docs/adr/ with sequential numbering (e.g., 0001-...) and stable filenames.
- Format: Markdown using the MADR template (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives, References).
- Status lifecycle: proposed → accepted/rejected → deprecated/superseded. ADR files are immutable after acceptance except for status or metadata; changes require a new ADR that supersedes the prior one.
- Scope: decisions with long-term impact on architecture, security, data, interfaces, runtime characteristics, or team-wide practices; ephemeral or purely tactical choices are excluded.
- Process: any contributor may draft an ADR; acceptance requires review via pull request with at least one architect and one affected stakeholder approving. Major PRs must cite relevant ADR IDs; new major architectural work must be preceded by a proposed ADR.
- Ownership: Architecture group curates, labels, and ensures consistency; code owners enforce checks on the docs/adr/ path.
- Discoverability: maintain an index at docs/adr/index.md; cross-link related ADRs and reference them in READMEs and system docs.
- Tooling: adopt adr-tools or equivalent scripts to create, link, and supersede ADRs; CI validates template conformance and status values.
- Language and clarity: write in concise, implementation-agnostic English, capturing decision drivers and trade-offs; include rationale and consequences.
- Governance: review ADRs at architecture syncs; periodically audit for relevance; deprecate when obsolete but preserve history.
- Integration: meeting outcomes proposing architectural changes must result in a corresponding proposed ADR within five working days.

This decision institutionalizes ADRs as the single source of truth for architectural choices, aligning design, implementation, and evolution.

## Decision

Adopt React Native as the cross-platform mobile framework for building and maintaining the iOS and Android applications. We will implement a single TypeScript codebase leveraging React Native core, with Expo for bootstrapping, OTA updates, and development tooling where feasible; we will eject only when native capabilities or build controls require it. UI will use a component library compatible with React Native (e.g., React Native Paper or NativeBase) and platform-specific styling via StyleSheet and platform selectors. Performance-sensitive features (e.g., heavy animations, background processing, Bluetooth) will use native modules or proven community packages; Reanimated and Gesture Handler will be standard for complex interactions. Networking will use fetch/axios with react-query for caching. Navigation will use React Navigation. State management will use Redux Toolkit or Zustand based on feature complexity.

We will maintain strict platform parity with selective platform-specific forks when necessary (file extensions .ios/.android). CI/CD will produce signed builds for both platforms and support OTA updates via Expo Updates or CodePush (subject to app store policies). Unit, integration, and end-to-end tests will be implemented with Jest, React Native Testing Library, and Detox.

Constraints and risks: some device-specific APIs may require custom native bridges; app size may increase versus fully native; extreme performance use cases may warrant native screens. Success is defined by achieving >80% shared code across platforms, app startup <2s on mid-tier devices, and meeting store compliance and accessibility baselines.

We will integrate with Cloud Foundry via the official Java client library (org.cloudfoundry:cloudfoundry-client-reactor) as the sole programmatic interface to the Cloud Foundry API. All platform interactions (app lifecycle, org/space management, routes, service instances/bindings, tasks, logs and metrics retrieval) will use the v3 API where available, with controlled fallbacks to v2 only when required by the library.

We will adopt the library’s reactive, non-blocking model (Project Reactor) but encapsulate it behind an internal abstraction layer to (a) isolate callers from Reactor types, (b) enable dependency injection and testing with mocks, and (c) preserve the option to replace Cloud Foundry or the client library with minimal impact. Public interfaces in our domain will expose futures/promises or synchronous facades as needed by callers.

Authentication will use UAA OAuth2 client credentials with short-lived tokens; secrets are sourced from the platform secret store and never logged. We will configure connection timeouts, TLS validation, proxy support, and implement retries with exponential backoff and circuit breaking (Resilience4j) for resiliency. Pagination, rate limits, and asynchronous job polling will be handled centrally in the adapter.

We will pin a tested version of the client compatible with our target foundations and JDK 17, track upstream changes, and run contract tests against a sandbox foundation; HTTP interactions will be tested with WireMock for isolation. We will not shell out to the cf CLI nor build bespoke REST calls except as temporary, reviewed workarounds. Telemetry (latency, error rates) and structured logs will be emitted with PII redaction. Configuration (API endpoints, org/space, timeouts) will be externalized and environment-specific.

We will secure the admin interface using enterprise Single Sign-On via OpenID Connect (OIDC) against the corporate Identity Provider (e.g., Okta/Azure AD/Google Workspace). The admin app will be a confidential client using the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. No local passwords will be maintained; all authentication and MFA are enforced by the IdP, with support for WebAuthn/FIDO2. Admin access is governed by least-privilege, role-based authorization derived from IdP group/claim mapping; provisioning and deprovisioning are handled via SCIM or automated claim-based assignment.

Tokens are short-lived: access tokens 5–15 minutes; refresh tokens are rotating with reuse detection and immediate revocation on suspected compromise. Sessions enforce inactivity timeout (15–30 minutes) and absolute lifetime (8–12 hours). Logout revokes refresh tokens and clears secure, HTTP-only, SameSite=strict cookies; CSRF protection is enabled for state-changing requests.

Conditional access is required for production: MFA always, compliant/managed device or secure network, and optional IP allowlists by environment. A monitored, break-glass account with hardware-key MFA is stored in a sealed vault and used only under incident procedures.

All admin authentication and authorization events (login, MFA challenges, token issuance/revocation, privilege elevation, policy changes) are centrally audited with immutable retention and alerts on anomalies. The admin interface is available only over TLS, fronted by a WAF with rate limiting and bot protection. Secrets (client credentials, signing keys) are managed in the organization’s secrets manager with automatic rotation. This decision standardizes on OIDC SSO to reduce credential sprawl, enforce consistent MFA and conditional access, and enable auditable, least-privilege admin operations.

We will implement a resource-oriented, RESTful HTTP API that exchanges JSON as the default representation. The API contract will be defined spec-first using OpenAPI 3.1, which will serve as the single source of truth for server stubs, client SDKs, documentation, and contract tests.

Versioning will use a URI prefix (e.g., /v1). Backward-compatible, additive changes are allowed within a version; breaking changes require a new major version. Deprecations will be communicated via Deprecation and Sunset headers and documentation.

Authentication and authorization will use OAuth 2.1/OIDC with JWT access tokens and fine-grained scopes; service-to-service calls will use client credentials, with optional mTLS for high-trust paths. CORS will be explicitly configured. Secrets are managed via a centralized vault.

Consistency and usability conventions:
- Resource names are plural nouns; snake_case fields in JSON.
- Standard HTTP methods and status codes; idempotency for PUT/PATCH/DELETE and POST with Idempotency-Key when applicable.
- Pagination via cursor-based parameters (page[cursor], page[size]); filtering and sorting via filter[*] and sort.
- Errors follow RFC 7807 (application/problem+json) with stable error codes.

Performance and resilience:
- Caching with ETags/If-None-Match and Cache-Control where safe.
- Timeouts, retries with backoff on transient 5xx/429, and circuit breaking at the gateway.
- Rate limiting and quotas enforced at the API gateway.

Security and quality:
- Input validation derived from OpenAPI schemas; OWASP ASVS-aligned controls.
- Comprehensive audit logging for security-sensitive operations.
- Observability with structured logs, correlation IDs (W3C Trace Context), metrics, and distributed tracing.

Deliverables include automated contract tests, linting, and CI pipelines to enforce spec compliance and backward compatibility.

## Decision

We will adopt the Symfony Messenger component as the standard mechanism for command, event, and async task handling across the application.

- Buses: We will use three logical buses—CommandBus, EventBus, and (optionally) QueryBus for CQRS separation. Commands are handled synchronously by default; events and background tasks are processed asynchronously.
- Transports: In production we will use RabbitMQ as the primary transport for async processing, with TLS-enabled connections. In development/test we will default to in-memory or Doctrine transport; local Dockerized RabbitMQ is supported for parity. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) will be configured per transport.
- Delivery semantics: At-least-once delivery with retry and exponential backoff. Messages that exceed max retries are routed to DLQ for manual inspection or automated compensating flows. Handlers must be idempotent.
- Ordering: We will ensure per-aggregate ordering by routing keys based on aggregate ID where ordering matters. Handlers must not assume global ordering.
- Serialization and schema: JSON serialization with explicit message versioning. Backward-compatible changes are required; breaking changes use new message versions. Sensitive data must not be embedded in payloads; prefer references.
- Outbox: Domain events emitted within transactions will use the Outbox pattern to guarantee publish-on-commit. A dedicated worker will relay outbox entries to the EventBus.
- Observability: CorrelationId and CausationId will be propagated via message headers. We will integrate structured logging, metrics (latency, throughput, retries, DLQ count), and distributed tracing.
- Security: Transport connections use TLS; credentials are managed via secrets. Message payloads are validated and size-limited. PII is minimized and, if unavoidable, encrypted at rest and in transit.
- Operations: Workers run as separate processes/containers with horizontal autoscaling driven by queue depth and SLOs. Graceful shutdown and heartbeat/health checks are required.
- Governance: Message contracts are owned and reviewed via ADRs and schema PRs. Handlers must include clear retry policies, idempotency keys, and compensating actions where applicable.

We will implement a decentralized, read-only Community Mirror network to distribute public artifacts and documentation, while keeping the primary origin as the sole source of truth. Mirrors will be community-operated, vetted through a lightweight onboarding process, and synchronized via pull-based replication (HTTPS rsync/rclone) on a scheduled basis (target: hourly) with content-addressed paths and immutable releases to minimize inconsistency.

All artifacts, indices, and release manifests will be cryptographically signed (Sigstore or GPG) and verified by clients; clients will trust signatures, not mirror identities. Client selection will use a mirrorlist API with active health checks, GeoDNS, and latency-aware routing; clients will automatically fail over to healthy mirrors and ultimately to the origin if needed. Mirrors will serve over HTTPS with HTTP/2 and support range requests; CDN fronting may be used by some mirrors for burst capacity.

Operational policy: mirrors are read-only; no user data is stored; logs are anonymized and rotated; minimal indexing metadata retained. Mirrors must meet uptime, bandwidth, and sync frequency guidelines; non-compliant mirrors can be temporarily delisted. The origin publishes canonical hashes and revocation lists; emergency takedown and blocklist procedures are defined. Governance includes a public registry, transparency dashboard, and periodic audits. This decision prioritizes resilience, community participation, predictable performance, and security without imposing hard SLAs on volunteer operators.

We will implement the backend using Ruby on Rails (v7.x) in API-only mode as the primary web framework. PostgreSQL will be the relational database via ActiveRecord; Redis will support caching and background processing. We will expose RESTful JSON endpoints, versioned under /api/v1, with json serialization via jsonapi-serializer. Authentication will use Devise with JWT (devise-jwt), with role/permission checks via Pundit. Rate limiting and basic abuse protection will be enforced with rack-attack.

Background jobs and scheduled tasks will run on Sidekiq backed by Redis. File storage will use Active Storage with Amazon S3 in non-local environments. Caching will use Rails cache with Redis, plus HTTP caching headers and ETags where appropriate. Puma will serve the app; containerization will be via Docker, and CI/CD will build and deploy containers to the chosen environment (e.g., AWS ECS/Fargate or Heroku), with zero-downtime migrations where feasible.

We will adhere to Rails conventions with thin controllers, using service objects, form/command objects, and query objects to encapsulate domain logic and keep models lean. Pagination will use Pagy. Observability will include structured logging with Lograge, distributed tracing/APM (e.g., New Relic), metrics, and health/readiness probes. Testing will standardize on RSpec, FactoryBot, and Shoulda Matchers, with request, model, and system specs. Configuration and secrets will be managed via Rails credentials and environment variables. Internationalization (i18n) will be enabled from the outset.

## Decision

Adopt a contract-first, REST-first API design approach standardized on OpenAPI 3.1 as the canonical specification format, with AsyncAPI 2.x for event-driven interfaces. Establish a centralized API Design Guide that enforces consistent resource modeling, naming, pagination, filtering, sorting, error handling, and versioning across all services.

Key standards and tools:
- JSON over HTTP with resource-oriented endpoints; prefer plural nouns and snake_case in JSON payloads; kebab-case in URLs.
- HTTP semantics: use appropriate methods (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE), idempotency for PUT/PATCH where applicable, and standard status codes.
- Versioning via URI prefix (e.g., /v1) with additive, backward-compatible changes favored; breaking changes require new major version and deprecation policy (minimum 12 months).
- Error format based on RFC 9457 (HTTP Problem Details) with organization-specific extensions.
- Pagination via cursor-based scheme by default; include total count when feasible.
- Authentication/authorization via OAuth 2.1 with OIDC; service-to-service via mTLS and JWTs; enforce least privilege scopes.
- Documentation generated from specs using Redocly/Swagger UI; examples and curl snippets required; SDK generation when justified.
- Linting and governance using Spectral with custom ruleset; pull-request checks mandatory; design reviews before implementation.
- Schema reuse via shared component library and common error/pagination schemas; strong typing encouraged.
- Change management through semantic versioning for specs, changelogs, and automated release notes; deprecation communicated via headers and portal.
- Backward compatibility verified with contract tests; consumers onboarded through a developer portal with searchable catalogs and SLA visibility.

All APIs MUST conform to the guide and pass governance gates before release; exceptions require architecture approval and documented rationale.

We will secure the API using Dropwizard’s built-in security capabilities to minimize custom code, align with framework conventions, and simplify operations.

- Transport security: Enforce HTTPS at the application via Dropwizard’s TLS configuration (server.applicationConnectors/adminConnectors with cert/key), or terminate TLS at a trusted proxy with secure upstream only. Reject plain HTTP in production.
- Authentication: Use dropwizard-auth with AuthDynamicFeature and a custom Authenticator to validate OAuth2 Bearer tokens. Prefer stateless JWT access tokens validated with the IdP’s JWKS (RS256/ES256) to avoid callback latency; fall back to introspection if required by policy. Inject the authenticated Principal via @Auth.
- Authorization: Implement a Role-based Authorizer and enforce permissions via @RolesAllowed on resource methods. Centralize permission mapping to roles in configuration to avoid scattering policy.
- Request handling: Register the authentication filter globally for protected paths; allow unauthenticated access only to explicitly whitelisted endpoints (e.g., health, readiness, public docs). Return standardized 401/403 responses.
- Configuration and secrets: All security parameters (issuer, audience, JWKS URL, token leeway, required scopes, TLS materials) are externalized in Dropwizard configuration and loaded from secure secret stores/environment at runtime.
- Operational hardening: Enable CORS only where necessary with strict origins. Add security headers (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options/COEP as applicable). Log authentication failures without sensitive data. Monitor token validation errors and certificate expiry.

This decision avoids bespoke security filters, leverages Dropwizard’s mature integration with Jersey, and keeps the service stateless and horizontally scalable.

We will adopt Elasticsearch 8.x as the primary distributed search and analytics engine for text search, relevance ranking, faceting, aggregations, and near real-time log/metric analytics across product domains. We will use Elastic Cloud (managed) with a production deployment in multi-AZ, hot-warm-cold architecture, and a separate staging environment. Core usage will include: keyword and BM25-based full-text search with custom analyzers, autocomplete via edge n-grams, aggregations for facets and dashboards, and time-series indexing for observability data.

We will standardize on one logical cluster per environment with segregated indices and strict RBAC for multi-tenant needs. Index design will follow ILM with hot (search), warm (less frequent), and cold/frozen tiers; rollover by size/time; compressed stored fields; and minimal mappings with explicit types to avoid dynamic mapping explosion. Ingest pipelines will handle normalization, enrichment (e.g., synonyms), and PII redaction where required.

Operationally, we will enable security by default (TLS in-transit, encrypted at rest, API key-based service access), snapshot backups to cloud object storage with daily retention, and observability via Elastic’s monitoring with alerting on cluster health, indexing latency, and search p95. Capacity will autoscale within preset bounds; we will provision dedicated master nodes and consider searchable snapshots for cost efficiency on historical data.

Clients will integrate via the official language SDKs, with query construction centralized in a shared library to enforce consistency and guardrails. We will not mix Elasticsearch with transactional source-of-truth responsibilities; authoritative data remains in relational stores, with Elasticsearch fed by CDC/ETL pipelines ensuring eventual consistency and idempotent updates.

Adopt AWS Image Builder as the standard mechanism for creating, hardening, testing, versioning, and distributing Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) across all environments and accounts. We will define Infrastructure-as-Code pipelines (CloudFormation/Terraform) that provision Image Builder components, recipes, and pipelines per image family (base OS, app runtime, bastion, tools), supporting both x86_64 and arm64.

Key parameters of the decision:
- Golden AMI pipeline: start from AWS-managed or our baseline hardened image; apply CIS/aligned hardening, security agents, and configuration via Image Builder components; run automated validation (Inspector, custom tests) before distribution.
- Versioning and promotion: semantic versioning per image recipe; promotion gates from dev → stage → prod via manual approval or automated policy; publish latest AMI IDs to SSM Parameter Store for consumption by EC2 Launch Templates/Auto Scaling.
- Multi-account/region distribution: use Image Builder distribution settings to replicate AMIs with KMS-encrypted snapshots and controlled sharing to target accounts/regions.
- Compliance and provenance: sign images and attest build metadata; enforce build-time SBOM generation; store build artifacts and logs in S3/CloudWatch; notify via SNS on success/failure; maintain audit trail.
- Lifecycle management: retain N latest versions per family; automate deprecation and snapshot cleanup; document rollback policy to previous known-good AMI versions.
- Security and access: least-privilege IAM roles for build, distribution, and parameter write; restrict component changes via code review; secrets sourced from SSM and never baked as plaintext.
- Integration: replace legacy manual/Packer-Jenkins baking for supported images; exceptions require architectural approval and documented equivalence for testing and compliance.

This decision standardizes AMI management, reduces drift, and ensures repeatable, compliant, and observable image delivery.

## Decision
Adopt PostgreSQL as the primary OLTP datastore using a normalized relational schema with explicit foreign keys, indexes, and constraints. Operate on a managed service (e.g., AWS RDS/Aurora or GCP Cloud SQL) with Multi-AZ/high-availability enabled, automated daily backups, and point‑in‑time recovery. Use server‑side encryption at rest (KMS-managed) and TLS in transit.

Employ a single database and shared schema with a tenant_id column for soft multi‑tenancy; enforce row‑level security (RLS) for application isolation. Reserve schema-per-environment (dev/staging/prod) and separate physical databases per environment. Define stable primary keys as UUIDv7; use bigserial only for internal surrogate needs. Apply time‑based partitioning on high‑volume tables to control index sizes and retention.

Set default isolation to READ COMMITTED with explicit transactions for multi-statement operations; use optimistic locking (version column) for concurrent updates. Introduce a lightweight connection pooler (e.g., PgBouncer) in transaction mode to cap application connections. Manage schema changes with versioned, forward-only migrations (Flyway or Liquibase) gated by CI/CD.

Create at least one asynchronous read replica for reporting and read-heavy workloads; route read-only traffic via application-level routing. Enable pg_stat_statements and query logging; enforce query timeouts and statement limits. Implement regular VACUUM/ANALYZE (auto-tuned), data retention policies, and periodic integrity checks. Secrets are stored in the platform secret manager; access is restricted via least-privilege roles and application-specific DB users.

Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document all significant architectural decisions.

- Repository location: version-controlled alongside code in docs/adr/, committed to main branches.
- Format: Markdown files, sequentially numbered (e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md), one decision per file, with sections: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives, References, Owners, Date.
- Status workflow: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded. Accepted ADRs are immutable; changes occur via a new ADR that explicitly supersedes prior ones.
- Scope: Decisions with lasting impact on architecture, quality attributes, cross-cutting concerns, external interfaces, data models, security, deployment, or cost. Team-level or trivial implementation choices are excluded unless they have systemic impact.
- Process: ADRs are created when a decision is identified, submitted via pull request, reviewed by designated architecture reviewers, and approved before or with the implementing change. Each PR that implements a significant decision must reference an ADR. Link ADRs to related issues, RFCs, and design docs; cross-reference superseded/superseding ADRs.
- Tooling: Prefer adr-tools or equivalent helpers for consistent naming and indexing. Maintain an index (docs/adr/README.md) generated or updated as part of CI.
- Visibility and compliance: CI checks validate ADR presence for flagged changes and verify links. ADRs are included in release notes when relevant and surfaced in onboarding materials.
- Ownership: The Architecture group stewards the process; decision owners are accountable for completeness and clarity.

## Decision
We will not permit direct Kubernetes API access from application workloads. Only designated platform components (e.g., GitOps controllers, autoscalers, admission controllers, operator reconcilers) and platform operators may interact with the Kubernetes API, and only with least-privilege, namespace-scoped RBAC.

Application teams will manage desired state declaratively via GitOps and/or platform-provided CRDs and APIs. Any need for imperative or programmatic interaction with cluster resources must be implemented in approved controllers/operators managed by the platform team.

Exceptions require a formal security review and a dedicated ADR. Approved exceptions must:
- Use dedicated, short-lived, namespaced service accounts with BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume and audience scoping.
- Be constrained by NetworkPolicies that explicitly allow egress only to the API server.
- Be governed by OPA Gatekeeper/Kyverno policies and labeled/annotated for audit.
- Use client-go (or equivalent) with exponential backoff, timeouts, and idempotent design.

Enforcement measures:
- Deny mounting kubeconfigs or long-lived static credentials into pods; prohibit cluster-admin bindings for service accounts.
- Enable admission policies to block pods requesting broad RBAC or unrestricted API access unless explicitly approved.
- Rotate tokens automatically; disable legacy service account token volume; prohibit hostPath mounts that could expose credentials.
- Centralize and retain API audit logs; alert on privilege escalations and cross-namespace access.
- Restrict API server exposure to private networks/VPN, protected by mTLS and IP allowlists; no public internet access.
- For multi-cluster operations, use a gateway/aggregator with per-cluster scoped credentials; no cross-cluster wildcard permissions.

Operational guardrails:
- Secrets and kubeconfigs must never be stored in source control or environment variables.
- Access reviews occur quarterly; RBAC drift is remediated automatically.
- Break-glass procedures exist for incident response with time-bound, audited elevation.

This decision reduces blast radius, enforces least privilege, improves auditability, and standardizes cluster interactions through controlled, declarative interfaces.

Adopt Python as the primary implementation language for application services, automation, data processing, and orchestration across the codebase. Standardize on CPython 3.13 for new development, with a compatibility floor of 3.11 where required by third‑party dependencies; retire 3.10 and earlier. All projects will use pyproject.toml (PEP 621) with Poetry/Hatch for builds and dependency management; ruff, black, and isort for linting/formatting; pytest for testing; and mypy/pyright with Pydantic v2 for runtime/data validation and static typing. Async services will use FastAPI + asyncio/uvloop; CLI tools will use Typer. Packaging will produce wheels and Docker images based on debian-slim; Alpine is disallowed for Python images.

Performance-sensitive paths will be profiled and, where needed, accelerated via vectorized libraries (NumPy/Pandas/Polars), multiprocessing/async IO, or native extensions (Cython or Rust via PyO3/maturin) behind stable Python interfaces. Long‑running CPU tasks must be offloaded to workers; IO-bound tasks should be asynchronous. Interoperability with non-Python components will use OpenAPI/REST or gRPC and Kafka/Event streams as applicable.

Security and supply chain: lock files are mandatory with hashes; vulnerability scanning (pip-audit/OSV), dependency review, and Bandit are required in CI. Images must be distroless or non-root containers with minimal OS packages. Observability: OpenTelemetry for traces/metrics/logs and standard structured logging.

Environment management will use uv/venv for local development and reproducible CI; deterministic builds and caching are required. Deprecation policy follows upstream Python EOL minus three months; library upgrades occur quarterly with automated compatibility testing. This decision centralizes skills, tooling, and ecosystem leverage while allowing targeted optimization where needed.

We will adopt CSS Modules as the default approach for component-level styling to ensure style encapsulation and prevent selector conflicts. Each component will have at most one co-located stylesheet named <Component>.module.css (or .module.scss where Sass is warranted), imported directly by the component. Class names are locally scoped by default; use :global only for intentional framework/global overrides. Global, cross-cutting styles (CSS reset, typography base, layout primitives, and third-party overrides) will reside in a limited set of global stylesheets (e.g., globals.css) and design tokens (CSS custom properties) defined at :root and/or via data-theme attributes.

Build configuration will generate human-readable class names in development and hashed class names in production. Our bundler (Vite/Webpack) will be configured accordingly, with source maps enabled in development. TypeScript projects will use typed CSS Modules (e.g., with a plugin or generated .d.ts) to provide autocomplete and type safety for class names.

Guidelines:
- One module per component; prefer BEM-like class names for readability within a module.
- Use CSS variables for theming and runtime toggles; avoid module-level hardcoding of theme values.
- Prefer composition via className arrays over deep selector chains; avoid element/type selectors leaking styles.
- Keep animations, keyframes, and media queries inside the module to retain locality.
- Testing should target data-testid or role-based selectors; avoid relying on generated class names.
- Use :global sparingly for required external library hooks or page-level wrappers.
- Migrate existing styles incrementally, starting with leaf components; shared legacy global rules will be reduced as modules are introduced.

Exceptions require review if a component must rely on utility-first or inline styles for performance-critical paths.

We will standardize on adr-tools to author, index, and manage Architectural Decision Records across all services and libraries, using a repository-local custom template to enforce our required structure and metadata.

- Tooling
  - Use adr-tools (Nat Pryce) pinned to version >= 3.0.
  - Provide Makefile/NPM scripts wrappers (adr:new, adr:link, adr:accept, adr:supersede) for consistent usage.
  - Store ADRs under docs/adr with sequential, monotonically increasing numbers; numbers are never reused.
  - Commit the custom template at docs/adr/.adr-template.md and configure ADR_TEMPLATE accordingly.

- Template
  - Required sections: Title, Status, Date, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives Considered, Trade-offs, Stakeholders, Related ADRs/Links, Implementation Notes, Owner.
  - Front-matter metadata: id, authors, reviewers, tags, component, scope.
  - Status lifecycle: Draft → Proposed → Accepted | Rejected → Deprecated | Superseded.
  - Include “Supersedes” and “Superseded by” link conventions.
  - Enforce concise Decision (2–400 words) and explicit consequences.

- Process
  - All architectural changes MUST be captured via adr-tools; PRs introducing changes must include or update an ADR.
  - Reviews: at least one architect and one owning team reviewer must approve ADRs before marking Accepted.
  - Superseding requires creating a new ADR linking both directions and updating statuses accordingly.
  - ADRs are immutable once Accepted except for metadata fixes; changes require a new ADR.

- Governance and enforcement
  - Add pre-commit hook to validate template conformance (section presence, status values, link integrity).
  - CI job validates ADR directory, numbering, status transitions, and cross-links; builds an index README.md via adr-tools generate.
  - Repository CONTRIBUTING.md updated with commands and workflow.
  - For multi-repo programs, each repo maintains local ADRs; cross-repo decisions are mirrored in the program-level architecture repo and linked.

- Migration
  - Existing ADRs will be renumbered as needed and normalized to the new template in a one-time migration PR; original titles/dates preserved.
  - Documentation will reference docs/adr as the single source of truth.

## Decision
We will capture all architectural decisions as Markdown ADRs in the project repository to ensure traceability, reviewability, and long-term maintainability.

- Location and naming: Store ADRs under /docs/adr with sequentially numbered filenames (e.g., 0001-use-markdown-adrs.md) and kebab-case titles.
- Template: Use the MADR template (Context, Decision, Status, Consequences, Alternatives, References) with YAML front matter (id, title, status, date, authors, related).
- Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded. Accepted ADRs are immutable; changes require a new ADR that supersedes the old one (typos/formatting excepted).
- Scope: One ADR per decision. Decisions apply to the whole system unless explicitly scoped to a subsystem. Cross-reference related ADRs.
- Process: Create/modify ADRs via pull requests. Require at least one architect reviewer (Architecture Guild) and relevant SMEs. Capture rationale and trade-offs; keep concise (<1 page when feasible).
- Tooling: Permit diagrams via Mermaid code blocks or linked images stored in-repo. Enforce markdown linting and template compliance in CI. Optionally generate a static index (e.g., mkdocs) but Markdown remains the source of truth.
- Discoverability: Maintain an index README in /docs/adr listing ADRs by status and topic. Link ADRs from relevant code/docs.
- Version control: ADRs live with code; releases snapshot decision state. Use tags to trace which ADRs apply to a given release.

We will implement a centralized, policy-driven managed domain verification and blocking mechanism across all apps.

- Verification: Domains must be verified via both (a) DNS TXT record with a signed token issued by our control plane and (b) HTTPS well-known endpoint serving the same token over TLS. Verification succeeds only if both methods agree and the certificate chain is valid.
- Management: An organization-wide allowlist and blocklist will be maintained in a central service, configurable via admin console and MDM. Apps will consume a signed, versioned policy bundle at startup and periodically (default 24h).
- Enforcement: Apps may initiate network requests only to verified, allowed domains. Non-verified or blocked domains are fail-closed for privileged operations and PII exfiltration paths; non-critical features may degrade gracefully with user messaging. Hard-block with telemetry for explicit blocklisted domains.
- Caching and revalidation: Local cache with short TTLs and ETag support; immediate revocation via push when risk is elevated. Domains are revalidated at least weekly or upon cert change.
- Environments: Separate policy bundles for prod, staging, and dev. Dev builds allow a scoped, signed local override with prominent UI watermarking.
- Observability: All allow/block decisions are logged with domain, reason, and policy version; aggregates feed a dashboard and alerting.
- Security: Policies and tokens are signed and time-bound; transport uses mTLS from apps where supported. Optional certificate pinning for high-risk domains.
- Rollout: Phased rollout with monitor-only mode, then soft-block, then hard-block.

- Format: Markdown using the MADR template (Context, Decision, Status, Consequences, Alternatives, References). Keep ADRs concise and self-contained.

  - Review: At least one architecture owner and one domain engineer must approve. Security and SRE review required for relevant topics.
  - Accept/Reject: Update status on merge; record rationale and consequences.
