- Use existing design system components; no new third-party search UI libraries. Leverage our shared focus state, tokens, and dark mode support.
- Accessibility: ARIA combobox pattern, proper roles for listbox/options, labels, live region for results count, high-contrast compliant, and full keyboard support. Provide Cmd/Ctrl+K shortcut.
- Performance: lazy-load search module on first focus or Cmd/Ctrl+K; cache suggestions per query prefix for 5 minutes; cap concurrent requests; cancel in-flight requests on new input.
- Privacy/Security: sanitize/encode input; limit payload size; log queries only with redaction rules; use GET for suggestions and POST for advanced filters; enforce rate limits and WAF rules.
- i18n/l10n: placeholder, empty states, and suggestion categories localized; support RTL layouts.
- Telemetry: track focus, suggestion impressions, selections, submit events, and latency; add feature flag for phased rollout with A/B guardrails.
- Failure modes: graceful degradation to server-side search results on errors or offline; display non-intrusive error/empty states.
- Ownership: Web Platform team maintains UI; Search Service team owns suggest API. Continuous contract tests ensure compatibility.

We will standardize on OCI image labels (annotations) as the authoritative store for non-sensitive build and release metadata on all container images. Labels will follow org.opencontainers.image.* for common fields (title, description, url, source, revision, version, created, licenses, authors, documentation, vendor) and a company namespace (io.company.*) for build/runtime integration (e.g., io.company.ci.build-url, io.company.ci.pipeline-id, io.company.vcs.branch, io.company.security.scan-id, io.company.meta-schema=v1). SBOMs and provenance will be referenced via labels pointing to registry artifacts/URIs (e.g., io.company.sbom.ref=oci://registry/org/app:sbom, io.company.provenance.ref=oci://…); we will not embed large artifacts in labels.

Labels will be injected at build time via Dockerfile LABEL or build tooling flags (e.g., buildx/buildkit --label). CI pipelines will populate and validate a mandatory label set; builds lacking required labels will fail. Admission/scanning policies will verify labels at deploy time. No secrets, tokens, or PII are permitted in labels; values must be concise (respecting OCI/Docker size constraints). For backward compatibility, we may emit legacy label-schema.org labels where external consumers require them.

This decision ensures consistent traceability, discoverability, and automation hooks across registries and runtimes with minimal image size impact. Governance for keys, formats, and retention is owned by the platform team; schema changes will be versioned under io.company.meta-schema.

We will integrate server-side rendered Termbox HTML into the page ParserOutput and persist it in ParserCache to eliminate redundant SSR calls and reduce TTFB on entity pages. The cached entry will be keyed by the entity revision ID, user interface language (including variant), Termbox bundle version hash, and a stable feature flag set, avoiding any per-user personalization to maintain high cache hit rates. The Termbox markup, required i18n strings, module styles, and boot configuration will be attached via ParserOutput extension data and module registrations; the page HTML will include a stable placeholder that is populated from the cached SSR fragment.

On cache misses, the renderer is invoked synchronously with a strict timeout; if it fails or times out, we fall back to client-side rendering while still storing a negative-cache marker to prevent thundering herds. ParserCache entries will inherit standard TTL and eviction policy; explicit invalidation will occur on entity term changes, sitelink changes that affect Termbox, and Termbox deployment (bundle hash change). Language-scoped purges will be triggered only for affected languages to limit blast radius. We will not vary on cookies, user groups, or skin; skin-specific differences, if any, will be restricted to CSS to keep the HTML identical across skins.

To reduce fragmentation, we will: (a) cap language variants to the UI language and its fallback chain; (b) include a Termbox API schema/version token to avoid stale-contract issues; and (c) coalesce concurrent renders with a per-key mutex. Monitoring will track cache hit rate, SSR latency, and fallback frequency, with feature flag rollback if error budgets are exceeded.

## Decision
We will implement time-based data extraction using event_time as the primary filter, with a deterministic fallback to ingestion_time when event_time is missing or invalid. All timestamps will be stored, transmitted, and compared in UTC using ISO 8601 format with millisecond precision.

Extraction windows will be half-open [start_time, end_time), ensuring no overlaps or gaps across consecutive runs. Incremental extraction will use a persisted high-watermark cursor composed of (last_event_time, last_id) to prevent duplicates and omissions at window boundaries; results will be ordered by (event_time ASC, id ASC) to guarantee deterministic pagination and cursor advancement.

To address late-arriving data, each run will overlap the previous high-watermark by a configurable lateness interval L, with idempotent de-duplication based on a stable primary key (or content hash where keys are absent). L will be tuned per source and monitored.

Data stores will be partitioned and/or indexed by event_time (fallback ingestion_time) to enable efficient pruning. APIs and ETL jobs will accept required parameters start_time and end_time in UTC; end_time is exclusive. Timezone inputs are not accepted; conversion to UTC is the client’s responsibility.

If neither event_time nor ingestion_time is available, records are excluded and flagged. Changes to the primary time basis require schema migration and reindexing, and will be controlled via a feature flag with backfill procedures.

## Decision
Adopt RFC-compliant UUIDs for all telemetry identifiers, standardizing on UUID version 7 (time-ordered) per the latest RFC (or RFC 4122-compatible implementation if RFC 9562 support is unavailable). UUIDv7 improves write locality and query performance in time-indexed stores while maintaining 128-bit uniqueness. Where UUIDv7 is not supported in a runtime, fall back to UUIDv4 using a cryptographically secure PRNG.

Scope:
- Apply to event IDs, trace/correlation IDs, and session IDs across all services and data pipelines.
- Disallow semantic or personally identifiable data in IDs.

Format and storage:
- Use canonical 36-character string representation (8-4-4-4-12, lowercase hex) at interfaces; prefer 16-byte binary storage in databases and telemetry backends when supported.
- Preserve byte order per RFC to maintain time-ordering benefits of v7.

Generation:
- Generate IDs at the service boundary closest to event creation; do not accept client-supplied IDs unless validated as compliant.
- Use platform-standard, vetted libraries; require CSPRNGs and stable time sources (UTC). For v7, use monotonic time when available to avoid regressions.
- Provide shared utility packages in supported languages to ensure consistent behavior and validation.

Validation and governance:
- Add lint and runtime checks to reject non-compliant UUIDs at ingestion.
- Document and monitor collision/error rates; treat any anomaly as a P0 incident.
- Migration plan: existing IDs remain valid; new telemetry uses v7 when available. Mixed v4/v7 datasets are supported; ordering-sensitive workflows should prefer v7 fields.

Security and privacy:
- Do not encode business context in IDs.
- Treat IDs as non-secret but avoid exposing them in user-facing URLs unless necessary.

Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as the standard mechanism to capture and govern architectural decisions across all products and services.

- Template: Use MADR (Markdown Any Decision Records) v3.0 with sections: Context, Decision, Consequences, Options, Pros/Cons, and References.
- Location: Store ADRs in each repository under /docs/adr; organization-wide decisions live in a central architecture repo and are referenced from dependent repos.
- Format: Markdown, one decision per file, immutable once Accepted except via a Supersede ADR; include metadata header (ID, Title, Status, Date, Owners, Related).
- Naming/Indexing: 0001-title.md sequential numbering per repo; maintain an index.md for discoverability.
- Status lifecycle: Draft → Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded.
- Process:
  - Initiation via lightweight RFC or spike summary linked in “References.”
  - Proposal authored by decision owner(s) with options and trade-offs.
  - Review via PR with architecture guild approval (2 approvers, including domain architect).
  - Acceptance recorded by merging; changes require a new ADR that supersedes prior ones.
- Scope: Decisions with cross-team impact, tech choices, patterns, data contracts, APIs, security/privacy controls, SLAs/SLOs.
- Traceability: Link ADRs to epics, code (via permalinks), runbooks, and deployment configs.
- Automation: CI validates ADR linting, broken links, and index; label PRs touching ADRs.
- Communication: Announce Accepted ADRs in architecture channel; summarize in release notes.
- Ownership: System architect is custodian; each team maintains their repo ADRs.

## Decision

We will standardize on using only the Value projection for all read models, query endpoints, and downstream integrations. All existing and future read concerns will be satisfied through a single, canonical Value projection per domain aggregate, computed from authoritative sources and published to consumers. No separate Key, Envelope, or Hybrid projections will be produced, stored, or exposed.

- Scope:
  - Read models: replace multiple projection variants with a single, normalized Value projection.
  - APIs: return Value projection DTOs; deprecate endpoints exposing non-Value shapes.
  - Data pipelines: publish only Value projection topics/streams/tables; remove parallel projection feeds.
  - Storage: persist only Value projection materializations; eliminate redundant projection stores.

- Principles:
  - Source of truth remains the write model/event log; Value projections are derived, idempotent, and rebuildable.
  - Value projections must be complete for consumer needs, versioned, and backward compatible via additive evolution.
  - Deterministic computation and observability (metrics, lineage, checksums) are mandatory.

- Constraints:
  - No consumer may rely on non-Value payloads or projection-specific metadata; such needs must be modeled explicitly within the Value projection.
  - Ordering, time-travel, and debugging requirements are addressed via metadata fields included within the Value projection (e.g., version, lastUpdatedAt, eventSequence), not separate streams.

- Migration:
  - Freeze non-Value projections; introduce Value projection v1 alongside existing outputs.
  - Provide adapters for critical consumers during transition; schedule deprecation and removal after adoption thresholds.
  - Full backfill and parity validation prior to cutover; documented SLAs for rebuild and freshness.

- Acceptance:
  - All queries satisfied from Value projection with equal or better latency.
  - No consumer depends on deprecated projections.
  - Automated rebuild passes determinism and completeness checks.

## Decision
- We will adopt Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) as the canonical mechanism to capture, communicate, and govern significant technical and architectural decisions across all products and platforms.
- We will use the MADR template (v3.x) with minimal adaptation to ensure consistency and ease of authoring; alternative formats require Architecture Council approval.
- Location and naming: each codebase will maintain ADRs in repo at docs/adr with zero-padded sequential numbering (e.g., 0001-title.md) and stable permalinks. Cross-cutting decisions live in a central architecture repo and are referenced from dependent repos.
- Lifecycle and status: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded. Accepted ADRs are immutable; changes require a new ADR that supersedes the prior one. Rejected ADRs remain for traceability.
- Scope: An ADR is required for decisions that materially affect architecture, quality attributes, cost, risk, data/contract schemas, external interfaces, security/privacy posture, runtime topology, or vendor/OSS selections.
- Process: ADRs are introduced and reviewed via pull request. Required reviewers include at least one domain engineer, one architect, and security/ops as applicable. Each ADR must link to motivating issues, options considered, and consequences.
- Traceability: Code, infrastructure, and runbooks must reference relevant ADR IDs. Release notes will include ADR references for impactful changes.
- Tooling: adr-tools or equivalent is recommended but not mandatory. A CI check will verify ADR presence for labeled “architectural” changes.
- Discoverability: ADRs are indexed in a lightweight catalog and published to the internal docs portal; search is enabled by tags and metadata.
- This decision is effective immediately for new work and will be retroactively applied to major ongoing initiatives.

We will standardize on the in-tree Kubernetes AWS EBS storage driver for all stateful workloads in current clusters. The in-tree plugin meets our present requirements (dynamic provisioning, gp2/gp3 volumes, encryption-by-default, topology-aware single-AZ binding) while minimizing operational overhead and avoiding additional controllers, sidecars, and IAM surfaces introduced by CSI at this time.

Scope:
- Use Kubernetes-provided in-tree aws-ebs plugin with StorageClasses for gp3 (default) and gp2 (legacy).
- Dynamic provisioning via in-tree provisioner; volume binding mode WaitForFirstConsumer to ensure AZ alignment.
- Default KMS encryption enabled; parameters for IOPS/throughput on gp3 where needed.

Constraints and implications:
- Volumes are AZ-scoped; stateful sets must be pinned to the same AZ as the PV.
- Access mode limited to RWO; no multi-attach read-write.
- Advanced CSI-only capabilities (online expansion edge-cases, snapshots, volume cloning) are not required by current workloads and will not be supported until migration.
- The in-tree driver is deprecated upstream; support depends on our managed Kubernetes versions.

Operational decisions:
- Maintain clusters on versions that continue to support the in-tree driver and enable CSIMigrationAWS=true as a no-op compatibility guard.
- Tag all volumes for ownership and cost allocation; enforce encryption and deletion policies via admission controls.
- Monitor EBS and PVC metrics; enforce quotas and StorageClass defaults via policy.

Migration plan:
- Reevaluate upon upgrading to a Kubernetes version where in-tree removal is imminent or when snapshot/clone features become required.
- Prepare a controlled migration to the AWS EBS CSI driver using CSIMigration to ensure zero-downtime PV handover, validated in staging before production rollout.

We will implement a unified text extraction service that uses a dual-path strategy: (1) native text extraction for born-digital documents and (2) OCR for scanned or image-only content. For born-digital PDFs, Office documents, and HTML, we extract text and basic structure via Apache Tika (PDFBox for PDFs; POI for Office; HTML parser), enriched with per-block/page coordinates when available. For pages lacking sufficient selectable text (configurable threshold), we fall back to OCR.

OCR will use Tesseract 5 with LSTM models and language packs (initially en, es, fr; extensible via configuration). A preprocessing pipeline (OpenCV) will perform de-skew, binarization, denoise, contrast normalization, and adaptive thresholding. PDFs requiring OCR are rasterized with Poppler at 300–400 DPI; large pages will be tiled to manage memory. The OCR engine is abstracted behind a provider interface to allow swapping in managed services (AWS Textract, Google Vision) per policy, cost, or accuracy requirements.

The service exposes an idempotent API that accepts documents via upload or URI, enqueues jobs, and streams progress. Outputs conform to a normalized schema: document > pages > blocks > lines > spans with text, language, confidence, reading order, and bounding boxes; plus a plain-text concatenation. We cache results keyed by content hash, persist intermediate artifacts for observability, and emit quality metrics (OCR confidence, coverage ratio, error rates).

Operationally, workers are containerized, sandboxed, and resource-capped; timeouts, size limits, and content-type validation are enforced. Sensitive content is processed in-region; no data is logged beyond telemetry. Tests will include golden files and benchmarks across representative corpora. This approach balances accuracy, cost, extensibility, and maintainability while providing a stable contract to downstream consumers.

Adopt Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for all deployable artifacts and public APIs. Production releases are immutable and identified by git tags vX.Y.Z; build metadata includes the commit SHA and build number. Only tagged commits produce release artifacts; all other commits produce ephemeral preview builds.

Use trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches and mandatory CI checks. Release candidates are cut from main and stabilized behind feature flags. The same signed, immutable artifact is promoted across environments (dev → staging → prod) via the CI/CD pipeline; no rebuilds occur between promotions.

Container images are published to the registry with both vX.Y.Z and sha-<commit> tags. Helm charts/manifests are versioned and stored alongside code; infra-as-code pins artifact versions.

Employ canary deployments by default with automated health checks and SLO-based guardrails; blue/green is used when canarying is not feasible. Rollbacks are executed by redeploying the last known good artifact; data changes follow expand/contract patterns to keep rollbacks safe.

Database migrations are forward-only, idempotent, and deployed with application releases. Backward-compatible schemas are maintained for at least one minor version. Destructive changes require deprecation windows and are gated behind ops approvals.

Public APIs are versioned (v1, v2) via URI or negotiated headers. MINOR and PATCH are backward compatible; MAJOR allows breaking changes. Deprecations include documented timelines and runtime warnings. We support the current and previous minor versions (N and N-1) in production.

Configuration is externalized via environment variables and secrets management; no environment-specific code changes are allowed. Feature flags control runtime exposure and allow progressive delivery and safe toggling.

All releases are changelogged, signed, and traceable to source. Observability (logs, metrics, traces) is required for promotion and automated rollback decisions.

## Decision
Adopt New Relic as the primary platform to collect, analyze, and present web analytics, leveraging New Relic Browser (RUM), APM, and NRDB dashboards.

- Scope: Use New Relic Browser Pro with SPA monitoring to capture page views, route changes, Core Web Vitals (LCP, FID/INP, CLS), JS errors, resource timings, and session traces. Correlate frontend telemetry with backend APM via distributed tracing for end-to-end user journey insights.
- Instrumentation: Embed the browser agent snippet via the web app shell; enable auto-instrumentation for supported frameworks. Emit custom events/attributes (e.g., tenantId, userRole, featureFlag, experimentVariant) via addPageAction and Telemetry SDK. Standardize tags (env, service, version) to support dashboards and SLOs.
- Presentation: Build role-based New Relic dashboards for Product (engagement funnels, cohorts), Engineering (performance, errors, Core Web Vitals), and Operations (availability/SLOs). Expose curated views via New Relic One and optionally embed via NerdGraph API into the internal portal.
- Governance and privacy: Do not collect PII; hash or drop user identifiers; truncate URLs/query params; honor consent/Do Not Track; anonymize IP where required; comply with regional data residency. Configure event sampling and retention to meet cost and compliance targets.
- Alerts and SLOs: Define SLOs for page-load, interaction latency, error rate, and availability; configure alerts and anomaly detection on NRQL queries. Integrate notifications with Slack/PagerDuty.
- Rollout: Start with non-prod, validate metrics parity and overhead (<2% load impact), then enable in production behind a feature flag. Provide dashboards and documentation for stakeholders.
- Exclusions: Retain existing marketing analytics (e.g., GA) for attribution; New Relic is the source of truth for performance and operational web analytics.

## Decision
Adopt Relay (Relay Modern) as the standard GraphQL client for all React front-end applications, foregoing Apollo for new development and phasing out existing Apollo usage. We will use Relay 15+ with React 18+, Relay Hooks API, relay-compiler for static analysis/codegen, normalized cache, and persisted queries enabled via the build pipeline.

The GraphQL schema must conform to Relay conventions: stable globally unique IDs (Node interface), Connections spec for pagination, server-driven pagination fields (edges/node/pageInfo), and fields suitable for @required/@defer/@stream where appropriate. The build will integrate relay-compiler, artifact generation, and CI checks to prevent schema/fragment drift. Type safety will be enforced via generated TypeScript types from Relay artifacts.

Data-fetching will be fragment co-located with components, using Relay environment per app, with network layer supporting persisted queries, authentication, retry, and error mapping. Pagination will use Relay’s Connection handlers; mutations will use updater functions for deterministic cache updates. Suspense-first patterns and incremental delivery (@defer/@stream) will be adopted where UX benefits.

Apollo is deprecated for new features; existing Apollo code will be migrated to Relay as touched by roadmap items, with an explicit deprecation timeline and compatibility shims limited to read-only paths during transition. Non-GraphQL data needs will use fetch/REST alongside Relay without introducing alternative GraphQL clients.

We will not require React for the Publisher-facing integration. The Publisher SDK and UI embeds will be framework-agnostic, implemented in vanilla TypeScript and distributed as lightweight ES modules (with a UMD fallback) to run on any site regardless of tech stack. Interactive units will be exposed as Web Components (Custom Elements) using Shadow DOM for style and DOM isolation, avoiding React runtime, JSX, or VDOM dependencies on Publisher pages. Communication with our backend and cross-frame coordination will use standardized browser APIs (postMessage, fetch, Events), and any optional overlays/portals will be pure DOM. We will provide thin optional wrappers for React, Vue, and Angular for developer ergonomics, but the core remains framework-neutral.

Build and delivery will optimize for minimal footprint and compatibility: no peer dependency on React, browsers targeted with transpiled ES2017+, CSS scoping within Shadow DOM, and graceful degradation for older browsers via documented polyfills. Styling will be themable via CSS custom properties and component attributes. Public API will be stable and declarative (data attributes/config object) to simplify copy‑paste integration. QA will include cross-framework and no-framework test matrices. This ensures the widest adoption by Publishers, avoids version conflicts, reduces bundle size, and decouples our release cadence from any specific frontend framework.

We will enforce namespace-scoped access to CloudHSM by constraining egress at both the Kubernetes and VPC layers, so only workloads in approved namespaces can reach the HSM ENIs.

- Use a default-deny egress posture cluster-wide and define explicit NetworkPolicies in allowed namespaces that permit egress only to the CloudHSM ENI IPs/ports.
- In EKS clusters that support Security Groups for Pods (SGP), assign a dedicated pod security group to each approved namespace via namespace labels and admission policies. The CloudHSM security group will allow ingress only from these pod security groups. Non-approved namespaces will not receive an SGP permitted by CloudHSM and will be blocked at the VPC layer.
- In clusters or environments without SGP, schedule HSM-enabled workloads onto a dedicated node group with a distinct node security group that is allowed by the CloudHSM security group. Enforce namespace-to-nodeGroup affinity via taints/tolerations and namespace-scoped admission controls to prevent other namespaces from landing on those nodes.
- Maintain a static allowlist of CloudHSM ENI IPs and ports in NetworkPolicies, updated automatically through IaC when HSM clusters scale or rotate ENIs.
- Block all egress to 0.0.0.0/0 from non-approved namespaces; only the minimal HSM endpoints and necessary AWS control-plane endpoints are allowed.
- Add runtime guardrails: validating admission policies to require the correct SGP/affinity for workloads declaring HSM access, and CI/CD checks ensuring NetworkPolicies and SG rules are present before deploying HSM clients.
- Monitor and audit with VPC Flow Logs and CNI metrics; alert on denied or unexpected egress to HSM from unapproved namespaces.

This decision provides layered enforcement (K8s policy + VPC SGs), namespace scoping, and clear operational controls while minimizing blast radius and accidental exposure.

Adopt a thin, standards-first authentication client that wraps a mature, FIPS-capable OAuth 2.1/OpenID Connect library and enforces secure-by-default flows. The client will support Authorization Code with PKCE for public clients (web SPA, mobile, desktop) and Authorization Code with client secret or mTLS for confidential clients (backend services), with optional DPoP where supported. Legacy Resource Owner Password flow and implicit grant are not supported; existing uses will migrate via an adapter layer and deprecation schedule.

The client will auto-discover provider metadata via OIDC Discovery, support multiple issuers/tenants via per-issuer configuration, and expose a minimal, consistent API for login, logout, token acquisition, and token refresh. Token storage will use platform-secure stores (Web: HTTP-only, same-site cookies with BFF pattern preferred over SPA token storage; Mobile/Desktop: OS keystore/Keychain; Server: in-memory or HSM-backed). Refresh-token rotation, replay detection, and automatic revocation handling are built-in. System browser or ASWebAuthenticationSession/Custom Tabs will be used; embedded webviews are disallowed.

The client will provide pluggable interceptors for attaching access tokens to HTTP requests, automatic token renewal, clock-skew handling, exponential backoff, and circuit-breaking. Telemetry hooks (metrics, structured logs, traces) and PII-safe error surfaces are included. WebAuthn/FIDO2 and MFA are supported via OIDC flows. Cryptography uses vetted primitives only; no custom crypto.

Initial implementations target TypeScript (web/Node), Kotlin (Android), Swift (iOS), and Java/.NET (server). Versioned configuration and feature flags enable gradual rollout. Security reviews and compliance gates (linting, SAST/DAST) are mandatory before release.

We will standardize on an Nginx configuration optimized for PHP-FPM and treat PHP-FPM as the only dynamic runtime behind Nginx for this service. Nginx will proxy PHP requests to PHP-FPM via a Unix domain socket by default (with optional TCP support for distributed deployments), use a canonical location ~ \.php$ block with try_files to prevent path traversal, and pass a minimal, explicit set of fastcgi_param variables (SCRIPT_FILENAME, DOCUMENT_ROOT, QUERY_STRING, REQUEST_METHOD, CONTENT_TYPE, CONTENT_LENGTH, SCRIPT_NAME, PATH_INFO). We will enforce security and correctness by disabling execution in upload/cache directories, denying access to hidden files and .php in media directories, and preventing direct access to .user.ini and composer/VC files.

Performance tuning will include: enabling sendfile, tcp_nopush, and gzip for static assets; serving static/content-addressed assets directly from Nginx with long-lived immutable caching; disabling caching for dynamic PHP endpoints; setting client_max_body_size per app requirements; tuning fastcgi_buffers, fastcgi_read_timeout, and keepalive for PHP-FPM throughput; and enabling microcaching only for explicitly whitelisted safe GET endpoints via dedicated locations.

Configuration will be modular: a shared base snippet (fastcgi_php.conf) and security/performance snippets included by all server blocks; per-app server blocks define server_name, root, and route-specific overrides. Error handling will use centralized error pages and structured access/error logs. Health and readiness endpoints will be served by Nginx (for liveness) and proxied to PHP-FPM (for readiness) as appropriate.

Non-PHP backends are out of scope for this configuration; separate server blocks/templates will be created if needed. The configuration will be codified as versioned templates and validated in CI with syntax tests and containerized smoke tests.

We will implement deterministic, idempotent, and distributed-safe mail queue cleanup via lease-based shard workers with explicit TTLs and state transitions.

- Each queued mail item will carry enqueue_ts, deliver_by_ts (expiration), max_attempts, attempts, and last_heartbeat_ts. Items exceeding deliver_by_ts or max_attempts transition to DEAD_LETTER; undelivered items with stale in-flight status (no heartbeat > processing_timeout) revert to READY.
- Cleanup will be executed by horizontally scalable workers that acquire leases per shard/partition using platform-native leader election (Kubernetes Lease/Endpoints) or database/Redis advisory locks as fallback. Only the lease holder processes a shard; leases are short-lived and renewed.
- Workers perform bounded, index-backed scans by status and cutoff timestamps in small batches, using compare-and-set updates on version fields to ensure idempotency and avoid double transitions under race.
- Expired or permanently failed items are moved to a DLQ with metadata for diagnosis and retained for a configurable period (default 14 days) before hard purge. Purge runs as a separate, throttled phase.
- Heartbeats mark active processing; lack of heartbeat beyond processing_timeout triggers safe reclamation. Visibility timeouts and processing heartbeats are enforced by the sender service; cleanup only reconciles stragglers.
- All transitions are audit-logged and metrified (counts, latency, reclaimed, DLQ, purged). Rate limiting and backpressure protect primary send throughput. Configuration (timeouts, batch sizes, retention) is centrally managed and hot-reloadable.
- This approach is storage-agnostic (RDBMS/Kafka/Redis queues) and ensures correctness, operability, and minimal duplicate sends in a distributed environment.

We will name each preservation object solely by the FileSet content digest, making the system content-addressable. The object key will be the SHA-256 digest of the FileSet’s canonical content and ordering, encoded as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. No additional metadata (e.g., work identifier, version, environment, timestamps, extensions) will be included in the name. The canonical digest is the already-established FileSet digest used for fixity/integrity; its definition (file ordering, path normalization, excluded metadata) is fixed and versioned in code.

Implications:
- Immutability and idempotence: any reingest of identical content yields the same key; metadata-only changes do not alter the name.
- Deduplication: identical FileSets map to the same object, preventing redundant storage.
- Consistency across environments: names are stable in all deployments and storage backends.

Specification:
- Algorithm: SHA-256 over the canonical FileSet representation.
- Encoding: lowercase hex (64 chars). Storage paths may fan out using leading prefix shards (e.g., ab/cd/<digest>), but the digest remains the name-of-record.
- Collision policy: if an incoming digest matches an existing object with different computed content, treat as integrity error and halt; if content matches, treat as duplicate and short-circuit storage.
- Scope: applies to all preservation backends (e.g., S3 keys, Glacier, tape indexes) and internal registries.
- Backward compatibility: existing objects retain legacy names; we maintain a lookup mapping legacy identifiers to the digest-based name for resolution. New ingests adopt the new scheme.
- Effective on next release; validation added to reject non-deterministic inputs to the digest.

We will standardize on OpenID Connect (OIDC) over OAuth 2.1 using a managed Identity Provider (e.g., Azure AD/Entra ID or Okta) as the single source of identity. Browser and native clients use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE; confidential backend services use Client Credentials for machine-to-machine.

Access tokens are JWTs, validated locally via IdP JWKS; they are short-lived (5–15 minutes) and contain only non-sensitive claims. Refresh tokens are used only by confidential clients and the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF); they are rotated with automatic revocation on reuse. Public browser clients do not store tokens; instead, a BFF issues HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=strict cookies and maintains server-side sessions to mitigate XSS/CSRF. CSRF protection is enforced via same-site cookies plus anti-CSRF tokens; CORS is restricted to trusted origins.

Authorization is enforced by a layered model:
- Coarse-grained access via OAuth scopes.
- Application-level RBAC via roles delivered as claims.
- Optional fine-grained ABAC via claims/policies, with centralized policy evaluation where appropriate.

Service-to-service calls require mTLS and JWT bearer tokens issued by the IdP (or workload identity) with audience constraints. Least-privilege scopes are required for all clients.

MFA is enforced by policy at the IdP; passwordless (WebAuthn/FIDO2) is supported where available. Account lifecycle (provisioning, deactivation) is delegated to the IdP. Break-glass access is provided via a minimal, audited local admin path.

Secrets are stored in the enterprise secret manager; keys use managed KMS. Comprehensive audit logging (auth events, admin actions, policy decisions) is enabled and retained per compliance. Session/logout use RP-initiated and back-channel logout where supported.

This decision prioritizes security, interoperability, and operability while minimizing custom auth logic in application code.

## Decision

Adopt GraphQL as the primary client-facing API for product and partner integrations, exposing a single versioned schema as the contract for all read/write operations. Implement a schema-first workflow with SDL as the source of truth, validated via CI, and generated types for server and clients. Use Apollo GraphQL (Gateway + Federation) to compose a unified graph from modular subgraphs owned by domain teams. Employ Apollo Server for Node.js-based resolvers, with DataLoader for request-scoped batching and caching to mitigate N+1 issues.

Retain REST endpoints only where clearly superior:
- Webhooks (incoming/outgoing)
- Large file uploads/downloads and streaming
- Health checks and internal service-to-service probes

Adopt GraphQL best practices:
- Cursor-based pagination (Relay-style)
- Explicit nullability and input validation
- Fine-grained authorization at field/resolver level
- Persisted and whitelisted queries for public clients; disable ad-hoc queries in production
- Deprecation via @deprecated and schema changelog; no versioned URLs

Operational decisions:
- Enforce depth/complexity limits, timeouts, and rate limits at the gateway
- Enable tracing, field-level metrics, and error redaction; integrate with central observability
- Cache at multiple layers (per-request DataLoader, CDN for persisted GET queries, and gateway response caching where safe)
- Blue/green rollout of the gateway; subgraphs deploy independently with backward-compatible schema evolution
- Backfill a minimal REST façade only if required by legacy consumers

Tooling:
- GraphQL Code Generator for types and operations
- Contract tests to prevent breaking changes
- Schema registry with checks in CI/CD

This decision standardizes external API access on GraphQL while pragmatically retaining REST for non-ideal GraphQL use cases.

We will adopt a stacked handler (pipeline/middleware) architecture for all request and message processing paths across services. Each request/command/event is processed by an ordered chain of small, single-responsibility handlers that implement a common interface (e.g., Handle(ctx, req) -> (resp, err)), where errors short-circuit the chain and context is used for cancellation, deadlines, and trace propagation.

Handlers will be stateless, composable, and configured per route/operation/consumer via dependency injection and declarative assembly. The handler stack is the mechanism for cross-cutting concerns including (but not limited to): authentication, authorization, validation, idempotency/deduplication, rate limiting, caching, circuit breaking, retries/backoff, timeouts, transactions/unit-of-work, schema transformation, observability (logging/metrics/tracing), auditing, feature flags, localization, pagination, and response shaping. Business logic remains in terminal handlers; cross-cutting logic remains in middleware.

Operational rules:
- Order is explicit and version-controlled; default stacks per service with per-endpoint overrides.
- Maximum stack depth 8 unless justified; per-handler latency budget ~1 ms (configurable); global timeout enforced.
- Handlers must be pure (no global mutable state), side-effect-safe, and idempotent where applicable.
- Errors are normalized; telemetry is emitted at entry/exit with correlation IDs.
- Context propagation is mandatory across async boundaries.

Testing and quality:
- Unit tests per handler with contract tests for chain composition.
- Performance benchmarks for hot paths; static analysis to prevent blocking I/O in shared stacks.

Adoption:
- All new endpoints/consumers use stacked handlers; existing paths are incrementally refactored with parity tests and metrics validation.

## Decision
Adopt a canonical file system convention organized as type/namespace/id with optional standardized subfolders and metadata to ensure discoverability, consistency, and tooling support.

- Canonical path: /{type}/{namespace}/{id}/
  - type: one of service, component, lib, dataset, job, pipeline, script, spec, doc, infra, env, tool (extensible via registry).
  - namespace: logical domain grouping using reverse-DNS or domain.tier (e.g., payments.core), no slashes.
  - id: immutable, lowercase kebab-case unique identifier (e.g., charge-processor).

- Required contents:
  - meta.yaml: machine-readable metadata (name, owner, description, version, tags, links).
  - README.md: human-readable overview.
  - Optional standard subfolders by type:
    - src/, config/, scripts/, docs/, tests/, assets/, ops/, migrations/, examples/
  - For datasets: schema/, samples/, contracts/
  - For infra: terraform/ or k8s/, modules/, overlays/
  - For specs: openapi/, proto/, adr/

- Naming and rules:
  - Lowercase, kebab-case for all names; no spaces; ASCII only.
  - Namespace segments separated by dots; max depth 3.
  - IDs are immutable; updates create new IDs or versions under the same id with versioning: /{type}/{namespace}/{id}/v{n}/
  - Cross-references via symlinks or index files; no deep nesting beyond the three-level root.
  - Reserved types and namespaces listed in a central registry; PRs to extend.

- Tooling and enforcement:
  - CI linting to validate structure, naming, required files, and metadata completeness.
  - Generators (scaffolding) to create compliant skeletons per type.
  - Backward compatibility via alias directories or symlinks with deprecation notices in meta.yaml.

- Environments/tenancy:
  - Environment overlays live under env/{env}/… within the id folder (e.g., env/prod/config/), not as additional path segments before id.
  - Multi-tenant variants use id suffixes (e.g., charge-processor--tenant-a) with shared base in the parent id.

Adopt Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR, v2.x) as the standard format for capturing, reviewing, and maintaining architectural decisions across the codebase.

- Scope: Required for decisions that affect system architecture, quality attributes, cross-cutting concerns, interfaces, data models, security, compliance, major dependencies, runtime topology, and cost. Minor implementation details may be documented elsewhere.
- Repository location: docs/adr/ (mandatory). Each decision is a single Markdown file.
- Naming and numbering: Zero-padded sequential IDs with a kebab-case title, e.g., 0001-use-madr.md. IDs are immutable once merged.
- Template: Use the MADR v2.x template (Title, Status, Deciders, Date, Context and Problem Statement, Decision Drivers, Considered Options, Decision Outcome with Consequences, Pros and Cons of the Options, Links). Provide the template in docs/adr/template.md.
- Status lifecycle: Draft → Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded. Superseding ADRs must link both ways. Deprecated/Superseded ADRs remain in the log for traceability.
- Process: Create/modify ADRs via pull requests. Reviews by designated architecture/code owners required for acceptance. Significant changes require a new ADR rather than editing accepted ones.
- Discoverability: Maintain an index at docs/adr/README.md listing ADRs in chronological order with status.
- Tooling: Author manually in Markdown; optional use of adr-tools or project scripts for scaffolding and indexing. CI will validate filename conventions and require a non-empty Status.
- Applicability: Effective immediately for all new decisions; existing decisions will be migrated to MADR as time permits without altering historical intent.

## Decision

Adopt a browser-based timed text editor built in-house as a React micro-frontend, using Slate.js for rich text editing and Yjs (CRDT) for optional real-time collaboration. Standardize on WebVTT as the canonical storage and interchange format; support import/export for SRT and TTML/IMSC via loss-aware converters. Maintain an internal millisecond timebase with frame-rate metadata to generate frame-accurate exports.

Integrate media playback via hls.js (HLS) and Shaka Player (DASH) with MSE fallback and precise seeking. Provide visual timing aids through client-side waveform rendering (Wavesurfer.js) backed by server-precomputed peak/spectrogram data (FFmpeg/SoX). Ensure sub-frame scrubbing, snap-to-boundaries, and collision detection between cues.

Persist editor state as a versioned JSON model mapped 1:1 to WebVTT cues, with autosave, draft publishing, and an immutable audit log. Expose a typed API (REST + WebSocket) for media metadata, waveform tiles, document lifecycle, and presence/collab signaling. Package the editor as a standalone micro-frontend embeddable in host products with theming and extension points (plugins for QC checks, linting, and batch operations).

Meet accessibility and localization requirements: WCAG 2.1 AA compliance, full keyboard control, screen reader support, RTL scripts, and custom lexicons. Defer native desktop clients; provide an offline-capable PWA profile for field use. Prefer permissive, well-maintained OSS dependencies; avoid GPL-licensed components to ease distribution. This decision aligns with our web-first delivery model, enables scalable collaboration, and minimizes format-lock-in.

We will standardize AMI resolution through a single “AMI Resolver” component used by all IaC and runtime provisioning paths. The resolver supports two strategies:

- AWS-managed AMIs: Resolve via AWS SSM public parameters (e.g., /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/... and service-specific parameters) with explicit OS, architecture, virtualization, and GPU/HVM variants. Resolution is region-aware and owner-restricted to AWS publishers.
- Custom/golden AMIs: Resolve by tags and semantic versioning (e.g., app=…, os=…, tier=…, version=MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) owned by our account(s) or an allowlisted publisher account. Latest is determined by semver with optional channel (stable/candidate).

To balance repeatability and agility:
- Production and long-lived environments use pinned AMI IDs committed to source control via an automated pipeline step that resolves, validates, and writes a lock file per region/arch.
- Ephemeral and non-prod environments may use “latest” lookups at deploy time, with optional max-age to avoid surprise drift.
- A nightly job proposes AMI bumps (PRs) with diffs, release notes, and rollback metadata; merges trigger controlled rollouts.

Hardening and safety:
- Owner allowlist enforced on all lookups.
- Mandatory tag schema validation and minimum age requirement (e.g., >24h) for custom AMIs.
- Fail-fast on ambiguous or missing results; no silent fallbacks to “latest.”
- Full audit logs of queries and selected AMI IDs.

This decision yields reproducible, auditable AMI selection across regions and accounts while enabling safe, automated updates and a single integration point for all provisioning workflows.

Adopt a declarative, externalized rules engine as the primary mechanism for expressing and executing business logic. Business rules will be authored in a human-readable DSL, version-controlled, and deployed independently from application code. A forward-chaining rules engine with conflict resolution (salience) will be used to infer outcomes from facts; rules must be side-effect free, idempotent, and deterministic. Facts are emitted from services/events, normalized into a shared schema, and evaluated in a stateless session with strict time and memory limits. Rule outputs are domain events or commands captured via well-defined adapters.

Governance will include: code review for rules, automated validation (syntax, static analysis, clash detection), unit and scenario tests, canary releases, and rollback. A central rules catalog documents ownership, dependencies, priorities, and rollout status. Observability requirements include per-rule activation metrics, trace correlation, and full audit logs of inputs, matches, and outcomes.

To ensure safety and performance, we will: (1) sandbox rule functions (no network/file access), (2) cap rule recursion and agenda depth, (3) precompile and cache rule sets, (4) partition rule evaluation by tenant/context, and (5) provide a feature-flagged kill switch. Imperative code remains for orchestration, I/O, and persistence; the engine is invoked via a stable interface. This decision enables faster change cycles for complex, evolving policies while preserving control, testability, and transparency.

## Decision

Adopt PostgreSQL (v15+) as the system-of-record relational database, provisioned as a managed service (e.g., AWS RDS/Aurora or GCP Cloud SQL) to provide ACID transactions, strong consistency, and operational reliability. Implement a normalized schema with clear ownership per bounded context, enforce referential integrity with foreign keys, and codify all DDL via versioned migrations (Flyway or Liquibase). Apply a strict migration workflow (dev → staging → prod) with automated checks and rollback procedures.

Access will occur through a data access layer/ORM supported by the application stack, with connection pooling (e.g., PgBouncer) and prepared statements. Implement row- and column-level constraints, unique indexes, and necessary composite indexes based on query profiles. For scale and resilience, enable automated backups with point-in-time recovery, encryption at rest and in transit, multi-AZ/high availability, and read replicas for read-heavy workloads. Plan for partitioning on time- or tenant-based keys where data volume warrants it.

Secrets will be managed via the platform’s secret manager; database roles will follow least-privilege and application-specific service accounts. Observability will include query logging, slow query analysis, and metrics/alerts on connections, replication lag, storage, and latency.

Data from the legacy store will be migrated via an ETL pipeline with validation and backfill, followed by a dual-write/verify window and a controlled cutover behind a feature flag. The legacy store will be deprecated post-cutover with a defined archival policy.

We will transfer artefact binaries between pipeline stages and environments by passing references to immutable binaries stored in a centralized artifact registry instead of re-building or re-packaging. All build outputs (JARs, ZIPs, OS packages, container images, etc.) will be uploaded once by the build stage to the registry (Artifactory/Nexus for generic/Java packages; OCI registry for container images). Each artefact is content-addressed and versioned with commit SHA and build number; artefacts are immutable and promoted across repositories (e.g., snapshots → staging → release) rather than re-published.

Integrity and provenance are enforced via:
- Cryptographic checksums (SHA-256) and mandatory signature (Sigstore/cosign or GPG) verification on download.
- Attached metadata: SBOM, build manifest, provenance (SLSA-compliant where possible), and security scan results.
- Policy gates that only allow promotion/consumption of artefacts meeting verification thresholds.

Transfers use HTTPS with retries, backoff, and resumable uploads/downloads for large binaries. Access is via short-lived, least-privilege tokens (OIDC/JWT from CI). Artefact retention and cleanup policies apply (e.g., snapshots 14–30 days, releases retained per compliance). For large artefacts or air-gapped promotion, we support signed, encrypted bundles exported/imported via S3-compatible storage as a controlled exception.

Consumers retrieve artefacts by coordinate only (group/name/version or OCI digest), never from source. Caching is enabled at edge runners to reduce egress while honoring immutability and checksum verification. No direct binary transfer between jobs; all hand-offs occur through the registry to ensure traceability, repeatability, and auditability.

## Decision
Adopt a dual-root (A/B) architecture with an independent data volume to enable atomic, safe OS/application updates and reliable rollback while preserving persistent state.

- Provision two immutable root partitions (rootA, rootB). Only one is active at a time; the other is the update target. Root filesystems are mounted read-only and integrity protected (e.g., dm-verity or OSTree). All writable paths are redirected to the data volume via bind mounts or overlay.
- Maintain a single persistent data volume (e.g., /data) for application state, configurations, secrets, logs, and caches. Optionally encrypt with LUKS. Define a strict directory contract (e.g., /data/etc, /data/var, /data/app) and bind-mount into standard FHS locations to keep root immutable.
- Use the bootloader (U-Boot or GRUB) for slot management with boot counters and health flags. After updating the inactive root, switch the boot slot. If post-boot health checks fail within a grace window, automatically roll back to the previous slot.
- Implement health signaling via a boot-complete service that records a success marker on the data volume after critical services start. Include watchdogs and telemetry to detect regressions.
- Updates are applied only to the inactive root and are transactional (whole-image or delta). Store update metadata and provenance on the data volume. Never modify the active root in place.
- Manage configuration through a layered approach: factory defaults baked into root, site-specific and runtime config read from /data and overlaid onto /etc. Provide versioned schema migrations for data on first boot after upgrades.
- Backups and disaster recovery target only the data volume; root partitions are reconstructed by reinstalling or re-updating.
- Enforce immutability in CI/CD and at runtime (mount options, policies) and provide developer tooling to work within the read-only model.

We will adopt a dual-queue architecture: RabbitMQ (via Bunny) for inter-service messaging and event distribution; Redis-backed Sidekiq for application-internal background job processing.

- RabbitMQ will be the authoritative event bus and command broker between services. We will use durable exchanges/queues, publisher confirms, consumer acknowledgments, dead-letter exchanges, and per-queue TTLs. Cross-service workflows, at-least-once delivery needs, routing by topic/headers, and fan-out patterns must use RabbitMQ. Producers will employ the Outbox pattern to ensure transactional publishing from the primary datastore. Payloads >256KB will be externalized to object storage with references.

- Sidekiq will handle in-app background tasks (e.g., email, cache warming, batch processing, scheduled jobs, idempotent retriable work) that do not cross service boundaries. Sidekiq is not to be used for inter-service integration, business event propagation, or contractual SLAs with other teams.

- Clear boundary rules:
  - Inter-service events/commands → RabbitMQ.
  - Intra-service async work → Sidekiq.
  - Do not chain RabbitMQ → Sidekiq → RabbitMQ within a single business transaction.
  - Use idempotency keys and deduplication in both systems; exactly-once is not assumed.

- Operational posture:
  - Separate HA deployments: RabbitMQ clustered with quorum queues; Redis with Sentinel/Cluster as appropriate.
  - Unified observability: metrics, traces, and logs for publish/consume rates, latency, retries, DLQs; alert on backlog thresholds and poison message rates.
  - Secure transport (TLS), authentication, and least-privilege credentials for both systems.

- Governance and contracts:
  - Message schemas versioned (JSON Schema/Avro) with compatibility checks.
  - Central registry for exchanges, queues, routing keys, and job queues; review required for new contracts.
  - Provide thin client libraries/wrappers to standardize headers, tracing, and error handling.

- Migration:
  - Existing cross-service Sidekiq jobs will be migrated to RabbitMQ within defined milestones; provide a bridge/adapter during transition.

## Decision
Adopt Living Documentation as a first-class practice to ensure architecture and system knowledge remain current, trustworthy, and discoverable.

- Treat documentation as code. All docs (ADRs, architecture views, runbooks, API specs, quality attributes) live in the repository, reviewed via pull requests with the same rigor as source code.
- Establish a single source of truth. Prefer generation from code and tests over manual prose:
  - Generate API/Schema docs (OpenAPI/AsyncAPI, database schemas) from source/annotations.
  - Maintain architecture diagrams and models as code; generate images in CI.
  - Use executable specifications (BDD/ATDD), contract tests, and observability dashboards to produce or link evidence of behavior.
- Automate currency and publishing:
  - CI enforces documentation linting, link checking, diagram generation, API spec validation, and stale content detection.
  - On merge to main, publish a versioned documentation site; provide PR preview environments.
  - Release tagging produces immutable doc snapshots aligned to artifacts.
- Governance and workflow:
  - Definition of Done includes updating or creating ADRs and affected docs.
  - PR template prompts for doc impact; architectural changes require an ADR reference.
  - Ownership is federated: each team maintains its domain docs; architecture guild curates cross-cutting sections.
- Information architecture and access:
  - Separate internal vs external views; enable full-text search and clear navigation.
  - Record doc debt as issues; track freshness metrics and audit key pages regularly.

This decision replaces static, manually maintained documents with continuously validated, versioned, and automated documentation integrated into delivery.

## Decision

Adopt Spring Framework as the foundational platform for the server component, implemented with Spring Boot 3.x on Java 21 LTS.

- Architectural style: layered (controller–service–repository), hexagonal ports/adapters where integration boundaries are required.
- Web stack: Spring MVC (blocking I/O) with Spring Web for RESTful APIs; consider WebFlux only for endpoints with proven high-concurrency/reactive requirements.
- Persistence: Spring Data JPA with Hibernate to PostgreSQL; Flyway for schema migrations.
- Security: Spring Security with OAuth2/OIDC support; method-level security enabled; CSRF protection for browser flows.
- Validation: Jakarta Bean Validation integrated at API boundaries and domain models.
- Observability: Spring Boot Actuator, Micrometer with OpenTelemetry exporters (traces, metrics, logs), health/liveness/readiness probes.
- Configuration: externalized via application profiles (dev/test/prod), environment variables, and config server readiness; secrets managed through platform secret stores.
- Messaging (if needed): Spring for Apache Kafka with transactional/outbox support; Retry/Dead-letter policies via Spring Kafka.
- API documentation: springdoc-openapi for OpenAPI 3 specification; contract-first where applicable.
- Testing: Spring Boot Test, Testcontainers for integration tests, WireMock for HTTP stubs.
- Packaging and runtime: layered Docker images via Spring Boot build plugins; readiness for AOT/native image (GraalVM) where startup/footprint justify it.
- Build tool: Gradle (Kotlin DSL) with dependency management via Spring BOM; reproducible builds in CI.
- Coding conventions: constructor injection, immutable configuration properties, component scanning constrained to application packages.

This positions the server for rapid development, consistency across services, and alignment with ecosystem standards while allowing modular evolution.

We will enable user-provided RelayState for SP-initiated SAML flows to control post-authentication navigation, with strict validation and secure handling.

- Accept an optional relay_state parameter via UI and API/SDKs.
- For HTTP-Redirect binding, cap RelayState to 80 bytes; for HTTP-POST binding, cap at 1024 bytes. Reject non-ASCII control characters.
- Use an opaque, server-issued nonce as the actual RelayState sent to the IdP. Map the nonce to the user-provided state in a short-lived, single-use cache (TTL 5 minutes) keyed to the AuthnRequest ID and user session.
- On callback, resolve the nonce to the stored state and invalidate it. If missing/expired/invalid, fall back to the default post-login destination.
- Enforce an allowlist for redirect targets and state payloads:
  - If the state encodes a URL/path, permit only registered first-party paths and pre-registered external domains. Normalize and compare after decoding to prevent open redirects.
  - If the state is opaque app data, require HMAC-signed payloads (server key), with issued-at timestamp and expiry; otherwise store server-side only.
- Do not echo or log user-provided state values. Log presence and validation outcomes only. Redact in error messages.
- Backward compatible: if relay_state is absent, behavior is unchanged.
- Configuration: per-tenant toggle, allowed domains/paths, TTL, and size limits (defaults as above).
- Not supported for IdP-initiated SSO (ignored).
- SDKs will expose a relay_state field and document constraints.

- Make in-app notifications the default channel; use email only for high-signal events. For each submission, send at most one email on creation (“Submission received”) and one at terminal state (“Approved/Rejected/Closed”). Intermediate workflow changes (assignment, comments, minor status updates) are in-app only by default.
- Provide role-based exceptions: submitters and external stakeholders get the two emails above; reviewers/managers receive a configurable daily digest summarizing all assigned submission changes instead of per-event emails.
- Implement a per-submission coalescing window (e.g., 5–10 minutes) to batch multiple rapid-fire events into a single email if thresholds are met; apply idempotency keys to prevent duplicates and deduplicate across retries.
- Replace attachments in emails with secure deep links to the portal; include a concise status summary and next-action CTA to reduce follow-up email chains.
- Centralize notification policy in a Notification Service with templating, throttling, and recipient-preference evaluation. Expose user/org-level preferences to opt into additional events or stricter digests, with sensible minimums to avoid zero-notice for compliance-critical steps.
- Gate rollout behind a feature flag, migrating groups incrementally and backfilling help content explaining the new model.
- Instrument metrics and alerts: emails-per-submission, suppression rate, digest open/click, SLA on critical notifications; review weekly and adjust thresholds/policies.
- Preserve an auditable event log of all notifications (suppressed, batched, sent) for support and compliance.
- Default policies are configurable per tenant but constrained by global caps to ensure the reduction objective is maintained.

We will integrate with Postcodes.io as the canonical service for UK postcode validation, normalization, and lookup (including geocoding, outcode/incode parsing, administrative areas, and NHS/ONS codes). The application will call the official public HTTPS API by default, with the base URL, timeouts, and retry/backoff policy configured via environment settings. To mitigate external dependency risks and rate limits, we will implement a read-through cache (in-memory for the app tier and optional Redis for multi-instance deployments) with TTLs appropriate to low-churn postcode data (default 30 days) and negative-cache entries (short TTL) for invalid postcodes.

Availability will be enhanced via an optional self-hosted Postcodes.io instance ( Docker ) as a hot-standby endpoint, with automatic failover if the public API is unavailable or degrades beyond SLOs. Requests will be idempotent and circuit-breaker protected. We will log request metadata but no raw postcodes in persistent logs unless hashed, to minimize PII exposure.

Returned fields will be restricted to those required by product features (normalized postcode, latitude/longitude, outcode, country, admin district). This decision limits scope to UK addresses; non-UK lookups are out of scope. Licensing of Postcodes.io (MIT) is compatible with our usage.

Adopt GitLab CI/CD as the single, authoritative platform for build, test, security scanning, release, and deployment across all services and repositories. Migrate existing pipelines from legacy providers to GitLab in a phased approach, prioritizing high-change, high-impact services first, and achieving like-for-like functionality before introducing optimizations. Standardize on shared GitLab CI templates and a central pipeline library for linting, build, test, SAST/DAST/Dependency scanning, container image build and signing, SBOM generation, artifact management, environment promotion, and deployment with approvals. Use GitLab-managed and autoscaling self-hosted runners (with Docker and Kubernetes executors) to match workload needs and control costs; enable caching and remote artifact storage for performance. Enforce policy-as-code via merge request approvals, protected branches/tags, required checks, and environment-level permissions. For deployments, adopt GitLab Environments with review apps, canary, and progressive delivery; record change evidence and compliance reports in GitLab. ## Decision

We will deprecate legacy Internet Explorer 6–8 support and transition to a reduced-support posture leading to full removal.

- Effective immediately, IE6–8 move to “best-effort, security-only” status: no new features, no layout/performance fixes, and no test coverage. Only critical security patches will be considered, time-boxed and risk-assessed.
- We will remove IE6–8 from our target browser matrix, CI pipelines, and release gates. Automated tests, polyfills, and CSS/JS hacks specific to IE6–8 will be phased out.
- Codebase changes:
  - Retire conditional comments, CSS filters/hacks, and legacy shims unique to IE6–8.
  - Adjust transpilation/polyfill targets to ES2017 → ES2019 with ES5 compatibility for supported browsers only (no IE8 ES3 constraints).
  - Split bundles: eliminate the legacy bundle; maintain a minimal “safe HTML” fallback (basic SSR markup and non-JS navigation) where feasible during the transition.
- User impact mitigation:
  - Serve an upgrade interstitial for IE6–8 with guidance to supported browsers and a link to a lightweight fallback experience for critical flows (auth, checkout).
  - Document known limitations and provide enterprise customers an opt-in, time-limited extended support path (up to 6 months) via a pinned legacy snapshot without feature parity or SLAs beyond security fixes.
- Timeline:
  - Now: deprecate and remove from CI; freeze non-security fixes.
  - +3 months: remove legacy assets from production; disable fallback except for contracted extensions.
  - +6 months: end all IE6–8 servicing.
- Ongoing:
  - Monitor traffic and error rates; if IE6–8 usage drops below 0.2%, accelerate removal.
  - Communicate changes via release notes, admin console banners, and enterprise channels.

We will maintain a human-readable CHANGELOG.md at the repository root that records user-visible changes for each release. The changelog will follow “Keep a Changelog” (v1.1.0) conventions and Semantic Versioning. Entries will be grouped under standard headings: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, and Security, with an Unreleased section at the top for pending changes.

Source of truth will be curated from pull requests and commits using Conventional Commits. We will generate a draft via tooling (e.g., conventional-changelog or git-cliff) and require manual review to ensure clarity, completeness, and user impact focus. Internal-only changes (refactors, CI, docs not affecting users) are excluded unless they change behavior or usage.

Each release will:
- Be tagged vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with release date.
- Include comparison links (Unreleased, and per-version diffs).
- Summarize breaking changes prominently with migration notes.
- Reference relevant issue/PR numbers.

Process and ownership:
- Every PR must carry a changelog label and/or a “Changelog: [category|skip]” directive; CI will fail if missing for non-trivial changes.
- Release managers are responsible for curating the Unreleased section into a new version on release.
- Automation will update CHANGELOG.md and publish GitHub Release notes from the curated content.

Scope:

Style and accessibility:

- All entries must describe user impact and, when applicable, include upgrade guidance.
