## Decision
- We will document all architectural decisions using Markdown-based ADRs following the MADR 3.x conventions, stored in-repo to live alongside code.
- Location: /docs/adr. Each ADR is a standalone Markdown file committed with the codebase.
- Naming: date-prefixed kebab-case filenames (YYYY-MM-DD-use-markdown-architectural-decision-records.md), with the first H1 title equal to the ADR title. A lightweight 2–3 sentence abstract follows the title.
- Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted → Deprecated → Superseded. Status must appear at the top of each ADR. Superseding ADRs must link to and from the prior ADR.
- Scope: ADRs capture decisions with long-term architectural significance (externally visible behavior, cross-cutting concerns, major dependencies, data contracts). Ephemeral or low-level implementation choices are excluded.
- Process: New ADRs are created in Proposed status on a feature branch using the MADR template. Acceptance requires code review via pull request by at least one architect and one senior engineer. Decisions should be made “just-in-time” and merged before or with the first implementing change.
- Discoverability: Maintain an index at /docs/adr/README.md listing ADRs by status and topic. Each ADR includes context, decision, consequences, alternatives, and links to related docs.
- Tooling: We will use adr-tools (or equivalent) to scaffold files and maintain the index; CI will verify presence of status, links, and filename format.
- Governance: The Architecture Working Group owns the process; any team may propose ADRs. Changes to accepted decisions require a new ADR.

We will standardize on JSON-LD 1.1 flattened form as the canonical representation for all self-encoded dialects across ingestion, validation, storage, and emission.

- Inputs must be self-encoded: each payload includes an embedded, versioned @context. Remote context fetching at runtime is disabled; contexts are resolved from an allowlisted, pinned cache (by IRI + hash) to ensure reproducibility and security.
- Parsing: we accept compact or expanded inputs but immediately normalize by expanding with the pinned context and flattening to a single top-level array of node objects with stable @id references. Blank nodes are preserved; list/value objects and language/datatype maps are honored.
- Validation and mapping: schema validation, constraints, and semantic mapping operate exclusively on flattened form to remove graph-structure ambiguity and to enable deterministic rule application across dialects.
- Emission: all outputs are produced in flattened form and include the authoritative embedded @context for the dialect. Optional client-specific compaction/framing is not performed by default; if required, it occurs only at the edge and never affects stored or signed representations.
- Determinism: for signatures, hashing, and diffing, we rely on flattened form combined with RDF dataset canonicalization (URDNA2015) when needed; JSON key order is not semantically significant and is not relied upon.
- Interop boundaries: internal services communicate using flattened JSON-LD only. External APIs may offer a compacted view as a convenience, clearly documented as a non-canonical projection.
- Backward compatibility: dialect evolution is handled via context versioning; multiple context versions may co-exist, but all are normalized to flattened form using their pinned contexts.
- Error handling: documents lacking an embedded context, referencing non-allowlisted contexts, or failing flattening/expansion are rejected with actionable diagnostics.

This decision yields a single, secure, deterministic JSON-LD shape for all self-encoded dialects, simplifying validation, storage, signing, and cross-dialect processing.

We will adopt OAuth 2.1 (OAuth 2.0 with the 2.1 recommendations) with OpenID Connect as the authentication mechanism across all clients and services. Browser and mobile clients will use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE; confidential server-side applications will use Authorization Code with client secret. A standards-compliant OpenID Provider (IdP) will be integrated (selection tracked separately); all apps will rely on the IdP for user authentication, MFA, session management, and JWKS key distribution.

Access tokens will be short-lived (≤15 minutes) and encoded as JWTs signed by the IdP; resource servers will validate tokens locally using the IdP’s JWKS and enforce authorization via scopes and claims. Refresh tokens will be enabled with rotation and reuse detection; compromise triggers revocation. For browser-based apps, we will adopt a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern: tokens are stored server-side and proxied via the BFF, with user session maintained using secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=strict cookies to minimize XSS/CSRF risk. Native/mobile apps will store tokens in platform-secure storage.

Scopes will be defined per service with least-privilege defaults; claims will include subject, issuer, audience, expiry, and app-specific roles/permissions as needed. Consent screens and fine-grained scopes will be used for third-party access where applicable. RP-initiated logout and IdP global logout will be supported; session timeouts align with compliance requirements.

SDKs and middleware from the IdP and vetted OSS libraries will be used to reduce custom code. Key rotation will follow the IdP’s JWKS rotation; clock skew and token leeway will be standardized across services. Non-functional requirements (availability, latency) will be met without token introspection dependencies. Existing authentication will be migrated incrementally via dual-stack support and feature flags.

## Decision
Standardize all serverless functions on a single, provider-agnostic entrypoint named handler that accepts an HTTP/JSON request and produces an HTTP response. The canonical signature is Request -> Response (e.g., Express-style req, res in Node.js, or equivalent in other runtimes). All non-HTTP triggers (Pub/Sub, queues, schedulers, storage events) will invoke the same handler via lightweight adapter shims that translate provider events into a normalized HTTP request (CloudEvents where available).

- Entrypoint name: handler (single exported symbol per function).
- Transport: HTTP/JSON over UTF-8; content-type application/json (or application/cloudevents+json for evented calls).
- Input normalization: adapters map provider-specific event/context into a normalized request with:
  - headers (including correlation/trace IDs and auth),
  - method and path,
  - query params,
  - body (raw and parsed),
  - event metadata under req.event (id, type, source, time).
- Output normalization: handler returns status code, headers, and JSON body; adapters map to provider response semantics.
- Cross-cutting concerns (authZ/authN, validation, idempotency, tracing, metrics, timeout handling) implemented as middleware executed before/after handler.
- Error handling: handler throws typed errors; adapters translate to structured problem+json with appropriate status codes and provider-compliant failures/retries.
- Idempotency: require idempotency-key header for non-idempotent operations; adapters map provider delivery identifiers when available.
- Observability: propagate W3C Trace Context; require request IDs in responses; log in structured JSON with request correlation.
- Backward compatibility: legacy functions expose thin wrappers delegating to handler until migrated.
- Local development: dev server runs the same HTTP handler; adapters are used only in deployment packages.
- Naming: each function directory/package contains exactly one handler; the deployment entry references handler.

This unifies execution semantics across providers, simplifies testing, and reduces duplicated boilerplate around triggers while preserving flexibility to support provider-specific events via adapters.

We will ship and support a single, canonical configuration file as the sole source of truth for runtime configuration. The file will be named config.yaml, located at the repository root and packaged with releases. All prior configuration files (e.g., app.conf, settings.json, feature-flags.yaml) are deprecated and will no longer be read after the next minor release.

Environment-specific customization will be achieved without additional files:
- Non-secret overrides via environment variables using a well-defined mapping (ENV_ prefixes) and command-line flags.
- Secrets will never reside in config.yaml; they must come from environment variables or the configured secret manager.
- Optional local developer overrides may exist as config.local.yaml but are git-ignored and never included in releases.

The config.yaml structure is versioned and validated at startup against a published JSON Schema; unknown keys cause warnings in the deprecation window and errors thereafter. Default values are embedded in the application and only deviations need to be specified in config.yaml.

Build and deployment tooling will reference only config.yaml. Documentation, examples, and templates will be consolidated accordingly. A migration tool and linter will be provided to convert legacy files into the unified format. Telemetry and logs will surface any legacy keys or files encountered during the grace period.

Ownership of config schema and evolution resides with the Architecture team; changes require schema PR review and a migration note.

- Implement the embedded application using C/C++ with strict MISRA-C compliance for safety and portability; adopt a layered architecture: Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) → Drivers → Services → Application (state machines).
- Use FreeRTOS as the RTOS to provide deterministic scheduling, time slicing, and isolation of concerns via tasks; prefer static task and queue allocation to avoid heap fragmentation.
- Employ an event-driven design with message queues for inter-task communication, plus lightweight publish/subscribe for decoupling; prohibit shared mutable state without explicit synchronization (mutexes with priority inheritance).
- Define clear timing budgets and watchdog integration; implement a system supervisor task to monitor liveness, stack usage, and timing violations.
- Persist configuration and critical telemetry in a wear-leveled, power-fail-safe storage (e.g., LittleFS or FlashDB) with CRCs; all I/O and storage operations are non-blocking or performed in dedicated I/O tasks.
- Abstract hardware via narrow interfaces to enable board portability; use vendor HAL only within the HAL layer and provide mocks for host-based tests.
- Enforce static memory patterns (no dynamic allocation after init), bounded queues, and compile-time configuration via Kconfig-style options.
- Provide a deterministic startup sequence with dependency-checked initialization and failure-safe modes; include OTA or field update via a dual-image, A/B bootloader with rollback on health check failure.
- Establish CI with cross-compilation, unit tests (Unity/CMock or GoogleTest for C++), hardware-in-the-loop smoke tests, and static analysis (clang-tidy, cppcheck) plus coverage where feasible.
- Instrument with lightweight logging (ring buffer, deferred output) and metrics; compile-time log levels to minimize runtime overhead.

## Decision

Adopt trunk-based development with short-lived branches and protected mainline.

- Default branch: main (protected; requires PR, 1+ reviewer, passing CI, up-to-date with main).
- Branch types and naming:
  - feature/<ticket-id>-<slug> for changes; lifespan ideally <2 days.
  - release/<version> for short stabilization windows (0–5 days) when needed.
  - hotfix/<ticket-id>-<slug> for urgent production fixes.
  - maintenance/<major.minor> only for supported LTS lines (if applicable).
- Merge strategy: squash-and-merge via PR to maintain a linear history; rebase locally to keep branches current; no direct commits to main.
- CI/CD gates: mandatory unit/integ tests, lint/type checks, security scan, code coverage threshold, build artifact, and change log generation. Status checks must pass before merge.
- Releases:
  - Regular releases are cut from main by creating a temporary release/<version> branch for final fixes; tag main with SemVer (vX.Y.Z) on release.
  - Environments: staging auto-deploys from main; production deploys only from signed tags.
  - Hotfixes: branch from the released tag or main as appropriate, merge to main, cherry-pick to active maintenance/<major.minor> branches, and retag with a patch version.
- Backports: changes land on main first; cherry-pick to maintenance branches with PRs referencing the original.
- Large/long-running work: use feature flags over long-lived branches; if unavoidable, gate merges behind flags and integrate incrementally.
- Repository settings: enforce branch protection, required reviews, linear history, signed commits/tags, and CODEOWNERS for critical areas.

This strategy optimizes flow and stability: frequent integration to main, rapid feedback, safe releases via tags, and controlled maintenance via explicit backports.

## Decision
Adopt a two-phase search strategy that balances time-to-value with scalability and relevance:

- Phase 1 (MVP): Implement application search using PostgreSQL native full-text search (tsvector/tsquery) with pg_trgm for fuzzy matching. Create GIN indexes on tokenized searchable fields and use language-specific dictionaries for stemming and stop-words. Use ts_rank for relevance scoring and seek-based pagination for stable result sets. Expose a simple query model (keywords, phrase match, field boosts, filters) via a search service interface to decouple callers from storage specifics.

- Phase 2 (Scale/Features): When query volume, data size, or feature requirements exceed Postgres capabilities (e.g., aggregations, suggesters, typo-tolerant ranking, vector/hybrid search), migrate the search backend to a managed OpenSearch/Elasticsearch cluster. Stand up a CDC-based ingestion pipeline (e.g., Debezium -> Kafka -> OpenSearch) to maintain near-real-time index freshness with replay/resilience. Adopt BM25 for ranking, add analyzers per language, and enable facets, synonyms, highlights, and autocomplete.

- Cross-cutting decisions: 
  - Define a stable domain-level Search API and query DSL to isolate clients from backend changes.
  - Implement relevance tuning via telemetry (click-through, dwell time) with offline evaluations and feature flags.
  - Ensure privacy and compliance by excluding sensitive fields from indexes and applying row-level filters.
  - Instrument end-to-end search latency, recall/precision proxies, and index health; set SLOs and alerts.
  - Provide blue/green index rebuilds and zero-downtime reindexing procedures.

## Decision
Adopt the selected frontend UI library as an external dependency managed via npm/pnpm, not vendored or forked. It will be declared as a direct dependency of each frontend app that uses it; the shared design-system package will expose thin wrapper components/adapters around library primitives to contain usage, enforce our tokens/a11y, and enable future replacement with minimal churn.

Dependencies will be pinned exactly in package.json with a lockfile committed; automated dependency updates (e.g., Renovate) will propose version bumps. We will accept patch updates automatically after CI passes; minor/major updates require review with visual and accessibility regression checks.

Only ESM, per-component imports will be used to maximize tree-shaking. Bundler configuration will ensure sideEffects is respected, CSS is extracted where applicable, and code-splitting is enabled for large components. Styles will be integrated using the library’s recommended approach; any global CSS will be isolated via CSS Modules or scoping to avoid collisions. The design system will provide theme tokens mapped to the library’s theming API; direct theme mutation in apps is prohibited.

SSR/CSR constraints will be respected by limiting client-only components to browser entry points and guarding DOM access. Browser compatibility will follow our browserslist; required polyfills will be injected centrally.

We will only adopt libraries with permissive licenses and active maintenance. A deprecation/exit path is maintained via the adapter layer; no app may import the library directly except through approved adapters, enforced by lint rules and code owners.

## Decision
We will establish a canonical domain model for the Catalog bounded context with the following core entities and invariants:

- Product (aggregate root): Represents a conceptual item for sale. Owns ProductVariants. Contains merchandising data (title, description, brand, collections, media), SEO, and lifecycle state (draft/active/archived). Identified by ProductId; public-facing slug is versioned and unique per locale.
- ProductVariant (entity): The sellable unit of a Product. Identified by VariantId and immutable SKU. Holds option selections, GTIN/MPN, physical dimensions, and variant-specific media and merchandising overrides. Variants cannot exist without a Product.
- Category (aggregate root): Hierarchical taxonomy for navigation and merchandising. Identified by CategoryId, supports multiple trees via CategoryType. Products can map to multiple categories. Slugs are unique within a tree and locale.
- Brand (aggregate root): Represents manufacturer/label for grouping and filtering. Stable BrandId and canonical name.
- Attribute (aggregate root) and AttributeValue: Extensible typed metadata (e.g., material, color). Attributes define cardinality, data type, and localization rules. Used for filtering and enrichment; not for variation axes.
- Option (aggregate root) and OptionValue: Define variation axes (e.g., Size, Color) used by ProductVariants. OptionValue combinations must be unique per Product.
- Collection (aggregate root): Curated, non-hierarchical grouping for campaigns.
- MediaAsset (value object reference): Images, videos, documents attached to Product/Variant with rendition metadata.
- Price (value object): Money with currency; list price and compare-at stored in Catalog; selling price resolved by Pricing context.
- Localization: All display fields are localized via Translation value objects; fallbacks are defined per locale policy.
- Inventory and Tax: Not modeled in Catalog. SKU is the integration key to Inventory, Order, and Pricing bounded contexts.
- Search/Indexing: Read-optimized projections (denormalized) are built from the authoritative write model for search and faceting.
- Integrity and governance: SKUs are immutable; deleting is soft by default with unique-key release on archival rules. Referential integrity is enforced by IDs; external references via stable URNs.
- Concurrency: Optimistic versioning on aggregates; changes are auditable with who/when/what.

This model balances flexibility (attributes/options) with clear sellable boundaries (variant/SKU) and isolates cross-cutting concerns (pricing, inventory, tax) into their own bounded contexts.

We will adopt TypeScript as the primary language for all new application and library code and progressively migrate existing JavaScript to TypeScript. Type safety is mandatory at compile time and enforced in CI.

Key implementation decisions:
- Enable strict mode and safety flags: "strict": true, "noImplicitAny": true, "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true, "strictNullChecks": true, "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true, "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true, "useUnknownInCatchVariables": true, "isolatedModules": true.
- Target and modules: target ES2022 (or platform baseline), module ESM, moduleResolution NodeNext, resolveJsonModule true, sourceMap true.
- Project structure: a root tsconfig.base.json shared by packages/apps; per-package extends with incremental builds and composite for project references when applicable.
- Tooling: ESLint with typescript-eslint and Prettier; type-check and lint as required CI gates; unit tests via Jest/Vitest with ts-jest/esbuild or SWC; type-check on commit via pre-commit hooks.
- Interop/migration: allowJs and checkJs during transition; prefer .ts over .js for new files; avoid namespace and decorators; prefer types over interfaces for aliases; avoid enums, use union literals; enforce exhaustive switch with never.
- Public APIs: export stable types; treat type changes as semver; emit declaration files for libraries; maintain a minimum 95% type coverage; any/unknown usage must be localized and documented; @ts-expect-error requires justification.
- Runtime boundaries: validate external inputs with Zod/io-ts and derive static types from schemas; generate types for API/DB schemas via codegen.
- Developer experience: tsx/ts-node for scripts; path aliases via baseUrl/paths; minimal barrel files; training and code review checklist include type quality.

We will implement a normalized relational schema (targeting 3NF) on PostgreSQL, emphasizing strict referential integrity, explicit constraints, and predictable naming. Tables will use snake_case, singular nouns (e.g., user, order), primary keys as UUID v7 (generated in-app) to support distributed ID generation and near-time-ordering. Foreign keys will be required where relationships exist, using ON DELETE RESTRICT by default, with ON DELETE CASCADE only for owned/containment relationships. Many-to-many relations will use junction tables with composite unique constraints.

All entities will include created_at and updated_at (timestamptz, default now()) and an optional deleted_at for soft deletion; unique constraints will be implemented with partial indexes that exclude soft-deleted rows where appropriate. Domain integrity will be enforced via CHECK constraints and reference tables for enumerations (avoiding PostgreSQL enum types for migration agility). Natural keys will be preserved with unique constraints where they carry business meaning.

Indexes will be created for all foreign keys, high-selectivity columns, and common query patterns (including composite indexes with leading columns ordered by selectivity). We will prefer covering and partial indexes where they materially improve performance and will document index rationales. For scalability, we will design hot tables with optional time-based partitioning (no premature partitioning; activate when thresholds are met). Text search needs will use PostgreSQL full-text indexes where required.

Schema changes will be managed through versioned, immutable SQL migrations (e.g., Flyway), with forward-only, backward-compatible steps, online-safe patterns (create-copy-swap for large changes), and automated validations in CI. Rollbacks will be implemented as new migrations. Data backfills will be idempotent and chunked.

We will adopt a schema-per-domain module (e.g., accounting.*, catalog.*, identity.*) to reduce coupling and clarify ownership. Triggers will be minimal; when cross-system publication is required, we will use an outbox table with transactional writes. All DDL and DML conventions, including column naming (_id suffix for foreign keys), nullability rules, and default values, will be codified in a style guide and enforced via linters where possible.

We will adopt Go modules and a module-aware workflow, abandoning GOPATH-centric layout. The repository will be a single Go module (go 1.21+) with a canonical module path (e.g., github.com/<org>/<project>). We will not vendor dependencies by default; reproducibility relies on go.mod/go.sum and the Go proxy. Vendoring may be temporarily enabled for constrained environments but is not committed by default.

Project layout:
- /cmd/<binary>: One folder per executable; main packages minimal, delegating to internal packages.
- /internal/...: Non-public application code (domain, app, adapters, infra). Everything not intended for external reuse lives here.
- /pkg/...: Public, reusable libraries only if we explicitly intend third-party consumption; otherwise avoided.
- /api/...: IDL and schemas (OpenAPI/JSON Schema/Protobuf) and generated artifacts (kept in subfolders, codegen reproducible).
- /configs/: Sample/config templates; no secrets.
- /deploy/: IaC and deployment manifests (e.g., Helm, K8s).
- /scripts/: Developer/CI scripts.
- /tools/: Auxiliary tooling (go:build tool deps pinned via tools.go).
- /docs/: Project documentation.
- /test/: Integration/e2e test assets that span packages.

Conventions:
- Package names are short, lower-case, no underscores; avoid stutter.
- Internal structure follows clear boundaries (e.g., internal/domain, internal/app, internal/adapters, internal/infra) but may evolve pragmatically.
- Imports from /internal are not used outside the module; any shared code intended for reuse is placed in /pkg or extracted to its own module.
- We default to a single-module repo; go.work is used only for local, multi-repo development and is not committed.
- main packages load configuration via environment/flags, wire dependencies, and expose health/metrics uniformly.

CI enforces module tidiness (go mod tidy), builds all /cmd targets, and verifies code generation determinism for /api.

- All assertion details will be validated centrally at the service boundary (API layer) using a versioned schema; requests failing validation are rejected with deterministic error codes and machine-readable messages.
- We will define an explicit, semver’d JSON Schema for assertions (v1 initially), covering required fields, types, formats, min/max lengths, enums, and regex constraints; cross-field and conditional rules (e.g., when type = X, fields A and B required) are enforced.
- Identifiers must be UUIDv4; timestamps must be RFC 3339 UTC; numeric ranges are bounded; strings normalized to NFC; empty/whitespace-only values are invalid unless explicitly allowed.
- Domain invariants are enforced: uniqueness where applicable, immutability of identity fields post-creation, referential integrity to related entities, and coherence between status fields and evidence.
- Evidence attachments are validated for allowed MIME types, size limits, and safe URLs; external links must use https; content hashes are required when provided and verified.
- Partial updates are validated against the full resulting document; unknown/extra fields are rejected by default; feature-flagged strict mode will be progressively rolled out, starting in non-critical endpoints.
- Validation occurs on create, update, bulk import, and background reconciliation jobs; ingestion pipelines perform pre-validate before persistence; DB-level constraints backstop critical invariants.
- Backward compatibility: legacy assertions are accepted under v0 relaxed rules and auto-migrated where possible; non-migratable records are quarantined with remediation guidance.
- Observability: all validation failures are logged with redaction, metrics are emitted per rule, and sample payloads are captured in secure debug storage.
- Tooling: shared validation library is generated from the schema for all SDKs; CI enforces schema linting and contract tests; schema changes require review and a migration plan.

Adopt TypeScript (tsc) as the single source of truth for type checking and use ESLint solely for linting and code-quality rules.

- Type checking: Run tsc with noEmit in CI and pre-push hooks to enforce sound typing, leveraging strict mode in tsconfig (strict: true and related strictness flags).
- Linting: Use ESLint with @typescript-eslint for stylistic and best-practice rules. Prefer non-type-aware ESLint rules for performance; enable type-aware ESLint rules only where TypeScript cannot express the intent (e.g., no-floating-promises, consistent-type-exports) and scope them to specific directories when needed.
- Rule overlap: Disable ESLint rules that duplicate TypeScript diagnostics (e.g., no-unused-vars, no-undef) in favor of the corresponding TypeScript checks via @typescript-eslint or tsc. Treat TypeScript errors as build blockers; ESLint violations follow project-defined severity.
- Developer workflow: 
  - IDE: ESLint runs on-save; TypeScript language service provides inline type feedback.
  - Git hooks: Pre-commit runs eslint --fix; pre-push runs tsc --noEmit and eslint --max-warnings=0 for changed files.
  - CI: Parallel jobs run tsc --noEmit and eslint across the repo; both must pass.
- Performance: Cache ESLint and tsc results; avoid enabling full-program type-aware ESLint across the entire codebase on every edit.
- Monorepo/projects: Each package has its own tsconfig for accurate type boundaries; a root tsconfig.build.json aggregates for CI. ESLint config is shared via a base config, with per-package overrides as needed.

This separation ensures fast feedback for style issues, authoritative type safety from the compiler, minimized duplication, and predictable build and CI behavior.

Adopt blue-green deployments with automated canary gating to achieve zero-downtime while preserving reliable end-to-end (E2E) testing:

- Provision a parallel “green” stack for each deploy (compute, runtime, and dependent services where feasible). Warm up and validate via health checks and synthetic probes.
- Route E2E test traffic explicitly to the green stack using a deterministic header/tenant marker to avoid interference with live users; shadow a subset of production traffic to green for observability without side effects.
- Run the full E2E suite against green before any user traffic cutover; block promotion on predefined SLOs (availability, latency, error budgets) and functional acceptance criteria.
- Perform database and schema changes using an expand-and-contract strategy with online, backward-compatible migrations; version contracts (APIs/events) and support dual-write/read compatibility during the transition window.
- For asynchronous systems, support parallel consumers/producers with versioned topics/queues or tolerant schemas; ensure idempotency and replay safety for test traffic.
- Use a traffic switch (load balancer/service mesh) for instantaneous cutover and immediate rollback to blue if gates fail; no restarts or draining required for live users.
- Isolate test data via namespacing/tenancy and automatic teardown to prevent cross-environment contamination.
- Make the deployment, test routing, gates, and rollback fully automated in CI/CD; all checks and promotions must be auditable and repeatable without maintenance windows.

This decision ensures zero downtime for users and deterministic, non-flaky E2E validation of each release candidate prior to exposure.

## Decision
Provide a single, high-level API help entry point that is both human-readable and machine-consumable, discoverable at GET / (default), GET /help, and via an OPTIONS response at the API root. The help content will be generated from the authoritative OpenAPI specification to ensure consistency and prevent drift, and exposed in multiple representations via content negotiation:
- text/plain and text/markdown for concise human consumption
- application/json and application/yaml for machine consumption (OpenAPI document and a curated “help summary” schema)

The help message will include:
- API purpose, supported versions, and deprecation policy
- Authentication methods with example headers/flows
- Common concerns: rate limits, pagination, filtering, sorting, idempotency keys, error model
- Media types and content negotiation guidance
- Environment endpoints (prod/stage/sandbox) and base URLs
- Links to SDKs, code samples, and detailed docs
- Contact and support channels, SLA, and status page link

Per-endpoint help is discoverable via:
- OPTIONS on each resource providing allowed methods, minimal semantics, and link to detailed docs
- “documentation” link relations (HAL/JSON Hyper-Schema style) from root and resources

Versioning:
- The root help advertises available versions; Accept/Accept-Version negotiates versioned help
- Deprecated items are flagged with sunset metadata and links to migration guides

Operational considerations:
- Responses are cacheable with ETag/max-age; help generation occurs at build-time with runtime overlays for dynamic quotas/limits
- Accessibility and i18n ready; default locale is English with optional locale negotiation via Accept-Language

We will persist any inbound application payload that fails validation in a dedicated, nullable JSON/JSONB column (invalid_payload) on ApplyApplication. When an ingest cannot be normalized into domain entities, we will create or reuse a minimal ApplyApplication record in an Invalid state, assign correlation identifiers, and atomically store the raw request plus structured error metadata (e.g., schema version, validation errors, received_at, source) in invalid_payload. No child records will be created for invalid applications, and invalid_payload will never be read for core business flows.

This change is backward compatible: the column defaults to NULL and is populated only on validation failure. We will not index invalid_payload; instead, we will add a lightweight partial index on status = 'invalid' for operational queries. Access is restricted to privileged/admin contexts; contents are encrypted at rest, redacted in logs/export, and excluded from full‑text search. Data is retained for up to 90 days or until successful remediation/reprocessing, after which invalid_payload is cleared and status updated.

Operational tooling will allow viewing, redaction, correction, and reprocessing; partial saves outside invalid_payload remain disallowed.

We will standardize on a TypeScript-first, JavaScript ecosystem with opinionated frameworks to optimize developer productivity, consistency, and long-term maintainability:

- Web frontend: Next.js (React 18) for SSR/SSG/ISR, routing, and performance. Styling: Tailwind CSS. Component library: Headless UI + Radix Primitives where needed.
- Mobile: React Native with Expo for cross-platform parity reusing domain and UI logic where feasible.
- Backend: NestJS (Node.js, TypeScript) for modular architecture, DI, and consistent patterns. HTTP API default is REST; GraphQL enabled via NestJS module only for use cases that benefit from client-driven queries.
- Data access: Prisma as the ORM for type-safe data models and migrations. Postgres as the primary relational database. Redis for caching and short-lived ephemeral data.
- Messaging/async: NATS or RabbitMQ (environment-dependent) via NestJS microservices package; default to NATS for cloud-native deployments.
- Auth: OAuth 2.1/OIDC using an external IdP (e.g., Auth0/Keycloak). Session tokens are JWTs with short TTL and refresh tokens managed by the IdP. RBAC enforced via NestJS guards.
- Monorepo: Turborepo with PNPM workspaces. Shared packages for types, utilities, and domain models. Path aliasing via TSConfig and consistent lint/format configs.
- Testing: Jest + Testing Library for unit/integration; Pact for consumer-driven contract tests; Cypress for E2E; k6 for performance testing on critical APIs.
- API documentation: OpenAPI (via NestJS Swagger) as the source of truth for REST; GraphQL schema published with versioning when used.
- Observability: OpenTelemetry instrumentation; logs via structured JSON; metrics and tracing exported to the chosen APM (e.g., Grafana Tempo/Prometheus or Datadog).
- Build and deploy: Containerized services with multi-stage Dockerfiles; CI/CD pipelines produce SBOMs and signed images. Infrastructure targets Kubernetes with Helm charts; local dev via Docker Compose.
- Accessibility and i18n: WCAG 2.1 AA baseline on web; React Native a11y APIs; i18next for localization in both web and mobile.
- Constraints: Avoid framework mixing outside these selections without ADR review. New services must use NestJS unless a justified exception is approved. Frontend variants must be Next.js to maintain SSR/SEO and shared tooling.
- Non-goals: Supporting legacy browsers beyond our defined baseline; poly-repo structures; server-side frameworks outside Node/NestJS in this phase.

We will migrate all custom method definitions from the legacy ad-hoc text/YAML shape to a canonical, versioned JSON format validated by JSON Schema (2020-12). The new format will standardize method metadata, inputs, outputs, and errors with the following decisions:

- Canonical representation: application/json files per method, with fields: name (kebab-case), namespace, version (semver), description, inputs (schema), outputs (schema), errors (enumerated, schema), idempotency, sideEffects, auth, tags, examples, and deprecation metadata.
- Validation: JSON Schema for inputs/outputs/errors; CI enforcement using schemaver + ajv; contract tests autogenerated from examples.
- Versioning: SemVer per method; breaking changes require new major; minor/patch allowed for additive/bugfix changes. Deprecations carry deprecationSince and removalIn.
- Namespacing: domain-scoped namespaces (e.g., billing.invoice.create) flattened to file paths (billing/invoice/create.json).
- Discovery: index.json manifest per package/service listing exported methods with versions; services expose /.well-known/custom-methods endpoint serving the manifest.
- Backward compatibility: a read-only compatibility loader will parse the legacy format at runtime and emit the new shape; authoring in the legacy format is frozen immediately. Legacy format support will be removed after two LTS releases.
- Tooling: a CLI (cmc) will scaffold methods, validate schemas, generate language-specific stubs/clients, and produce markdown docs.
- Rollout: new format allowed immediately; all new methods must use it. Existing methods will be migrated incrementally with dual-publish. Completion target: end of next quarter for Tier-1 services.
- Governance: changes require review by API Council; CI blocks merges that violate schema or versioning rules.

Adopt the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern and introduce separate BFF services per client application (e.g., Web, Mobile) as the sole backend interfaces consumed by those clients. Each BFF will expose a client-tailored API, orchestrate and aggregate calls to downstream services, enforce client-specific security and authorization policies, and perform response shaping, caching, and protocol adaptation as needed. BFFs will encapsulate client-centric business logic, reducing coupling to domain services and shielding clients from backend changes.

We will:
- Create one BFF per client surface with independent deployability and release cadence aligned to its client.
- Maintain backwards compatibility of BFF APIs with explicit versioning and deprecation policies.
- Centralize cross-cutting concerns at the BFF layer (auth, rate limiting, input validation, error mapping, observability, feature flags, and limited edge caching).
- Prefer pass-through of domain logic to backends; only client-specific composition lives in BFFs.
- Enforce strict contracts with downstream services and apply resilience patterns (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers) at the BFF boundary.
- Provide consistent telemetry (structured logs, metrics, traces) and budgeted latency SLOs for BFF endpoints.
- Limit data storage in BFFs to ephemeral caches; persistent data remains in domain services.
- Ensure BFFs are owned by the respective client teams, with shared platform standards for security, SDK generation, and documentation.

This decision decouples clients from backend evolution, optimizes payloads and performance per client, and concentrates client-specific complexity in a manageable layer.

## Decision

The IAM API will use human-readable, unique names as the primary identifiers for all externally addressable resources (e.g., users, groups, roles, policies) instead of UUIDs.

- Resource addressing: All endpoints use names in paths and parameters (e.g., /v1/users/{userName}, /v1/groups/{groupName}). Responses return names; UUIDs are not exposed.
- Uniqueness and scope: Names must be unique within their defined scope (e.g., tenant/organization). Cross-scope references must include scope qualifiers.
- Stability: Names are the stable external identifiers. Renames are supported only via an explicit rename operation that atomically updates the canonical name and ensures referential integrity; otherwise names are immutable.
- Canonicalization and validation: Names are case-insensitive with canonical lowercase storage and comparison; allowed chars: [a-z0-9-], 3–63 chars, no leading/trailing hyphen, no consecutive hyphens. Reserved names and prefixes are disallowed.
- Errors and semantics: 409 Conflict on duplicate names; 404 Not Found for unknown names; 422 Unprocessable Entity for invalid names. Sorting and pagination default to name.
- Backward compatibility: Existing UUID fields in payloads are deprecated and removed from responses; clients must use names. Internally, opaque IDs (e.g., UUIDs) may remain for storage/joins but are not part of the public contract.
- Security and authorization: Policy definitions and access checks reference resources by canonical names; name changes trigger policy revalidation.
- Observability: Audit logs and metrics record names (and internal IDs for forensic correlation).

## Decision
Implement a first-class “check.performed” event to count automated checks, with authoritative classification at authentication/edge and consistent propagation across services.

- Definition: A “check” is any programmatic verification executed by non-human principals (e.g., bots, CI, schedulers, external webhooks) that evaluates code, configuration, security, policy, or health of artifacts; routine service liveness/health probes are excluded.
- Classification: Principal type is set at auth time using:
  - Service accounts and API tokens flagged as automated (principal_type=bot|ci|scheduler|webhook).
  - JWT/OAuth claims and token metadata to mark automation.
  - An optional X-Automation-Context header (enum: human|bot|ci|scheduler|webhook) may narrow classification; human UI requests cannot self-declare as automated.
  - Heuristics (allowlisted IPs, known user-agents) are used only when principal is unknown; such events are tagged classification=inferred.
- Event emission: Middleware in all relevant services emits check.performed exactly-once with idempotency key, excluding health endpoints. Required fields: event_time, principal_id, principal_type, source_system, check_type, target (repo/project/env), outcome, latency_ms, request_id, classification_confidence, schema_version. No PII is included.
- Telemetry pipeline: Events stream to Kafka (or equivalent), aggregated to:
  - Time-series store (e.g., Prometheus) for real-time counters.
  - Analytics warehouse (e.g., BigQuery/Snowflake) for historical reporting.
  Rollups are computed hourly and daily; no sampling for cardinal metrics.
- Governance: Event schema is versioned; data quality dashboards and alerts monitor volume, nulls, and inferred rates. A canonical metric “automated_checks_count” is exposed by principal_type, source_system, check_type, and target.
- Scope and rollout: Forward-only adoption from decision date; no backfill required. Dashboards and APIs will provide organization-, project-, and system-level counts with filters.

## Decision
All network communications must enforce TLS with certificate and hostname verification enabled by default across all environments (dev, test, staging, prod). Disabling verification (e.g., InsecureSkipVerify, rejectUnauthorized=false, CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0) is prohibited. Self-signed certificates are not allowed unless issued by the organization’s approved private CA and distributed via managed trust stores.

- TLS 1.2+ is required; prefer TLS 1.3 where available. Weak ciphers and deprecated protocols are disallowed.
- Server certificate validation and hostname verification must fail closed. Retries are permitted; bypasses are not.
- Centralized trust management will use OS trust stores or a centrally managed CA bundle. Certificate issuance/renewal is automated via ACME/enterprise PKI with short-lived certs and monitored expiry.
- For service-to-service traffic, mutual TLS is required where supported; otherwise, server-side verification remains mandatory.
- For local development, verification remains enabled: developers use endpoints with valid certs, a sanctioned internal root CA distributed via dev trust stores, or a local TLS proxy that presents valid certs. No environment may ship with verification disabled.
- Production flags to disable verification do not exist. Any emergency override must be time-bound, environment-scoped, security-approved, auditable, and removed within a defined SLA.
- Tooling enforces compliance: CI/CD blocks insecure flags, SAST rules detect verification bypasses, and integration tests assert verification behavior. Runtime metrics/logs capture TLS handshake and verification failures.
- Certificate pinning (CA/SPKI) may be applied to high-risk clients with a defined rotation strategy and recovery path.
- Non-compliant endpoints will be deprecated on a published timeline until they meet these requirements.

## Decision
We will minimize configuration surface area and complexity to favor sensible defaults and convention over configuration. Each deployable will accept a single, flat, declarative config with a strict, versioned schema and validation at startup. Required options are limited to identity, network bindings, and external dependencies; all other behavior is driven by documented defaults.

Configuration hierarchy is constrained and predictable:
- Base defaults (bundled)
- One optional application config file
- Environment variables for operational overrides
- Command-line flags for ad‑hoc/local overrides

We will not support dynamic logic in config (no conditionals, templates, includes, evaluation, or cross-file imports). Nesting depth and cardinality are limited; feature flags and plugin settings must be encapsulated under a single namespaced key without arbitrary extension points. Secrets are not stored in config files; they are supplied via environment variables or the secret manager.

Backward compatibility is maintained via explicit schema versions and automated migrations for non-breaking changes; deprecated keys warn before removal. Tooling includes a generated reference, example config, and a linter/validator. Any new feature must justify new config keys, prefer deriving behavior from existing inputs, and default to “off” if risk‑bearing. If a capability requires significant logic or branching, it belongs in code, not configuration.

We will enable extractToLink for JSON-LD expanded emission and default to link-by-@id semantics instead of inlining. Concretely:
- Any node with a stable identifier (IRI) or a deterministically generated @id will be emitted once as a top-level node, and all subsequent occurrences will be emitted as references containing only @id.
- Nodes without a resolvable @id (true blank nodes) will remain embedded; no implicit skolemization is performed unless explicitly configured.
- The emitter guarantees uniqueness per @id within a document and deduplicates repeated structures, preserving outbound and inbound edges by linking.
- Cyclic and shared subgraphs are represented via links, avoiding recursive embedding and duplication.
- The behavior is gated by an emitter option: expanded.extractToLink=true (default). It can be disabled per call or via configuration for backward compatibility.
- When disabled, existing embedding behavior is preserved.
- The decision applies only to expanded form; compacted or flattened forms may still re-embed according to context and framing rules.
- Validation ensures that referenced @id nodes exist in the document (or are resolvable externally), otherwise falls back to embedding for that node.
- Migration notes: version the emitter configuration, provide a linter to detect large embedded graphs that benefit from linking, and offer a toggle to force skolemization if consumers require link-only graphs.

Adopt Kotlin as the primary programming language for all new Android applications and JVM-based services in this codebase. Existing Java code will be maintained and integrated via Kotlin/Java interop; migration to Kotlin will be incremental and opportunistic (touch-when-changing), not a wholesale rewrite.

Standards and tooling:
- Kotlin 2.x with JVM target 17 (updated as part of regular platform upgrades).
- Gradle Kotlin DSL for build scripts.
- Official Kotlin coding conventions; enforce with ktlint and detekt in CI.
- Prefer KSP-based processors; avoid kapt unless required by an unreplaceable dependency.
- IntelliJ IDEA/Android Studio as the standard IDEs with Kotlin plugins.

Language/features:
- Use coroutines and Flow for concurrency and reactive streams; apply structured concurrency and cancellation.
- Prefer data classes, sealed hierarchies, value classes, and null-safety idioms.
- Avoid extension abuse and operator overloading that reduces readability.

Testing:
- JUnit 5 + kotlinx-coroutines-test; allow Kotest/MockK where appropriate.

Frameworks/libraries:
- Prefer frameworks with first-class Kotlin support (e.g., Spring with Kotlin extensions, Android Jetpack).
- Use Kotlinx libraries (serialization, datetime, immutable collections) where suitable.

Scope/constraints:
- New modules default to Kotlin; Java may be used only when interop with Java-only libraries or specific performance constraints warrant it.
- Kotlin Multiplatform is opt-in per module after feasibility assessment; not a blanket default.

People/process:
- Provide team training and code review guidelines focused on idiomatic Kotlin.
- Apply static analysis and CI gates to ensure consistent adoption.

We will standardize on Dapr as the application sidecar runtime and adopt a controlled release process to ensure stability and predictable upgrades across environments.

- Versioning and pinning: All services will pin to a specific Dapr runtime and CLI minor version (e.g., 1.x.y), with patch updates permitted automatically; minor updates require an ADR and release plan. Components and SDKs will be pinned to compatible versions per Dapr’s compatibility matrix.

- Packaging and distribution: Dapr will be provisioned via official Helm charts and validated container images from the Dapr project. All artifacts will be cached in our internal registry and verified via checksums/signatures.

- Environment rollout: Releases follow dev → staging → prod with automated conformance, e2e, and performance tests at each gate. Canary rollout (10% → 50% → 100%) is mandatory for minor upgrades in production.

- Backward compatibility: We will only adopt Dapr versions that maintain backward compatibility for enabled features. Any breaking component spec changes require a migration playbook and dual-run period.

- Configuration management: Dapr configs (MTLS, tracing, retries) and components (pubsub, state, bindings, secret stores) are managed as code in a central repo with environment overlays. Changes require code review and automated validation.

- Observability and SLOs: We will enable Dapr metrics, logs, and traces by default and define SLOs for sidecar startup, request latency overhead, and error budgets. Telemetry regressions block promotion.

- Security and compliance: mTLS remains enabled; cert rotation and token auth are enforced. Images undergo vulnerability scanning; CVEs with critical severity trigger expedited patch releases.

- Rollback and support: A one-click rollback to the previous minor/patch is required. We support N-1 minor versions; older versions are deprecated with a 90-day sunset.

We will allow TODO/FIXME comments only as traceable, time-bound technical debt with enforced ownership and closure.

- Required format: // TODO(username | team) [ISSUE-1234] YYYY-MM-DD: short imperative summary. Optionally append due: YYYY-MM-DD and priority: P1–P3.
- Every TODO/FIXME must link to a tracked work item (issue/ticket) except in spike branches. Untracked TODOs are blocked by CI.
- No TODOs without a named owner. Ownership may be a team alias if rotating.
- Lifespan: default max 30 calendar days from creation; P1 within 7 days, P2 within 30, P3 within 90. Past due items fail CI unless explicitly labeled accepted-debt in the linked issue and approved by the code owner.
- Scope: TODOs must be small, concrete, and local. Larger or cross-cutting work must be represented only by an issue; comments should reference the issue without duplicating plans.
- Enforcement: a linter/CI job validates format, presence of issue links, dates, and SLA. Release branches cannot contain untracked or overdue TODOs. Counts and aging are reported on dashboards.
- Closure: when addressing the work, remove the TODO comment and include “closes ISSUE-1234” in the PR. If the TODO is no longer applicable, delete it and close the issue with rationale.
- Exceptions: generated or vendored code is ignored; test-only TODOs follow the same rules.
- Cadence: teams review open TODOs weekly and during release readiness; overdue items must be reprioritized or eliminated.

## Decision
We will assign each Report a globally unique, immutable, externally-visible reference generated at creation time using UUID v7 (time-ordered UUID). The reference will be:

- Generated in the application layer upon Report creation; no client-supplied values.
- Persisted in the database as reports.report_ref (UUID) with a unique, non-null, immutable constraint and a supporting unique index.
- Used as the canonical identifier across APIs, events, logs, and inter-service communication. All foreign keys and cross-entity links will reference report_ref.
- Exposed externally as a read-only string. For human readability, we will present it with a “REP-” prefix and the UUID v7 string (e.g., REP-018f1c1a-...); we will not shorten or re-encode to avoid ambiguity.
- Backfilled for existing records via a one-time migration that generates UUID v7 values and enforces the uniqueness constraint.

Operational considerations:

- Because UUID v7 is k-ordered, it improves index locality and query performance for recent reports.
- On write conflicts (extremely unlikely), we will retry generation once.
- The reference is never updated or reused; deleted report references are not recycled.
- All create endpoints will return report_ref; all subsequent operations must use it.
- Analytics and auditing will store and display report_ref to ensure traceability.

We will containerize all application services using Docker to standardize build, test, and runtime environments across local, CI, and production. Each service must include a maintained Dockerfile (multi-stage builds, BuildKit-enabled) and .dockerignore. Images will be minimal, preferring distroless or Alpine where appropriate, with non-root users, read-only filesystems where feasible, no shell in runtime layers, and no privileged mode. Secrets will be injected via orchestrator secret stores (not baked into images) and configuration provided via environment variables and mounted config files.

Images will be tagged with semantic versions and immutable digests (git SHA) and pushed to the central container registry after passing CI (linting, unit/integration tests, SBOM generation, vulnerability scanning, and license checks). Healthchecks, exposed ports, and resource hints must be defined. Applications should be stateless; persistence is externalized to managed data services or explicitly defined volumes with clear ownership and backup policies.

Local development and integration testing will use Docker Compose for service orchestration and parity. Production deployment will consume the same images via the target orchestrator (e.g., Kubernetes), inheriting runtime constraints (CPU/memory limits, probes). Network egress is least-privilege; capabilities are dropped by default.

Backward deployment paths that rely on host-installed runtimes are deprecated and will be phased out. Performance baselines must be captured; image size and startup time budgets are enforced via CI gates. Documentation for build/run instructions, environment variables, and operational playbooks must accompany each service’s Docker configuration.

We will introduce compile-time feature flag support for Storefront SCSS using a centralized, namespaced feature map and helper API, enabling incremental, opt-in rollout of styling changes without shipping unused CSS.

- Implement a central _features.scss that defines a $sf-features: () map with all flags and their default values. Flags default to false for breaking/visual changes and true for additive, non-breaking enhancements.
- Provide helpers:
  - @function sf-feature($name) -> boolean
  - @mixin when-feature($name) { @if sf-feature($name) { @content } }
  - @mixin unless-feature($name) { @if not sf-feature($name) { @content } }
- Enforce early import of _features.scss as the first SCSS import so subsequent partials can branch styles.
- Allow overrides via build-time configuration:
  - sass-loader additionalData or Sass include to inject a $sf-features override map before imports.
  - Environment variable STOREFRONT_FEATURE_FLAGS (e.g., new-cart=true,legacy-grid=false) parsed by the build to generate the override map.
  - Theme/customers can override by defining $sf-features prior to importing Storefront bundle.
- Adopt naming convention sf.feature-name (kebab-case), single-purpose, non-nested flags, with JSDoc-style comments documenting intent, defaults, deprecation plan, and removal version.
- Backwards compatibility: when a feature flag is false, legacy styles remain authoritative; gated styles only compile when true, preventing CSS bloat.
- Governance: new flags require an ADR entry, tests (visual/regression where applicable), and a removal timeline; flags slated for removal will flip to true by default one minor before deletion.
- Scope: SCSS only; no runtime JS toggles. Uses Dart Sass. No dynamic user-level switching.

Adopt React Context API to manage cross-cutting, low-churn application state such as authentication/session, theme, localization, feature flags, and user preferences. For high-frequency or large, mutable state, continue to use specialized libraries (e.g., Redux/Zustand) and React Query/SWR for server cache; Context must not be used as a general-purpose state store.

Implement domain-scoped contexts (AuthContext, ThemeContext, I18nContext, FeatureFlagContext) with custom hooks (useAuth, useTheme, etc.), colocating providers near consumers while exposing a top-level composition provider for app bootstrap. Keep context values minimal, stable, and memoized; export functions that wrap state transitions to prevent unnecessary re-renders. Split contexts to avoid unrelated updates; consider use-context-selector for fine-grained subscriptions if profiling reveals bottlenecks.

Type all contexts with TypeScript, provide null-safe hooks that throw on missing providers, and expose test utilities to mount providers with fixtures. Ensure SSR compatibility by deriving initial values from request-bound sources and hydrating consistently on the client.

Migration will replace prop drilling with context-backed hooks in targeted slices, proceeding per domain. Success criteria: reduced prop plumbing, stable render performance (no significant increase in commit times), and clearer ownership boundaries for cross-cutting concerns.

## Decision

Standardize on Docker Compose v2 as the sole orchestration tool for local development, integration testing, and lightweight environment provisioning. All teams will use the docker compose (CLI plugin) command; the legacy docker-compose (v1) binary is deprecated and unsupported.

We will:
- Migrate all Compose manifests to the v2-compatible schema and features, consolidating into a single canonical compose.yaml per service group with profiles for optional components.
- Update developer tooling, Makefiles, and scripts to use docker compose commands and flags; remove any explicit dependencies on the v1 Python binary.
- Update CI/CD runners and ephemeral environments to Docker Engine and Docker Compose plugin versions that fully support v2 (minimum Docker Engine 20.10+ and Docker Compose v2.x matching the LTS toolchain).
- Provide a short-lived shim for legacy commands (docker-compose -> docker compose) where necessary, and remove it after the migration window.
- Align secrets, buildx, and extension usages with v2 capabilities; disallow features deprecated in v2.
- Enforce the version via pre-commit checks and CI verification steps; builds will fail on detection of v1 usage.

Ownership and timeline:
- Platform Engineering owns the migration, validation, and documentation.
- A two-sprint migration period is allocated; after that, v1 is blocked in CI and removed from developer setup scripts.

Success criteria:
- All pipelines and developer workflows run using docker compose v2 without regressions.
- No references to docker-compose remain in code, docs, or tooling.

## Decision
We will separate all externally consumed contracts from their concrete implementations into distinct, independently versioned packages and build artifacts.

- Structure:
  - <domain>.api: Public interfaces, DTOs, error types, constants, feature flags, and minimal factories/builders necessary for construction and testing. No runtime logic or network/IO.
  - <domain>.spi (optional): Service Provider Interfaces for pluggable implementations.
  - <domain>.impl: Concrete implementations and internal utilities. Not exported as a dependency to consumers.
- Dependency direction: impl and spi depend on api; api depends on no internal modules. No code in api may import impl. Cross-module references must flow api → spi (optional) → impl only.
- Encapsulation/enforcement:
  - Use JPMS/exports or package visibility to hide impl.
  - Publish api as a separate artifact with semantic versioning and strict compatibility guarantees; impl versions may evolve independently.
  - Apply architectural tests and build rules to forbid impl leakage into api and to prevent consumers from depending on impl.
- Compatibility:
  - API follows semver with deprecation periods and replacement guidance; removals only in the next major version.
  - DTOs in api are stable, serialization-friendly, and free of implementation dependencies.
- Extensibility:
  - Pluggability via spi + service loader/DI. Default implementations live in impl and are swappable.
- Runtime wiring:
  - Applications depend on api (compile) and select one or more impl artifacts (runtime).
- Tooling:
  - Separate repositories or submodules with ownership boundaries.
  - CI publishes api and impl independently; contract tests validate impl against api.
- Documentation:
  - API is fully documented; impl notes remain internal.

## Decision
We will document significant architectural decisions using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

- Format and template:
  - Use MADR 3.x style ADRs with sections: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Options, Pros/Cons, Links.
  - Provide a canonical template at docs/architecture/decisions/_template.md.
- Location and naming:
  - Store ADRs in docs/architecture/decisions/.
  - Name files as NNN-title-slug.md with a monotonically increasing zero-padded number starting at 000.
- Scope:
  - Required for decisions with substantial architectural impact: cross-cutting concerns, system boundaries, public interfaces/contracts, data models and migrations, infrastructure/platform choices, security/privacy, availability/performance/SLA/SLO, cost implications, and technology selection/deprecation.
- Lifecycle and states:
  - States: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded.
  - Accepted ADRs are immutable; changes require a new ADR that supersedes prior records.
- Process:
  - Create ADRs early (before implementation) and iterate via pull requests.
  - Each ADR must list alternatives and trade-offs and link to related issues/PRs.
  - Approval requires at least two reviewers, including a designated architecture owner.
  - Record rationale for rejections; keep Rejected ADRs for traceability.
- Tooling and discoverability:
  - Optional use of adr-tools or templates to scaffold.
  - Render ADRs in project docs (e.g., MkDocs) and link from README and internal wiki.
  - Tag ADRs with domain labels at the top (e.g., [security], [data], [infra]).
- Governance:
  - The architecture owner curates consistency, numbering, and status transitions.
  - Teams must reference relevant ADRs in design docs and PR descriptions.

Adopt optimistic concurrency as the default concurrency control strategy across services and data stores. Each mutable aggregate/entity will carry a monotonic version (e.g., rowversion/timestamp in SQL, _etag in document stores, expectedVersion for event streams). Updates must include the last-seen version (e.g., If-Match/ETag for HTTP, version column in SQL UPDATE WHERE clause). On version mismatch, the operation fails with a 409 Conflict (or equivalent), and the client may refresh state and retry.

Implement compare-and-swap semantics in repositories and APIs; no long-lived locks or distributed transactions. Use small, single-aggregate transactions. Client SDKs will provide a retry policy with jittered exponential backoff and a bounded number of attempts, and all write operations must be idempotent (idempotency keys for commands; deduplication at consumers).

For event-sourced components, use expected version checks per stream. For message-driven workflows, use an outbox pattern combined with OCC on the outbox record and consumer-side deduplication.

Provide conflict-resolution strategies per domain:
- Silent retry for idempotent, commutative updates.
- Automatic merge for well-defined fields (e.g., additive counters).
- User-facing merge UI for conflicting edits on non-commutative data.

Define hot-spot mitigation: detect high-conflict entities via telemetry; allow targeted fallback to pessimistic locking or queue-based serialization behind a feature flag for those aggregates only.

APIs will standardize error semantics and headers (409 Conflict, ETag/If-Match) and log conflicts for observability. Schema requirements: add version columns/indexes; enforce updates by version in data access layers. Testing will include conflict injection and retry behavior.

Scope excludes cross-service distributed locks and two-phase commit. This decision is mandatory for all new write paths; legacy paths will be migrated incrementally.

Adopt a relational, normalized (3NF) core data model on PostgreSQL with the following conventions and structures:
- Primary keys: UUIDv7 (surrogate keys) for all tables; natural keys enforced via unique constraints.
- Core columns: created_at, updated_at (UTC), created_by, updated_by, and deleted_at for soft deletes; hard deletes disallowed for business entities.
- Multi-tenancy: tenant_id on all tenant-scoped tables with composite unique indexes including tenant_id; Row-Level Security enabled per tenant.
- Referential integrity: mandatory foreign keys with ON UPDATE RESTRICT and ON DELETE RESTRICT by default; explicit CASCADE only where derived data can be safely regenerated.
- Domain modeling: business concepts modeled as first-class tables; enumerations modeled as lookup tables (or PostgreSQL enums when stability is guaranteed).
- Extensibility: JSONB attributes column on select entities for low-volatility, optional properties; promote frequently queried JSONB fields to first-class columns as usage stabilizes.
- Concurrency: optimistic locking via integer version column (or xmin) on write paths.
- Auditing: append-only audit tables (or logical decoding stream) for critical entities; changes captured with before/after values and actor.
- Naming: snake_case table and column names; singular table names; fk_<table>_<column> and idx_<table>_<columns> naming for constraints/indexes.
- Indexing: btree indexes for FKs and high-selectivity columns; partial indexes for soft-deleted data; GIN indexes for JSONB where needed.
- Migrations: versioned, backward-compatible migrations managed via <tool> and executed in CI/CD with automated rollback plans.
- Data privacy: classify PII columns; apply column-level encryption or pgcrypto where required.
- Versioning: schema semver and ERD snapshots maintained with each release.

This initial model prioritizes integrity, auditability, tenant isolation, and measured flexibility while avoiding premature denormalization.

We will not implement an explicit state machine within Services to govern domain state transitions. Instead, Services and domain aggregates will enforce invariants and transitions through explicit intent methods (e.g., approve(), cancel(), fulfill()) with guarded validations and business rules co-located in the domain layer. Transition eligibility will be expressed via predicate methods and policy/specification objects where complexity warrants it. Orchestration of multi-step processes will reside in application services or sagas/process managers, using idempotent commands, retries, and compensations as needed, without a generic state-machine framework.

Persistence will store current state as explicit fields plus derived read models as required; no generic transition tables will be maintained. Observability will rely on domain events and structured logs to audit transitions. Validation errors will be surfaced as typed domain exceptions with machine-readable codes.

This decision applies to all new Services and refactors; existing state-machine code will be sunset opportunistically and replaced when touching related areas. Exceptions may be granted for externally mandated workflows or complex long-running orchestrations; those cases should use a dedicated workflow engine at the boundary, not embedded in core Services.

We will revisit this decision if transition logic becomes unmanageably complex (e.g., >10 states with dense conditional transitions), if compliance requires formalized workflow proofs, or if metrics indicate frequent defects traceable to ad hoc transition handling.

## Decision
Adopt a consistent, pragmatic REST standard for all external and internal HTTP APIs to ensure interoperability, maintainability, and observability:

- Resource design: Use plural, noun-based, hierarchical URIs (e.g., /v1/orders/{id}/items). No verbs in paths; represent actions via state transitions or sub-resources.
- Methods: GET (safe), POST (create/commands), PUT (full replace), PATCH (partial update via JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7386), DELETE (idempotent).
- Status codes: Use standard semantics; include 202 + Location for async operations; 201 + Location on create; 204 on successful no-content; 409 for conflicts; 422 for validation errors; 429 for rate limits.
- Media types and payloads: Default application/json; support content negotiation via Accept. JSON uses camelCase, UTC ISO-8601 timestamps, RFC 3339 formatting, and stable field names.
- Errors: Conform to RFC 7807 (application/problem+json) with type, title, status, detail, instance, and domain-specific error codes.
- Versioning: URI versioning (/v1) with deprecation and Sunset headers; maintain backward compatibility within a major version.
- Filtering, sorting, pagination: Filtering via query parameters (e.g., filter[status]=), sorting via sort=field or sort=-field, cursor-based pagination (page[cursor], page[size]) with RFC 5988 Link headers.
- Caching: Support ETag/If-None-Match and Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since; define cache-control where safe; enable conditional requests.
- Idempotency: Require Idempotency-Key for unsafe, retryable POST operations; ensure PUT/DELETE are idempotent.
- Observability: Return a Correlation-Id header; log it end-to-end; expose rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-*) where applicable.
- Security: Enforce TLS; OAuth2/OIDC for auth; JWT access tokens; least-privilege scopes; avoid sensitive data in URLs.
- Documentation and contracts: OpenAPI 3.0+ as the single source of truth; include examples and schemas; CI to validate spec conformance.
- Consistency: No envelope wrappers for lists; use HATEOAS links selectively; maintain stable SLAs for performance and availability.

We will standardize on accepting file uploads as Base64-encoded content in request payloads across public and internal APIs for small-to-medium files, prioritizing transport-agnostic simplicity and consistent developer experience over raw throughput.

Scope:
- Applies to synchronous API endpoints where files are part of a larger JSON request.
- Intended for files up to 5 MB by default; larger payloads must use the binary/multipart or pre-signed URL path.

Key choices:
- Payloads carry Base64-encoded content plus required metadata (filename, MIME type, byte length before encoding, checksum).
- Servers will decode in a streaming-safe manner, validate length/checksum, and reject payloads exceeding limits.
- Rate limits and WAF rules will be tuned for the 33–37% size overhead of Base64.
- Virus/malware scanning, content-type sniffing, and extension/MIME consistency checks are mandatory post-decode.
- Audit logs will record metadata only; content is not logged.

Non-goals and exceptions:
- Not intended for very large files or high-throughput ingestion; those must use direct-to-storage uploads with pre-signed URLs.
- Real-time chunked streaming over Base64 is out of scope for now.

Migration and compatibility:
- Existing multipart endpoints remain supported; new clients are encouraged to adopt Base64 for small files.
- We will expose both modes behind capability negotiation, with deprecation only after adoption metrics meet targets.

Operational notes:
- Enforce per-request and per-tenant size quotas.
- Monitor decode errors and latency; auto-fallback guidance in 4xx responses for oversized payloads.

We will implement a Hybrid Tech Radar as the authoritative catalog of technologies and practices, combining curated expert judgment with automated telemetry.

- Structure: Four quadrants (Languages & Frameworks; Techniques & Practices; Platforms & Infrastructure; Tools & Services) across four rings (Adopt, Trial, Assess, Hold).
- Dual-sourcing: Curated inputs from the Architecture Guild and domain SMEs, augmented by automated signals (repo adoption, dependency freshness, vulnerability trends, incident/cost impact, performance/quality metrics).
- System of record: Backstage with the open-source Tech Radar plugin as the publishing surface; a versioned JSON/YAML registry in Git for change history; data pipeline pulling from GitHub/GitLab, Jira, SonarQube, Snyk, artifact registries, cloud cost and observability platforms.
- Governance: Architecture Review Board owns taxonomy, criteria, and ring decisions; domain custodians own specific entries; contributions via lightweight RFC/PR workflow with defined acceptance criteria and sunset policy.
- Cadence: Quarterly review and publication; monthly telemetry refresh; ad-hoc updates for critical items (e.g., CVEs, EOL).
- Decision criteria: Fitness functions weighted across security, reliability, operability, cost, delivery velocity, ecosystem health, and strategic fit; thresholds inform ring movement.
- Usage: Mandatory reference for solution and platform proposals, tech selection ADRs, and procurement; exceptions require recorded rationale and time-bounded re-evaluation.
- Transparency: Organization-wide read access; rationale, evidence, and examples documented per entry; changelog maintained.
- KPIs: Coverage (percentage of material techs captured), adoption alignment, time-to-ring-change, exception rate, and risk reduction signals.

This hybrid model becomes the single source guiding technology choices while remaining responsive to real-world usage and risk signals.

Decide to implement a design-tokens–first theming system with CSS variables as the runtime mechanism and Style Dictionary as the single source of truth for token generation. Tokens (color, spacing, typography, elevation, motion) will be maintained in a repository as platform-agnostic JSON, versioned and validated via CI. Style Dictionary will emit platform-specific artifacts: web (CSS variables under :root and [data-theme]), mobile (iOS/Android resource files), and design tooling exports.

On web, themes (e.g., light, dark, high-contrast, brand variants) will be applied by toggling a data-theme attribute on the html element. Default theme follows prefers-color-scheme with user override persisted in localStorage and inlined server-side to prevent flash of incorrect theme. Components and Tailwind configuration will consume CSS variables only; no hardcoded values. Tailwind colors will reference CSS variables to preserve runtime theming while retaining utility ergonomics. Component libraries must read tokens via variables and avoid per-component JS theme logic.

Token names follow a semantic, tiered convention (core → semantic → component), enabling brand theming by overriding semantic layers without breaking components. Accessibility requirements (WCAG AA minimum contrast) are enforced at token level with automated checks.

No SCSS theme maps or runtime CSS-in-JS color computations are allowed. Theming changes must be zero-JS where possible, limited to setting data-theme. New themes are added by defining token overrides and regenerating artifacts. This approach ensures consistency across platforms, minimal runtime cost, and scalable, auditable theming evolution.

We will standardize on TypeScript version 3.4.5 across the codebase and build pipeline. The exact version will be pinned in devDependencies for all packages and enforced via lockfiles to ensure deterministic builds. CI will verify the compiler version (tsc -v) and fail if a divergent TypeScript version is detected. All developers’ IDEs must use the workspace TypeScript (Use Workspace Version) to avoid discrepancies.

All build tools and plugins that integrate with the compiler (e.g., ts-loader, ts-jest, ts-node, eslint typescript parser/plugin) must be set to versions compatible with TypeScript 3.4.5. New dependencies that require a higher TypeScript version will not be introduced without a separate ADR to upgrade. Existing tsconfig settings remain in effect; any required adjustments for compatibility with 3.4.5 are permitted but must not change public runtime behavior.

Release and CI images will include TypeScript 3.4.5, and any containerized or ephemeral environments must install this exact version. Monorepo packages must not override the root TypeScript version; if necessary, they may add local tsconfig overrides without changing the compiler version.

We will not adopt language or type-system features introduced after 3.4.5. Security or correctness issues attributable to the compiler will trigger an expedited proposal to revise this decision. This decision remains in force until superseded by an ADR specifying an upgrade path and migration plan.

We will standardize URI design and derive API tags directly from the URI structure.

- URIs will be lowercase, kebab-case, resource-oriented nouns, pluralized (e.g., /v1/customer-orders).
- Versioning will use a mandatory leading segment: /v{major} (e.g., /v1).
- Compound words use hyphens; no file extensions; no trailing slashes; stable identifiers in path parameters.
- Path parameters use camelCase (e.g., /v1/orders/{orderId}).
- Actions are modeled as sub-resources with POST (e.g., /v1/orders/{orderId}/cancellations) rather than verbs in paths.
- Nested resources reflect containment (e.g., /v1/orders/{orderId}/items).
- Query conventions: pagination page, pageSize; sorting sort (field[, -field]); filtering via field=value; sparse fields fields=.
- Non-domain endpoints: /health, /metrics, /status.

URI tags (for OpenAPI grouping, RBAC scopes, and observability) are auto-derived:
- Tag = the first domain resource segment after version (plural, kebab-case). Example: /v1/orders -> orders.
- For nested resources, tag = top-level resource; optional secondary tag orders-items for fine-grain dashboards.
