- Non-domain endpoints use platform.

Enforcement:
- OpenAPI lint rules validate naming and tag derivation.
- API gateway templates and instrumentation extract tags from request paths.
- CI blocks changes that violate conventions; compatibility routes maintained during migration via gateway rewrites.

- Adopt HTMX as the primary client-side interaction layer, favoring server-rendered HTML over JSON APIs for UI concerns.
- Use progressive enhancement: all core flows must work without JavaScript; HTMX augments behavior via hx-* attributes.
- Render UI via server-side templates; expose endpoint actions that return HTML fragments (partial templates) optimized for HTMX swaps.
- Standardize patterns:
  - hx-boost for link/form enhancement; hx-get/post/put/delete for actions.
  - hx-swap and fragments with stable IDs for targeted updates.
  - hx-push-url for navigable state; rely on browser history (no SPA router).
  - Out-of-band swaps for toasts, modals, and global UI updates.
  - hx-trigger for debounced inputs and lazy loading (on load, reveal, etc.).
- Use Server-Sent Events for one-way live updates (hx-sse); evaluate WebSocket channels only for bidirectional, low-latency needs.
- Keep client-side state minimal. For localized interactivity (e.g., dropdowns), allow lightweight helpers (e.g., Alpine.js or small bespoke JS). Avoid heavy SPA frameworks.
- Establish HTML component conventions: reusable server-rendered partials, deterministic IDs, and accessibility-first semantics (ARIA, focus management).
- Error handling: return HTMX-friendly error fragments; use HTTP status codes; surface validation near fields and global notices via out-of-band swaps.
- Security: enforce CSRF protection via headers; validate and sanitize all server-rendered HTML; constrain hx-headers and CORS appropriately.
- Performance: cache server-rendered fragments where safe; paginate and stream where applicable; minimize asset size; defer non-critical JS.
- Testing: snapshot test HTML fragments; integration test end-to-end flows with HTMX interactions; monitor for regressions in swap targets and IDs.
- Opt-out criteria: when rich client-side state, offline capability, or complex canvas/WebGL is required, encapsulate those islands as Web Components or micro-frontends, integrated within the HTMX-driven shell.

We will introduce a MutableMessageFactory to construct Message instances via a controlled, reusable, and performant builder-style API. The factory will provide mutable builders for assembling messages incrementally, and will produce immutable Message objects upon build, ensuring post-construction immutability and validation guarantees.

Key aspects:
- Provide MutableMessageBuilder instances via the factory; these are recyclable and obtained from a bounded pool (thread-local first, then shared) to minimize allocations and GC pressure.
- Builders expose setters for all message fields and support incremental composition (e.g., headers, payload, metadata) and zero-copy views where possible. Input is copied only when required for safety.
- Validation occurs at build(); invalid states yield deterministic errors. Successful build() returns an immutable Message and clears/sanitizes the builder for reuse.
- Messages remain deeply immutable and thread-safe; builders are not thread-safe and must not be shared across threads.
- All direct Message constructors and ad-hoc mutators are deprecated; new code must use the factory. Existing code will be migrated behind a compatibility layer that routes to the factory.
- Serialization/deserialization pathways will integrate with the factory: parsers populate builders; serializers operate on immutable Messages.
- Memory hygiene: builders scrub sensitive buffers on reset; pooled capacity is capped to prevent unbounded growth; metrics and leak detection (in-use counters, timeouts) are included.
- Configuration: pool sizes, maximum retained buffer size, and validation strictness are configurable per service.
- Backwards compatibility: Message schema remains unchanged; wire format unaffected.
- Concurrency: one builder per thread per workflow; factory enforces single-ownership with optional tryAcquire semantics under pressure.
- Performance target: ≥25% reduction in allocations on message-heavy paths and no regression in p99 latency; feature can be disabled via config if targets are not met.

We will adopt strict, unambiguous boolean semantics across all layers to eliminate truthy/falsy ambiguity and data inconsistency.

- Canonical representation: Boolean only (true/false). No string, numeric, or custom sentinel substitutes (e.g., "yes/no", "0/1", "Y/N") in domain models, APIs, or persistence.
- Serialization: JSON booleans (true/false) exclusively. Reject or normalize non-boolean inputs at boundaries; respond with 400 for invalid types.
- Type systems: Strongly-typed booleans in all languages:
  - TypeScript/JS: boolean (no any; no coercion; eslint rule no-implicit-coercion enabled).
  - Python: bool (disable reliance on truthiness for collections/strings in conditionals via linters).
  - SQL: BOOLEAN (or BIT(1) mapped to boolean where BOOLEAN unsupported).
- Nullability: Default to NOT NULL with explicit default false unless business rules require tri-state logic. Where tri-state is required, use Nullable Boolean with explicit semantics documented (null = unknown/not set); avoid overloading false.
- Migrations: Convert legacy values via deterministic mapping:
  - Accept: true, 1 → true; false, 0 → false.
  - Reject/flag: "true"/"false" strings, "Y/N", "yes/no", empty strings, null (where NOT NULL).
- API contracts: OpenAPI/Proto schemas declare boolean types; backward-compat shims normalize known legacy encodings at edge services only.
- UI/UX: Render booleans with explicit labels; avoid double negatives. Default toggles to false unless specified.
- Testing and linting: Add unit/contract tests for boundary normalization and linters/precommit checks to prevent introduction of truthy/falsy patterns.

We will designate a Primary Person (Directly Responsible Individual, DRI) for this decision and its resulting work. The Primary Person is accountable for driving the outcome to completion, coordinating stakeholders, maintaining the decision record, and ensuring alignment with standards and timelines. They have authority to make day-to-day technical and prioritization calls within established guardrails; strategic scope or policy changes require approval from the Architecture Council.

Selection and tenure:
- Nominated by the relevant Engineering Manager and approved by the Architecture Council.
- Serves through the decision’s implementation and stabilization, or for a maximum of six months, whichever comes first, with quarterly review.
- The Primary Person must name a documented deputy to mitigate bus factor risks.

Responsibilities:
- Maintain the ADR and related artifacts (RFCs, diagrams, runbooks) and keep them current.
- Create and track an execution plan, risks, and dependencies; report status in agreed cadences.
- Coordinate cross-team work, manage interfaces and contracts, and ensure non-functional requirements are met.
- Facilitate decisions, seek input, and document rationale; call out trade-offs and compliance impacts.
- Define and monitor success metrics; drive post-implementation review and handover to steady-state ownership.

Operational policies:
- Contact details and ownership are recorded in CODEOWNERS/OWNERS and the architecture registry.
- If the Primary Person is unavailable >5 business days, the deputy acts; for unresponsiveness >3 business days, escalate to the Engineering Manager and Architecture Council.
- Ownership transfers require a written handover (scope, open issues, risks, next steps) and Council acknowledgment.

This role is execution ownership, not line management; it may be held by a tech lead, senior IC, or architect.

## Decision

Adopt Taurus (bzt) as the standard framework for authoring and running all benchmark/performance tests across services.

- Author tests in Taurus YAML, stored alongside service code under tests/perf with a shared, versioned base profile. JMeter will be the default executor; Locust or Gatling may be used via Taurus when justified.
- Containerize the runner (pinned Taurus and executor versions) and execute in CI: smoke load on pull requests (opt-in label), baseline on merges to main, and full benchmarks nightly and before releases.
- Define SLAs/SLOs as Taurus pass/fail criteria (latency percentiles, error rate, throughput, CPU/memory ceilings via custom metrics) so builds are gated automatically on violations.
- Standardize outputs: retain raw logs, artifacts, and final reports; publish summarized metrics to the metrics backend and store detailed artifacts in centralized object storage with retention policies. Generate trend dashboards from these data sources.
- Use a dedicated, production-like performance environment with controllable data volume and test fixtures; load generation will originate from isolated runners sized to avoid test-induced throttling.
- Provide templates, example scenarios, and a shared library of test fragments (auth, ramp patterns, datasets) to promote reuse and consistency.
- Enforce reproducibility: fixed seeds for data feeders where applicable, deterministic test windows, and explicit environment/configuration capture in artifacts.
- Security and compliance: never embed secrets in test configs; retrieve via CI secret stores. Scrub PII from logs and reports.
- Governance: changes to shared perf profiles require review by the performance guild; each service team owns its scenarios and SLO definitions.

## Decision
We will refactor the type system to a unified, structural, and schema-driven model centered on algebraic data types (ADTs) and tagged unions, replacing inheritance-heavy nominal hierarchies. The codebase will adopt strict typing end-to-end with:

- Language/tooling: TypeScript 5.x in strict mode as the source of truth for static typing.
- Data modeling: Discriminated unions and interfaces for domain variants; no subclassing for polymorphism.
- Runtime validation: zod schemas co-located with types, with type inference from schemas to ensure parity between compile-time and runtime.
- Contracts and persistence: JSON Schema generated from zod for API and storage validation; OpenAPI and database typings will be code-generated from the same source to eliminate drift.
- Boundaries: All I/O boundaries (HTTP, messaging, persistence) will validate and normalize data at ingress/egress using the shared schemas.
- Backward compatibility: A compatibility layer will decode legacy payloads into the new ADTs via explicit adapters; deprecated fields will remain accepted for one major version with telemetry to measure usage.
- Incremental migration: Start with leaf domains, introduce mappers from old types to new, and progressively flip feature flags to enforce strict validation. Mixed mode is allowed temporarily via adapter modules.
- Guidelines: Composition over inheritance, exhaustive switch handling for discriminants, immutable value objects, and no implicit any or unknown in public APIs.
- Tooling and quality gates: CI will fail on type holes, schema drift, or uncovered discriminants; codegen artifacts are versioned and regenerated on build.

This decision standardizes types across components, ensures runtime safety, and enables contract-first evolution while minimizing integration drift.

We will persist user-denied permission responses on the client, per device and per permission, to reduce repeat prompts, respect user choice, and guide UX. A DeniedPermission record will be stored in secure client storage (Keychain/Secure Enclave on iOS, EncryptedSharedPreferences on Android, secure keystore on desktop; localStorage with encryption wrapper on web where available) and will include: permission identifier, status (denied | denied_permanent/never_ask_again), firstDeniedAt, lastPromptAt, promptCount, nextEligibleAt, appVersion, and an optional rationaleShown flag. No PII is stored in this record; when authenticated, we key by account locally but do not sync this artifact across devices.

Re-prompting will be throttled: after an initial denial, defer system prompts and show an in-app rationale on next relevant feature use; then apply exponential backoff (e.g., 24h, 3d, 7d) up to a max of 7 days. If the OS indicates “never ask again”/permanent denial, we will not prompt again; instead we surface a non-blocking call-to-action to open system settings. Users can proactively change decisions via an in-app Settings entry point. Uninstalling the app clears records; updates preserve them unless a migration explicitly resets strategy.

Only aggregated, anonymized counts of denials may be sent to analytics (opt-in where required). No server-side persistence of individual denials will occur. QA and support can toggle a debug override to reset local records.

Implement a server-side proxy for ORCID’s OAuth2 flow within our Auth Service behind the API Gateway. All applications will initiate authentication via /auth/orcid/login (redirect to ORCID) and complete via a single whitelisted callback /auth/orcid/callback on our domain; no frontend will communicate directly with ORCID or handle client secrets.

Enforce PKCE, state, and nonce on all authorization requests. On callback, the proxy exchanges the code for tokens, normalizes errors, and returns only the minimum required user attributes (ORCID iD and granted scopes) to clients. Access and refresh tokens are stored server-side only, encrypted at rest and in transit; clients receive a short-lived session (HTTP-only, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookies for browsers; opaque token for non-browser clients). Refresh, revoke, and token introspection are exposed as internal endpoints; refresh tokens are rotated on use.

Support ORCID sandbox and production via configuration, separate credentials, and isolated redirect URIs. Apply strict origin allowlists, CORS where applicable, and rate limiting, with circuit breaking, timeouts, and retries with backoff to ORCID. Instrument with structured logging, metrics, and trace context; redact secrets in logs. Manage credentials via the secret manager with rotation. Align scopes with least privilege and ORCID policies, and maintain a passthrough of ORCID terms and consent screens. This centralizes security, observability, and compliance while providing a consistent integration surface for all clients.

## Decision
We will remove Discourse as a first-class component of the DataLab stack and decommission its deployment, operations, and support from core distributions. Discourse will no longer be provisioned by default in any environment (local, staging, production), and all infrastructure elements dedicated to it (container images, Helm/K8s manifests, Terraform modules, Postgres/Redis instances, backup jobs, monitoring alerts) will be retired from the main repository and release artifacts. The Discourse integration points (SSO/OIDC, user profile links, in-app deep links, notification webhooks) will be decoupled and replaced with a generic “Community” integration surface that supports linking to external platforms (e.g., GitHub Discussions, Slack, or a separately managed Discourse instance) via configuration.

Existing Discourse content will be exported and archived; a read-only static archive will be hosted for historical reference, and HTTP redirects will be provided where feasible. A migration guide will document how to point DataLab to an alternative community solution, including SSO patterns, link mapping, and notification routing. Backups for the retired Discourse database will be retained per data retention policy for a limited period.

This decision does not affect DataLab’s core APIs, UI contracts, or upgrade paths beyond removal of Discourse-specific settings, which will be marked deprecated in the next release and removed in the subsequent major release. Optional community integrations will remain pluggable and out-of-tree.

We will standardize on Kubernetes Service type LoadBalancer for all external ingress traffic, fronting a dedicated ingress controller (e.g., NGINX/HAProxy/Traefik). In cloud environments, we will use the managed cloud load balancer. In on‑premises or bare‑metal environments, we will provision an L2/L3 software load balancer (e.g., MetalLB, Cilium LB/IPAM) or integrate with an existing hardware LB. HostNetwork will not be used for ingress in production due to security, operability, and scalability constraints (port conflicts, node coupling, reduced isolation). HostNetwork may be employed only for exceptional edge/single‑node scenarios with explicit approval, strict firewalling, and documented blast‑radius controls.

Consequences:
- Improved isolation, portability, and HA with native health checks, TLS offload, and session affinity managed by the LB.
- Clear IP/port management and avoidance of node‑level port contention.
- Requires LB provider integration, IP pool planning, and may incur cloud/LB costs.
- Network policies, source IP preservation (externalTrafficPolicy=Local when needed), and PROXY protocol settings must be configured per service requirements.
- Operational runbooks will cover LB lifecycle, certificate management, and autoscaling of the ingress controller.
- Migration path: replace HostNetwork exposures (if any) with Services of type LoadBalancer; for dev-only clusters, NodePort or port-forwarding may be used.

We will distribute the LaTeX assets as a set of versioned .tex source files (templates and modular includes) rather than as an installable package (.sty/.cls or CTAN entry). The canonical distribution will be a public Git repository and signed release archives. Consumers will integrate by copying the files into their projects or by referencing them via \input from a vendored subdirectory; no system-wide installation or package manager is required.

To ensure maintainability and reuse:
- Provide a minimal, dependency-free core split into small, composable .tex modules.
- Embed semantic version and compatibility notes in the file headers and maintain a CHANGELOG.
- Offer example main.tex files demonstrating typical compositions and an integration guide.
- Stabilize public macros and interfaces; changes that break compatibility will trigger a major version.
- Tag releases and publish checksums; avoid runtime code download.

To ease updates, we will:
- Keep a single “bundle” directory layout to allow drop-in replacement.
- Provide a migration guide for any breaking changes.
- Maintain long-term support branches for the last two minor versions.

We will deprecate the prior package distribution, provide a final transitional release pointing to the .tex bundle, and archive the package after one LTS cycle. Licensing remains unchanged and is included in each file header.

## Decision
We will provide first-class RDF/SPARQL support by standing up a standards-compliant SPARQL 1.1 endpoint backed by a dedicated triple store. The endpoint will be read-only initially (SELECT/ASK/DESCRIBE/CONSTRUCT), with SPARQL Update disabled; all mutations will continue to flow through our application APIs and ETL pipelines. We will use Apache Jena Fuseki over TDB2 as the default deployment, with an abstraction layer (RDF4J-compatible interfaces) to allow substitution with other SPARQL 1.1 stores if needed.

Data will be modeled in RDF using stable, dereferenceable IRIs and a curated set of vocabularies (SKOS, Dublin Core, PROV, and domain ontologies), partitioned into named graphs for provenance, access control, and lifecycle management. SHACL will be used for schema/constraint validation at ingest. Lightweight RDFS reasoning will be enabled offline to materialize frequently used inferences into dedicated named graphs; no runtime OWL reasoning.

Operational safeguards will include query timeouts, result row and payload size limits, pagination (via OFFSET/LIMIT), and query whitelisting for critical integrations. Authentication/authorization will be enforced at the API gateway (OAuth2/OIDC), with per-tenant graph-level access controls. The endpoint will be documented with example queries and a public service description.

RDF serializations (Turtle, N-Triples, JSON-LD) will be supported for import/export. Dataset versioning will be handled via immutable snapshots of named graphs and change sets recorded in PROV. The service will be deployed as a containerized Fuseki instance with persistent storage, backups, and monitoring (latency, timeout rates, heap, I/O). This decision enables standards-based interoperability while preserving our existing write pathway and operational controls.

Adopt a centralized, role-based access control model for CRUD operations on records configuration, with deny-by-default and least-privilege principles. Define explicit permissions: records.config:create, records.config:read, records.config:update, records.config:delete. Permissions are scoped by tenant and optional namespace/resource attributes to enable fine-grained control (e.g., per-record-type). Roles (e.g., Admin, ConfigManager, Auditor, Reader) map to these permissions; only Admin and ConfigManager may create/update/delete, while Readers/Auditors may read. Authorization is enforced at two points: at the API gateway for coarse checks and within service middleware for resource-scoped checks, using a signed, cacheable authorization decision. All permission assignments and CRUD operations are fully audited with immutable logs (actor, action, scope, target, correlation ID).

Expose dedicated endpoints to manage role-permission mappings and subject-role assignments; only Admins may modify assignments. Support hierarchical inheritance (global → tenant → namespace) with the most specific rule winning and explicit deny overriding allow. Implement optimistic concurrency control on configuration updates, along with validation and dry-run to prevent invalid configs. Soft-delete configurations with retention to enable recovery and audit continuity; hard-delete restricted to Admins.

Authorization data is stored in a dedicated authz store with read-through caching and short TTL to balance performance and revocation latency. Changes to permissions trigger cache invalidation via events. Seed default roles and scopes via migration, and provide feature flags to roll out enforcement per endpoint. Provide clear error semantics (403 for unauthorized, 404 for hidden resources) and redact sensitive fields from responses when read access is partial.

Adopt a single-repository model that co-locates all automated tests with their corresponding production code. For each module/service, place unit tests adjacent to the implementation (for example: src/... with tests in tests/ or filename.test.* conventions), and keep integration/e2e tests under a top-level tests/integration and tests/e2e directory. Consolidate the existing test repository into the production repository, preserving history where feasible.

Configure build and packaging to exclude test code and fixtures from production artifacts and images (for example: build tool exclude patterns, devDependencies for test-only libraries, .dockerignore for tests/ and fixtures/, and separate test-specific resources). Ensure test-only code paths are not compiled into runtime bundles.

Update CI/CD to:
- Run unit, integration, and e2e test stages with clear tags/selectors.
- Enforce coverage thresholds and required checks on pull requests.
- Parallelize test suites and cache dependencies to keep feedback fast.
- Publish test reports, coverage, and artifacts for traceability.

Mandate that feature PRs include or update corresponding tests, reviewed together with code changes. Provide shared test utilities as internal test-only packages/modules to avoid duplication without leaking into production builds.

For data and security, segregate test secrets via dedicated secret scopes and sanitize test fixtures. For large datasets, host them as on-demand test artifacts rather than committing binaries.

This decision improves change coupling, reviewability, and version alignment between code and tests while reducing drift. Risks of accidental inclusion of tests in production deliverables are mitigated by explicit build exclusions, CI validation, and release gates. Continuous enforcement will be added via repository policies and linters to maintain structure and conventions.

We will introduce a mandatory egress proxy tier for all self-hosted CI runners to centralize network control, observability, and compliance while keeping runners on private subnets with no inbound exposure. Each runner will be configured to use an authenticated HTTPS proxy endpoint (TLS passthrough with optional mTLS) for all outbound traffic to SaaS endpoints and package registries. The proxy tier will be implemented as a horizontally scalable, stateless pool (HAProxy/Envoy) fronted by regional load balancers and paired per region/zone for high availability and controlled failover. An allowlist-based egress policy will be enforced at the proxy, with DNS pinning and SNI filtering for critical domains, and optional per-tenant route maps. All requests will be logged centrally with redaction, short-retention hot logs, and privacy-safe aggregates retained per compliance requirements.

Proxies will expose health and metrics endpoints for autoscaling and SLOs; capacity planning will target N+2 redundancy and drain/rotate procedures. Configuration will be delivered via immutable images plus environment-scoped overlays; emergency blocks can be pushed via a signed config channel. Secrets for proxy auth and mTLS will be managed through the existing vault and rotated automatically. Runners without proxy configuration will be rejected at provisioning; existing runners will be migrated via phased rollout and feature flags.

No inbound access to runners will be permitted; debugging will occur via ephemeral jump tasks initiated by runners. Direct internet egress from runner subnets will be disabled; only proxy subnets will be allowlisted externally. This decision standardizes network control for runners, improves reliability under load, enables precise cost/traffic accounting, and satisfies egress compliance without increasing runner complexity.

## Decision
Adopt Lerna to manage package versioning and releases in the monorepo. Use independent (per-package) versioning to allow granular, package-specific release cadence while minimizing unnecessary version bumps. Enable Conventional Commits as the single source of truth for semantic versioning decisions and changelog generation.

Key elements:
- Versioning: lerna version --conventional-commits in independent mode, generating per-package changelogs and git tags.
- Publishing: lerna publish to the npm registry, using two-factor auth in CI as required. Pre-release channels supported via prerelease identifiers (e.g., alpha, beta, rc).
- Change detection: Only packages with changes (and their dependents as needed) are versioned; Lerna will bump dependents when API-affecting changes are detected.
- Changelogs and releases: Auto-generate CHANGELOGs and GitHub Releases from commit history; include compare links.
- Branching: Release from the main release branch; support release branches for hotfixes and pre-releases as needed.
- CI/CD: Automate versioning and publishing on protected branches with required checks. Use canary releases for PR validation where useful.
- Commit quality: Enforce Conventional Commits via commitlint and CI. PR titles must conform when squash merging.
- Package manager: Use existing workspace tooling for install/build/test; Lerna is scoped to versioning/releasing.
- Tags: Create annotated git tags per published version; follow npm dist-tags (latest, next) for channel management.
- Rollback: Support revert via git revert and republish with corrected version, updating dist-tags accordingly.

We will standardize eventing on Symfony’s EventDispatcher as provided by Shopware. Concretely:
- Prefer subscribing to existing Shopware core/DAL events (e.g., EntityWrittenEvent, EntityDeletedEvent) where they cover our needs; only create custom events when no suitable core event exists.
- Define custom domain events as immutable value objects (readonly properties) implementing Symfony\Contracts\EventDispatcher\Event (or Shopware\Core\Framework\Event\ShopwareEvent), with descriptive, namespaced names (e.g., acme.product.repriced).
- Dispatch custom events only after successful state changes to avoid side effects inside transactions. Where possible, trigger them from write-result listeners (EntityWrittenEvent) or explicit post-commit application services to ensure consistency.
- Register consumers via dedicated EventSubscriber classes (implements EventSubscriberInterface), autowired and tagged automatically by Symfony/Shopware. Keep handlers idempotent and side-effect bounded; offload heavy/IO work to async messages.
- For Flow Builder/business events exposure, provide dedicated flow-aware wrappers implementing FlowEventAware and defining AvailableData for payload fields, so non-technical users can react to our events in flows. Keep domain event separate from the flow wrapper to avoid coupling application logic to Flow Builder.
- Use clear contracts for event payloads (UUIDs, scalar snapshots) and avoid leaking entities; include contextual metadata (salesChannelId, languageId, context).
- Version event names/payloads when making breaking changes (e.g., acme.product.repriced.v2); maintain backward compatibility windows.
- Prohibit write operations in listeners that can cause recursion or deadlocks; validate via code review and static checks.
- Provide test coverage with unit tests for event emission and handler behavior, and integration tests ensuring dispatch points align with transactional boundaries.

## Decision
- License the project’s source code under Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0) to enable broad adoption, permissive reuse (including commercial), explicit patent grant, and clear contribution terms.
- License project documentation, tutorials, and design docs under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0). Project branding and trademarks are excluded and reserved.
- Prohibit inclusion of strong copyleft dependencies (e.g., GPL, AGPL) in shipped artifacts and core modules. Such dependencies may only be used in development tooling or optional integrations that are clearly isolated and not distributed as part of core releases.
- Require SPDX license identifiers in all source files and maintain root-level LICENSE and NOTICE files. Include third-party attributions and licenses in a THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES file, generated as part of the release process.
- Adopt a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) workflow with signed-off commits for contributions. Substantial external contributions must include explicit confirmation that the contributor has the right to license the work under Apache-2.0.
- Distribute container images, binaries, and Helm charts under the same license as the source code, with embedded license and notice files.
- Permit dual-licensing of optional, non-core enterprise extensions under a commercial license in a separate repository/package, avoiding linkage that would alter the open-source licensing obligations of the core.
- Enforce license checks in CI (SPDX scanning, dependency license compliance) and block releases on violations.
- Apply versioned license headers and maintain a CHANGELOG entry for any licensing policy changes.

## Decision
We will use client-initiated polling as the default mechanism for detecting and retrieving updates between components and external integrations. Polling is chosen over push-based approaches (webhooks/streams) to optimize for simplicity, network/firewall compatibility, operational reliability, and clear backpressure control. Two modes are supported: short polling for interactive UX and long polling for reduced request overhead when near-real-time is desired without maintaining server-initiated connections.

Key parameters and safeguards:
- Default intervals: 15s (interactive) and 60s (background); configurable per client/use case.
- Long-poll timeout: up to 25s with immediate return on change; server responds 204/304 on timeout/no-change.
- Adaptive backoff: exponential with jitter on 429/5xx; ceiling 5 minutes; resume normal on 2xx.
- Conditional requests and caching: ETag/If-None-Match and/or If-Modified-Since; servers return 304 where applicable.
- Delta/cursor support: incremental endpoints (since/cursor) to minimize payloads; consistent pagination with stable cursors.
- Idempotency and statelessness: idempotent GET/HEAD; side-effecting operations guarded by idempotency keys.
- Rate limits: published budgets; clients self-throttle to stay within quotas.
- Concurrency control: cap parallel polls per resource; coalesce requests where possible.
- Observability: metrics for poll rate, hit/miss ratio, latency, error/backoff rates; alerts on sustained 4xx/5xx or quota saturation.

This decision targets bounded staleness (typically <= 2× interval) with predictable load and simplified failure modes. We will revisit push/webhook or streaming approaches if substantiated requirements emerge for sub-second latency, guaranteed event delivery, or materially reduced request overhead under high churn, and if partner environments can reliably support outbound connectivity and signature verification at scale.

## Decision

- Standardize on Create React App for bootstrapping React front-end projects using the official TypeScript template.
  - Scaffold command: npx create-react-app <app-name> --template typescript
  - Pin to create-react-app/react-scripts 5.x until further notice.
- Use Node.js LTS (>=18.x) and npm (>=9) as the sole package manager across local and CI environments.
  - Commit package-lock.json; do not allow yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml.
  - Add .yarn*, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml to .gitignore.
  - Enforce npm via preinstall guard: "preinstall": "npx only-allow npm"
  - Configure .npmrc with package-lock=true, fund=false, audit=false (CI uses audit on demand).
  - Set engines in package.json to enforce Node/npm versions.
- Dependency workflow:
  - Local installs/updates: npm install / npm update.
  - CI: npm ci for deterministic installs.
  - Publishing/internal registries use npm configs and .npmrc; no Yarn Berry/Plug’n’Play.
- Project scripts (baseline):
  - start: react-scripts start
  - build: react-scripts build
  - test: react-scripts test
  - eject: react-scripts eject (prohibited without architectural approval)
  - lint/format/test:coverage as project-specific additions.
- Repository hygiene and policy:
  - PRs introducing Yarn/Pnpm configuration or lockfiles are rejected.
  - Any change to package manager or bootstrapping tool requires an ADR update and approval.

Adopt XChart as the standard plotting library for generating static charts in our Java-based tools and services. Use it for common chart types (line, bar, scatter, pie, histogram) in both desktop (Swing/JavaFX embedding) and server-side, headless report generation. XChart is selected for its lightweight footprint, simple API, permissive Apache-2.0 license, minimal transitive dependencies, and adequate export capabilities (bitmap and vector formats such as PNG and SVG). This choice optimizes developer productivity and build times while meeting current visualization needs.

Scope and constraints:
- Intended for static plots and embedded UI previews; interactive, browser-based visualizations are out of scope.
- Suitable for small-to-moderate datasets; for very large datasets, apply downsampling/aggregation.
- For server use, ensure headless operation (e.g., set java.awt.headless=true) and avoid UI components.
- Standardize themes, fonts, and color palettes via a shared styling utility to ensure consistent branding.

Implementation guidelines:
- Introduce a plotting abstraction (e.g., PlotRenderer) to decouple business logic from the library and allow future replacement.
- Centralize chart construction in a plotting module; prohibit direct XChart usage outside this module.
- Pin a minor version line and monitor upstream changes; add golden-image/regression tests for critical chart outputs.
- Provide helpers for common exports (PNG at 2x DPI, SVG for print) and for chart downsampling strategies.

Risks and mitigation:
- If requirements evolve to rich web interactivity or very large-scale plotting, evaluate web-native options (e.g., ECharts/Plotly) behind the same abstraction.

Adopt a single, versioned global namespace to expose a minimal, stable public API for legacy/host integrations: window.App. Internal modules remain ES modules; only a curated facade is attached to window.

- Provide a dedicated “legacy integration” bundle (UMD/IIFE) that, when included, attaches window.App.v1 with:
  - Facade functions, event emitters, and selected Web Component constructors needed by hosts.
  - No exposure of internal framework instances, stores, or mutable state.
- Freeze and seal the exposed namespace (Object.freeze) and prevent reassignment via a non-configurable property. Expose read-only getters for lazily loaded features to minimize initial payload.
- Version the API (window.App.v1) and keep a deprecated alias (window.AppLegacy) for two minor releases. Breaking changes increment the version (v2) and do not change older versions.
- Initialize after DOMContentLoaded; heavy modules load on first access (dynamic import). Namespaces are attached only on pages that load the legacy bundle; the SPA continues to consume ES modules.
- Ship TypeScript ambient declarations (global.d.ts) describing the public surface for host consumers.
- Enforce an allowlist for exposed symbols via a build-time manifest; CI fails if unreviewed globals are added.
- Add lightweight usage telemetry and console deprecation notices to guide migration.
- Security: no secrets on window; inputs validated; no eval; CSP-compatible.
- Support guaranteed API stability for LTS period; deprecations follow documented schedule.

We will use Docker named volumes for all high-churn and large I/O paths on macOS to mitigate poor bind-mount performance. Specifically, the following will run on named volumes instead of host bind mounts: databases (db-data), caches (cache-data), search/queue stores (search-data, queue-data), persistent uploads (uploads), dependency and build artifacts (node_modules, vendor, .m2/.gradle, build/cache), and any service state directories. Application source code will remain a bind mount only when live editing is required; otherwise, a named volume will be used with explicit sync/build steps. For teams needing hot reload with near-native speed, we will optionally employ Docker Desktop’s VirtioFS (default on recent versions) or Mutagen/colima sync profiles, but dependency directories will still reside in volumes to avoid excessive file watcher churn.

Compose will define named volumes by default with a macOS-specific override file enabling the above layout. Data backup/restore will be handled via volume snapshot scripts (docker run --rm -v <volume>:/data …). CI/CD and production remain unchanged as they already rely on volumes or managed storage.

This decision reduces filesystem translation overhead on macOS, leading to faster startup, builds, and tests, while isolating persistent data from the host. Developers may need one-time bootstrap tasks to populate volumes (e.g., dependency install, DB seed). We accept the trade-off of less direct host visibility into those directories in exchange for significantly improved performance.

## Decision

Adopt Google Cloud Storage (GCS) as the primary object storage backend for all binary assets (user uploads, media, artifacts, static site assets, logs, and backups). Use environment-scoped buckets with standardized naming (e.g., org-app-{env}-{purpose}) and Uniform Bucket-Level Access. Production buckets will be dual-region; non-production will be single-region. Enable bucket versioning and object lifecycle rules for cost control (transition to Nearline/Coldline/Archive by age and delete expired temp objects). Enforce retention policies where compliance requires.

Access will be via the GCS JSON API using official Google Cloud client libraries. All access is authenticated with workload identities/service accounts following least-privilege IAM (objectAdmin for writers, objectViewer for readers; no broad storageAdmin in runtime). External clients will use short-lived signed URLs for direct upload/download. Internal access is restricted through Private Google Access and VPC Service Controls where applicable.

Encrypt all data at rest with CMEK using Cloud KMS; rotate keys per policy. Enable Cloud Audit Logs (Admin/Data Access) and configure Monitoring alerts for errors, latency, storage growth, and lifecycle failures. Use Pub/Sub notifications for object events where required by downstream processing. Serve public/static content via Cloud CDN with backend buckets; set appropriate Cache-Control headers.

Abstract storage behind an internal interface to allow future backend substitution if needed, but standardize on GCS features (lifecycle, signed URLs) in the current implementation. Provide migration tooling to move existing assets to GCS with checksum verification and minimal downtime. Document egress patterns to control costs and prefer in-region processing. This decision is effective immediately for new services; existing services will migrate incrementally.

Adopt a schemaless, namespaced key-value “properties” bag on supported resources to enable extensible metadata without core schema changes. Each resource will expose a properties field (map of string key → JSON value) persisted as a JSONB column (or equivalent document field) with GIN indexes for equality/containment queries on whitelisted keys. Keys must be lowercase, dot-namespaced (e.g., vendor.feature.flag), ≤64 chars, and may not use reserved prefixes sys.* or internal.*. Values must be valid JSON (scalar, array, or object), with limits: ≤100 keys per resource, per-value serialized size ≤8 KB, total properties payload ≤64 KB.

API surface: properties is readable via standard GETs; partial updates supported via PATCH with JSON Merge Patch semantics. Deletes occur by setting a key to null or using PATCH remove operations. Bulk property updates are idempotent and conflict-detected via ETags. SDKs expose properties as a Map<String, Object> (or language equivalent). Server enforces RBAC: read/write of properties requires explicit permissions; exposure in list/search responses is limited to an allowlist of keys. Write-time validation rejects reserved prefixes, size/shape violations, and forbidden keys.

Auditing: all property mutations are recorded with actor, timestamp, and diff. Backups and exports include properties. Search: optional secondary indexes are created only for allowlisted keys; others remain queryable via containment at reduced performance.

Migration: add nullable JSONB properties column defaulting to {} for new rows; no downtime required. Backward compatibility is maintained as existing clients ignore the new field. Operational guards include request size limits, rate limits on property writes, and monitoring of JSONB index bloat.

Adopt GitLab as the single system of record for release orchestration and delivery. All release automation will migrate from GitHub (Actions, Releases) to GitLab CI/CD and GitLab Releases. Source code for active products will be hosted in GitLab with protected branches (main/release), code owners, and required approvals; GitHub will be retained only for public mirroring and issue redirection where necessary.

Key elements:
- Standardize on GitLab CI/CD pipelines for build, test, security scanning (SAST/DAST/Dependency), packaging, and deployment across environments using GitLab Environments and Deployments.
- Use Git tags and GitLab Releases to produce immutable, traceable artifacts, release notes (auto-changelog from conventional commits), SBOMs, and release evidence.
- Enforce Semantic Versioning with release tags generated via pipeline jobs gated by approvals; restrict tagging and release jobs to maintainers via protected tags/branches.
- Use GitLab Runners (shared or dedicated) with caching and Docker-in-Docker where required; store artifacts and container images in GitLab Package/Container Registry.
- Gate production deployments with environment-specific approvals and change controls; use feature flags for progressive delivery where applicable.
- Integrate compliance policies (merge request approvals, security findings thresholds) and audit logging in GitLab; deprecate GitHub release permissions and workflows.
- Maintain one-way mirroring to GitHub for visibility; disable GitHub Releases to avoid duplication and confusion.

This decision centralizes governance, security, and traceability in GitLab, simplifies tooling, and reduces operational fragmentation of the release process.

We will enforce a single-active signer per validator key with defense-in-depth controls to prevent and contain double-signing. All signing will be performed by an external signer fronted by a strongly consistent, HA slashing-protection store that maintains fork- and slot/height-aware indices. A time-bound, renewable fencing lease (via quorum-backed distributed coordination, e.g., etcd/Consul/ZK) is required to enable signing; instances without an active lease must refuse to serve. Lease acquisition and renewal are guarded by strict liveness and clock-drift checks; on lease loss or missed heartbeats, the signer immediately halts (“fail closed”).

Validator keys are held in an HSM/TEE with monotonic counters/nonces and per-chain context verification to reject replay or equivocation attempts. Automatic failover is permitted only when the new instance first: (a) restores and verifies the latest slashing-protection state, (b) atomically acquires the fencing lease, and (c) passes connectivity and fork-choice health checks. Auto-restarts that could create concurrent actives across zones/regions are disabled unless lease preemption is proven.

Operationally, we maintain cold or warm standbys that remain offline until an explicit runbook-driven activation acquires the lease and validates state parity. Disaster recovery requires restoring the slashing-protection database before bringing any signer online. Network partitions are treated conservatively: inability to renew the lease or confirm quorum causes self-suspension.

Comprehensive observability is mandated: lease status, signer liveness, fork-choice alignment, HSM counters, and slashing DB lag are monitored with paging alerts. Configuration changes, key rotations, and software upgrades follow two-person review and staged rollout to preserve single-actor guarantees.

Adopt a unified Git style guide across all Decentraland repositories to ensure consistent history, automated release workflows, and efficient collaboration.

- Branching model: trunk-based with short-lived branches. Protected branches: main (always releasable) and release/* (stabilization only). Branch naming: feature/<ticket-id>-<slug>, fix/<ticket-id>-<slug>, chore/<slug>, docs/<slug>, refactor/<slug>, hotfix/<slug>.
- Commit messages: follow Conventional Commits (type[scope][!]: subject). Types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert. Subject ≤ 72 chars, imperative mood. Body paragraphs wrap at 72 chars, explain rationale and impact. Footer includes issue references (Closes #123), breaking changes (BREAKING CHANGE: …), and Signed-off-by (DCO).
- Commit practices: small, atomic commits; no “WIP” commits on shared branches; no committing generated artifacts or large binaries (use Git LFS for assets >10MB).
- Merge strategy: squash-merge PRs into main to maintain linear history; disallow merge commits. Rebase feature branches on latest main before merge; resolve conflicts locally. Hotfixes may be cherry-picked to release/* as needed.
- Reviews and checks: require at least one maintainer approval (two for core repos), passing CI, static analysis, tests, and security checks before merge. Enforce CODEOWNERS where applicable.
- Versioning and releases: Semantic Versioning; tag releases as vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Generate changelogs from Conventional Commits. Automated release pipelines cut tags from main; release/* branches only for stabilization and backports.
- Security and provenance: require signed commits (GPG/SSH) and DCO sign-off for all contributions.
- Tooling/enforcement: commitlint with Conventional Commits, husky pre-commit/pre-push hooks (lint, tests, secret scan), lint-staged, .editorconfig, .gitattributes, Git LFS, and repository branch protection rules. PR templates and ISSUE templates standardized across org. Submodules discouraged; prefer packages or vendoring with clear update policies.

## Decision
We will adopt MkDocs as the standard tool for authoring, building, and publishing project documentation.

- Authoring: Documentation will be written in Markdown and stored under the docs/ directory in the repository. The MkDocs configuration file (mkdocs.yml) will live at the repo root. We will use explicit nav in mkdocs.yml to control information architecture.
- Theming and UX: Use the Material for MkDocs theme for accessibility, responsive design, built‑in search, and a rich component set.
- Plugins:
  - mkdocstrings (with appropriate handlers) for auto‑generated API reference from source docstrings
  - mike for versioned documentation aligned with release tags
  - mkdocs-mermaid2 for architecture and sequence diagrams
  - mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized for last-updated metadata
  - redirects and tags as needed
- Diagrams: Prefer Mermaid in Markdown; allow PlantUML via plugin if required.
- Linting and quality: Enforce Markdown style, links, and anchors via pre-commit hooks (markdownlint, mdformat, link-checker). PRs must pass doc build and link checks.
- CI/CD: On each commit to main, build and publish docs to GitHub Pages (or internal static hosting). For pull requests, publish ephemeral previews via PR environments. Releases trigger mike version updates (e.g., latest, 1.x).
- Contribution workflow: Changes to docs follow the same review process as code. ADRs live under docs/adr/ with stable permalinks. Code examples are tested when feasible (doctest or snippets).
- Scope: This decision covers public and internal developer documentation, including getting started, guides, concepts, reference (API), and ADRs.
- Rollout: Introduce mkdocs.yml, base nav, theme, and CI pipeline; migrate existing docs; document authoring guidelines in CONTRIBUTING.md.

We will adopt Brakeman as the standard static application security testing (SAST) tool for all Ruby on Rails codebases.

- Scope: All Rails services and engines in this organization must include and maintain Brakeman. New projects must start with zero findings; legacy projects will establish a time‑boxed remediation plan.
- Execution: Brakeman will run in CI on every pull request and on default branch builds. Pull requests with Critical/High findings will fail; Medium may warn or fail based on repo policy; Low/Info will not block merges.
- Configuration: Each repo will maintain a committed brakeman.yml for rules, paths, and checks. False positives require explicit, reviewed ignores in .brakeman.ignore with justification and expiry where feasible; blanket or auto‑generated ignores are prohibited.
- Reporting: CI will publish SARIF (preferred) or HTML/JSON reports. For platforms supporting code scanning, SARIF will be uploaded to surface annotations inline with code.
- Developer workflow: A fast local task (e.g., bin/brakeman or make scan) will be provided; optional pre-commit hooks may run a subset of checks. Teams must fix blocking findings before merge.
- Performance/Determinism: Runs will use a pinned Brakeman major/minor version via a lockfile or container image. Tooling will cache as supported to keep CI times acceptable.
- Governance: Security/AppSec owns global policy, version upgrades (at least quarterly), and rule exceptions; teams own remediation. Changes to thresholds or global config require AppSec approval.

Adopt AWS Elastic Container Service (ECS) as the standard platform for hosting containerized applications. Use ECS on Fargate as the default launch type to minimize operational overhead; fall back to ECS on EC2 only for specialized workloads (e.g., GPU, custom AMIs, daemonset-like agents) with documented exceptions. Container images will be stored in Amazon ECR. Networking will run in a multi-AZ VPC with services in private subnets, fronted by Application Load Balancers (ALB) and protected by security groups and WAF where applicable.

Standardize on:
- One ECS cluster per environment (dev, staging, prod) per account, following a multi-account strategy (segregated blast radius).
- Service discovery via AWS Cloud Map where ALB is not used.
- Autoscaling using ECS Service Auto Scaling driven by CloudWatch metrics.
- Blue/green and canary deployments via AWS CodeDeploy (or ECS rolling update where appropriate).
- Secrets and configuration via AWS Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store.
- Observability with CloudWatch Logs, Metrics, and X-Ray/OpenTelemetry exporters; optional Prometheus/Grafana for deep metrics.
- IAM roles for tasks (IRSA equivalent) with least privilege.
- Infrastructure as Code (Terraform or CloudFormation/CDK) as the only provisioning mechanism; no manual console changes.

Operational policies:
- Health checks and circuit-breaking at ALB and container levels.
- Resource limits/requests defined per task; capacity constraints enforced with budgets and cost allocation tags.
- Multi-AZ high availability with minimum two tasks per service in distinct AZs.
- Rolling back via CodeDeploy or task definition version pinning.
- Disaster recovery via multi-AZ design and ECR image immutability; optional cross-region replication for ECR and stateful dependencies.

This decision is effective immediately for all new services; existing workloads will be migrated incrementally based on risk and value.

Adopt a third‑party, compliant e‑signature platform as the system of record rather than building in-house. Primary provider: DocuSign; secondary: Adobe Acrobat Sign. Implement a provider-agnostic abstraction to allow switching with minimal impact.

All signature workflows (preparation, routing, identity verification, audit trail, and certificate issuance) are executed by the provider to ensure ESIGN/UETA and eIDAS compliance. The application prepares documents and recipients, then creates “envelopes” via server-to-server OAuth/JWT. Identity assurance uses provider features (email link, SMS OTP, KBA, government ID verification, SSO) selected per use case and geography; advanced/qualified signatures in the EU leverage the provider’s qualified trust services.

Executed artifacts (final PDF and the provider’s completion certificate/evidence summary) are persisted in our storage as the authoritative copy, with:
- Immutable retention using S3 Object Lock (WORM), server-side encryption (KMS), and tenant-scoped buckets.
- Content-addressable integrity (SHA‑256 hash) recorded at send time and verified on receipt.
- Trusted timestamping via provider; optionally augmented with RFC 3161 timestamping if required.

We store minimal metadata (envelope ID, participants, timestamps, status, hashes) in our database; no raw PII beyond necessity. Status changes are consumed via webhooks with idempotent handlers and dead-letter retries. Templates and fields are managed in the provider; our app references template IDs and injects runtime data.

Consent disclosures are presented and recorded by the provider. Data residency is configurable per tenant; retention and purging align with policy and legal holds. Wet-sign fallback is available for edge cases; offline/native drawn signatures are not implemented outside provider capabilities. We will not implement custom cryptographic signing. Continuous legal and security review governs provider configuration and changes.

## Decision

- Adopt Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 across all public deliverables: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
  - PATCH: backwards-compatible bug fixes.
  - MINOR: backwards-compatible features and deprecations.
  - MAJOR: breaking changes only.
- Public HTTP APIs are versioned via URI prefix (/v{MAJOR}). Minor/patch changes must be non-breaking. Deprecations are announced in a MINOR release and removed in the next MAJOR after a minimum 6-month deprecation window.
- Event and schema versioning:
  - Include an explicit version field in event payloads and schemas.
  - Use a schema registry with “backward compatible” evolution rules for MINOR/PATCH; breaking schema changes require a MAJOR.
- Database schema is versioned with forward-only migrations (e.g., Flyway/Liquibase). Each application version declares the required migration set. MINOR/PATCH migrations must be additive or backward compatible; destructive changes are gated to MAJOR with expand-and-contract patterns where needed.
- Packaging and distribution:
  - Git: tag releases as vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; maintain release branches per MAJOR.MINOR for patches; hotfixes from tags.
  - Containers: publish tags for MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, MAJOR, and latest (latest tracks the default branch, not necessarily a release).
  - Libraries/SDKs: publish SemVer versions; avoid pinning transitive dependencies; declare compatible ranges for runtime deps; applications use lockfiles to pin exact versions.
  - Pre-releases use SemVer pre-release identifiers (e.g., -alpha.1, -rc.1) and are not considered stable.
- Compatibility and support:
  - We guarantee backward compatibility within a MAJOR for public APIs, events, and CLIs.
  - We support the current MAJOR and the previous MAJOR (N and N-1) for security and critical fixes for 12 months after a new MAJOR.
- Communication and governance:
  - Every breaking change requires an approved ADR and a migration guide.
  - Changelogs follow Keep a Changelog format and clearly label breaking changes, deprecations, and migrations.
  - Automated CI enforces version increments consistent with commits (conventional commits) and blocks breaking changes without a MAJOR bump.

Store all moment-in-time values in UTC and exchange them in ISO 8601/RFC 3339 format with explicit offset (e.g., 2026-01-23T15:04:05.123Z). Use Instant/OffsetDateTime (or equivalent) for timestamps, LocalDate for date-only values, and LocalTime only when no date or zone is meaningful. Time zone conversions occur only at the presentation layer based on user’s IANA time zone.

Databases:
- PostgreSQL: use TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (timestamptz); persist in UTC.
- MySQL/MariaDB: use DATETIME with server/session time_zone=UTC; enforce UTC at connection.
- Do not store local times or offsets in timestamp columns; store user’s chosen IANA zone separately.

APIs:
- Require and return ISO 8601 with offset; reject ambiguous or zone-less local datetimes for moment-in-time fields.
- For date-only fields, use YYYY-MM-DD without time or zone.
- Normalize inbound timestamps to UTC on receipt; emit UTC by default (Z).

Precision and arithmetic:
- Standardize millisecond precision in APIs; round/truncate inbound higher precision; preserve higher precision internally if supported.
- Use Duration/Period types for math; avoid manual DST-sensitive arithmetic.

Scheduling/recurrence:
- Store recurrence rules separately (RFC 5545 RRULE) with an associated IANA zone; compute next occurrences zone-aware.

Testing and reliability:
- Abstract time source (Clock) for deterministic tests.
- No implicit defaults for time zone; require explicit user preference.
- Handle DST/ambiguous times by deferring to standard libraries; never invent offsets.

## Decision

Adopt JSON Web Tokens (JWT, RFC 7519) as bearer access tokens for API authorization across all services.

- Tokens will be issued by the centralized Auth Service/IdP using asymmetric signing (RS256 or ES256). Public keys are exposed via a JWKS endpoint; tokens carry a kid for rotation.
- Required claims: iss, aud, sub, iat, exp, jti. Authorization claims: scope (primary), with optional roles and tenant/org identifiers where needed. No PII in tokens.
- Access tokens are short-lived (5–15 minutes). No server-side session state is maintained for access tokens.
- Refresh tokens are opaque, rotated on every use, and stored securely:
  - First-party browser clients: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies.
  - Native/service clients: secure OS keychains/secret stores.
- APIs (gateway and services) must validate: signature against JWKS, exp/nbf, iss, aud, jti (if blocklisted), and required scopes. Allow up to 60s clock skew.
- Service-to-service auth uses client credentials flow issuing JWT access tokens with service scopes; mTLS is required for sensitive internal calls.
- Token propagation is via Authorization: Bearer <token>. Downstream services re-validate or rely on gateway validation plus signature/claim checks for defense in depth.
- Key management: rotate signing keys at least every 90 days or on compromise; maintain overlapping JWKS during rotation. Immediately invalidate compromised keys.
- Revocation: maintain a short-lived blocklist of jti for high-risk events until token expiry; rely on refresh token rotation for user-driven logout and compromise recovery.
- Error handling: on auth failures, return 401 with WWW-Authenticate and standardized error codes; 403 for insufficient scopes.
- Size and performance: limit token size (< 2 KB), minimize custom claims, and avoid JWE unless sensitive claims are strictly required; prefer claim indirection via resource lookups.
- Compliance and auditing: log token metadata (iss, aud, sub, jti) only, never raw tokens; redact in transit logs.

We will adopt a conservative deprecation policy for the 0.x series to provide predictability while allowing iterative improvement.

- Versioning discipline:
  - Patch (0.y.z): no breaking changes; bug and security fixes only.
  - Minor (0.y+1.0): may introduce breaking changes only after a prior deprecation period.

- Deprecation lifecycle:
  - N: Introduce new API/behavior and deprecate the old. Annotate with deprecation markers, docstrings, and replacement guidance. Emit structured runtime warnings once per process (and compile-time annotations where applicable).
  - N+1: Maintain deprecated API. Default flips to new behavior via feature flag where relevant; old behavior still available by opt-in flag.
  - N+2: Remove deprecated API/behavior and associated flags. Provide clear error messages and migration pointers.

- Communication and tooling:
  - Record all deprecations in CHANGELOG and a living DEPRECATIONS.md with N/N+1/N+2 milestones.
  - Tag deprecations with stable codes to enable CI fail-on-deprecation (env/flag).
  - Provide migration guides and, where feasible, automated codemods.
  - CLI and server components log deprecation notices; libraries use standard deprecation channels.

- Backward compatibility for data/config:
  - During N and N+1, read legacy config keys and data formats; write in the new format and emit warnings when legacy inputs are detected.
  - Removal at N+2 with clear errors and upgrade instructions.

- Support window:
  - Maintain the last two minor releases with critical bug and security fixes; deprecation notices are not backported.

- Exceptions:
  - Security, data-loss, or correctness issues may trigger accelerated removal with a documented rationale and mitigation steps.

This policy remains in effect for all 0.x packages until 1.0, at which point standard SemVer deprecation and removal timelines will be established.

We will build a time-boxed, throwaway prototype to de-risk the highest-uncertainty aspects of the solution. The prototype will target 1–2 critical end-to-end user journeys and the most uncertain non-functional requirements (performance at target scale, reliability under failure modes, and integration with key third-party services). External systems will be stubbed or sandboxed; synthetic, non-PII data will be used.

The prototype will use the intended target technologies only where risk needs validation; elsewhere, speed-first choices are acceptable. We will instrument the prototype for basic logging, tracing, and benchmarking to produce objective evidence.

Success criteria:
- Demonstrate the critical flows working E2E with acceptable UX.
- Meet provisional performance thresholds (e.g., p95 latency, throughput) under a representative load profile.
- Validate feasibility of priority integrations and identify any blocking constraints.
- Produce effort/complexity estimates within ±30% for the MVP backlog.

Constraints and governance:
- Time-box: 3 weeks with weekly checkpoints.
- Team: 2 engineers, part-time UX, QA consult for test design.
- Isolated branch and environment; no production data or users; access restricted.
- Security is minimal but responsible (secrets management, dependency scanning).

Deliverables:
- Running demo and automation to reproduce it.
- Measured benchmarks and test scripts.
- Findings report with recommendations (proceed, pivot, or change approach/stack).
- Updated ADRs and a prioritized risk/assumption register.
- A hardening plan if we choose to evolve parts of the prototype; otherwise, code is disposable and not promoted to production.

## Decision
Adopt the Argo CD App-of-Apps pattern to declaratively compose and operate all applications and platform components, with one “root” Application per environment that owns the lifecycle of child Applications generated by ApplicationSets.

- Repository model:
  - A single “platform-config” Git repo contains environment directories (e.g., envs/prod, envs/stage) that define the root app, ApplicationSets, and shared platform components.
  - Each product/service maintains its own “app” repo with Helm/Kustomize overlays per environment (apps/<service>/overlays/{dev,stage,prod}).

- Root application:
  - One Argo CD Application per environment points to envs/<env>, which contains:
    - ApplicationSets that generate Applications for each service from a declarative manifest list, directory generator, or Git generator.
    - Platform apps (ingress, cert-manager, logging, metrics) as first-class Applications.
  - Automated sync enabled with prune and self-heal.

- Application boundaries and security:
  - Argo CD Projects per domain/team to scope destinations, repos, and namespaces.
  - Each child Application deploys into a dedicated namespace with least-privilege RBAC.
  - Secrets managed via External Secrets Operator or Sealed Secrets; no plaintext secrets in Git.

- Multi-cluster and promotion:
  - ApplicationSet cluster generators target multiple clusters; environment overlays encode cluster-specific configuration.
  - Promotion is Git-driven via PRs updating image tags/versions in environment overlays.

- Ordering and resilience:
  - Use sync waves and optional sync hooks to sequence platform before workloads and manage dependencies.
  - Health checks, retry/backoff, and revision history limits configured for safe rollouts and rollback.
  - Bootstrap via a minimal “bootstrap” manifest that installs Argo CD, then applies the root Application.
  - Disaster recovery by reapplying bootstrap and syncing from Git; no imperative state required.

This structure standardizes onboarding, scales to many services/clusters, enforces guardrails via Projects/RBAC, and centralizes environment orchestration while preserving team autonomy over app repos.

## Decision
We will standardize custom HTTP header handling across all services via a shared middleware/library that enforces naming, validation, normalization, propagation, and security controls.

- Naming: Use a project-specific, non-“X-” prefix per RFC 6648 (e.g., App-Request-Id, App-Tenant-Id). Kebab-case, ASCII alphanumerics plus hyphen only. No underscores or mixed delimiters.
- Casing: Treat headers case-insensitively on ingress; emit canonicalized casing on egress.
- Validation: Enforce allowlists for known custom headers and value schemas (length, charset, regex). Reject malformed values with 400 for client-originated requests; drop invalid headers from internal calls and log.
- Limits: Cap custom header count and size to prevent abuse (e.g., ≤ 16 custom headers, each ≤ 1 KB, total ≤ 8 KB).
- Normalization: Map allowed custom headers into a structured request context (tenant, correlation, features). Downstream services must read from context, not raw headers, when possible.
- Propagation: Only propagate an explicit allowlist of headers downstream. Strip all custom headers at trust boundaries (public egress, third-party calls) unless explicitly required and reviewed.
- Security: Forbid overriding standard security headers (e.g., Authorization, Cookie, Host, Forwarded) via custom equivalents. Block hop-by-hop and sensitive headers. Apply PII scrubbing in logs/metrics; never log full values for sensitive headers.
- Compatibility: Temporarily accept legacy X-App-* headers and map to new names; emit deprecation warnings and remove support after one release cycle.
- Observability: Standardize correlation via App-Request-Id; interop with W3C Trace Context when present.
- Delivery: Provide language-specific middleware/filters and a contract test suite; services must adopt the library and disallow ad hoc custom header handling.

## Decision

We will officially support only Node.js versions that are receiving security updates from the Node.js project (Active LTS and Maintenance LTS). When a Node.js version reaches End-of-Life (EOL) and no longer receives security updates, we will deprecate and subsequently drop support for that version.

Policy and implementation:
- engines policy: package.json will declare the minimum supported Node.js version as the lowest LTS that still receives security updates. We will not set an artificial upper bound; compatibility with new majors will be validated via CI within 30 days of their release.
- CI strategy: our test matrix will include all Node.js versions currently in security support. CI will automatically update the matrix as versions transition (via release schedule monitoring/automation).
- Release management: dropping support for a Node.js version is a breaking change for libraries and will be released in a new major version. For applications, we will schedule the runtime upgrade as part of regular platform maintenance.
- Deprecation and communication: we will announce deprecation at least one minor release in advance and, when feasible, a minimum of 60 days prior to the upstream EOL date. Release notes and migration guides will accompany drops.
- Security posture: we will not backport fixes to unsupported Node.js versions. Critical exceptions require explicit approval and must not introduce security risk.
- Tooling alignment: TypeScript targets, lint rules, polyfills, and Docker base images will align with the minimum supported Node.js version.
- Review cadence: quarterly review of the Node.js release schedule to adjust the minimum supported version and CI matrix.

We will remove support for Google’s Sitelinks Searchbox across all web properties. Specifically, we will:
- Delete all schema.org “WebSite” JSON-LD (or microdata) containing potentialAction/SearchAction from layouts, CMS components, and any tag-manager injections.
- Add <meta name="google" content="nositelinkssearchbox"> on canonical homepages to explicitly opt out while Google reprocesses pages.
- Retain all other structured data (e.g., Organization, Breadcrumb, Article, Product) unchanged.

Rationale: The Sitelinks Searchbox yields low-quality query routing, inconsistent localization, and diluted brand experience; it conflicts with our new on-site search UX and provides negligible CTR/SEO benefit per analytics. Removal reduces SEO maintenance overhead and avoids misaligned SERP behavior.

Scope and rollout:
- Apply to all production domains and environments.
- Gate behind a feature flag; validate in staging.
- Use Google’s Rich Results Test and URL Inspection to confirm removal.
- Monitor Search Console (Enhancements, Search Appearance, Rich Results), branded SERPs, and traffic/CTR for 4–8 weeks post-deploy.

Risks and mitigations:
- Google may cache prior markup; the meta opt-out accelerates deprecation.
- Third-party scripts may reintroduce markup; audit and block via tag manager review and code scanning.
- Potential minor SERP real estate loss; monitor brand query KPIs and revert via flag if negative impact exceeds thresholds agreed with SEO/Marketing.

This decision stands until future evidence shows material benefit from reintroducing the feature.

## Decision
Adopt a Composite Handler design to orchestrate request processing via a uniform Handler interface, enabling ordered aggregation of child handlers under a single composite. The composite will support three execution policies selectable per use case: (1) First-Success (short-circuit on first handler that returns Handled), (2) All (fan-out to all handlers, aggregate results), and (3) Fail-Fast (abort on first error). Handlers are discovered and wired via dependency injection, ordered by explicit priority metadata; absent metadata, insertion order is preserved.

The Handler interface returns a Result type (Handled | Skipped | Failed(error)), never throws for expected conditions. The composite normalizes exceptions to Failed and, under All policy, aggregates errors for reporting. Idempotency and statelessness are required for handlers by default; stateful handlers must declare thread-safety guarantees. The composite is immutable after construction to ensure predictability and safe concurrent use.

Configuration is externalized: handler registration, ordering, and policy are defined via configuration profiles to enable environment-specific compositions. Feature flags may enable/disable handlers without code changes. Observability is built in: each handler invocation is traced with timing, outcome, and correlation IDs; the composite emits structured events and metrics (count, latency, error rate, skip/handle ratios).

Performance considerations: the composite supports optional parallel fan-out for the All policy when handlers are independent and side-effect free; otherwise it executes sequentially. Backpressure and timeout policies are enforced at the composite level. The design allows easy extensibility by adding new handlers without modifying the composite, enabling incremental evolution and safer rollout through canarying and staged priority adjustments.

We will interact with Docker via the Docker Engine API using a maintained Docker client library instead of shelling out to the docker CLI. We will standardize on the language’s actively maintained SDK (e.g., Go: official client; Java: docker-java; Python: docker-py; Node.js: dockerode) and encapsulate it behind an internal interface to allow mocking, replacement, and future upgrades without broad refactors.

Connection policy:
- Local: Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock) on Linux/macOS; named pipe on Windows.
- Remote: TCP with mutual TLS; no plaintext.
- Avoid mounting the Docker socket into untrusted containers; if unavoidable, access through a restricted proxy/sidecar with scoped authorization.

Operational scope:
- Container lifecycle: create, start, stop, inspect, remove.
- Image management: pull, tag, remove; optional build via buildkit where available.
- Logs, events, and stats streaming with backpressure support.
- Prune operations guarded behind explicit feature flags and role checks.

Reliability and compatibility:
- Pin Docker API version and enable negotiated compatibility; maintain a compatibility matrix in docs/ops.
- Configure timeouts, retries with exponential backoff, and circuit breakers for long-running streams.
- Enforce idempotency where possible (e.g., name-based reconciliation).

Security and governance:
- Store Docker credentials and TLS materials in the secret manager; rotate regularly.
- Enforce least-privilege with scoped registries and rate limits; redact sensitive fields in logs.
- Disallow Docker-in-Docker for production; prefer remote daemon or privileged host service.

Observability and testing:
- Emit structured metrics (latency, error rates, stream duration) and minimal, scrubbed request logs.
- Provide a fake client and record/replay harness for tests; use ephemeral environments (e.g., Testcontainers) in integration.

Fallback to CLI is prohibited in production; it may be used only in dev tooling with explicit opt-in.

## Decision
Establish a single source of truth in a managed cloud relational database (PostgreSQL) hosted in the primary region. All data creation, updates, and deletions occur exclusively through backend domain services exposed via authenticated APIs; clients never write directly to the database. The service layer enforces validation, authorization, and transactional integrity.

Adopt a pragmatic CQRS pattern: write operations target the primary database; read operations may be served from read replicas and a managed in-memory cache (Redis) for low-latency access. Caches are strictly ephemeral and treated as non-authoritative; cache invalidation follows write-through or explicit eviction on successful commits.

Implement change data capture (CDC) from the primary database to downstream consumers (search index, analytics warehouse) via an event stream, ensuring decoupled propagation and eventual consistency for non-critical projections. All mutations are synchronously persisted to the primary database before emitting events.

Support offline/draft use cases with client-side temporary storage limited to user drafts; synchronization occurs through the same APIs with conflict detection using optimistic concurrency (ETags/version columns). Maintain comprehensive audit logging of all mutations at the service layer and, where required, database-level row change auditing.

No data is stored permanently on client devices or edge caches beyond drafts and session tokens. Backups, encryption at rest/in transit, and point-in-time recovery are enabled for the primary database; read replicas are disposable and can be rebuilt from the primary.

## Decision

Adopt a managed feature flag platform (LaunchDarkly) as the standard mechanism for progressive delivery, experiment enablement, and operational kill switches across all services and clients. Use server-side evaluation for backend services and client-side SDKs where necessary, with all flags defined and managed centrally per environment (dev, staging, prod).

- Flag taxonomy:
  - Release flags (short‑lived, default off, gate incomplete code)
  - Ops kill switches (long‑lived, default on with rapid disable)
  - Experiment flags (time‑boxed, tied to analytics)
  - Permission/config flags (long‑lived, rarely changed)

- Governance and hygiene:
  - Each flag requires an owner, description, rollout plan, default/fallbacks, and explicit expiry/cleanup date.
  - Naming convention: <domain>.<service>.<feature>.<purpose>.
  - PR checks require a referenced flag ID for guarded code paths.
  - Flags older than 90 days (non-permission) trigger automatic review; experiments auto-expire.

- Rollout practices:
  - Use percentage rollouts, attribute/segment targeting, and per-region enablement.
  - All production rollouts are gradual with real-time monitoring and automated rollback via flag kill switch.
  - Mobile/edge clients use bootstrapped values and SDK caching with safe defaults to prevent outages.

- Operationalization:
  - Integrate flag change events with audit logs, alerting, and incident response.
