- Permissions: Implement separate, user-initiated flows for background location; respect auto-reset of unused permissions; review and reduce permission surface.
- Package visibility: Declare queries in manifest for required packages and intents; replace broad package scans with targeted APIs.
- Foreground services: Specify foregroundServiceType where applicable (location, mediaPlayback, dataSync, etc.); ensure proper notification channels.
- Background execution: Audit and refactor background work to WorkManager/JobScheduler; eliminate implicit background starts.
- Networking and security: Confirm cleartext traffic policy via networkSecurityConfig; validate TLS and strict mode in debug.
- Intents and components: Replace deprecated/broad implicit intents; tighten exported component definitions; add android:exported as required when we later target 31+.
- Libraries/CI: Upgrade Android Gradle Plugin, Gradle, and dependencies compatible with API 30; update lint and static analysis rules.

Rollout:
- Ship behind feature flags where possible; run full regression on Android 8–13 devices/emulators.
- Provide data migration where file paths change; communicate user-visible changes.
- Use staged rollout with crash/ANR gating and telemetry to validate storage, permissions, and background work behavior.

This decision is mandatory for continued Play Store updates and reduces platform-induced failures while modernizing app security and privacy.

## Decision

We will deploy the proxy node as a stateless, containerised service on the GDS Supported Platform, leveraging its managed Kubernetes runtime, ingress, and security controls. The service will be built and packaged as an OCI image, deployed via GitOps-driven Terraform and platform-native pipelines, and exposed through the platform-managed Ingress with WAF, TLS termination, and mutual TLS to upstream/back-end services where required.

Key elements:
- Stateless by design; no local persistence. Configuration and secrets provided via platform secret management and ConfigMaps.
- High availability through multi-AZ deployment, horizontal pod autoscaling, and pod disruption budgets. Rolling and blue/green deployments for zero-downtime releases.
- Network policy enforcement for least-privilege ingress/egress, with egress restricted to approved endpoints via the platform’s egress controls. Private networking preferred; public exposure only through managed ingress.
- Authentication and authorisation integrated with platform-supported mechanisms (mTLS, OIDC/JWT validation) and request/response filtering at the proxy.
- Centralised logging, metrics, and tracing using platform observability (structured logs, Prometheus scraping, alerts in PagerDuty/Slack); synthetic probes for external availability.
- Compliance with GDS controls: CIS baselines for images/nodes, supply-chain scanning (SCA, image scanning), signed images, and SBOM publication.
- Disaster recovery via redeployability from IaC and container registry; no data backup required for the service itself. Runbooks and SLOs defined (e.g., 99.9% availability, P99 latency budget).
- Decommission legacy VM-based proxy once parity, performance, and resilience criteria are met and cutover completes.

We will represent all in-memory pixel data as a single, contiguous double-precision array using interleaved per-pixel channel layout.

- Buffer layout: double[] length = width × height × channels; row-major order; pixel stride = channels; channel order RGBA (absent alpha implies A=1.0).
- Value domain: normalized linear values in [0.0, 1.0]; NaN permitted to denote missing/invalid samples; values will be clamped to [0.0, 1.0] at API boundaries unless explicitly disabled.
- Color space: values are linear; any gamma/transfer conversion occurs at I/O and UI boundaries.
- Precision: all internal computations on pixel buffers use double; intermediate temporaries may use double or vectorized float as long as results are stored back as double with error < 1 ULP of double at [0,1] range endpoints.
- Conversions:
  - On decode/ingest: convert from source bit depth (8–16 int, 16f/32f) to double [0,1] linear.
  - On encode/export and GPU upload: convert from double to required format (e.g., 8/16-bit int, float16/32). Rounding: round-to-nearest, ties-to-even; clamp before quantization.
- Memory/tiling: default is a single slab buffer; optional tile views/slices reference the same underlying array (no copies).
- Threading: read-only access is multi-thread safe; writers must ensure external synchronization. Functions operating in-place must document aliasing constraints.
- SIMD: implementations may downcast to float32 internally for vectorization; must meet precision requirement above.
- Endianness/portability: standard IEEE-754 doubles; no platform-specific layouts assumed.

This decision applies to all core image processing stages and shared APIs accepting or returning pixel buffers.

Adopt Microsoft Playwright as the primary framework for browser-based functional (end-to-end) testing of our web applications. Implement Playwright Test with TypeScript as the standard, running headless in CI and using the official Playwright Docker image for reproducibility.

Scope and coverage:
- Default CI runs on Chromium; daily smoke on Chromium/Firefox/WebKit; full cross-browser regression on release branches.
- Mobile emulation for critical journeys; real-device testing remains out of scope.
- API/contract tests remain in the existing framework; only UI-driven journeys are in Playwright.

Standards and conventions:
- Use data-testid attributes as the preferred selector strategy; prohibit brittle CSS/XPath selectors against presentation.
- Centralize auth, test data seeding, and environment setup via Playwright fixtures.
- Enable retries for known flaky tests and trace/video on failure for debuggability.
- Isolate third-party dependencies via network interception/mocking where feasible.

Operationalization:
- Integrate with CI for parallel sharding and artifacts (traces, videos, screenshots).
- Provide a base test template, project config per environment, and a minimal page object pattern where it adds value.
- Freeze new tests in Selenium/Cypress immediately; migrate critical paths first, complete migration in phased waves over two quarters.

Risks and mitigations:
- Learning curve mitigated with templates and training.
- Flakiness addressed through robust waits, idempotent test data, and retries.
- Infrastructure load managed via CI concurrency limits and containerized runners.

This decision standardizes on Playwright to improve reliability, speed, and maintainability of functional tests while enabling consistent cross-browser coverage.

We will not use thread-level interruption or forced termination to stop work (e.g., Thread.interrupt/Abort/stop/suspend, pthread_cancel, Future.cancel(true), or signal-based thread kills). Instead, all cancellation and shutdown will be cooperative and structured.

- All long‑running or blocking tasks must accept a cancellation/deadline context and periodically check it at well-defined safe points, then exit gracefully on cancellation.
- Blocking I/O and waits must be bounded via timeouts or cancelable APIs; where possible, prefer closing the underlying resource or using non-blocking, async, or selectable primitives to unblock.
- Work must run on managed executors/thread pools; raw thread management is discouraged. Do not hold locks while performing unbounded or non-cancelable operations.
- Each task must implement idempotent teardown and release resources deterministically on cancellation, error, or timeout.
- Services must propagate cancellation/deadlines across boundaries (RPC, DB, queues) and prefer structured concurrency or async task hierarchies to ensure children are cancelled with parents.
- Operationally, if a task becomes unresponsive despite cooperative cancellation, escalate by isolating the unit (circuit breaker/bulkhead), and, if necessary, restart the process/container rather than attempting thread-level interruption.
- Instrumentation must report cancellation latency, stuck task detectors, and shutdown time budgets; tests must cover cancellation checkpoints and timeout behavior.

This policy improves safety, predictability, and debuggability, avoiding inconsistent state, lost invariants, and deadlocks commonly caused by mid-flight interruption.

We will institutionalize automated, enforceable code quality gates across the development lifecycle.

- Enforce formatting and linting via pre-commit hooks and CI (lint warnings treated as errors). Use language-appropriate tools (e.g., ESLint+Prettier for JS/TS, Black+Flake8 for Python, Checkstyle/SpotBugs for Java, EditorConfig across repos).
- Adopt centralized static analysis and coverage reporting (e.g., SonarQube/SonarCloud). Minimum thresholds: ≥80% line coverage and ≥70% branch coverage per PR and on default branch; thresholds are ratcheted upward quarterly where feasible.
- Require unit, integration, and property-based tests where applicable; tests must be deterministic and parallelizable. Flaky tests are quarantined within 24 hours and fixed within one sprint.
- Mandate peer review on all changes via pull requests, with CODEOWNERS for critical areas and a lightweight architecture checklist. Small, focused PRs (<300 LOC diff) are preferred.
- Apply SAST (e.g., Semgrep), dependency scanning (e.g., Dependabot/Snyk), and license compliance checks in CI; high/critical issues block merges.
- Use Conventional Commits and PR templates to ensure traceability and consistent documentation. All public APIs require docstrings and usage examples.
- Establish “quality fitness functions” (lint, test, security, performance smoke) as CI gates; merges to protected branches are blocked on failure.
- Allow temporary waivers via documented, time-bound exceptions approved by tech lead and recorded in ADRs.
- Audit compliance and metrics monthly; publish dashboards and act on regressions within the next sprint.

## Decision
Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as the canonical mechanism for capturing, communicating, and evolving significant architectural decisions across the codebase.

- Storage and structure:
  - Maintain ADRs in the repository under docs/adr/.
  - One ADR per decision, immutable once Accepted except via Superseding ADRs.
  - Use sequential numbering (e.g., 0001, 0002) and descriptive titles (kebab-case filenames).

- Template and format:
  - Use the MADR template (v3.x) with sections: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Options, and Links.
  - Write in concise, implementation-neutral language; include rationale and trade-offs.

- Status workflow:
  - Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded.
  - Changes to Accepted decisions require a new ADR that supersedes the prior one and explains migration/impact.

- Process and governance:
  - ADRs are created via pull requests and require review/approval from the architecture owner(s) and affected teams.
  - Every significant architectural change (e.g., tech selection, cross-cutting concerns, data contracts, deployment topology, SLAs) requires an ADR before implementation.
  - Minor refactors and non-architectural changes do not require ADRs.

- Traceability and discoverability:
  - Link ADRs from related code, docs, and tickets; cross-link alternatives and superseded records.
  - Maintain an index in docs/adr/README.md with statuses and summaries.

- Tooling and automation:
  - Optionally use adr-tools or repo templates to bootstrap ADRs.
  - Enforce presence and status via CI checks for PRs labeled as “architecture.”

- Retrospective coverage:
  - Backfill ADRs for critical legacy decisions as “Accepted (retrospective)” where feasible.

## Decision

Adopt a standardized, governance-driven lifecycle for all channels (topics/queues/websocket rooms) across environments to ensure predictability, safety, and auditability.

- Lifecycle states: Proposed → Provisioned → Active → Deprecated → Archived → Deleted.
  - Proposed: defined in ADR + IaC PR, assigned owner and SLOs.
  - Provisioned: infrastructure created via IaC in a non-prod environment.
  - Active: promoted to prod, usage monitored and SLOs enforced.
  - Deprecated: read-only announcement issued; new producers/consumers blocked.
  - Archived: writes blocked; retention set to minimum; access restricted.
  - Deleted: resources destroyed; metadata retained for audit.

- Changes via code only (GitOps/IaC). Manual creation/modification is prohibited and blocked where possible.

- Ownership and metadata registered in the Service Catalog (owner, data classification, retention, encryption, SLOs, contact, purpose).

- Naming convention enforced: <domain>.<bounded-context>.<purpose>.<version>.<env> with linting in CI.

- Schema/versioning:
  - Backward-compatible changes allowed within version; incompatible changes require a new versioned channel.
  - Schema registry required; consumers must tolerate additive fields.

- Access control:
  - Least-privilege IAM roles per producer/consumer; secrets managed by KMS/Secret Manager.
  - PII channels require encryption at rest/in transit and access reviews.

- Retention and cleanup:
  - Default retention by classification; inactivity TTL triggers auto-archive after N days, auto-delete after M days post-archive unless exemption is approved.

- Observability:
  - Mandatory metrics (throughput, lag, DLQ rate), alerts, and dashboards; drift detection on IaC.

- Migration:
  - Deprecation requires a migration plan, dual-publish/dual-consume window, and cutover date; CI blocks new deps on deprecated channels.

- Emergency controls: freeze switch to block new channels during incidents; break-glass with audit for urgent changes.

We will adopt OpenSearch as the primary full-text search engine for user-facing search and discovery, separate from the transactional database. OpenSearch will power relevance-ranked queries, autocomplete, filtering/faceting, highlighting, and analytics dashboards; the relational database remains the source of truth.

- Deployment: Use managed OpenSearch (e.g., AWS OpenSearch Service) in production for availability, scaling, and operational burden reduction; use containerized OpenSearch locally and in CI.
- Data flow: Perform near–real-time indexing via an asynchronous pipeline fed by database change data capture (CDC) events; batch backfills handle reindexing and schema changes. The application will treat indexing as eventually consistent and retry on failures.
- Index design: Define explicit mappings, language-specific analyzers, and use keyword + text fields for exact match and relevance. Apply alias-based index versioning (blue/green) for zero-downtime reindexing.
- Multitenancy: Use per-tenant index prefixes when isolation is required; otherwise, a shared index with a tenant_id filter and filtered aliases. Enforce tenancy at query time via mandatory filters.
- Security and compliance: Do not index secrets or highly sensitive PII; store only derived or tokenized fields where needed. Enable encryption at rest and in transit and enforce IAM/role-based access.
- Observability and SLOs: Track ingestion lag, query latency, error rate, and index health; set alerts on shard allocation and disk watermarks.
- Fallbacks: If OpenSearch is temporarily unavailable, degrade to limited database-backed search for critical flows and queue index operations for later replay.
- Cost and scaling: Start with modest cluster size, enable autoscaling where supported, and review shard/replica counts per data volume growth.

## Decision

We will enforce business invariants by failing fast with domain-specific exceptions thrown at the point of violation within the domain layer (entities, value objects, aggregates, domain services). Invariants will not be represented as nullable returns, sentinel values, or generic error codes.

- Introduce a domain exception hierarchy with a non-technical base (e.g., BusinessRuleViolationException) and specific subtypes per invariant (e.g., InsufficientBalance, InvalidStateTransition, DuplicateOrder). Messages must be actionable and include invariant names and key identifiers.
- Differentiate concerns:
  - Invariants (must always hold): enforced via exceptions in domain logic.
  - Input validation (shape/format): handled before entering the domain; return structured validation results, not exceptions.
  - Technical faults (timeouts, IO): throw/propagate technical exceptions; do not map to business exceptions.
- Application layer will catch domain exceptions to:
  - Map to user-visible outcomes (e.g., HTTP 409/422 or equivalent codes/events).
  - Trigger compensating actions as needed.
  - Ensure transactions roll back; no partial side effects remain. Outbox/event publication is contingent on success.
- Do not log domain exceptions at every layer. Log once at the boundary with correlation/tenant/context; internal layers enrich and rethrow without duplicative logging.
- Avoid using exceptions for normal control flow (e.g., absent optional data). Use Option/Maybe/Result for expected absence or query-time conditions where no invariant is violated.
- Public APIs and message handlers will translate domain exceptions into stable error contracts. Exception details will be sanitized; a stable error code is required per invariant type.
- Asynchronous and reactive pipelines must propagate domain errors on the error channel and maintain cancellation/rollback semantics.
- Performance: guard clauses make invariant checks O(1) where possible. Hot paths with predictable “negative” outcomes should prefer pre-checks to avoid exception costs.
- Testing: each invariant has explicit unit tests asserting both the allowed transitions and the exact exception type/code on violation. Exceptions double as living documentation of business rules.
- Versioning: adding a new invariant requires a new exception subtype and API error code; treat as a backward-compatible change only if existing flows remain valid.

We will not base any functionality, data model, rendering, or indexing on images that contain text (including TeX/LaTeX-rendered equations saved as bitmaps, screenshots of code/docs, rasterized PDFs). Images-of-text will not be treated as canonical sources for any pipeline.

- Canonical sources must be structured, machine-readable text/markup: Markdown, HTML, LaTeX source, MathML, JSON/YAML, protobuf/Avro, or SVG with embedded text. Mathematical content must be stored as LaTeX/MathML; rendered outputs may be SVG with selectable text.
- Ingestion: assets detected as text-in-image are rejected by default. If business-critical, they undergo OCR with confidence thresholds and human verification; the canonical stored result is text/markup, and the image remains optional decorative media with alt text.
- Rendering: clients and services render from canonical text/markup. Where raster output is unavoidable (e.g., email previews), we also include accessible text equivalents (alt, ARIA, hidden text).
- Search/indexing: only canonical text/markup is indexed; images are excluded except for metadata and alt text.
- Tooling and enforcement: add CI/CD checks to flag/deny merges introducing text-in-images; content linters for repos; migration tasks to replace existing text-images with text/markup or SVG. Provide authoring guidance and converters.
- Exceptions: third-party binaries may be stored for reference but are not used as sources of truth or indexed. Diagram images are allowed only when accompanied by their editable source (e.g., Mermaid, draw.io) and a textual description.
- Governance: any temporary deviation requires architecture approval, a documented rationale, and a time-boxed remediation plan.

## Decision
Implement a dedicated Service History Service (SHS) as a separate bounded-context microservice that records the complete lifecycle of service-related activities across domains. The SHS will use an append-only, event-sourced model where each ServiceEvent is immutable; corrections occur via compensating events, not updates. We adopt CQRS: a command API for validated writes and read-optimized projections for queries.

Event ingestion will use a write API with idempotency keys and the outbox pattern to publish to a Kafka topic. A consumer persists canonical events to partitioned PostgreSQL (time- and tenant-partitioned) as the system of record and builds projections to OpenSearch for flexible filtering, full-text search, and timeline queries. Reads are served from projections; the write log remains the source of truth.

Event schemas are versioned (backward compatible), with strict schemas enforced via schema registry. The domain model includes tenant_id, subject_id (e.g., asset, customer, ticket), event_type, occurred_at, actor, and payload (opaque, schematized). Multi-tenancy isolation is enforced at both storage and index layers.

Security and compliance: minimize PII in events; encrypt at rest and in transit; implement per-tenant RBAC and service-to-service auth; support legal erasure via redaction/erasure events and cryptographic erasure of payload references. Retention is policy-driven with data lifecycle management.

Operationally, the SHS provides 99.9% availability with eventual consistency targets under 5 seconds for projections, supports backfill/import pipelines, and offers SLIs on write latency, projection lag, and query latency. The API and event contracts are versioned and backward compatible to enable safe evolution without breaking consumers.

We will standardize on Kotlin as the primary programming language for all new application code targeting JVM and Android, and, where applicable, Kotlin Multiplatform for shared logic. Kotlin 2.x (K2 compiler) will be the default, upgraded on a regular cadence aligned with ecosystem compatibility (Android Gradle Plugin, Spring/Build tools).

Scope and usage:
- New features and modules must be implemented in Kotlin. Existing Java code remains supported and will be migrated opportunistically (Boy Scout Rule) rather than via big-bang rewrites.
- Interoperability with existing Java libraries is permitted; Java will only be introduced for platform gaps or third-party constraints.
- For concurrency and async, use Kotlin coroutines and Flow; do not introduce new Rx-based code.
- Adopt Kotlin data/inline classes, sealed hierarchies, null-safety, and extension functions to express domain models and invariants.

Tooling and standards:
- Gradle with Kotlin DSL is the default build configuration language.
- Enforce ktlint and detekt with the official Kotlin style guide; treat style violations as CI failures.
- Enable strict compiler flags (e.g., -Werror for warnings agreed by the team, explicit API for libraries, progressive mode where stable).
- Use Dokka for API documentation.
- Prefer kotlinx libraries (serialization, datetime, coroutines) where suitable.

Testing:
- Write tests in Kotlin using JUnit 5 and Kotest (or MockK for mocking); avoid mixing Java test frameworks for new tests.

Platform targets:
- JVM target aligns with the project baseline (e.g., 17 for server, AGP defaults for Android). For KMP, restrict targets to those with mature tooling; add others only when justified.

Governance:
- Any deviation from Kotlin-first requires an ADR. Library choices and language feature usage (e.g., inline classes, context receivers) follow a lightweight RFC before adoption.

Adopt CSS-in-JS using styled-components (v6) as the standard mechanism for authoring and composing UI styles in React across all new features and refactors. Co-locate styles with components; avoid global CSS except for a minimal reset and root variables via createGlobalStyle. Centralize design tokens (colors, spacing, typography, radii, z-index) in a single theme consumed via ThemeProvider; all components must consume tokens, not hard-coded values. Use styled primitives (e.g., Box, Text, Button) as the base for composition to ensure consistency and reduce duplication. Enable SSR style injection and deterministic class names in all runtimes; include the Babel plugin for extraction/labeling and transient props to prevent prop leakage to the DOM. Prefer variants and style helpers over ad-hoc conditional logic; keep dynamic styling bounded to props that map to tokens to control runtime cost. Disallow inline styles for themable properties; permit inline styles only for truly dynamic, non-themable values (e.g., canvas dimensions). For third-party components, wrap with styled() adapters to align theming. New code uses styled-components exclusively; legacy SASS/CSS Modules may remain but must be migrated opportunistically during touchpoints. Document component-level theming contracts and test dark/high-contrast modes. Performance budgets apply: avoid deep nesting, limit complex interpolations, and use asProp/polymorphism judiciously.

We will implement a dedicated Barcode Querying service that standardizes all retail barcodes to a canonical GTIN-14 format (normalizing UPC-A, EAN-8/EAN-13, ITF-14; validating and computing check digits; stripping/addding leading zeros as needed). QR/DataMatrix content handling is out of scope and deferred to a separate ADR.

Query flow:
- Validate and normalize input to GTIN-14.
- Lookup in an in-memory/read-through distributed cache.
- Fallback to internal product catalog keyed by GTIN.
- Final fallback to external providers via an adapter interface; providers are pluggable and prioritized, with circuit breakers, exponential backoff, and timeouts.
- Successful external responses are normalized, enriched into our canonical ProductIdentifier and ProductSummary schemas, annotated with provenance and confidence, and cached with configurable TTLs (short for misses, longer for hits).

Non-functional decisions:
- SLO: p95 latency ≤150ms for cache/catalog hits, ≤1.5s for external lookups; 99.9% availability.
- Strict rate limiting and request coalescing for identical in-flight GTINs to prevent thundering herds.
- Idempotent, deterministic normalization and responses; no PII transmitted to external providers.
- Observability: structured logs (redacted inputs), metrics (hit/miss, latency, error codes), and traces across provider adapters.
- Degraded/offline behavior: return minimal normalized identifier with “unknown product” classification and reason codes; no blocking on external failures.
- Versioned schemas and adapter contracts to enable provider changes without client impact.

APIs:
- Synchronous GET /barcodes/{code} for real-time clients.
- Async batch endpoint for large imports; results delivered via callback/webhook.

Security/compliance:
- Input sanitation, length/type checks, and allowlist of symbologies.
- Configuration for region-specific prefix rules and data residency for caches and external calls.

## Decision
Adopt a globally unique, human-readable, and versionable identifier scheme for extension indicators using reverse‑DNS namespacing with canonical lowercase slugs and semantic version suffixes.

- Format: <namespace>.<domain>.<product>.<extension>.<indicator>@<semver>
  - Namespace is reverse-DNS owned by the publisher (e.g., org.example.analytics).
  - Components after the namespace are dot-separated, lowercase, kebab-free tokens (a–z, 0–9), max 32 chars each.
  - The semantic version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is mandatory for published indicators; “@latest” is an alias resolved at runtime.
- Uniqueness: The tuple (<identifier without version>, <version>) MUST be unique and immutable. Identifiers MUST NOT be recycled.
- Case and charset: Identifiers are ASCII, lowercase, digits, and dots only; comparisons are case-sensitive but canonical form is lowercase.
- Ownership and registry: Each namespace owner maintains a signed registry of their indicators. A central catalog aggregates registries and enforces uniqueness by namespace. Publishing requires proof of domain ownership.
- Stability and evolution: Changes breaking meaning or shape require MAJOR version increment; additive, backward-compatible changes increment MINOR; fixes increment PATCH. “latest” may move only forward within the same MAJOR by default.
- Deprecation: Deprecated versions remain resolvable with a deprecation flag and sunset date; removal requires a minimum deprecation window.
- Resolution: APIs accept fully qualified IDs with version or “@latest”. Storage persists fully qualified IDs to ensure reproducibility. UI may display friendly names but must store canonical IDs.
- Validation: Enforced via shared library and schema (length <= 200 chars total; no leading/trailing dots; no empty segments). Invalid IDs are rejected at publish and at runtime boundaries.
- Backward compatibility: Existing nonconforming IDs are mapped once to compliant canonical IDs and aliased; aliasing is preserved for one MAJOR release before removal.

Adopt restricted deletion with soft-delete as the default and hard-delete as an exceptional, controlled operation. All domain entities gain deletion metadata (deleted_at, deleted_by, deletion_reason, deletion_source) and transition to a Deleted state; records remain queryable only to privileged roles via include_deleted filters. DELETE APIs perform soft-delete, are idempotent, require a reason code, and return 202 Accepted; subsequent GETs behave as 404 for non-privileged callers. A restore endpoint enables undo within a defined grace window.

Hard-deletes are prohibited in application paths and executed only by a controlled data stewardship job after policy-driven retention periods, dependency checks, and approval workflow. Legal hold flags supersede deletion requests. PII follows data-class rules: where retention is mandated, fields are redacted/tokenized rather than removed; where erasure is required, purge occurs at retention expiry.

Referential integrity is enforced with ON DELETE RESTRICT at the database layer and application-level guardrails: aggregates cannot be deleted if active children exist; cascades are limited to derived/cache tables only. Event-sourced streams emit Deleted/Restored events; projections honor Deleted state.

Access control restricts deletion to specific roles with contextual ownership checks; dual authorization is required for high-risk domains. All delete/restore actions are fully audited (who, when, why, from where) and emitted as security events; metrics and alerts monitor anomalies.

Backups and analytics stores are included in the purge workflow, ensuring eventual consistency with retention policies. Rollout is feature-flagged, with data migration to backfill deletion metadata and read paths updated to filter Deleted by default.

## Decision

We will expose a public, versioned REST API over HTTPS using JSON as the wire format and define the contract with an OpenAPI 3.1 specification as the single source of truth.

- API style and structure: Resource-oriented REST with predictable, plural nouns and hierarchical paths. JSON field names use camelCase; timestamps use ISO-8601 UTC. ETags are returned for cache validation.
- Versioning: Major versions in the URI (/v1), with additive, backward-compatible changes within a major version. Deprecations follow a documented schedule and are signaled via headers and changelog.
- Authentication and authorization: OAuth 2.1 with OIDC (Authorization Code + PKCE) for end-user flows; OAuth 2.0 client credentials for server-to-server. JWT access tokens with short TTL; scopes control fine-grained access. All endpoints require TLS 1.2+.
- Error model: Consistent HTTP status codes with RFC 7807 problem+json responses containing machine-readable codes, human messages, and correlation IDs.
- Pagination and filtering: Cursor-based pagination default; explicit page size limits. Standardized filtering, sparse fieldsets, and sorting via query parameters.
- Idempotency and safety: Idempotency-Key header for POST operations that create or trigger side effects; PUT/PATCH are idempotent by design. Retries are safe when idempotency keys are honored.
- Rate limiting and quotas: Enforced per API key/client with standard headers (X-RateLimit-*) for visibility and 429 responses on exceedance.
- Observability: Correlation-ID is accepted/returned; structured logging, metrics, and audit trails for all authenticated actions.
- Asynchrony: Long-running tasks return 202 with a job resource and webhooks for completion; webhooks are signed and retried with exponential backoff.
- Compatibility and SDKs: The OpenAPI spec is validated in CI and used to generate client SDKs and reference docs; contract tests gate breaking changes.
- Internal services MAY use gRPC; the public contract remains REST. CORS is enabled for trusted origins only.

## Decision
We will remove Smartdown from the stack and standardize on CommonMark-compatible Markdown rendered via remark/rehype with a small set of custom plugins to preserve required interactive capabilities. All Smartdown artifacts (syntax, runtime, and build-time dependencies) will be deprecated and replaced with:

- Content: Migrated to Markdown with frontmatter and fenced code blocks; interactive elements expressed via MDX components (for web) or shortcodes/macros (for non-MDX targets).
- Rendering: remark/rehype pipeline with vetted plugins; no client-side runtime beyond the components strictly required for interactivity.
- Authoring: Linting and previews via unified/remark tooling; CI enforces format and link checks.

Scope includes all user-facing docs, embedded help, tutorials, and any runtime interpretation of Smartdown content. A compatibility layer (parser transforms) will be provided short-term to auto-convert 90%+ of existing Smartdown constructs; remaining edge cases will be manually refactored.

Rollout plan:
1) Freeze new Smartdown content immediately.
2) Implement conversion transforms and CI checks.
3) Migrate high-traffic content first, then remainder.
4) Remove Smartdown deps and code paths behind a feature flag, then delete after two releases.

Success criteria: zero Smartdown files in main, equivalent rendering and interactivity, reduced bundle size and build times, and simpler authoring workflow.

We will implement a Selenium-based scraping subsystem to reliably extract Koshvani data that is rendered dynamically with client-side JavaScript and guarded by interactive flows. The scraper will run a headless Chromium browser via Selenium WebDriver, emulate standard user behavior (including waiting for XHR-completed DOM states), and capture data through structured DOM queries rather than screen scraping.

Key parameters and practices:
- Use explicit waits for stable selectors; avoid brittle XPath where possible in favor of semantic attributes.
- Run in headless mode by default; enable visible mode for diagnostics.
- Centralize page object models for navigational flows and form interactions to improve maintainability.
- Implement robust retry with backoff for transient failures, network issues, and dynamic content timeouts.
- Respect site policies: adhere to robots/legal terms, throttle requests, introduce randomized human-like delays, and schedule off-peak runs.
- Detect and gracefully handle anti-bot measures (CAPTCHA/OTP); if encountered, pause the job and route to a manual review/assisted workflow rather than attempting to bypass.
- Log structured telemetry (navigation steps, request timings, selector versions) and capture screenshots/HTML snapshots on failure for auditability.
- Containerize the runtime (e.g., Selenium + Chrome in Docker) for consistent CI/CD execution; run under a job orchestrator with concurrency controls.
- Persist extracted data via idempotent upserts with schema validation; maintain source hashes and timestamps for traceability.

If Koshvani introduces a stable public API or bulk export endpoints, we will reassess and prefer those over browser automation.

## Decision

Adopt a multi-project solution within a single repository to enforce clear architectural boundaries, improve modularity, and support independent evolution of components. The solution will be organized into the following projects:

- Domain: Pure domain model and business rules; no external dependencies.
- Application: Use cases, orchestration, and ports; depends only on Domain.
- Infrastructure: Adapters and implementations (persistence, messaging, external services); depends on Application (and transitively Domain) and external libraries.
- API (or Web): Delivery layer (HTTP/GRPC/UI); depends on Application (and on Infrastructure only via composition root).
- Contracts: DTOs/schemas shared across boundaries (if needed for integration); packaged for reuse where appropriate.
- Shared/Commons (minimal): Cross-cutting utilities that cannot live in a specific layer (kept small to avoid coupling).
- Tests: Dedicated test projects per production project.

Dependency direction is strictly inward: API/UI -> Application -> Domain; Infrastructure implements ports defined in Application and is wired at composition root. Domain remains dependency-free.

Building and deployment will allow per-project pipelines, enabling targeted builds, tests, and artifact publication. Contracts (and select libraries) may be versioned and distributed as internal packages; other coupling will use project references to simplify development.

Enforce boundaries with static analysis and solution-level conventions (e.g., no Infrastructure references from Application or Domain). Provide a single runnable entry point per deployable (API/UI, workers) that composes Infrastructure at startup.

This structure enables parallel development, clearer code ownership, faster builds via incremental compilation, and safer change management while keeping the system in one cohesive codebase.

## Decision

Adopt Jest as the primary test runner, assertion, and mocking framework, and React Testing Library (RTL) for component testing. Tests will emphasize user-centric behavior and accessibility by querying via role/label/text and simulating interactions through RTL utilities, avoiding implementation details.

- Environment: jsdom. A shared setupTests.ts initializes @testing-library/jest-dom, configures RTL cleanup, and starts/stops MSW for API mocking.
- Test placement: co-locate tests as *.test.ts(x) next to source; integration tests may reside in __tests__ when spanning modules.
- TypeScript: use babel-jest for transpilation for speed; type-checking runs as a separate CI step (tsc --noEmit). Source maps enabled for actionable failures.
- Mocking: prefer MSW for network boundaries; use jest.mock for module boundaries; use modern fake timers where needed. Avoid shallow rendering and Enzyme.
- Snapshots: allowed only for stable, presentational output with strict review; otherwise prefer explicit assertions via jest-dom matchers.
- Coverage: enforce project-wide thresholds (min 80% lines/branches; higher for core utilities). Allow targeted file-level exceptions via per-file overrides with justification.
- Execution: local watch mode enabled; in CI, run jest with --runInBand for flakey suites if needed, otherwise parallelize with a capped --maxWorkers to balance CPU/memory. Generate JUnit and lcov reports; publish coverage to the reporting service.
- Testing strategy: favor fast unit tests and RTL integration tests; delegate end-to-end flows to Playwright/Cypress outside this scope.
- Accessibility: require queries by role and accessible name first; eslint-plugin-testing-library and jest-dom rules enforced in CI.

We will not introduce Enzyme or alternative runners. This standard applies to all new React code; legacy tests will be incrementally migrated during maintenance.

Adopt a standardized, stable error code scheme for all user-visible fatal errors across UI, API, and CLI. Each fatal error will present a concise, non-sensitive message plus a mandatory immutable error code and a per-incident correlation ID. Error codes will be short, human-readable identifiers with category prefixes (e.g., AUTH-1001, IO-2003, SVC-3007). Codes are version-agnostic and never repurposed; any semantic change requires a new code. A central registry will govern code creation, ownership, documentation, and deprecation. For APIs, codes will be included alongside HTTP status and machine-readable details; for CLI, codes will be printed to stderr and mapped to non-zero exit statuses; for UI, codes will appear in error toasts/dialogs with a “Copy details” action.

No sensitive implementation details will be exposed in messages; only the code, correlation ID, timestamp, and safe context will be shown to users. Full diagnostics will be captured in logs/telemetry keyed by correlation ID and error code. Offline/air-gapped contexts will still display the code and correlation ID.

We will provide a public troubleshooting guide mapping codes to causes, remediation steps, and support playbooks. A default fallback code (GEN-0000) will be used if classification fails, with automated alerts to close gaps. Internationalization will localize messages only; codes remain invariant. Backward compatibility will be preserved by maintaining old codes indefinitely and documenting replacements.

Adopt a consistent Git branch naming convention to improve traceability, automation, and collaboration.

Pattern:
- <type>/<issue-key>-<short-kebab-description>

Types:
- feature, bugfix, hotfix, release, chore, docs, refactor, test, spike, poc

Rules:
- All lowercase; kebab-case for descriptions; ASCII letters/digits/hyphens only.
- Single forward slash after type; no additional slashes.
- Include tracker key (e.g., ABC-123). If none, use noissue.
- Description ≤ 50 chars; meaningful, avoid stopwords and PII.
- Examples:
  - feature/ABC-123-user-auth-oauth2
  - bugfix/ABC-456-fix-null-pointer
  - hotfix/ABC-789-critical-cache-leak
  - release/v1.4.0
  - chore/noissue-update-deps

Release and hotfix:
- Release branches: release/v<semver> (e.g., release/v2.1.0).
- Hotfix branches from main: hotfix/<issue-key>-<desc>, merge back to main and the latest release line as applicable.

Merging and lifecycle:
- Prefer squash merges to main; delete branches after merge.
- Do not rebase shared branches; keep up to date by merging main.
- Main and release branches are protected; direct pushes are disallowed.

Scope:
- Applies to all repositories in the organization; enforced via repository branch protection and CI checks on branch name pattern.

We will implement a layered test strategy aligned to the test pyramid, structured into distinct suites with clear ownership and gating: (1) Unit tests validate pure functions and classes in isolation with fast, deterministic execution; (2) Integration tests validate module boundaries and infrastructure adapters against ephemeral, production-like dependencies; (3) Contract tests enforce API and event compatibility between services using consumer-driven contracts; (4) End-to-end tests validate critical user journeys through the system; (5) Non-functional tests (performance, security, accessibility) run on scheduled pipelines.

Test artifacts live near the code under test with consistent naming and folder conventions. Unit tests are mandatory for all new logic; integration and contract tests are required at boundary changes; end-to-end tests cover a minimal, risk-based set of flows. Minimum coverage thresholds: 80% lines/branches at unit level per module, 100% for safety-critical paths. Coverage does not gate integration/e2e suites.

Tests must be deterministic, parallelizable, and hermetic. External dependencies are mocked/stubbed in unit tests and replaced with ephemeral, containerized services in integration tests. Test data uses factories/fixtures; e2e uses seeded datasets. Snapshot tests are limited to stable, low-noise artifacts. Time, randomness, and clock are controlled via fakes or seeds.

CI gates: all suites relevant to a change must pass before merge; flaky tests are quarantined within 24 hours with an owner and SLA; quarantined tests do not block releases but create alerts. Nightly pipelines run full non-functional suites. Any behavior change requires updating corresponding tests and contracts.

## Decision

We will document all significant architectural decisions using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) stored alongside the codebase.

- Repository and location: Maintain ADRs in version control under docs/adr/.
- Format: Use Markdown with the MADR template (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives, References, Date, Authors).
- Naming and numbering: Sequential numeric prefix (e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md); do not renumber after merges—supersede instead.
- Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded. Superseding ADRs must link both ways.
- Scope: Required for decisions that impact architecture, cross-cutting concerns, security, scalability, data model, external contracts, runtime topology, or significant cost/operational posture.
- Creation and timing: Draft ADR before implementing substantial changes; reference the ADR in design docs and PRs.
- Review and governance: ADRs are submitted via pull request and approved by the Architecture Working Group (or designated maintainers). Minor clarifications may be edited; substantive changes require a new ADR that supersedes the prior one.
- Traceability: Each ADR must reference related issues/PRs and affected components; code changes should link back to ADR IDs.
- Discoverability: ADRs are indexed in docs/adr/README.md and published to the project docs site.
- Tooling: Prefer MADR-compatible templates; adr-tools (or equivalent) may be used but is optional.
- Enforcement: CI checks ensure ADR presence for labeled “architecture-impact” changes.

We will adopt smart contract wallets as the primary user account model and support meta-transactions to abstract gas from end users for key workflows. Wallets will be minimal proxy contracts deployed on demand and will expose: EIP-712 signatures, batched transactions, spending limits, session keys, social recovery, and upgradeability via timelocked modules.

Meta-transaction support will follow EIP-2771 with a trusted forwarder contract per network. We will operate a first-party relayer with API auth, rate limiting, and observability, and integrate a third-party relayer provider as failover. Gas sponsorship will be enabled for onboarding, recovery, and defined growth/retention flows; all other transactions can still use meta-tx with user-paid gas or be sent directly from the wallet.

Security controls will include: allowlisted target contracts and function selectors for sponsored calls, per-user and per-period spend limits, per-call gas caps, strict nonce management and replay protection, signature expiry windows, and configurable pausing. Upgrades to wallet and forwarder logic will require multi-party approval and a delay.

Compatibility requirements: EOAs remain supported for read-only access and migration to a smart contract wallet; direct execution paths are preserved for advanced users and integrations. The solution will be deployed on Ethereum mainnet and supported L2s/sidechains with environment-specific forwarders. Operational SLOs, monitoring, and incident response for relayers are in scope.

Adopt Express.js (Express 4.18.x) as the standard HTTP server framework for all Node.js services in this system, running on Node.js LTS 20.x and TypeScript 5.x. All new HTTP APIs must be implemented with Express and existing Node HTTP services will migrate to Express during their next significant refactor. Express 5 will be evaluated and adopted once it reaches stable GA and compatibility is validated.

Implementation directives:
- Project setup: TypeScript with strict mode; tsconfig aligned across services; use tsx for local runs and tsc for builds.
- Structure: Layered architecture (routes → controllers → services → repositories); no business logic in route handlers; reusable middleware in /middleware.
- Routing: Versioned base path (/api/v1); mount modular routers; enable trust proxy when behind load balancers.
- Middleware: helmet for security headers; cors with explicit allowlist; body parsing with size limits (JSON 1MB default); compression enabled selectively; express-rate-limit on public endpoints.
- Validation: zod schemas for params/query/body; central request validator middleware; reject unknown fields.
- Errors: Central error-handling middleware; standardized Problem+JSON (RFC 7807) responses; map domain errors to HTTP codes; include correlation/request IDs.
- Logging/Observability: pino-http for structured logs; OpenTelemetry instrumentation for traces/metrics where supported; prometheus-client for /metrics (protected).
- Docs: OpenAPI via swagger-jsdoc and swagger-ui-express; CI enforces spec validity.
- Testing: Jest + Supertest for unit/integration; contract tests against OpenAPI.
- Performance/Resilience: Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM with in-flight drain; HTTP keep-alive enabled; connection timeouts set; run behind TLS-terminating proxy; horizontal scaling via process manager/container orchestrator.
- Security: Disable x-powered-by; sanitize/escape outputs; dependency scanning in CI; periodic framework updates.

Exceptions to using Express require architecture review approval.

Adopt a version-controlled, forward-only migration strategy for both schema and data changes to enable safe, auditable, and zero/near‑zero downtime releases. All migrations will be stored alongside application code in the monorepo, reviewed via pull requests, and executed automatically by CI/CD as part of deployments. We will use a standard migration runner (e.g., Flyway/Liquibase for relational stores; framework-native change sets or scripted jobs for NoSQL/message stores) with strict ordering, checksums, and environment-aware execution.

Key constraints:
- Forward-compatible, additive-first changes (expand/contract pattern): add new structures/columns/indices and dual‑write/read behind feature flags; remove legacy structures only after verified backfills and read-path cutover.
- No destructive changes in the same release that introduces them; deprecation windows defined per data domain.
- Idempotent, re-runnable scripts with clear pre/post conditions and validation queries; guardrails to fail fast on drift.
- Large data backfills executed as online, chunked, retryable jobs with rate limiting and observability; scheduled outside peak hours.
- Roll-forward as the primary recovery strategy; emergency rollback only via pre-planned compensating migrations.
- Per-migration ownership, naming convention (timestamped, descriptive), and classification (schema vs. data; blocking vs. online).
- Automated smoke tests in ephemeral environments and canary migrations in production with metrics and alerting.
- Cross-store changes coordinated via a migration plan that defines ordering, contracts, and fallbacks to maintain consistency.
- Access control restricts production writes to the migration runner; manual changes are prohibited.

Success is measured by zero failed deploys due to migrations, bounded migration times, no unplanned downtime, and full traceability from commit to production state.

We will use AWS Application Load Balancer target group HTTP(S) health checks against explicit, unauthenticated readiness endpoints exposed by each service at /healthz. Health checks will be configured per target group with the following parameters unless a service-specific override is justified:
- Protocol/port: HTTPS on service listener port (fallback to HTTP only for internal, non-TLS services)
- Path: /healthz
- Success codes (matcher): 200-299
- Interval: 15 seconds
- Timeout: 5 seconds
- Healthy threshold: 2
- Unhealthy threshold: 3
- Deregistration delay: 30 seconds
- Stickiness: unaffected by health check status
- Health check port: traffic port (use override only when service exposes a dedicated health port)
- ECS healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds (if applicable): 60-120 seconds to mask startup transients

Readiness checks will verify only in-process readiness (e.g., app boot complete, critical in-memory caches warmed) and shallow dependencies that are highly available (e.g., connection pool established), but will not depend on downstream, non-critical services to avoid cascading failures. Liveness checks (if exposed separately, e.g., /livez) are not used by ALB and remain for runtime/ orchestrator diagnostics.

Security groups will allow inbound health check traffic from the ALB only; the /healthz endpoint will not require authentication and must not expose sensitive data. Services must return a deterministic 2xx on readiness; any 5xx/timeout will mark the target unhealthy. Blue/green and rolling deployments will rely on ALB health to transition traffic; target deregistration and connection draining must complete before instance/task termination.

Adopt a layered, vendor-agnostic malware scanning strategy for all user-supplied binaries, documents, images, and archives. All uploads are intercepted by an event-driven scanning service that runs in isolated containers with least privilege and no outbound access except to definition/IOC feeds. For high-risk types (executables, scripts, archives) and files ≤50 MB, perform synchronous scanning; for larger files and low-risk types, accept into quarantine storage and scan asynchronously before making content available. Use a pluggable scanner adapter supporting multiple engines: default to ClamAV (signature) plus YARA rules (heuristics) and optional hash reputation lookups; enable configuration to add commercial engines without code changes. Detonations of unknown executables occur in a disposable sandbox where supported.

On detection of malware or policy violations, permanently block the file, record evidence, and notify producers/consumers via webhook and audit logs; on inconclusive results or engine failure, retry with exponential backoff and escalate to manual review after threshold; fail-closed for high-risk types, fail-open-with-warning for low-risk types when all engines are unavailable. Maintain per-tenant policies (allowed types, size limits, sensitivity) and scheduled rescans on definition updates. Store immutable scan manifests (hashes, engine versions, results, timestamps) for audit and downstream enforcement. Automatically update signatures/rules, monitor scanner health, and enforce SLAs (timeouts, concurrency caps).

## Decision
We will remove redundant and unused database indexes across transactional stores to reduce write amplification, storage footprint, and maintenance overhead, without degrading read performance.

Scope:
- All non-clustered/secondary indexes on OLTP databases.
- Excludes primary keys, unique constraints, foreign key-supporting indexes, partitioning keys, and indexes mandated by vendor features or compliance.

Selection criteria (must meet at least one and violate none of the exclusions):
- Zero or negligible usage over a sustained observation window (≥60–90 days) from engine telemetry (e.g., pg_stat_user_indexes, sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats).
- Fully redundant with another index (duplicate definition) or subsumed by a left-prefix, covering, or composite index.
- Demonstrably harmful (high maintenance cost vs. benefit), e.g., high bloat/write cost with no corresponding plan usage.
- Overlapping indexes consolidated into a single, better-designed composite index.

Process:
- Identify candidates via automated telemetry and schema analysis; review with query plans and workload traces.
- Validate in staging with representative load; if needed, introduce improved replacement indexes first.
- Apply changes via versioned migrations (e.g., Flyway/Liquibase) using online/CONCURRENTLY DDL where supported.
- Roll out incrementally per service/environment, one index per release where risk is higher, with real-time monitoring of error rates, p95/p99 latencies, plan regressions, and replication lag.

Rollback:
- Maintain recreate scripts within the same migration set; immediate rollback on detected regressions.

Governance and ownership:
- Data Platform team approves candidate list; service owners sign off per domain.
- Document decisions and rationale per index in the schema catalog.

Success metrics:
- ≥X% reduction in index storage and maintenance time; no statistically significant degradation in read latencies or throughput.

## Decision

We will standardize on contract-first, auto-generated test doubles and a minimal, consistent interaction-verification policy:

- Mocking approach: Prefer interface-based, auto-generated mocks for external/system boundaries and complex collaborators. Use hand-written fakes/stubs only when behavior is non-trivial and stable. Discourage ad-hoc/manual mocks.
- Tools: Adopt one mocking framework per runtime and a single code generation tool per language. Generators run as part of the test/build pipeline; generated code is not committed to VCS. Deterministic generation is enforced via pinned tool versions and config files.
- When to mock: Mock only across architectural boundaries (IO, third-party services, time/uuid, process, network) or for expensive/unstable components. Within a module, prefer real implementations or lightweight fakes to preserve refactorability.
- Assertion strategy: Prefer state-based assertions over interaction verification. Use interaction assertions (verify calls, counts, order) only when the behavior is defined by collaborator interaction (e.g., messaging, retries, idempotence). Keep at most one primary interaction assertion per test.
- Strictness: Use strict mocks by default (unexpected calls fail tests). Explicitly stub all expected interactions with argument matchers; avoid overspecifying order unless required by the contract.
- Test structure: Follow Arrange-Act-Assert. Reset/rehydrate mocks between tests. Avoid partial mocks and spying on concrete classes unless necessary for legacy code.
- Organization: Place mock interfaces/contracts alongside production code; place generators and templates under tooling/config. Generated artifacts go to build/test-only directories. Naming: <Interface>NameMock, Fake<Thing>, Stub<Class>.
- CI: Lint to block manual mocks in prohibited areas, verify no ungenerated mocks exist, and run codegen in CI to ensure reproducibility.

Adopt serverless-offline as the primary local emulation of API Gateway + Lambda for developer workflows. We will use it to run HTTP APIs and Lambda handlers locally with fast feedback and hot reload, without deploying to AWS for routine development.

Scope and constraints:
- Scope: HTTP APIs (REST or HTTP API) and Lambda invocation paths only. Do not rely on serverless-offline to emulate AWS managed services (e.g., SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, S3) beyond basic stubs.
- Complement: Use LocalStack (preferred) or dedicated local emulators (e.g., DynamoDB Local) for AWS services. Integration tests targeting AWS services run against LocalStack or deployed ephemeral environments, not serverless-offline.
- Stages: Enabled only for local and dev stages; disabled for CI/CD, perf, security, and production-like testing.
- Runtime: Node.js 18+ lambdas supported; non-Node runtimes are out of scope for offline.
- Ports and scripts: Standardize npm run dev to launch serverless-offline on fixed ports (e.g., 3000/3001) with watch/hot reload.
- Configuration: Load environment from .env.local; disallow loading production secrets. Enforce CORS and authorizer behavior consistent with deployed configuration where feasible; document known gaps.
- Parity management: Where offline behavior diverges (request/response mapping, authorizers, binary/timeout limits), add contract tests that run against deployed/staging. Critical paths must have at least one deployment-validated test.
- Exit criteria: If drift materially impacts defect rates or developer throughput, reevaluate in favor of LocalStack-only or fully ephemeral preview environments.

## Decision
Adopt a runtime-agnostic, Kubernetes-backed Container API that exposes a stable, RESTful, OpenAPI-defined surface for managing containers and related resources. The API will model higher-level domain concepts and translate them to Kubernetes primitives (Pods, Deployments, Jobs, Services, Ingress, PersistentVolumeClaims, Secrets, ConfigMaps) via controllers and CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs) for App and Task.

Key facets:
- Protocol and schema: HTTPS/JSON with OpenAPI 3.1; explicit resource schemas, validation, and error contracts; pagination, filtering, and sorting for list endpoints.
- Versioning: URI versioning (e.g., /v1). Backward-compatible changes only within a major version; deprecations announced with sunset headers and minimum two-release overlap.
- Operations: Synchronous for fast reads; asynchronous for create/update/delete of workloads, returning an Operation resource with polling and optional server-sent events (SSE). All mutating POST/PUT/PATCH support idempotency keys.
- Events: Outbound domain events published as CloudEvents over webhooks and optional Kafka topic for automation and audit.
- Authn/Authz: OAuth2/OIDC bearer tokens; fine-grained RBAC bound to tenants and namespaces; support for service accounts for automation. Every request is evaluated against namespace-scoped policies to enforce multi-tenancy.
- Resource model: Project, Environment, App (CRD for long-lived workloads), Task (CRD for run-to-completion jobs), Image (OCI reference), Release, Secret, Config, Volume, NetworkPolicy, Operation, Log/Metric query endpoints.
- Runtime and registry: OCI-compliant images and registries (Distribution spec); controller targets Kubernetes (default) and remains portable to other orchestrators via an abstraction layer.
- Reliability: Declarative state with reconciliation; retries with exponential backoff; transactional semantics achieved via idempotency and reconcile loops rather than distributed transactions.
- Observability: Correlation IDs, structured logs, metrics, and traces for all API calls and reconciler actions.
- Backward compatibility: CRD versioning and conversion webhooks to evolve the schema without breaking clients.

This decision avoids a bespoke container API surface, maximizes interoperability with OCI/Kubernetes ecosystems, and provides a stable, secure, multi-tenant abstraction aligned with our domain.

## Decision
The ViewModel will expose a single, immutable UIState object as the sole source of truth via StateFlow (or equivalent), rather than multiple discrete data streams. All UI-relevant data will be represented as fields within UIState, updated atomically through reducer-like intents, ensuring consistency and preventing impossible intermediary states. The UI will observe the entire state and render declaratively, relying on structural equality and distinctUntilChanged to minimize unnecessary recompositions.

One-off effects (navigation, toasts, dialogs) will be emitted through a separate, ephemeral effects channel (e.g., SharedFlow) to avoid polluting persistent UIState. For performance-sensitive subtrees, we may provide memoized selectors/derived flows that map from the single state to specific slices, without introducing additional sources of truth. Large collections or paged data may be modeled as dedicated sub-states or integrated with Paging constructs while remaining referenced from UIState.

State transitions will be driven by intent handlers in the ViewModel, producing a new UIState via pure transformations where feasible, enabling deterministic behavior and snapshot testing. Domain-to-UI mapping occurs once in the ViewModel, with UIState kept serialization-friendly for persistence and process death recovery.

This approach standardizes unidirectional data flow, simplifies reasoning and testing, and reduces UI coupling. Exceptions to whole-state exposure require justification (e.g., extreme performance constraints) and must retain the single-source-of-truth invariant by deriving from UIState rather than creating independent streams.

We will standardize on GNU Make as the primary task runner for all local and CI build tasks across the repository. A top-level Makefile will define canonical, idempotent targets for common workflows: help (default), init, deps, build, test, lint, fmt, coverage, run, clean, dist/package, docker-build, docker-run, and ci. All user-facing targets will be .PHONY and will produce deterministic results when re-run. Make will orchestrate existing toolchains (e.g., language-specific build tools, linters, container tooling) rather than replace them.

We will require GNU Make ≥ 4.3. Linux and macOS use system GNU Make; Windows users run via WSL2 or MSYS2. A thin PowerShell wrapper may be provided for developer ergonomics but is not authoritative. Incremental builds will be modeled with explicit file and directory dependencies where feasible to gain caching benefits; where not feasible, targets remain phony and self-contained.

Make variables will centralize configuration (e.g., BUILD_DIR, VERSION, DOCKER_IMAGE), allow overrides from the environment, and provide sane defaults. Each target will produce concise logs and fail fast with non-zero exit codes. The Makefile will include a help target that documents targets and common parameters.

CI pipelines will call the same Make targets (e.g., make ci, make test) to ensure parity with local development. Complex logic will be kept in scripts under scripts/, which Make invokes, to keep the Makefile readable and maintainable.

Adopt PostgreSQL as the system-of-record relational database for all transactional workloads. Use a managed PostgreSQL offering in the target cloud (e.g., AWS RDS/Aurora PostgreSQL, GCP Cloud SQL, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL), provisioned per environment. Start with one multi-AZ cluster per environment with a single writer and 1–N read replicas; scale vertically first, then horizontally via read replicas and partitioning as needed.

Version: standardize on the latest cloud-supported major release (currently v15+) with minor versions auto-patched in a defined maintenance window.

Topology and tenancy: each product domain/service receives a separate logical database within the shared cluster initially; no cross-database joins; evolve to separate clusters for high-throughput/isolated domains when justified.

Schema and migrations: enforce strong schema with server-side constraints; manage migrations via Flyway (or Liquibase) executed in CI/CD. All timestamps in UTC, database encoding UTF-8.

Connectivity and pooling: require TLS for all connections; prefer IAM/AD-integrated auth where available; use PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode for application connections.

Extensions: enable pgcrypto, uuid-ossp (or use gen_random_uuid), pg_trgm, btree_gin, and pg_stat_statements; enable PostGIS only for services requiring geospatial features.

Resilience and backups: enable automated snapshots and point-in-time recovery with ≥30-day retention; test restores quarterly. Use logical replication for CDC/analytics; no triggers for business logic.

Security: encrypt at rest with cloud KMS-managed keys; manage credentials via Secrets Manager/Key Vault; least-privilege roles per service; row-level security where applicable.

Observability: collect metrics/logs to centralized monitoring (e.g., CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Datadog); enable query sampling and slow query logs; capacity and cost alerts.

Infrastructure: provision via Terraform; parameterize instance class, storage autoscaling, and IOPS; codify maintenance windows and parameter groups.

Adopt Knative Eventing as the eventing control plane and programming model for Kyma. Standardize on CloudEvents 1.0 as the canonical event format. Provide a default Namespaced Broker per workload namespace, with Triggers as the primary subscription and filtering mechanism. Use Knative Sources and custom adapters to onboard external event producers; expose an HTTP ingestion endpoint via the Kyma API Gateway.

Select a pluggable data plane: InMemoryChannel for local/dev profiles; KafkaChannel as the production default for durable, scalable delivery with at-least-once semantics, partition-based ordering within keys, retry with exponential backoff, and dead-letter queues. Configure per-namespace isolation, resource quotas, and label-based multi-tenancy. Enforce transport security via the service mesh (mTLS) and request authentication/authorization via JWT/OIDC and namespace-scoped policies.

Guarantee at-least-once delivery; do not provide exactly-once or global ordering. Support event size and retention limits aligned with the chosen channel backend. Provide out-of-the-box observability using Knative Eventing metrics, traces, and structured logs; surface health and SLO dashboards. Enable DLQ routing and replay for operator-driven remediation.

Deprecate legacy event-bus components; provide a guided migration to Brokers/Triggers and CloudEvents with compatibility shims where feasible. Manage Knative via Kyma modules with version pinning and blue/green upgrades to maintain cluster stability. Keep the backend pluggable to allow future alternatives (for example, NATS, cloud-managed Kafka) without changing the developer-facing model.

We will persist synthesized audio as immutable, content-addressed files in MediaWiki’s standard FileRepo (LocalFileRepo), leveraging the site’s configured backend (local FS/Swift/S3) and CDN. Files will not be stored in the database or an external object store managed outside MediaWiki.

- Storage model: one artifact per unique input variant. The cache key includes normalized source text (or source wikitext rendering), language, voice, engine, engine version, synthesis parameters (rate, pitch, format, sample rate), and extension version. Filename pattern: tts/<lang>/<voice>/<format>/<engine>-<version>/<hash>.<ext>, where <hash> is SHA-256 of the canonicalized key. Files are immutable; new variants produce new files.

- Metadata: a dedicated extension table maps hash to source page/revision, parameters, duration, and engine provenance; minimal metadata also stored in file props for quick lookup. This enables deduplication across pages and auditability.

- Access control: artifacts inherit visibility from the source page. Public pages use the public repo; restricted pages use the private repo. URLs are not guessable but security relies on repo ACLs, not obscurity.

- Lifecycle: generation occurs asynchronously via JobQueue; synchronous fallback is allowed behind a feature flag for small snippets. Reuse occurs on hash hit; regeneration happens when any key element changes. Purge hooks invalidate and optionally requeue synthesis on page edit, deletion, or parameter change. A GC job reference-counts and deletes unreferenced artifacts after a grace period.

- Delivery: served via FileRepo with long-lived cache headers (immutable) and CDN support. Range requests are supported. Quotas and size limits follow site upload configuration, with per-namespace overrides.

This decision maximizes reuse, respects MediaWiki’s storage/security model, and simplifies operations by using existing file infrastructure.

We will adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document significant architectural and cross-cutting technical decisions across all services and components.

- Format: MADR v3.0 in Markdown to ensure consistency and readability.
- Location: /docs/adr in each repository (or in the platform “standards” repo for organization-wide decisions). Filenames: ADR-<NNN>-<kebab-title>.md (e.g., ADR-001-adopting-adrs.md).
- Scope: Decisions with long-term impact, architectural structure, technology choices, data contracts, operational standards, security/privacy, and patterns that affect multiple teams. Minor implementation details are excluded.
- Content: Title, Status (Proposed|Accepted|Rejected|Superseded|Deprecated), Date, Decision Drivers, Considered Options, Decision, Consequences, and References. Authors and reviewers are listed.
- Workflow: New ADRs start as Proposed via the template; discussed via PR/issue; approval by the Architecture Working Group (or designated Tech Leads) results in status Accepted/Rejected. Any change to an Accepted ADR requires a new ADR that references and supersedes the prior one.
- Governance: The Architecture Working Group stewards the ADR process, curates cross-repo decisions, and ensures traceability.
- Tooling: Provide a template and script (e.g., adr-tools) to generate ADR stubs; CI enforces presence of required metadata and unique numbering.
- Visibility: Link the ADR index from README and publish to the internal docs portal.
- Backfill: Create ADRs for critical past decisions as time permits to improve historical traceability.

## Decision

Adopt a 12-factor compliant configuration management approach with clear separation of concerns:
- Non-secret, environment-specific configuration is supplied via environment variables at deploy time.
- Secrets (credentials, tokens, keys) are stored and retrieved from a cloud-managed secrets service backed by KMS; secrets are never committed to source control.
- Service defaults reside in versioned, application-local configuration files (e.g., YAML/JSON) committed to the repository.

Configuration precedence:
1) Environment variables
2) Secret references (resolved at runtime)
3) Application defaults (in-repo)

Operational model:
- Configuration is read at process start; changes require a redeploy to ensure determinism and auditability.
- Feature flags are managed through a dedicated flag service to enable safe, dynamic behavior toggling without redeploys.
- All configuration is strongly typed and validated at startup against a shared schema; invalid configs cause fail-fast with clear diagnostics.
- Each service owns its config schema; shared settings (e.g., observability, networking) are defined in a common module to ensure consistency.

Security and compliance:
- Access to secrets is least-privilege and audited; rotation is supported without code changes.
- Sensitive values are never logged or exposed in metrics.
- CI/CD injects configuration via environment and secret mounts; changes are tracked through version control and deployment metadata.

Portability and observability:
- Local development uses .env files and a developer secrets store; production paths are identical in shape.
- Effective configuration (with secrets redacted) can be exported for troubleshooting.

We will maintain the CSSK as a single authoritative source of truth in a monorepository, consolidating all core libraries, templates, reference implementations, documentation, and tooling. The monorepo will use a modular package structure with clear boundaries (e.g., /core, /adapters, /examples, /docs), enforce compatibility via shared contracts and interfaces, and publish versioned artifacts from a centralized CI/CD pipeline.

Key elements:
- Single repository with mandatory code ownership and review policies to safeguard cross-cutting integrity.
- Semantic versioning at the package level with automated changelog generation and dependency graph awareness; coordinated releases for breaking changes.
- Unified build and test orchestration with hermetic toolchains and reproducible builds; mandatory integration tests across modules before release.
- Standardized contributor workflow (trunk-based with short-lived feature branches) and pre-merge quality gates (lint, type-check, SAST, license/sca).
- One documentation source co-located with code; API docs auto-generated; versioned docs tied to releases.
- Distribution via automated publishing to artifact registries and creation of curated “bundles” for common adoption paths.
- Backwards compatibility policy with deprecation periods and migration guides maintained in-repo.
- Governance model defining module ownership, RFC/ADR process, and exception handling for vendor- or client-specific forks.

This decision prioritizes consistency, discoverability, and coordinated evolution over distributed autonomy, with limited exceptions requiring explicit approval and synchronization back to the monorepo.

## Decision
- Adopt a microservices architecture for core domain services, with clear bounded contexts and independently deployable services.
- Implement services in Kotlin on JVM using Spring Boot for consistency, maturity, and performance; allow Go for high-throughput/low-latency edge cases with prior approval.
- External interfaces: REST over HTTP/1.1 with JSON, documented via OpenAPI 3; long-lived streaming via server-sent events or WebSocket where required.
- Internal service-to-service communication: gRPC with Protocol Buffers; maintain backward-compatible protobuf schemas and API versioning.
- Persistence: PostgreSQL as the primary relational database; Redis for caching, ephemeral data, rate limiting, and distributed locks; Kafka for durable asynchronous messaging and event streaming.
- Data ownership: each service owns its schema; no cross-service DB access; use CDC or Kafka topics for data sharing; schema migrations via Flyway.
- Containerization and orchestration: Docker images deployed to Kubernetes; Helm charts for release management; horizontal pod autoscaling; resource quotas enforced.
- Security: OAuth 2.1 / OIDC for authN via a centralized IdP; JWT access tokens validated at the API gateway and services; mTLS for internal traffic; secrets managed via HashiCorp Vault or Kubernetes Secrets (sealed).
- Networking: API gateway (Kong or Envoy) for routing, rate limiting, auth, and request shaping; optional service mesh (Istio) for traffic policy, mTLS, and observability in multi-team/multi-cluster scenarios.
- Observability: OpenTelemetry instrumentation; metrics via Prometheus; logs to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch; tracing via Jaeger/Tempo; dashboards in Grafana; alerting via Alertmanager.
- CI/CD: trunk-based development; GitHub Actions (or equivalent) pipelines with build, test, security scans (SAST/DAST), container scan, SBOM generation, and progressive delivery (blue/green or canary) using Argo Rollouts or Flagger; IaC via Terraform.
- Quality gates: contract testing (Pact) for APIs; integration tests against ephemeral environments; performance baselines with k6; resilience verified with chaos testing on staging.
- Configuration and feature management: environment-agnostic configs via 12-factor principles; feature flags via LaunchDarkly (or OpenFeature-compliant provider).
- Reliability: idempotent handlers; retries with backoff; circuit breakers and bulkheads (Resilience4j); request timeouts standardized; UTC-only timekeeping.
- Compliance: SBOM and dependency policies enforced; third-party libraries vetted; PII handled per data classification; encryption at rest and in transit mandatory.

## Decision
Establish a synthetic “root tenant” to represent the platform-wide scope in our multi-tenant architecture.

- Purpose and scope:
  - Centralize global configuration, default policies, feature flags, platform roles/permissions, and cross-tenant service principals.
  - Host system-owned resources (e.g., audit sinks, global webhooks, templates, baseline quotas) not attributable to a customer tenant.
  - Serve as the anchor for bootstrap flows (first admin, default RBAC, org provisioning defaults) and cross-tenant reporting/aggregation.

- Identity and visibility:
  - Assign a well-known, immutable ROOT_TENANT_ID.
  - Not listable via tenant discovery APIs; only addressable by privileged platform services.
  - Non-billable, non-deletable, non-transferable; cannot be assumed by end users.

- Access control and isolation:
  - Authorization layer recognizes root-scope operations by tenant_id == ROOT_TENANT_ID with explicit, separate permissions.
  - Root policies are inheritable as defaults but can be overridden per tenant where applicable; no implicit elevation.
