  - No customer PII or tenant-owned data stored under root; only references or aggregated, anonymized metrics when necessary.

- Data and routing:
  - Physically isolated storage partitions/namespaces for root data; separate encryption context and keys.
  - Service routing treats root traffic as a distinct segment for rate limiting, monitoring, and incident blast-radius reduction.

- Governance and safety:
  - Changes to root resources require elevated approvals, MFA, and break-glass procedures with time-bound, audited access.
  - All root mutations are logged to an immutable audit log with heightened alerting.
  - Backups, disaster recovery, and schema migrations treat root as a first-class environment with explicit runbooks.

- Implementation notes:
  - Introduce ROOT_TENANT_ID constant across services; update schemas and indexes to include/allow root scope.
  - Gate UI/CLI endpoints for root behind feature flags; default off in non-platform workspaces.
  - Provide migration scripts to move existing global artifacts into the root tenant and remove ad hoc exceptions.

This decision enables clear separation of platform-level concerns from tenant data, simplifies global feature delivery, and improves security, auditability, and operability without exposing elevated capabilities to end users.

## Decision

Adopt the node-vibrant library as the standard mechanism for extracting color palettes from images across our services. We will use the latest stable node-vibrant release compatible with our Node.js runtime and browsers, pin the exact version, and wrap it behind an internal ColorPalette service interface to isolate third-party dependency details.

The service will produce a normalized palette containing at minimum Vibrant, Muted, DarkVibrant, LightVibrant, DarkMuted, and LightMuted swatches, each exposing RGB, HEX, and population values. We will default to MMCQ quantization with a configurable maximum color count and quality setting, and we will cap input image dimensions to control CPU and memory usage. In browser contexts, we will execute palette extraction off the main thread (Web Worker) and in Node we will parallelize with a bounded worker pool. Results will be cached per image content hash to avoid repeated computation.

Security and compliance: only process images from trusted sources or after sanitization; enforce timeouts and size limits; respect the library’s MIT license and include attribution in third-party notices.

Operationally, we will add lightweight metrics (latency, error rate, palette completeness) and feature flags to enable gradual rollout and safe fallback to a neutral theme when extraction fails. If node-vibrant shows maintenance risk or blocks required capabilities (e.g., WASM quantizers, streaming), we will evaluate alternatives behind the same interface without impacting consumers. Periodic review every 6 months will confirm performance, accuracy, and ecosystem health.

## Decision
Adopt a versioned, declarative configuration model for the Subject Viewer based on JSON documents validated against a JSON Schema, with layered overrides and strict backward compatibility guarantees.

- Represent Subject Viewer behavior (layout, tools, permissions, data sources, feature toggles, accessibility options) in a schema-versioned JSON config (configVersion semver).
- Validate all configurations at build time and at runtime using JSON Schema; unknown fields are rejected in strict mode, logged and ignored in permissive mode per environment setting.
- Implement hierarchical configuration layering with deterministic precedence: base → product → environment → tenant → subject → user/session. Later layers override earlier ones via deep-merge-on-keys; arrays use replace-by-default with optional merge semantics via explicit directives.
- Distribute configs via a centralized Config Service exposing signed, cacheable endpoints with ETag and max-age; clients cache and hot-reload on ETag changes. Local fallbacks are bundled for offline and bootstrap.
- Secure configurations with signing and signature verification; restrict dynamic execution (no embedded code). Only whitelisted URI templates are allowed for remote assets.
- Integrate feature flags by referencing stable flag keys; flag evaluation occurs client-side with server-provided context, with defaults encoded in config to ensure deterministic behavior.
- Maintain backward compatibility within a major configVersion; deprecations are announced one minor ahead and enforced after two minors. A migration tool auto-upgrades configs between schema versions.
- Provide an extension registry for viewer plugins declared in config by capability name and version range, resolved at runtime; unresolvable extensions degrade gracefully.
- Observability: emit configId/configVersion in telemetry; log validation and resolution outcomes for supportability.
- Rollout is progressive via environment and tenant scopes with kill switches at each layer.

Adopt an event-driven, rules-based feedback routing architecture:

- Normalize all feedback into a versioned canonical schema; enrich with metadata (source, product area, user segment, severity, locale, consent).
- Publish feedback as events to a durable message bus; decouple producers from consumers.
- Implement a stateless routing service that evaluates declarative rules from a centralized config store to determine destinations (e.g., team inboxes/queues, issue tracker, analytics lake, support CRM, alerting).
- Support multi-cast routing with priority, rate limiting, deduplication, and idempotency keys.
- Enforce privacy and compliance: automatic PII detection/redaction, regional data residency, consent-aware routing, and retention policies.
- Guarantee delivery semantics: at-least-once with retries and backoff; dead-letter queues for poison messages; replay capability via event retention.
- Provide operational visibility: structured logs, distributed tracing, per-destination metrics (throughput, latency, failure rate), and rule evaluation audit trails.
- Allow dynamic rule changes without redeploy; validate changes via dry-runs and staged rollouts.
- Expose self-serve tooling for rule authoring with linting and tests; maintain version history and approvals.
- Ensure scalability and resilience via horizontal scaling, partitioning/sharding by routing key, and zonal redundancy.
- Define ownership and SLAs per destination integration; isolate failures with circuit breakers and bulkheads.

This decision standardizes feedback flow, enables flexible routing, and supports compliance, observability, and future integrations.

Adopt a modular monolith backend as the initial architecture. Implement domain-aligned modules as independently versioned packages/libraries within a single deployable process. Enforce strict boundaries: no cross-module data access or imports beyond explicitly defined public interfaces; dependencies flow inward (domain) and via adapters (hexagonal/clean architecture). Provide inter-module communication using in-process synchronous interfaces for commands/queries and in-process domain events for notifications. Introduce an event bus abstraction and transactional outbox to enable later promotion of selected events to external messaging with minimal change.

Persist data in a single database, using schema-per-module (or table namespaces) and repository interfaces per module; prohibit cross-module joins and direct table access. Keep transactions module-local where possible; cross-module consistency is achieved via eventual consistency using domain events. Expose a unified external API (HTTP/GraphQL) composed from module controllers, with backward-compatible contract versioning.

Establish guardrails: static analysis to block forbidden imports, architectural tests to enforce dependency rules, CI checks for module boundaries, and clear code ownership per module. Provide shared kernel only for truly cross-cutting concerns (logging, tracing, auth) via stable abstractions.

Prepare for future extraction to microservices by maintaining deployment-agnostic interfaces, isolating side effects behind ports/adapters, keeping modules independently testable, and documenting context maps. When scale, team boundaries, or autonomy needs justify it, extract modules incrementally using the strangler pattern with minimal code changes.

We will use Jenkins as the single integration point to access and manage network path storage for build artifacts, caches, and release bundles. Jenkins controllers and all build agents will mount the approved enterprise network share (SMB/NFS) and expose it to pipelines via standardized environment variables (e.g., ARTIFACT_SHARE, CACHE_SHARE, RELEASE_SHARE) and shared library steps. Pipelines will interact only through these abstractions; no job will reference hard-coded UNC/NFS paths in code repositories.

Access to the network share will be governed by Jenkins Credentials and Credentials Binding with least-privilege service accounts per namespace/project. Secrets will never be stored in source control; rotation is handled centrally. Directory layout is standardized per org/project/job/build with write-once, immutable release locations and time-bounded retention for caches and intermediate artifacts. Audit logging is enabled at the storage layer; Jenkins job metadata (who/when/what) is correlated in a central log.

All static agents must have the share mounted at a consistent path; ephemeral/containerized agents will receive the mount via node templates or sidecar volumes. Pipelines will fail fast if the share is unavailable and will not silently fall back. For agents that cannot mount the share (e.g., SaaS runners), a controlled proxy stage on a mounted agent will perform upload/download.

Encryption at rest is enforced by the storage system; in-transit encryption is required (SMB3/NFS over TLS/VPN). Concurrency-safe file writes are implemented via atomic moves and file locks provided by the platform. Quotas and retention are enforced to prevent unbounded growth. This decision replaces ad hoc direct network access from build scripts with a governed, observable Jenkins-managed pattern.

Adopt a unidirectional data flow. Parent-to-child communication uses typed props; child-to-parent uses callback props. Sibling interactions are handled by lifting state to the nearest common ancestor. Co-locate state with the component that owns it and prefer deriving state over duplicating it.

Use React Context sparingly for stable, low-churn, cross-cutting concerns (e.g., theme, authentication, localization). Avoid using Context as a general global store; split contexts to minimize rerenders.

Standardize Redux Toolkit for shared, high-churn client state that spans distant parts of the tree or requires orchestration (e.g., optimistic updates, undo/redo, complex workflows). Encapsulate store access and mutations in feature-scoped slices and typed selectors. Prohibit ad-hoc event buses or global singletons.

Treat server state separately: use TanStack Query for fetching, caching, synchronization, invalidation, and background refetching. Do not place server state in Redux except for rare integration needs. Represent navigation and shareable view state in the URL via React Router.

Encapsulate communication patterns in reusable, typed custom hooks; expose narrow interfaces to components. Apply React.memo, useCallback, and useMemo selectively; split contexts and components to contain rerenders.

All props, callbacks, and store contracts are typed with TypeScript. Real-time updates (WebSocket/SSE) update server cache via TanStack Query or dispatch RTK actions, with query invalidation where appropriate.

We will use a locally generated RFC 4122 UUID as the Installation ID, specifically UUIDv4 (random) for unpredictability and negligible collision risk. The ID is generated on first launch/installation without network calls, stored persistently in platform-appropriate secure storage (e.g., iOS Keychain with iCloud backup excluded, Android EncryptedSharedPreferences/Keystore with auto-backup disabled, Windows DPAPI-protected store, macOS Keychain, Linux file with OS permissions). It persists across app updates and is removed on uninstall; users and administrators may reset it via an in-app control or documented CLI flag, which triggers regeneration on next launch.

The ID is treated as opaque, non-PII, and never derived from device hardware, user accounts, or environment data. It is transmitted to services only when necessary (e.g., telemetry opt-in, licensing, feature rollout) over TLS and included as a request header or field named Installation-Id. We use the canonical lowercase 36-character hyphenated format; services validate format only and do not rely on sort order. For server-side indexing needs, services may independently store a UUIDv7 derivative alongside, but the client Installation ID remains v4.

The ID is excluded from logs and analytics by default; when correlation is required, only a salted hash is logged. Backups and sync mechanisms must not propagate the ID across devices. Collision handling is best-effort: servers reject improbable duplicates and request client regeneration. Migration from legacy IDs includes a one-time mapping and immediate deprecation of old identifiers.

- Adopt a schema-driven, headless content model with strict separation of content and presentation. All content will be stored as structured types in the CMS and rendered by the frontend via APIs.
- Define core atomic content types: Page, Article, Product, Collection, Person/Author, Asset (media), Taxonomy (Category, Tag), and Block. Blocks are reusable, nestable components (e.g., RichText, ImageGallery, Callout, Hero, FormEmbed) enabling page composition without bespoke templates.
- Use a block-based “Page = Layout + Blocks” paradigm. Content editors assemble pages by ordering blocks; layout controls are constrained to preserve design consistency.
- Standardize common fields across types: title, summary, slug, locale, SEO (title/description/open graph), canonical URL, publish window, status, version, and ownership.
- Relationships are explicit (e.g., Article → Author(s), Product → Collection(s)) with referential integrity and denormalized snapshot fields for resilience (e.g., author name).
- Implement global taxonomies (categories, tags) with hierarchical support and localized labels. Content-to-taxonomy mappings drive navigation, recommendations, and faceted search.
- Implement localization at the field level with locale fallback. Slugs and URLs are locale-aware (/locale/slug). Default locale content is the source of truth.
- Media assets are managed as first-class entities with renditions, focal points, captions, alt text, and usage tracking. Content references assets by ID, not URLs.
- Content versioning and editorial workflow (draft/review/publish) are mandatory; changes are audit-logged. Structured migrations evolve schemas with backward compatibility.
- URL strategy: stable, human-readable, immutable slugs; redirects maintained on slug changes.
- Support lightweight rich text via MDX/portable rich text within RichText blocks, with whitelisted components only.
- Nonbreaking changes to the content model require deprecation windows and migration tooling; breaking changes require RFC and cross-team approval.

## Decision
- Command handlers will return a standardized Result envelope rather than domain entities or view models. The envelope captures:
  - Status: Success, ValidationFailed, NotFound, Conflict, Forbidden, or UnexpectedError.
  - Correlation/CommandId for idempotency tracing.
  - AggregateId and NewVersion (if applicable) on success.
  - Optional Payload with minimal identifiers of created resources (e.g., newly assigned IDs), never rich read models.
  - Errors: list of structured error codes with machine-readable metadata and human-friendly messages.
- Handlers remain the sole place to produce state changes; all user-facing data must be retrieved via queries (CQRS). Command responses are not a data retrieval channel.
- Domain events are persisted and dispatched via the outbox; events are not returned by handlers.
- Concurrency violations yield Conflict with expected vs. actual version metadata; the command performs no partial updates.
- Validation failures are returned as ValidationFailed with all collected violations; no state changes occur.
- Missing aggregates/resources return NotFound; authorization issues return Forbidden; unexpected exceptions are mapped to UnexpectedError without leaking internals.
- Idempotency is enforced per CommandId: duplicate commands return the prior Result (Status, AggregateId, NewVersion, Payload) with Idempotent=true.
- Handlers are synchronous within a transaction boundary for decision and persistence; any long-running work is offloaded to async processes and not awaited by the command path.
- No transport-specific concerns leak into handlers; HTTP/gRPC mapping is done at the edge based on the Result envelope.

## Decision
Adopt react-hook-form (RHF) v7+ as the standard library for all data-editing forms in the React application.

- Scope: All create/update flows, including complex, nested, and dynamic (add/remove) field sets. Exceptions only for non-React surfaces or highly bespoke widgets that cannot interoperate via Controller.

- Rationale: RHF’s uncontrolled-input model minimizes re-renders, improves performance on large forms, and reduces boilerplate. It offers robust form state management (dirty, touched, errors), first-class TypeScript support, and clean integration with schema validators and component libraries.

- Implementation guidelines:
  - Initialize with useForm; derive types from a shared domain schema. Use a resolver (Zod preferred; Yup acceptable where legacy exists) for synchronous validation; complement with server-side validation on submit.
  - For async-loaded data, pass defaultValues when available; otherwise reset(...) after fetch to avoid dirty flag drift. Preserve user edits when refetching by selectively setValue.
  - Use Controller only for controlled or third-party components; prefer native/uncontrolled inputs elsewhere.
  - Model dynamic collections with useFieldArray.
  - Display server validation via setError; map API field paths to form fields consistently.
  - Trigger validation on submit, with onBlur for UX-critical fields.
  - Disable submit while isSubmitting; show progress/state. Reset form on successful submit when appropriate.
  - Compose forms via FormProvider to share context across nested components.
  - Keep field state local to RHF; do not mirror into global stores. Use React Query (or equivalent) for data fetching/mutations; wire onSuccess/onError to form actions.
  - Ensure accessibility with labeled inputs and error messaging.

- Outcome: Standardized, performant, testable, and accessible editing flows with clear patterns for validation, async data, and complex fields.

## Decision
We will standardize ABCI error handling with a deterministic, module-scoped, and machine-readable model to ensure consensus safety, diagnosability, and client interoperability.

- Structured taxonomy:
  - Each module owns a codespace and a reserved uint32 code range.
  - Canonical error constants are defined per module and never reassigned.
  - A common base error type wraps causes and maps to ABCI Code/Codespace with optional details.
- Determinism:
  - All errors emitted from DeliverTx and end-block/begin-block paths must be deterministic across nodes (no timestamps, addresses shortened deterministically, no localized text).
  - Non-deterministic diagnostic content (stack traces, node-specific info) is only allowed in CheckTx.Info or server logs, never in DeliverTx.Log/Info.
- ABCI response mapping:
  - Code and Codespace reflect the canonical error.
  - Log contains a stable, succinct, human-readable message.
  - Data is reserved for protocol-defined binary payloads; not used for free-form text.
  - Events are still emitted for failed txs only when safe and explicitly defined.
- Unknown failures:
  - All unexpected panics or unclassified errors are caught and mapped to a reserved InternalError code with Codespace “core”; the node continues processing.
- Backward compatibility:
  - Existing codes are preserved; deprecated codes remain mapped for at least one major release with telemetry warnings.
- Observability:
  - Emit metrics by codespace/code and count of InternalError occurrences.
  - Optionally include a compact, redaction-safe error fingerprint in Log for correlation.
- Client integration:
  - gRPC/REST translate ABCI errors to structured error envelopes preserving codespace/code and message.
  - SDKs are provided a registry for reverse-lookup and localization on the client side only.
- Governance:
  - A central registry tracks code allocations and changes; additions require review.

We will use React Context to manage low-churn, cross-cutting, app-wide state and configuration, while avoiding it for complex or high-frequency updating data.

Scope:
- Use Context for: authentication/session (current user and tokens), theme, localization (locale/strings), feature flags, and UI preferences.
- Do not use Context for: server cache/state (use React Query), complex domain state or business workflows (use Redux/Zustand/XState as needed), or high-frequency UI state (keep local or use dedicated stores).

Implementation:
- Define narrowly scoped contexts: AuthContext, ThemeContext, I18nContext, FeatureFlagsContext, PreferencesContext. Split contexts to minimize re-renders.
- Expose each via typed custom hooks (useAuth, useTheme, useI18n, etc.). Prohibit direct Context consumption outside hooks.
- Memoize provider values and callbacks; avoid passing mutable objects; prefer stable references and derived selectors.
- For fine-grained subscriptions, consider context selector pattern (e.g., use-context-selector) where necessary.

Composition:
- Place providers at the app root with minimal nesting; group providers in a Providers component for readability and testability.
- Support SSR by ensuring default values and deterministic initialization; defer client-only initialization (e.g., reading localStorage) to effects.

Performance and testing:
- Add lint rules/docs discouraging overuse; include guidance on splitting contexts and measuring re-renders.
- Provide test utilities to render with providers and supply overrides/mocks.

Migration and review:
- Review any proposal to add new contexts via ADRs.
- If usage grows beyond this scope, plan migration to a dedicated state library without breaking public hooks.

We will standardize on platform buildpacks for application packaging and deployment on our primary PaaS, foregoing custom container images for the default path. All new services and most existing services will be built and deployed via supported buildpacks (e.g., Cloud Native Buildpacks on our PaaS), leveraging automated detection, curated runtimes, and opinionated build/deploy workflows.

Scope:
- Applies to web apps, APIs, and workers in languages with first-class buildpack support (e.g., Node.js, Java, Python, Go).
- CI will produce buildpack images or slugs; CD will deploy directly to the PaaS using the native pipeline.
- Operational add-ons (logging, metrics, APM) will use PaaS-native integrations where available.

Exceptions:
- Services requiring OS-level dependencies, custom system packages, nonstandard runtimes, GPU/accelerator access, sidecars, or advanced networking not supported by the PaaS/buildpacks may use container images orchestrated on a managed container service.
- Data plane components and stateful systems remain outside this decision.

Security and compliance:
- Only vendor-maintained or organization-approved buildpacks are permitted.
- SBOMs and provenance from the buildpack pipeline are required artifacts.
- Runtime configs and secrets are managed via PaaS config/secrets stores.

Operational implications:
- Teams relinquish base image maintenance in favor of PaaS-managed runtime patching.
- Build-time customization is limited to buildpack configuration and approved extensions.
- Performance tuning is constrained to PaaS-provided knobs (e.g., instance size, concurrency).

Timeline:
- New services adopt buildpacks immediately.
- Existing containerized services are evaluated and migrated opportunistically; non-qualifying workloads remain on containers with documented justification.

## Decision

We will keep Study as a pure Data Transfer Object (DTO) used solely for data interchange across process and layer boundaries. Study will contain only structural data (fields) with simple accessors, no business logic, side effects, domain invariants, or persistence concerns. It will be immutable where language supports it, and serialization-friendly (e.g., JSON/Protobuf-safe types).

All domain behavior and validation rules will reside in dedicated domain models/services. Semantic validation and invariants are enforced in the domain layer; DTO-level validation is limited to shape/type and basic constraints. Persistence models (if distinct) will not reuse Study; repositories will work with domain entities/aggregates, and explicit mappers will convert between persistence/domain and Study DTOs.

API endpoints, messaging, and external integrations will accept/return Study DTOs (or versioned variants). DTOs may be versioned to maintain backward compatibility; mapping adapters will handle evolution between versions and between DTOs and domain models.

We will maintain explicit mapping functions (manual or via a mapper library) in the application layer; mappers are the only place allowed to translate between Study DTOs and domain constructs. No framework/ORM annotations or transport-specific concerns will be added to Study beyond serialization hints.

This decision preserves a clear separation of concerns, reduces coupling between API contracts and domain/persistence models, and enables safe evolution of the external contract without forcing internal refactors.

Adopt a standardized labeling/naming strategy across all Terraform configurations by mandating the use of a single label module based on Cloud Posse’s terraform-null-label. We will provide and require a thin organizational wrapper module (org/label) that pins a stable minor version (~> 0.27), encodes defaults, and exposes only approved inputs (namespace, environment, stage, name, attributes, tags, tenant, workload, component). The wrapper will enforce: lowercase kebab-case, “-” delimiter, deterministic attribute order, max-length guards with safe truncation + hashes, and consistent tag propagation to all taggable resources.

Decision scope:
- All new Terraform modules and stacks must source org/label for names and tags; direct ad-hoc naming is prohibited.
- Existing modules will migrate incrementally; any resource that would be replaced by name changes requires an explicit migration plan (e.g., create-before-destroy, data migration windows).
- Version updates to org/label follow semantic versioning; breaking changes require ADR and migration guidance.
- Defaults (e.g., namespace, environment) come from a shared context.tf and can be overridden only via approved variables.
- Global and module-specific tags are merged with module tags taking precedence on key conflicts; reserved keys (e.g., Name, CostCenter, Owner, Environment) are controlled centrally.

Governance and enforcement:
- TFLint/OPA policies will flag resources not using org/label outputs or violating reserved tag rules.
- Provider/resource-specific quirks (length/charset) are captured in org/label and tested in CI with golden cases per provider.
- Exceptions require architecture approval and must document risk and rollback.

Outcomes:
- Consistent, predictable resource names and tags across clouds/providers.
- Easier cost allocation, ownership, and environment scoping.
- Reduced drift and copy-paste errors; simpler module reuse and automation.

We will serve all application static assets via a global CDN in front of object storage. Build-time assets (JS, CSS, images, fonts) will be produced by the front-end build pipeline (Vite) with content-hashed filenames for immutable caching. Artifacts will be uploaded to object storage (e.g., S3) under a versioned prefix per release; the CDN (e.g., CloudFront/Fastly) will be the public origin. User-uploaded assets will be stored in a separate bucket/origin with distinct policies and limited cache lifetimes.

Caching and performance:
- Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for hashed assets; shorter (e.g., 5–15m) for user uploads with revalidation.
- Compression: Brotli and Gzip at edge; HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
- Image optimization: use responsive variants and modern formats (WebP/AVIF) generated at build or via an image optimization service.

Integrity and security:
- Subresource Integrity for critical third-party/static JS/CSS.
- Strict Content Security Policy with allowed asset origins.
- SVG sanitization and EXIF stripping for uploads; no inline SVG from users.

Deployment:
- CI/CD uploads assets atomically, then updates release manifest. No CDN invalidations required for hashed assets; fallback invalidations only for HTML or non-hashed files.
- HTML entry points are short-cached and reference the manifest to latest hashed assets.

Local development:
- Dev server serves assets with hot reload; production parity verified via a preview environment using the CDN.

Observability and continuity:
- Enable CDN logs and object access logs; monitor cache hit ratio, error rates, and latency.
- Rollback by switching manifest/version prefix; retain previous versions for a defined TTL.

## Decision

Adopt Tachyons as the primary utility-first CSS framework for all new UI development and for incremental migration of existing styles. Styling will be composed directly in markup using Tachyons utility classes; bespoke CSS will be minimized and reserved for cases not expressible via utilities (e.g., complex animations). We will:

- Install Tachyons via npm and include it in the build pipeline; enable CSS purging (e.g., PurgeCSS) with a safelist for dynamically constructed class names to keep the final bundle minimal.
- Standardize on Tachyons’ spacing, typography, and layout scales; define a thin “design tokens” layer (CSS variables or a small overrides file) mapping brand colors, spacing, and type to Tachyons scales. Where customization is required, extend via a small, project-specific utilities file prefixed with u- to avoid collisions.
- Use Tachyons responsive and state variants (e.g., -ns, -m, -l; hover-, focus-) for adaptive layouts and interactions; avoid authoring custom media queries unless necessary.
- Prefer composition of utilities over component-scoped CSS or BEM; only create component CSS when utility composition becomes unwieldy, and name it with a c- prefix.
- Document usage patterns, class recipes for common components, and accessibility conventions; enforce via lint rules and code review checks to prevent reintroduction of ad-hoc CSS.
- Migrate legacy styles opportunistically: new features use Tachyons exclusively; existing components are refactored when touched.
- Measure and enforce performance budgets on CSS size; gzip and cache static assets.

This decision centralizes styling in a well-documented, composable utility system, improving consistency, velocity, and maintainability while controlling CSS bundle size.

We will adopt AppArmor as the primary Mandatory Access Control (MAC) mechanism on Linux hosts (Ubuntu/Debian) and enforce per-workload least-privilege confinement. For containerized workloads (Docker/containerd), we will use Bane to generate and maintain AppArmor profiles that explicitly declare allowed capabilities, syscalls, file paths, network access, and mount points. All production containers must run with an explicit AppArmor profile (no --privileged; no docker.sock mounts). Profiles will default to deny and allow only what is required by the workload.

Operationalization:
- Profiles are versioned in-repo alongside service code; changes require security review.
- CI will lint profiles (bane verify), validate loading, and run smoke tests in aa-complain before promotion to enforce.
- Staging runs new/modified profiles in complain mode for one release to capture audit events; production runs enforce mode.
- AppArmor audit logs are shipped to the SIEM; recurring denials feed profile updates via a defined SRE/SecOps workflow.

Scope and exceptions:
- Mandatory for all Linux services on AppArmor-capable hosts; systemd units for non-container processes will be bound to profiles.
- Explicit, time-bound exceptions require risk acceptance and compensating controls (e.g., tightened seccomp, read-only FS).
- Hosts without AppArmor support are temporarily permitted to run with hardened seccomp and capability drops; migration to AppArmor is required before production certification.

Reliability and compatibility:
- Pin Bane and profile schema versions; test against supported kernel/container runtime versions.
- Provide a minimal base profile library per language/runtime to reduce drift.
- Blue/green rollout of profile changes to minimize disruption; immediate rollback path via profile reversion and complain mode.

This decision strengthens isolation, reduces blast radius, and standardizes policy-as-code for runtime confinement across our fleet.

We will provide first-class support for deserializing text/plain payloads through a dedicated PlainTextDeserializer integrated into the existing content-negotiation and conversion SPI.

- Registration: Activate when Content-Type is text/plain (default charset UTF-8; honor explicit charset if provided).
- Mapping rules:
  - String and byte[] targets: direct assignment (respecting charset).
  - Single-argument value objects: use public String constructor, static of(String)/from(String)/valueOf(String)/parse(CharSequence), in that order.
  - Primitives/wrappers/BigDecimal/BigInteger/UUID: standard parsers; temporal types use ISO-8601.
  - Enums: match by name; case sensitivity configurable (default case-sensitive).
  - No implicit mapping to complex/nested objects; collections/arrays unsupported unless an explicit converter is registered.
- Whitespace and empties:
  - Default: trim leading/trailing whitespace before parsing.
  - Empty payload ⇒ null by default (configurable to empty string or type-specific default).
  - Configurable option to preserve whitespace.
- Error handling:
  - 415 Unsupported Media Type if text/plain is not declared/allowed.
  - 400 Bad Request on parse failure with consistent error codes/messages; include charset and first N characters for diagnostics (redacted by length limits).
- Limits and streaming:
  - Apply configurable max size; stream to buffer with cap to prevent memory pressure and DoS.
  - Reject control characters outside standard whitespace unless explicitly allowed.
- Configuration:
  - Feature is enabled for endpoints/consumers that declare consumes: text/plain; otherwise opt-in via configuration/annotation.
  - Pluggable converters can extend support for additional types.
- Backward compatibility and docs:
  - No change to existing JSON/XML behavior.
  - Provide clear documentation and examples, including charset, trimming, and error semantics.

## Decision

Introduce a new, versioned set of domain-centric element models within dotcom-rendering (DCR) to replace the legacy, CAPI-shaped element structures. The new models (ElementV2+) will:
- Be strictly typed with discriminated unions to represent each element kind (e.g., Text, Image, RichLink, Interactive, Media, Callout, Ad, Embed).
- Remove implicit/null semantics, using explicit option types and defaults to reduce rendering ambiguity.
- Encapsulate presentation concerns required by DCR (e.g., role, weighting, display hints) while isolating upstream CAPI variability behind a mapping layer.
- Support forward-compatible extension via additive fields and non-breaking union variants, governed by semantic versioning.

A dedicated translation layer will map CAPI (and other sources) to the new models on the server-side before hydration, enforcing validation against a published schema. Both legacy and new models will be supported in parallel behind a feature flag, with per-route opt-in and metrics to monitor correctness and performance. New rendering components will only accept the new models.

We will publish JSON Schemas and TypeScript types for all element variants, along with conformance tests and golden fixtures. Migration will proceed element-by-element with an explicit deprecation schedule for legacy elements once parity is validated in production. This decision aims to stabilize rendering, reduce conditional logic, improve developer ergonomics, and enable safer evolution of element capabilities without coupling to upstream API changes.

We will support direct ingestion of Scratch project.json as a first-class import path, in addition to existing .sb3 uploads. The import pipeline will be refactored to accept either: (a) an .sb3 archive (zip) or (b) a raw project.json payload via file upload, paste, or API request. Internally, both paths will normalize to the same canonical project model.

Key points:
- Add a project.json parser/validator with strict schema validation, size limits, and safe string handling. Reject malformed JSON; surface actionable errors.
- Asset handling: when JSON is provided without embedded assets, we will:
  - Resolve assets by md5ext references against our asset store/CDN if available.
  - Optionally accept an asset manifest mapping to external URLs (config gated).
  - If unresolved, create stubs and mark assets missing, allowing partial import with clear warnings.
- Version detection: support Scratch 2/3+ JSON variants; apply migration transforms as with .sb3 imports.
- API/UX: new “Import project.json” option in UI and corresponding API endpoint with Content-Type application/json; maintain .sb3 backward compatibility with no behavioral change.
- Security and limits: enforce maximum JSON size, depth constraints, and timeouts; disallow remote fetches unless explicitly enabled; audit logging of source/provenance.
- Output parity: downstream features (rendering, analysis, export) remain identical regardless of import path; exporting will still support .sb3 packaging by assembling assets when available.
- Testing/monitoring: add conformance tests for representative JSON samples and metrics on import failures to guide iteration.

## Decision
Adopt GitHub Actions as the standard CI/CD orchestrator for all provisioning workflows, integrating tightly with our Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform) and configuration management. Provisioning will occur exclusively via version-controlled pull requests; direct console or ad-hoc script changes are disallowed and will be deprecated.

Key workflow decisions:
- PR validation: on each change, run terraform fmt, validate, init, and plan; publish plan as an artifact/comment; block merges on failures and policy violations.
- Policy and compliance: enforce OPA/Conftest policy checks and static analysis (tflint, tfsec/checkov) as required checks.
- Environment promotion: use environment-specific workflows (dev → staging → prod) with manual approvals and environment protection rules; apply only from protected branches/tags.
- Credentials and secrets: use OIDC-based federated identity to cloud providers for short-lived, least-privilege credentials; manage non-federated secrets in GitHub Environments/Secrets with tight scoping.
- State management: require remote state backends with locking; enable automated state backup before applies.
- Drift and hygiene: schedule nightly drift detection (plan-only) and alert on deltas; auto-close stale plans.
- Reusability and scale: provide organization-level reusable workflows and composite actions; leverage matrices and caching for multi-module execution; enable concurrency controls and path filters to scope runs.
- Observability and audit: emit structured logs/metrics, persist artifacts (plans, reports), and integrate notifications (Slack/Teams); retain audit trails via required checks and environment approvals.
- Rollback: codify rollback via versioned IaC, state snapshots, and “last-known-good” tags.
- Governance: require code owners and branch protection; changes to CI definitions follow the same PR process.

This decision standardizes, secures, and accelerates provisioning while ensuring traceability, policy enforcement, and repeatability across all environments.

## Decision
Adopt a consistent naming convention that uses the suffix “Helper” for components that provide stateless, cross-cutting utility functions not tied to a specific domain entity, service lifecycle, or infrastructure driver.

- Scope: Applies to classes/modules/functions whose primary responsibility is cohesive, reusable utility logic (e.g., formatting, parsing, mapping, lightweight orchestration without external side effects).
- Non-scope: Do not use “Helper” for domain services, repositories, controllers, handlers, adapters, clients, or any stateful/long-lived component.
- Prohibited alternatives: “Utils,” “Utilities,” “Common,” “Support,” or similar suffixes. Consolidate under “Helper.”
- Structure:
  - Java/Kotlin/C#: ClassNameHelper in a helpers package/namespace.
  - JS/TS: File or module named NameHelper in a helpers folder.
  - Python: name_helper.py in a helpers package.
- Design constraints: Helpers must be stateless, side-effect-free (except explicitly documented pure I/O helpers), dependency-light (no DI required), and expose cohesive, verb-oriented methods.
- Enforcement: Add linting/static analysis and code review checks to flag nonconforming names. Provide templates and examples.
- Migration: Rename existing *Utils/*Utility/*Support artifacts to *Helper. Offer compatibility shims or re-exports only until the next major release, then remove.
- Documentation and tests: Each Helper includes brief usage docs and dedicated unit tests mirroring the Helper name.

We will manage application and infrastructure configuration as code in Git. All non-secret configuration will be stored in version-controlled repositories: either colocated with the service code or in a dedicated configuration repository when shared across services/environments. Configuration will be represented in machine-readable formats (YAML/JSON/HCL) with validated schemas, defaults, and environment-specific overlays (e.g., directory per env, Helm values, or Kustomize). Reusable modules and templates will minimize duplication.

Secrets will not be stored in plaintext. They will be referenced via an external secret manager (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault) or stored encrypted using SOPS with KMS/GPG. CI/CD will have least-privilege read access to decrypt or fetch secrets during deploy; plaintext secrets are prohibited from the repo and commit history.

All configuration changes will follow the same SDLC as code: pull requests, code review, automated validation (lint, schema, policy-as-code), and traceable approvals. Git history forms the audit log; releases will be tagged and rollbacks performed by reverting commits. Branch protection, required reviews, and signed commits will enforce integrity. Ownership, review paths, and change windows will be defined per directory or repo.

Deployments will be driven by Git (GitOps where applicable) so that the live state converges to the desired state from the repository. Promotion across environments will occur via PRs or tag-based automation to ensure parity and controlled drift.

We will migrate existing configurations into the repository incrementally, introducing schemas, tests, and documentation, and replacing ad-hoc runtime edits with PR-based changes. Runtime mutable state is out of scope and will remain in its respective data stores.

We will record all significant architectural decisions as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) stored in the repository under docs/adr as Markdown files. ADRs will be lightweight, one decision per file, numbered sequentially (e.g., ADR-0001), and follow a standard template including: Title, Status (Proposed | Accepted | Rejected | Deprecated | Superseded), Date, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives Considered, Owners, and Links.

Creation and lifecycle:
- ADRs are authored by the proposing engineer(s) at the time of decision discovery, not retroactively.
- All architecture-impacting changes require an ADR referenced in the pull request; inclusion is part of the Definition of Done.
- Review and approval occur via the normal PR process; cross-cutting decisions require Architecture Board approval.
- Supersessions must link both ways (supersedes/superseded-by) to preserve traceability; deprecated decisions remain in history.

Scope and criteria:
- An ADR is required for decisions affecting system qualities (performance, security, reliability), public interfaces, data models, dependencies/technology choices, deployment topology, or cross-team contracts.
- Keep ADRs concise (preferably ≤2 pages) and focused; non-architectural process or minor implementation choices belong in issues or RFCs.

Discoverability and tooling:
- Maintain an index (docs/adr/README.md) and tags (e.g., domain, component) for navigation.
- Use a standard template (e.g., MADR) and optional tooling (adr-tools) with linting in CI.
- Publish ADRs to the internal wiki/portal automatically on merge.

Governance and maintenance:
- Conduct periodic (e.g., quarterly) reviews to validate relevance and update statuses.
- Ensure security/privacy implications and threat models are referenced where applicable.
- Decisions become effective upon “Accepted” status and are versioned with the codebase.

We will adopt GitHub Dependabot to continuously detect and remediate vulnerabilities in third‑party dependencies across all repositories in this organization.

- Scope and ecosystems: Enable Dependabot for security and version updates for npm/yarn/pnpm, Maven/Gradle, Pip/Poetry, Go modules, Dockerfiles, and GitHub Actions. Configure a single .github/dependabot.yml per repo (monorepos included) with directory-specific manifests.
- Update cadence: Security updates daily; version updates weekly. Group updates by ecosystem and severity to reduce PR noise.
- Auto-merge policy: Auto-merge patch/minor updates after green CI and policy checks. Major updates require manual review and sign-off by CODEOWNERS.
- CI and policy gates: All Dependabot PRs must pass tests, SCA, linters, and license checks. Branch protection will require status checks and at least one reviewer for non–auto-merged PRs.
- Credentials: Use GitHub Dependabot secrets to access private registries and internal packages; rotate credentials regularly.
- Alerting and SLAs: Enable repository and org-level Dependabot alerts. Triage critical/high CVEs within 24 hours; medium within one sprint; low as capacity permits. Escalate critical issues via on-call.
- Exceptions and ignores: Configure ignore rules for deprecated/unmaintained packages only when compensating controls exist; document rationale in the PR or security record.
- Ownership and workflow: CODEOWNERS will route PRs to the responsible team. Renovation PR descriptions and release notes must be reviewed for breaking changes and runtime impacts.
- Visibility and metrics: Track open vulnerability counts, time-to-remediate, and auto-merge rates; report monthly.
- Rollback: If an update causes regressions, revert via GitHub and open an issue to apply a pinned version with follow-up actions.

Adopt Amazon Cognito as the managed identity platform for the product. Use Cognito User Pools as the primary user directory and OIDC/OAuth 2.0 authorization server, with optional Identity Pools only when temporary AWS credentials are required for direct access to AWS services.

- Authentication flows: Use hosted UI with OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code + PKCE for public/mobile/web clients; enable SSO with external IdPs (OIDC/SAML) per tenant as needed.
- Authorization: Issue OIDC ID/Access JWTs; define custom scopes via Resource Servers; map User Pool Groups to application roles and, where applicable, to IAM roles via claims.
- Token handling: Access token 15 minutes, ID token 15 minutes, refresh token 30 days; validate JWTs via JWKS in services and API Gateway/Lambda authorizers; rotate keys per Cognito defaults.
- Security: Enforce strong password policy for password-based accounts; enable optional TOTP MFA, with adaptive risk checks via Lambda triggers if required; configure custom domains for TLS and brand consistency; disable client secrets for public clients; use confidential app clients with secrets only for trusted server-to-server flows (client credentials).
- UX and compliance: Use email-first sign-up/sign-in with verified email; support social logins via federated IdPs; implement account recovery via email; minimize PII in profiles; comply with GDPR/CCPA with data export/delete via Admin APIs and triggers.
- Extensibility: Use Pre/Post Authentication, Pre Token Generation, and Custom Message Lambda triggers for custom claims, attribute validation, and policy enforcement.
- Operations: Provision via IaC (Terraform/CloudFormation), isolate per environment with distinct User Pools and domains, monitor via CloudWatch metrics/alarms, and document runbooks for incident response and user migration.
- Migration: For existing users, use staged migration with “Define Auth Challenge”/“Pre Auth” triggers to import on first login or bulk import where feasible.

## Decision
We will centralize ownership of Address readiness in the Prober package. The Prober is the single writer of readiness state for Address entities, responsible for performing liveness/health checks, computing readiness, and updating the authoritative readiness status. All other packages (e.g., discovery, routing, reconciliation, controllers, and APIs) must treat readiness as read-only and must not directly set or mutate it.

- The Prober exposes an interface to:
  - Request (re)probe of one or more Addresses.
  - Subscribe to readiness change events.
  - Query current readiness.
- The Prober maintains the readiness state machine, including retries, backoff, timeouts, hysteresis/debounce, and failure thresholds. Readiness decisions are idempotent and thread-safe.
- The Prober is the exclusive updater of the Address.status.ready field (or equivalent), enforcing a single-writer invariant to eliminate races and split-brain conditions.
- Configuration of probe parameters (timeouts, intervals, thresholds) is sourced only from the Prober’s config; other components cannot override runtime probe behavior.
- Observability (metrics, logs, trace spans) for probe outcomes is emitted by the Prober; other components consume these signals but do not infer or set readiness independently.
- Persistence semantics (e.g., optimistic concurrency/CAS on status updates) are implemented by the Prober to ensure consistency.
- Existing code paths that set readiness outside the Prober will be deprecated and removed, replaced with calls to the Prober interface.

## Decision

We will adopt User Stories as the primary unit of work for capturing, prioritizing, and delivering product functionality.

- Structure: Each story will follow the template “As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit].”
- Acceptance Criteria: Mandatory, expressed in clear, testable terms using Given-When-Then examples. Where appropriate, use executable specifications (Gherkin) tied to automated tests.
- Sizing: Estimate relatively using Fibonacci story points (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13). Stories larger than 8 points must be split before commitment.
- Splitting: Apply standard patterns (e.g., workflow step, data slice, happy path first, defer edge cases, CRUD split) to maintain vertical slices delivering user-visible value.
- Readiness: A story is “Ready” when it has clear value, defined acceptance criteria, identified dependencies, testability, and is small enough to complete within a sprint/iteration.
- Done: A story is “Done” when acceptance criteria pass, code is peer-reviewed, integrated, covered by automated tests, security and accessibility checks are completed, documentation is updated, and deployed to the agreed environment.
- Backlog Management: Maintain a single prioritized backlog with periodic refinement; use story mapping to visualize scope and release slices.
- Non-Functional Needs: Capture cross-cutting quality attributes as acceptance criteria within relevant stories; create technical stories only when vertical slicing is not feasible.
- Workflow: Track stories through a defined lifecycle (e.g., Backlog → Ready → In Progress → In Review/Test → Done) with WIP limits to preserve flow.
- Traceability: Link stories to epics, design artifacts, tests, and releases to ensure end-to-end visibility.

## Decision

We will provision a net-new Salesforce Sales Cloud production org dedicated to CRM, separate from any existing Salesforce orgs, to serve as the single source of truth for accounts, contacts, leads, opportunities, activities, and related sales processes. This greenfield org avoids legacy technical debt, enables a clean data model and governance, and supports a configuration-first approach with minimal custom code.

Scope and operating model:
- Adopt Salesforce standard objects and features wherever possible; custom objects/automation only when clear gaps exist.
- Install only vetted managed packages; avoid unmanaged third-party code.
- Establish a single production org with Dev, QA/UAT, and Full sandboxes; implement CI/CD pipelines and version control for metadata.

Security and access:
- Enforce SSO with corporate IdP, MFA, role hierarchy, profiles/permission sets, FLS, and audit logging. Use Shield (encryption, event monitoring) if required by compliance.
- Apply least-privilege and data residency policies aligned to GDPR/CCPA.

Data and migration:
- Migrate cleansed, deduplicated current data (accounts, contacts, open opportunities/cases); archive deep history off-platform with governed access.
- Define canonical data model and stewardship; implement ongoing data quality rules.

Integrations:
- Use standard REST/Bulk APIs and event-driven patterns (Platform Events/Change Data Capture) via the corporate iPaaS (e.g., MuleSoft); prohibit point-to-point custom integrations.
- Establish mastership rules and SLAs for upstream/downstream systems.

Licensing and adoption:
- License Sales Cloud Enterprise (and Service Cloud if needed); use Platform licenses for light users.
- Provide role-based training, enablement, and change management; define KPIs (adoption, data quality, pipeline hygiene).

Governance and delivery:
- Create a CRM governance board for backlog, standards, and release management (monthly releases, emergency hotfixes).
- Sunset the legacy CRM on a staged timeline with dual-run only as necessary and a defined rollback plan limited to cutover window.

We will colocate all component-specific styles with their components to ensure tight cohesion, ease of maintenance, and safer refactoring.

- For React components, use CSS Modules with SCSS: ComponentName.module.scss placed alongside ComponentName.tsx in the same folder.
- Class names remain local by default; no global selectors within component styles.
- Use design tokens (colors, spacing, typography) via CSS variables and shared SCSS maps imported from the design-system package; do not hardcode brand values in component styles.
- Prefer composition over inheritance: use CSS Modules’ composes or SCSS @use for shared patterns; avoid cross-component style imports.
- Theming uses CSS variables set on :root and theme-[name] scope elements; components read variables only.
- Global styles are limited to:
  - CSS reset/normalize, base typography, and root layout primitives.
  - @font-face declarations.
  - Third-party overrides isolated in a dedicated global-overrides.scss.
- Co-locate style-only assets (SVGs used as backgrounds, component-specific icons) within the component folder.
- Naming: export class names in camelCase from modules; avoid BEM since scoping is provided by modules.
- Storybook examples must use the same colocated styles.
- Linting/CI will enforce no global leakage and disallow importing module styles across component boundaries, except for approved shared primitives.
- Migration of legacy global styles will be incremental, moving rules into the owning component folders.

We will adopt Jasmine as the primary unit testing framework for all JavaScript/TypeScript units in this codebase. Tests will be written in Jasmine’s BDD style (describe/it) with built-in matchers and spies for mocking/stubbing. For Node-executed tests, we will use jasmine-npm as the runner; for browser-based components (if applicable), we will run Jasmine via Karma. Code coverage will be collected with Istanbul/nyc (or karma-coverage), with minimum thresholds enforced in CI.

Scope:
- Mandatory for unit tests across frontend and backend JS/TS modules.
- End-to-end and performance testing are out of scope and will use dedicated tools.
- Snapshot testing will not be used; approvals or explicit assertions will be preferred.

Standards and conventions:
- Test files colocated with source as *.spec.ts|js.
- AAA (Arrange-Act-Assert) structure, one behavior per test.
- Deterministic tests only; no network/real time dependencies—use spies/fakes.
- Coverage thresholds: lines/branches/functions/statements ≥ 85% (subject to revision).

Tooling and integration:
- TypeScript support via ts-node/tsconfig paths or pre-compilation.
- CI pipeline runs Jasmine suites in parallel where feasible; fail build on test/coverage failure.
- Reporters: spec (console) and JUnit/XML for CI.

Migration:
- Existing unit tests in other frameworks will be incrementally ported; sinon/chai usage will be replaced by Jasmine spies/matchers where practical.

Revisit criteria:
- If requirements emerge for features poorly served by Jasmine (e.g., extensive snapshot testing or advanced watch-mode ergonomics), we will reassess the framework choice.

We will make creation of Route53 resources optional and controlled via configuration. A top-level flag (e.g., dns.manageRoute53 = true|false) will determine behavior per environment/workspace.

- When dns.manageRoute53 = true:
  - Provision Route53 resources required by the workload (hosted zone if absent, and DNS records such as A/AAAA/ALIAS/CNAME/TXT for validation).
  - Support both public and private zones via dns.zoneType and optional vpc associations for private zones.
  - Optionally manage ACM DNS validation records when certificates are issued by the stack.

- When dns.manageRoute53 = false:
  - Do not create or modify any Route53 zones or records.
  - Require inputs for externally managed DNS, such as existing hosted zone ID or domain name, and publish desired record data as outputs to be applied outside this stack.
  - Support a hybrid mode to create records in an existing hosted zone (no zone creation) via dns.existingZoneId.

Defaults:
- Default to dns.manageRoute53 = false to avoid unintended DNS changes, enabling explicit opt-in.
- Enforce validations preventing simultaneous zone creation when an existingZoneId is provided.

Outputs and contracts:
- Expose canonical DNS names, record targets, and validation values regardless of mode.
- Maintain idempotency and import capabilities for preexisting records/zones when toggled on.

Operations and security:
- Restrict Route53 IAM permissions to be conditional on the flag.
- Tag all created DNS resources consistently and include TTL/alias policies.
- Provide environment-specific configuration allowing dev/test to enable management while prod can remain externally managed.

This decision ensures safe, configurable DNS management without coupling deployments to Route53 where not desired.

We will enforce automated, programmatic formatting across the codebase using language-native formatters and a uniform workflow:

- Adopt canonical formatters per language: e.g., Prettier (JS/TS/JSON/Markdown/YAML), Black (Python), gofmt/goimports (Go), rustfmt (Rust), dotnet format (C#), and shfmt/shellcheck-fix (Shell). Where no canonical tool exists, use EditorConfig + lint autofix.
- Centralize configuration in the repository (.prettierrc, pyproject.toml, .editorconfig, etc.) to ensure deterministic, version-pinned formatting across all environments.
- Integrate formatting into developer workflow via pre-commit hooks (pre-commit framework), with local auto-fix on staged files and fast failure on unfixable issues.
- Enforce formatting in CI: run format check on all changed files and fail the pipeline on diffs; provide an automated “format” job artifact or bot commit for convenience on protected branches.
- Exclude generated, vendored, and migration artifact directories via .gitignore and formatter ignore files; store formatter include/exclude rules in the repo.
- Provide one-time migration: repository-wide formatting commit, followed by enabling checks to keep history readable and minimize noisy diffs.
- Document formatter usage and commands (make format, make check-format) and provide IDE/editor integrations via checked-in settings to reduce friction.
- Treat formatting as non-negotiable; code reviews should not discuss style. Exceptions require an ADR or documented ignore with justification and minimal scope.

We will implement a layered, schema-driven validation strategy with a single source of truth and fail-fast enforcement:

- Single source of truth: Define request/response contracts using OpenAPI with JSON Schema. Generate validators and typings for clients and services to eliminate duplication.
- Boundary validation: Validate all external inputs at service edges (API gateways, message consumers) using the generated schema. Reject invalid payloads with structured error responses; do not execute business logic on invalid input.
- Domain validation: Enforce domain invariants in the domain layer using explicit, composable validators (e.g., FluentValidation for .NET or equivalent). Domain rules are authoritative and cannot be bypassed by boundary validation.
- Error reporting: Return deterministic, localized, field-level error objects with codes, human-readable messages, and paths; include all non-dependent field errors in one response. Use localization keys for i18n.
- Cross-field and async checks: Support cross-field rules within validators. Perform async/external validations (e.g., existence/uniqueness) via dedicated services; cache-safe where possible. Async checks do not block schema validation but must succeed before command execution.
- Client-side validation: Mirror schema and basic rules on the client (e.g., Zod/Yup) for UX, but server remains source of truth. Keep client rules generated or derived from the shared schema.
- Security: Treat validation as part of input sanitization; enforce strict typing, size limits, canonicalization, and allowlists. Strip unknown fields by default; optionally enable permissive mode for backward compatibility.
- Observability: Emit structured metrics (validation failures by rule/code) and logs with correlation IDs; create alerts on spikes.
- Performance: Precompile validators and reuse; short-circuit on fatal errors; cap error counts per request.
- Versioning and evolution: Version schemas; support tolerant readers during transitions. Validation rules that tighten constraints require explicit version bumps and migration plans.

Adopt distributed tracing via OpenTelemetry across all services and do not expose a public “tracing” API for span ingestion. Instead:
- Instrument services with OpenTelemetry SDKs, propagate context using W3C Trace Context (traceparent/tracestate) and baggage, and export spans to the OpenTelemetry Collector via OTLP/gRPC.
- Add a trace-id response header (e.g., X-Trace-Id mirroring the current root span id) on all API responses to aid user support and cross-correlation in logs.
- Provide a non-production, authenticated, and IP-allowlisted debug endpoint at /_trace that returns the current request’s trace identifiers and sampled status for troubleshooting. This endpoint is disabled by default in production and can be temporarily enabled via a feature flag with time-bounded access.
- Enforce server-side sampling: default 5% baseline probability sampling with rules-based upsampling for error/latency outliers and downsampling for high-throughput low-value paths; sampling policies centrally managed in the collector.
- Redact or avoid capturing sensitive fields (PII/PCI/PHI) via attribute filters in SDKs/collector processors; cap event/attribute sizes and drop bodies by default except on explicitly whitelisted endpoints.
- Secure all telemetry transport with TLS; no tracing data is accepted from external clients. Retain spans per compliance policy (e.g., 7–30 days) in the backend (Jaeger/Tempo/Elastic APM) managed by SRE.
- Document header usage and trace correlation in the API guide; provide runbooks and dashboards for trace health. This decision balances observability needs with security, performance, and privacy.

## Decision
Adopt a managed external search service as the system-of-record for application search, selecting Algolia as the initial provider for product and content search across web and mobile. We will not self-host Elasticsearch/OpenSearch at this time.

- Scope: All end-user search experiences (global search, category search, autocomplete, faceting). Back-office admin search remains in the primary database.
- Integration: Implement an internal Search Adapter interface to abstract provider SDKs. The initial adapter targets Algolia; we will maintain a provider-agnostic index schema and export/import tooling to enable future migration to Elastic Cloud/OpenSearch Serverless if required.
- Indexing: Use an event-driven pipeline (outbox + queue + worker) to push incremental updates on create/update/delete. Nightly full reindex jobs ensure consistency. Only whitelisted, non-sensitive fields are indexed; identifiers are opaque IDs, with selective hashing for join keys.
- Relevance: Manage synonyms, ranking, and facets via provider configuration and versioned rules. A/B test relevance settings behind feature flags.
- Performance and resilience: Set strict client timeouts (e.g., 500–800 ms), retries with backoff, and a circuit breaker. Provide graceful degradation: cached last-known-good results for popular queries and local filtering for small result sets. Autocomplete falls back to local suggestions when unavailable.
- Security and privacy: Use per-environment API keys with least privilege, secured via server-side proxy; short-lived, signed search tokens for authenticated contexts. Enforce data residency by selecting regional indices and disabling logging of query bodies where required.
- Observability: Emit SLIs (availability, p95 latency, error rate), index lag, and quota utilization. Alert on budget burn, throttle events, and indexing failures. Track search analytics to guide relevance tuning and cost optimization.
- Cost control: Apply rate limiting, cache hot queries, segment indices to minimize record/operation counts, and archive stale records. Review pricing monthly and adjust index design accordingly.
- Rollout: Phased enablement via feature flags per surface area; dual-run with baseline search for validation; cutover after SLOs are met.
- Review: Reassess build-vs-buy each 12 months or if costs exceed threshold or SLOs are unmet for two consecutive quarters.

Adopt a lightweight, deterministic HTML5 parser for tests instead of the production parser/engine. Specifically, we will use Cheerio (backed by parse5) for all unit and integration tests that need HTML parsing, querying, or serialization. The production runtime remains unchanged (browser DOM/Nokogiri/serving layer as applicable). We will introduce a thin test-only abstraction (DOMTestAPI) that wraps common operations (querySelector/querySelectorAll via CSS selectors, attribute/text retrieval, normalization, and serialization) to avoid coupling tests to parser-specific behavior.

Parser configuration in tests will be standardized: HTML5 mode, entity decoding enabled, void-element handling per spec, consistent whitespace normalization, and lowercasing of tag/attribute names where applicable. Test helpers and fixtures will be updated to normalize HTML before assertions (trim, collapse whitespace where needed) to reduce brittle diffs.

A small cross-compatibility sanity suite will parse a representative set of fixtures with both the production parser and Cheerio to detect material differences in semantics; if differences appear, adjust the test abstraction or fixtures rather than asserting on parser quirks. New tests must rely on DOMTestAPI and must not assert on serialization details that are parser-dependent (e.g., attribute ordering).

Rollout will switch existing tests incrementally via the abstraction, starting with parsing-heavy suites. If unforeseen incompatibilities arise, we can temporarily fall back to JSDOM/production parser per suite behind a feature flag. This change aims to improve determinism, performance, and maintainability of HTML-related tests without affecting production behavior.

## Decision

Store all ETL outputs in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (ADLS Gen2) using Delta Lake as the default table format. Data will be organized into medallion zones (bronze/raw, silver/cleansed, gold/curated) within separate containers per environment (dev/test/prod) and per domain. Tables will be partitioned by ingestion/processing date (yyyy=MM/dd) and additional high-cardinality business keys where beneficial. Small to medium dimension-like outputs may be additionally materialized to Azure SQL Database/Synapse Serverless views for consumption; ADLS remains the system of record.

Access will be enforced via Azure AD RBAC with least-privilege roles, managed identities for compute (Databricks/Synapse/Data Factory), and Private Endpoints with storage firewalls enabled. Data is encrypted at rest with Microsoft-managed keys (with support for CMK if required) and in transit via HTTPS. Soft delete and versioning (via Delta Lake time travel) will be enabled to support reproducibility and rollback.

Lifecycle management policies will transition bronze to cool/archival tiers per retention requirements; silver and gold will retain hot storage for active windows, then down-tier. RA-GRS redundancy will be used for production; lower environments use LRS to control cost. Schema enforcement and evolution will be managed through Delta constraints and table properties; data contracts define allowed changes.

Operational practices include: naming conventions, metadata cataloging in Purview, automated compaction/Optimize and vacuum schedules, and cost governance with budget alerts. This decision standardizes on open, scalable, and analytics-optimized storage while enabling secure, governed, and cost-effective access for downstream consumers.

Adopt PostCSS as the primary CSS transformation layer in the build pipeline across all web frontends. All stylesheets (including framework- or library-generated CSS) will flow through a centralized postcss.config.js, with a shared Browserslist to define target environments.

Standard plugin baseline:
- postcss-import for modular CSS composition
- postcss-nesting to enable native-like nesting
- autoprefixer to ensure cross-browser compatibility
- cssnano (production only) for minification
- postcss-custom-media and postcss-custom-properties for design tokens and responsive primitives
- postcss-calc to normalize calc() expressions

Integration:
- Wire PostCSS into the existing bundler (e.g., Vite/Webpack) and Storybook.
- Enable source maps in development; disable in production.
- Enforce configuration via a shared package to ensure consistency across repositories.

Scope and coexistence:
- PostCSS is the required baseline; utility frameworks (e.g., Tailwind) and CSS-in-JS may coexist if they output standard CSS compatible with this pipeline.
- Preprocessors (e.g., Sass) are allowed only where necessary; their output must also pass through PostCSS. New features should prefer PostCSS capabilities over preprocessor-specific ones.

Operational decisions:
- CI will validate PostCSS configuration and run stylelint with PostCSS syntax.
- Production builds must pass PostCSS processing to ship.
- Version pinning for plugins and scheduled updates to track CSS spec evolution.

This decision standardizes CSS processing, improves portability and performance, and centralizes control of cross-browser behavior.

## Decision
Adopt a demand-driven, priority-aware capacity assignment mechanism for cells using a min-max fairness objective with hard constraints, implemented via integer linear programming (ILP) with a deterministic greedy fallback.

- Objective: Maximize minimum satisfaction ratio across cells (served_capacity / demanded_capacity), then secondarily maximize total served capacity, enforcing priority tiers and reservation quotas.
- Inputs: Near-real-time telemetry, short-term demand forecasts, policy constraints (per-cell hard caps, backhaul limits, spectrum blocks), and tenant priorities/SLAs.
- Constraints: Per-cell physical capacity, inter-cell interference budgets, regional/regulatory caps, reserved capacity for emergency/critical services, and maintenance blackouts.
- Priority handling: Weighted fairness by tier; critical/emergency traffic preemptively reserved; enterprise/tenant quotas enforced with ceilings and floors; burst credits allowed within safety margins.
- Algorithm: Solve ILP every 15 minutes (or on significant topology/risk events). If solver times out or data is incomplete, use a deterministic greedy heuristic that:
  1) Satisfies hard reservations,
  2) Distributes remaining capacity by weighted water-filling until caps reached,
  3) Applies local smoothing to reduce oscillations.
- Stability: Apply hysteresis and minimum hold times; cap per-interval reallocation deltas; simulate changes in a shadow environment before promotion in high-risk regions.
- Interfaces: Expose decisions via a versioned API and publish to the orchestration plane; all decisions are auditable with inputs, solver metadata, and diffs.
- Rollout: Progressive regional rollout with guardrails and automated rollback on KPI regressions.
- Non-goals: Long-horizon planning and spectrum re-farming; those remain with offline planning tools.

## Decision
We will eliminate “invalid address” faults caused by unterminated control flow by requiring explicit program termination and by hardening runtime bounds checks.

- Introduce an explicit EXIT/HALT instruction that must be reachable on all control-flow paths. The assembler/linter will statically validate that every function/program has at least one terminating instruction and that all branches converge to a terminator or a well-defined tail call.
- Treat fall-through past the last instruction as an implicit HALT only for backward compatibility in the current minor release; emit a warning during assembly/validation. In the next major release, remove implicit HALT and treat missing EXIT as a build-time error.
- Add VM/interpreter program counter (PC) bounds checks on each fetch/decode cycle. On PC == code_length, return a structured HALT status; on PC > code_length or any misaligned/invalid target, raise a defined TRAP with an error code (e.g., VM_ERR_INVALID_PC) instead of dereferencing an invalid address.
- Enforce target validity on indirect/direct jumps and returns: verify target is within [0, code_length) and to a valid instruction boundary; reject otherwise at load-time when possible, and at runtime as a trap when dynamic.
- Update toolchain: assembler enforces EXIT presence; optimizer preserves terminators; verifier performs control-flow graph (CFG) reachability and termination checks.
- Provide migration guidance and tests to ensure no production path relies on implicit termination; log metrics on traps to detect residual violations.

## Decision
All Katas in this repository must conform to a single, canonical formatting standard as described herein to ensure consistency, discoverability, and automation support.

- Required sections (in order) in a single Markdown file per Kata: Title, Overview, Problem Statement, Constraints/Assumptions, Input/Output Specification, Examples (incl. edge cases), Provided Artifacts/Starter Code, Evaluation Criteria, Hints (optional), Extensions/Follow-ups (optional), References.
- Mandatory front matter (YAML) at top of file: id, title, version (semver), status (draft/active/deprecated), difficulty (beginner/intermediate/advanced), estimated_time, tags, primary_language(s), required_prerequisites, author(s), reviewer(s), created_at, last_updated, license.
- File and directory conventions:
  - One directory per Kata: katas/<kebab-case-id>/
  - Primary spec file: README.md (with required front matter and sections).
  - Assets under katas/<id>/assets/, starter code under katas/<id>/starter/<lang>/, solutions under katas/<id>/solutions/<lang>/ (solutions optional and gated).
  - Test fixtures under katas/<id>/tests/<lang>/ with instructions in README.md.
- Content rules:
  - Use Markdown; code blocks fenced and language-tagged; avoid inline HTML.
  - Deterministic I/O specs; avoid ambiguous phrasing; define error handling.
  - Examples must match I/O spec and include at least one edge case.
  - Diagrams as images in assets with alt text; link relatively.
  - Keep line length ≤ 120 chars; use US English.
- Validation and tooling:
  - Front matter validated against JSON Schema; CI enforces schema, section order, and broken links.
  - Pre-commit hook provided to lint Markdown and front matter.
  - A template (templates/kata-template.md) must be used for all new Katas.
- Versioning and lifecycle:
  - Changes follow semver in front matter; breaking spec changes require MAJOR bump and migration notes.
  - Deprecations must state replacement and end-of-support date.
- Governance:
  - PRs must include checklist confirming conformity; non-compliant Katas cannot be merged.

## Decision
Adopt a single Git monorepo for all deployable applications, backend services, shared libraries, infrastructure, and tooling. Manage JavaScript/TypeScript workspaces with pnpm and orchestrate builds/tests/linting with Turborepo (with remote caching enabled in CI). Use Changesets for independent package versioning and automated release notes. Enforce ownership with CODEOWNERS and per-folder reviewers.

Directory layout:
- apps/: End-user deployables (e.g., web, mobile, api-gateway). No cross-imports between apps; depend only on packages/libs.
- services/: Backend services (e.g., billing, auth). Same dependency rules as apps.
- packages/: Shared libraries (UI components, domain modules, SDKs, utilities). Published as versioned packages.
- libs/: Internal-only shared code not published externally (e.g., internal tooling, feature flags).
- infra/: Infrastructure-as-code (terraform/, helm/, k8s/, env overlays). Service-specific manifests live under infra/<service>.
- tools/: Repo-wide scripts, code generators, custom CLIs.
- configs/: Centralized configurations (eslint, prettier, tsconfig base, jest/vitest base).
- docs/: Architecture docs, ADRs, runbooks.
- .github/ or ci/: CI/CD workflows, reusable actions, pipeline templates.

Conventions and policies:
- Each project has its own README and package.json/Makefile with scripts that delegate to root configurations.
- Strict module boundaries enforced via tooling (TypeScript project references, eslint-plugin-boundaries, import path rules).
