- Third-party dependencies are declared in leaf packages; apps/services depend on packages/libs, not each other.
- API contracts and schemas live in packages/contracts; services consume them to avoid drift.
- Environment-specific configuration uses twelve-factor principles; secrets managed outside the repo.
- CI uses affected-graph execution (only build/test what changed), type-checks at project level, and caches artifacts.
- Code generation outputs are checked in only when necessary and isolated under generated/ with lint ignore.
- Release flow: Changesets drives version bumps and changelogs; publishing is automated per package.
- Branch protection and review rules enforced at folder granularity; test coverage thresholds per project.

This structure prioritizes clear boundaries, high cache reuse, fast incremental builds, and scalable ownership while enabling shared code reuse and consistent governance across the portfolio.

## Decision

Adopt TypeScript as the primary language across the stack to ensure type safety, shared domain models, and consistent developer experience.

- Web framework: Next.js 14 (App Router) with React 18 as the primary web application framework.
  - Rendering strategy: Prefer Server Components and SSR for dynamic routes; use SSG/ISR for content that benefits from caching; enable Edge runtime where latency matters.
  - Styling/UI: Tailwind CSS for utility-first styling; Radix UI (headless) for accessible primitives; component tokens centralized in a design system package.
  - State/data fetching: React Query for server state; minimal global client state via Zustand when needed; React Hook Form for forms.
  - Routing/i18n: Next.js built-in routing and internationalization.

- Backend/API: Node.js 20 LTS with NestJS.
  - API style: REST-first with versioned routes; OpenAPI/Swagger for contract; consider GraphQL for aggregate/query-heavy use cases later if justified.
  - Validation/serialization: class-validator/class-transformer at boundaries; Zod for shared schemas where appropriate.
  - Persistence: PostgreSQL (v15+) using Prisma ORM; migrations via Prisma Migrate; connection pooling via PgBouncer.
  - Caching: Redis for session/cache/invalidation patterns.
  - Authentication/authorization: OIDC/OAuth2 using NextAuth on the web side with JWT sessions and rotating refresh tokens; RBAC enforced in NestJS guards.
  - Observability: Structured logging (pino), metrics (OpenTelemetry/OTLP), tracing propagated through both Next.js and NestJS.

- Packaging and delivery: Docker images for both web and API; CI/CD pipelines produce SBOMs, run tests, and sign images. Deploy on a Node-compatible platform (Kubernetes or Vercel/Render/Fly); use CDN for static assets. Environment config via Twelve-Factor principles and runtime env validation.

- Quality: Unit tests (Vitest/Jest), integration tests (Supertest), and E2E (Playwright). Linting/formatting with ESLint/Prettier; commit hooks enforce standards.

This decision standardizes on a modern, type-safe, JavaScript/TypeScript stack that supports hybrid rendering, strong DX, scalability, and clear contracts while allowing future evolution (e.g., GraphQL) without replatforming.

Adopt CSS-in-JS as the default styling approach for new UI components in React, using Emotion (runtime with Babel preset for extraction) to enable co-located, type-safe, themeable styles with deterministic class names and SSR support. Continue to support existing global styles and utility classes; legacy SCSS and design tokens will be progressively migrated into an Emotion theme and design-token package.

Enable SSR style extraction and critical CSS for first paint, and configure the build to use the Babel Emotion plugin for dead code elimination, label injection, and minification. Standardize on the ThemeProvider for color, spacing, and typography tokens; enforce usage via ESLint rules and a stylelint setup. Restrict dynamic styles to props that materially impact UX and avoid generating styles inside hot render paths; prefer variants/polymorphic components over ad-hoc inline conditionals. For large data grids, animations, or print styling where runtime cost or specificity is a concern, prefer static CSS (CSS Modules) as an exception.

Provide Storybook theming, visual regression tests, and a codemod path for migrating styled-components where encountered. Document patterns for responsive styles, dark mode, and RTL via theme tokens. Establish performance budgets (no more than 5% render time attributable to styling) and include a CI check to fail on Emotion SSR regressions. This decision will be revisited if platform targets expand beyond React web or if runtime overhead becomes a sustained bottleneck.

Adopt incremental, event-driven popularity updates with eventual consistency. Popularity-affecting events (e.g., view, like, add-to-cart, purchase, share) will be emitted to a durable stream and consumed by stateless processors that update per-entity aggregates in near real time. We will compute a configurable, time-decayed, weighted popularity score from multiple rolling windows (e.g., 1h, 24h, 7d) maintained as additive counters. For unique-user signals, we will use approximate distinct structures (e.g., HLL) when needed.

The serving layer will read from a fast store (e.g., Redis) holding hot-window aggregates; periodic compaction writes consolidated snapshots to a durable store (e.g., Postgres/BigQuery) for cold queries and recovery. Consumers will be idempotent via event IDs and deduplication; offsets/checkpoints enable replay. In case of sustained backlog or drift, a nightly batch job will reconcile by recomputing scores from source-of-truth events and correcting aggregates.

Configuration (signal weights, decay half-lives, window definitions) will be externally managed and hot-reloadable. SLO: 99th percentile propagation under 60 seconds; correctness within 1% of batch reconciliation for top-N entities. On failures, we degrade to last persisted snapshot. Access controls ensure only aggregated, non-PII data is stored in the fast path. Telemetry (lag, error rate, skew vs. batch) and alerts are mandatory.

Adopt Cypress as the primary framework for browser-based integration and end-to-end testing of the web application. Cypress will be used to validate user flows across the UI and backend, including authentication, navigation, input/validation, and critical business workflows. Unit tests remain in the existing test frameworks; API/contract tests continue in their designated tooling.

Implement Cypress e2e tests under cypress/e2e, using data-test attributes for resilient selectors. Prefer test isolation with deterministic test data via seed/reset hooks or dedicated test fixtures; avoid cross-test state. Use network stubbing only when external dependencies are unstable or non-deterministic; prefer hitting real services in non-prod environments for high-fidelity coverage.

Run Cypress in headless mode in CI with parallelization and retries enabled to reduce flakiness. Enforce a PR-time smoke suite; execute the full regression suite on merge to main and on nightly schedules. Persist screenshots, videos, and junit reports as CI artifacts. Fail builds on regressions.

Target Chrome-family and Firefox browsers supported by Cypress; use Cypress viewport emulation for common device sizes (not a substitute for native mobile testing). Where Cypress has limitations (e.g., multi-tab/window, file downloads, certain browser APIs), complement coverage with lower-level tests.

Guardrails: no secrets in test code; stable, unique test data; timeouts tuned to app SLA. Engineering owns tests adjacent to their features; QA curates cross-cutting scenarios and maintains testing standards.

We will replace legacy, generic PIMS redirects with canonical deep links from search results to the specific PIMS entity detail pages. Links will be generated using a centralized URL builder that maps record type to path templates (e.g., /properties/{pid}, /leases/{id}, /projects/{id}) and supports optional tab/section anchors. The PIMS base URL will be environment-configured (dev/test/prod) via application configuration, not hardcoded.

All PIMS links will open in a new tab/window (target=_blank with rel=noopener noreferrer) to avoid disrupting the user’s search workflow. Where supported by PIMS, we will append a returnUrl parameter encoding the current search route and filters to enable a seamless “Back to results” experience within PIMS or the browser. We will include standardized analytics parameters (e.g., utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign) for click tracking.

Before rendering a link, the UI will validate that the record contains the identifiers required by the corresponding PIMS route; otherwise, the link will be disabled with an explanatory tooltip. For entities without a known deep link, we will fall back to the nearest valid parent route or omit the link.

Backward compatibility will be maintained by keeping the existing redirect endpoint for one release cycle, returning HTTP 301 to the new deep link patterns. Feature rollout will be gated behind a feature flag to allow incremental verification and rollback.

Security and privacy will be preserved by not embedding sensitive data in query strings and by relying on existing SSO/SSO-initiated login flows; unauthenticated users will be redirected by PIMS as usual. All links will be tested across environments, and automated tests will verify URL construction, presence of required identifiers, and analytics emission.

We will standardize a canonical, human-readable, and machine-friendly URL schema:

- Protocol and host: Enforce HTTPS; redirect HTTP→HTTPS (301).
- Case and characters: Lowercase only; words separated by hyphens; UTF-8 with percent-encoding of unsafe characters. No spaces or underscores.
- Trailing slashes: No trailing slash for resources; enforce canonical form via 301 redirects (/path/ → /path).
- File extensions: Omit (content negotiated by Accept headers or inferred).
- Resource structure (API): RESTful plural nouns and shallow nesting (max depth 1): /v1/users, /v1/users/{user_id}, /v1/users/{user_id}/orders. Use path parameters for identity; query parameters for filter/sort/pagination.
- Versioning (API): Major version in path (/v1); minor/patch backward-compatible and not reflected in the path.
- Identifiers: Stable opaque IDs (UUIDv7) in APIs; SEO slugs for public web pages with collision-safe suffixes (e.g., /blog/my-article and /blog/my-article--a1b2).
- Pagination and filtering (API): ?page=, ?per_page=, ?sort=field[, -field], filter as explicit keys (?status=active&created_after=2025-01-01T00:00:00Z). Timestamps ISO 8601 UTC (Z).
- Localization (web): Optional locale prefix /{locale}/path (e.g., /en/products). API URLs are not localized.
- Multi-tenancy: Tenant isolation via subdomain ({tenant}.example.com) with a canonical tenant identifier; optional /t/{tenant} fallback for non-DNS contexts.
- Assets and downloads: Static assets under /assets/... served via CDN; signed, time-limited URLs for private downloads under /downloads/.
- Canonicalization and redirects: Single canonical URL per resource; permanent redirects for moved content; preserve query strings on redirects.
- Reserved words and collisions: Maintain a denylist for top-level segments; validate slug uniqueness case-insensitively.
- Backward compatibility: Provide redirect maps for legacy URLs during migrations and deprecate old versions with scheduled sunset headers.

We will implement the new product pages using Next.js 14 (App Router) with React and TypeScript to achieve a performant, SEO-friendly, and maintainable solution.

- Rendering strategy:
  - Default to static generation with incremental static regeneration (ISR) for product detail and listing pages with stable content.
  - Use server-side rendering (SSR) for personalized/pricing-sensitive or rapidly changing sections.
  - Enable Edge runtime for latency-sensitive geolocated content when feasible.

- Component model:
  - Prefer React Server Components for data-heavy, non-interactive sections.
  - Use Client Components only where interactivity is required (e.g., configurators, add-to-cart).
  - Adopt an islands/partial hydration approach to minimize client JavaScript.

- Data access:
  - Fetch via server components from existing backend APIs (REST/GraphQL) with caching controls aligned to ISR/SSR needs.
  - No direct CMS coupling in the UI layer; integrate via API abstraction.

- Internationalization and accessibility:
  - Implement i18n with localized routes and domain/locale negotiation (e.g., next-intl).
  - Enforce WCAG AA compliance and semantic HTML; include structured data for SEO.

- Styling and design system:
  - Use Tailwind CSS with our component library; co-locate styles with components; enforce design tokens.

- Performance and SEO:
  - Use next/image, route segment-level metadata, and performance budgets (LCP, CLS, TTI).
  - Canonical URLs, hreflang, and Open Graph/Twitter metadata.

- Build, testing, and deployment:
  - TypeScript strict mode; linting and formatting enforced.
  - Unit (Jest), component (React Testing Library), and e2e (Playwright) tests required.
  - Vendor-agnostic deployment on Node 18+; compatible with Vercel or containerized Kubernetes.

- Migration:
  - Preserve existing URLs where possible; otherwise provide 301 redirects and telemetry to monitor impact.

We will standardize all tracking responsibilities on the CoreTracker service and the CoreTrackable interface, deprecating the LegacyTrackable interface effective immediately. No new code may reference LegacyTrackable. Existing implementations must be migrated by implementing CoreTrackable directly or by using a temporary adapter. For interoperability during the transition, we will provide:
- LegacyToCoreTrackableAdapter to wrap LegacyTrackable implementations where immediate refactoring is not feasible.
- CoreToLegacyTrackableAdapter only where external dependencies still require LegacyTrackable (to be minimized and removed).

Dependency injection bindings will be updated to resolve CoreTracker as the default tracker in all services. Any modules exposing LegacyTrackable will register the adapter until they are refactored. Public APIs will preferentially expose CoreTrackable; if backward compatibility is required, dual signatures may be offered for one minor version.

We will introduce a build-time lint rule and CI check to block new usages of LegacyTrackable. Telemetry and audit trails will be routed through CoreTracker, with parity tests ensuring behavior equivalence to LegacyTrackable in critical paths. Performance baselines will be captured before and after migration; regressions >2% in hot paths must be addressed prior to removal.

Deprecation timeline:
- Current release: deprecate LegacyTrackable, ship adapters, update docs and examples.
- +1 minor release: remove dual signatures; adapters remain.
- +2 minor releases: remove adapters and LegacyTrackable types.

Roll-back plan: retain feature flag to switch selected modules back to LegacyTrackable for one minor release if critical defects are found. Ownership for migration is assigned to each domain team; architectural sign-off required before removing adapters.

Proceed with splitting the current combined system into two independently deployable products: (1) Audit Tool and (2) Content Performance Manager (CPM). Each product will own its domain, codebase, and database. Cross-domain data sharing will occur via published domain events and read-only queries through versioned APIs; no direct database access across products is allowed.

Authentication and authorization will be centralized via the existing IdP, with shared SSO and product-scoped roles/permissions. Shared UI components will be extracted into a design system library; any remaining shared logic becomes a separately versioned SDK to avoid tight coupling.

Deployment pipelines, scaling policies, and on-call rotations will be separate. Observability (logs, metrics, traces) will use consistent conventions and correlation IDs across both products. Feature flags will control any cross-cutting release dependencies.

Migration will be incremental:
- Freeze net-new cross-domain features in the monolith.
- Extract CPM first (content metrics, dashboards, reporting), then Audit Tool (checks, evidence collection, remediation).
- Introduce anti-corruption layers and strangle references until all direct calls are replaced with API/event integrations.
- Maintain a compatibility façade for legacy clients for one release cycle, then deprecate.

Data ownership: CPM owns performance metrics, content taxonomy, and reporting aggregates; Audit Tool owns audit definitions, runs, findings, and remediation status. Shared identifiers (content IDs) will be standardized via a canonical registry.

Non-functional targets: independent releases, <30 min rollback, P95 API latency unchanged, and no loss of audit history or performance metrics during cutover.

We will migrate all third‑party and backend API calls from the client (browser/mobile) to the server, establishing the backend as the single integration layer (Backend‑for‑Frontend pattern). The server will own authentication, authorization, request signing, secrets handling, rate limiting, input validation, schema normalization, response shaping, caching, retries, and circuit breaking. Client applications will interact only with first‑party endpoints exposed by the server. For web, pages that benefit from SEO or protected data will use SSR/ISR where applicable; purely interactive components will fetch from our server APIs. Real‑time features will use server‑mediated WebSockets/SSE as needed.

Implementation scope and rules:
- Introduce a BFF service per client surface or a unified gateway with client‑aware routes.
- Replace client SDK usage of third‑party APIs with server adapters; deprecate and remove direct calls.
- Centralize auth (OAuth/OIDC/JWT) and token exchange on the server; remove secrets from clients.
- Add server‑side caching (in‑memory + Redis) and request deduplication; enforce idempotency where possible.
- Standardize error contracts and pagination; implement observability (structured logs, traces, metrics).
- Harden egress with allowlists, timeouts, and exponential backoff; add WAF and input sanitization.
- Update CORS to allow only our domains to our server; block cross‑origin calls to third‑party APIs.
- Provide feature‑flagged, incremental rollout with dual‑write/dual‑read where necessary; maintain backward compatibility during transition and publish client SDK updates.
- Establish SLIs/SLOs for the new server endpoints and capacity plan accordingly.

We will forbid the use of HTML meta tags that trigger reloads or client-side redirects across the product surface. Specifically, we will strip and/or block <meta http-equiv="refresh"> (including timed reloads and URL-based redirects) and any non-standard/legacy “location” meta directives in all first-party templates and all user-supplied HTML content. All redirects must be implemented via HTTP 3xx responses (server-side) or via our client router/navigation API in controlled code paths. All periodic data refresh requirements must be implemented via application-level polling, server-sent events, or WebSockets; full-page reloads, if absolutely necessary, must be invoked explicitly in code, not via meta tags. Sanitization pipelines will actively remove these meta tags, and CI/static checks will fail builds containing them. Exception requests (e.g., constrained kiosk/dashboards) require security and accessibility review, product sign-off, a feature flag, and must document the user impact (focus/assistive tech, SEO) and recovery behavior. CSP and HTML sanitization rules will be updated to enforce this decision. This ensures predictable navigation, improves accessibility and UX, avoids SEO penalties, prevents open-redirect and clickjacking vectors, and centralizes navigation logic.

## Decision

We will separate type definitions from executable functions across the codebase to enforce clear boundaries, reduce coupling, and enable safer evolution.

- Create a dedicated, dependency-free types module that contains only data shapes (e.g., interfaces, DTOs, domain entities as immutable records) and serialization contracts. Types must not include behavior, I/O, or framework references.
- Place all business logic and reusable operations in function modules (use-cases/services), expressed as pure functions where possible. Functions may depend on the types module but types must not depend on functions.
- Isolate side effects (I/O, persistence, messaging, frameworks) in adapter modules. Adapters depend on types and may invoke functions; functions must not depend on adapters.
- Prefer composition over methods on data structures; validation, mapping, and transformation are implemented as functions. If runtime schemas are needed, colocate schema artifacts with types but keep generation and validation logic in functions/adapters.
- Establish package boundaries and import rules (e.g., lint/ABI checks) to prevent circular dependencies and enforce one-way dependencies: adapters → functions → types.
- Use a single source of truth for external contracts (e.g., OpenAPI/Proto/JSON Schema) to generate types. Code generation outputs only types; any generated helpers reside outside the types module.
- Manage change via semantic versioning of the types module; prefer additive, backward-compatible changes. Breaking changes require coordinated function and adapter updates.
- Testing: contract tests assert conformance to types; function tests operate on in-memory types; integration tests cover adapters.
- Document naming conventions, directory layout, and review gates to ensure ongoing adherence.

Adopt a centralized Identity Provider (IdP) to provide common authentication for all internal and customer-facing applications. The IdP must support OpenID Connect (OIDC) and OAuth 2.1, with SAML available for legacy integrations.

- Single Sign-On (SSO) and MFA are mandatory across all applications, with conditional access policies as needed.
- Flows:
  - Web apps: Authorization Code with PKCE via a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) where feasible; otherwise secure same-site cookies.
  - SPAs/mobile: Authorization Code with PKCE.
  - Server-to-server: Client Credentials.
  - Legacy: SAML 2.0 where OIDC is not yet possible.
- Tokens:
  - Use short-lived JWT access tokens (≤15 minutes) with asymmetric signing (kid rotation) and audience scoping.
  - Use opaque, rotating refresh tokens with sender-constrained binding (DPoP/MTLS where supported).
  - Enforce strict scopes and least privilege; include standard OIDC claims.
- Session management:
  - Centralized logout via IdP; propagate logout to relying parties.
  - Support step-up authentication for sensitive actions.
- Authorization integration:
  - Applications consume identity via OIDC and enforce authorization locally using RBAC/ABAC from IdP-managed roles/attributes.
  - Externalize fine-grained authorization where appropriate (e.g., policy engine), but authentication remains centralized.
- Provisioning and lifecycle:
  - Integrate user and group provisioning/deprovisioning via SCIM 2.0.
  - Synchronize with corporate directories/HRIS as sources of truth.
- Security and compliance:
  - Enforce MFA (TOTP/WebAuthn/passkeys preferred), passwordless where supported.
  - Implement anomaly detection, account lockout, and risk-based controls.
  - Maintain audit logs for auth events; align with applicable compliance requirements.
- API enforcement:
  - Validate tokens at API gateway and services; prefer gateway offload with defense-in-depth validation in services.
  - Forward identity context via standard headers only after successful verification.
- Developer experience:
  - Provide SDKs/config templates, environment-isolated tenants, and automated client registration.
- Migration:
  - Wrap legacy apps via gateway or SAML bridge; phase out embedded credentials.
  - Sunset bespoke auth mechanisms and centralize configurations in the IdP.

We will use Amazon DynamoDB as the primary persistence and event source to model realistic AWS Lambda usage patterns. Concretely:
- Provision per-environment DynamoDB tables (dev/test/stage/prod) with on-demand capacity, point-in-time recovery enabled, and TTL for automatic data cleanup of ephemeral records.
- Use DynamoDB Streams (NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES) to trigger downstream Lambdas for event-driven workflows (e.g., projections, notifications, CQRS-style read models), with retries and DLQ/SNS for poison-pill handling.
- Adopt a pragmatic single-table design for the demo domain to illustrate access patterns, conditional writes, and transaction APIs (TransactWrite/TransactGet) where appropriate; document partition/sort keys and GSIs to demonstrate query patterns.
- Implement strict IAM least-privilege policies per Lambda, scoped to table and stream ARNs; enforce idempotency with conditional expressions and deduplication keys.
- Use AWS CDK/SAM for infrastructure as code, integrating table, stream, event source mappings, alarms, and dashboards (consumed RCUs/WCUs, throttles, stream iterator age, Lambda errors/durations).
- Support local development with DynamoDB Local and seed scripts; provide synthetic data generators to simulate realistic workloads and contention.
- Apply server-side encryption with AWS-managed KMS keys by default; enable PITR backups and lifecycle policies for cost control; add cost guardrails (CloudWatch/Cost Anomaly alerts).
- Prefer on-demand capacity initially; if sustained traffic patterns emerge, evaluate provisioned capacity with auto scaling.
- Exclude relational features from this scope; RDS/Aurora will not be used for these Lambda use cases.
- Success is measured by demonstrable event-driven patterns, operational visibility, cost predictability, and ease of reproducing real-world Lambda interactions end-to-end.

- Accept metadata payloads that include unrecognized fields without rejecting the request.
- Treat unrecognized fields as opaque: do not affect core behavior, authorization, or business logic unless explicitly whitelisted in a released schema.
- Preserve unrecognized fields end-to-end (create/update → storage → read APIs → emitted events) to enable round-tripping and forward compatibility, except where blocked by policy.
- Enforce guardrails: total metadata size limits, depth limits, and JSON-serializable primitive types only; reject executable content and disallowed types; reserve and block system-controlled field names/prefixes from client use.
- Apply schema versioning with tolerant parsing: known fields validated strictly; unknown fields allowed across versions. Introduce new behaviors only after explicit promotion of a field to “recognized.”
- Security and privacy controls apply uniformly: run unknown fields through PII redaction, secret scanning, and content filtering pipelines; exclude preserved unknown fields from indexing/search unless explicitly allowed.
- Observability: collect metrics and sampled logs on unknown-field occurrence and size; emit warnings (not errors) to clients when feasible; provide admin tooling to inspect and purge unknown fields if needed.
- Compatibility: maintain round-trip fidelity for clients that depend on preserving extra fields; provide migration hooks to backfill or drop fields when they become recognized or deprecated.
- Feature flags/governance: support per-tenant or environment switches to disable acceptance/preservation if required by compliance; maintain an allow/deny list for field names.

## Decision

We will remove PostgreSQL as a runtime dependency across all environments and adopt a temporary lightweight persistence strategy, while preserving a clear path to reintroduce PostgreSQL.

- Introduce a storage abstraction (Repository/DAO or ORM-agnostic ports) and provide a default SQLite provider for dev, test, and current production needs that fit our scale and concurrency profile. Keep the PostgreSQL provider in the codebase but disabled behind a feature flag.
- Decommission PostgreSQL infrastructure from IaC, docker-compose, and CI pipelines (migrations, health checks), retaining modules/config stubs disabled for rapid reactivation.
- Freeze and snapshot existing PostgreSQL data; export required operational subsets to seed SQLite where applicable. Archive full snapshots to object storage for retention/compliance and analytical access.
- Update configuration to select storage via environment variable and feature flag; default to SQLite. Disable Postgres-specific extensions, migrations, and connection pools.
- Adjust observability to reflect the new storage backend and update SLOs that were tied to Postgres availability/latency.
- Document functional and non-functional limitations of SQLite (concurrency, locking, extensions) and gate high-write or complex transactional features until PostgreSQL (or another scalable store) is reinstated.
- Provide a rollback path: maintain schema definitions and migration scripts for PostgreSQL, keep connection parameters in secrets management, and validate a blue/green reintroduce-Postgres procedure in staging.
- Reassess within one quarter with explicit triggers (data size, write throughput, concurrency, feature needs) to decide on reintroducing PostgreSQL or selecting an alternative managed datastore.

We will implement a unified, language-agnostic Generator API that accepts both OpenAPI v3.1 and OData v4 (CSDL/metadata) inputs, normalizes them to a single intermediate representation, and produces consistent outputs (SDKs, server stubs, typed models, clients, and reference docs). OpenAPI will be the primary interchange format; OData inputs will be transformed to OpenAPI via a standards-aligned mapping, after which the same pipeline is used. For OData and OpenAPI parity and cross-language SDK quality, we will adopt Kiota as the primary code generator, supplemented by OpenAPI Generator for ecosystems not covered.

Key decisions:
- API shape: asynchronous job model with idempotent submissions keyed by content hash; presigned artifact retrieval; deterministic builds for cacheability.
- Inputs: OpenAPI v3.1 JSON/YAML; OData CSDL (XML/JSON) and $metadata URLs. Optional overlays for auth, servers, tags, and naming.
- Outputs: clients (at GA: TypeScript, C#, Java); optional server stubs (Node/ASP.NET initially); Markdown/HTML reference docs.
- Validation: strict schema and rule validation with configurable lints; fail-fast on breaking issues, warnings otherwise.
- Feature scope: OData v4 core, query options, pagination, enums, inheritance; defer complex functions/actions binding, containment, and batch until phase 2.
- Versioning: semantic versioning of the generator; reproducible outputs via pinned toolchain container images.
- Extensibility: plugin hooks pre/post-IR and pre/post-emission; stable IR contracts.
- Security/limits: size/time quotas, spec fetching with allowlists, redaction of secrets, SBOM for generated artifacts.
- Observability: structured logs, job tracing, artifact provenance (spec hash, tool versions).

Risks are mitigated by converging on OpenAPI as the normalized path, leveraging Kiota for OData fidelity, strict validation, and deterministic builds with caching.

## Decision

Adopt Azure Table Storage as the primary persistence layer for non-relational, high-volume, key-value entities that require scalable, cost-effective storage with simple query patterns. Use it for operational workloads that can be modeled around PartitionKey/RowKey without cross-entity joins or complex transactions.

- Data modeling: Design entities with explicit PartitionKey/RowKey to support the top read/write patterns; avoid hotspots via synthetic partitioning where needed.
- Access and SDK: Use Azure.Data.Tables with Managed Identity and role-based access; enforce optimistic concurrency via ETags; use upsert semantics where appropriate.
- Indexing: For secondary lookups, maintain denormalized “index tables” updated within the same write operation; accept eventual consistency for derived indexes.
- Limits and fit: Respect 1 MB per entity, no server-side joins, and no cross-partition transactions; for scenarios requiring aggregations/analytics, replicate to a downstream store (e.g., Azure Synapse/ADLS) via periodic export.
- Reliability and DR: Use GRS with read-access where required; enable soft-delete/versioning at the account level; implement periodic backups/exports and tested restore procedures.
- Security: Enforce private endpoints, VNet integration, CMK where mandated, and encryption at rest; audit with Azure Monitor/Activity Logs.
- Observability: Emit request metrics, latency, throttling, and retries; set SLO-aligned alerts.
- Lifecycle: Define TTL via scheduled cleanup; implement schema evolution via additive changes and backfills.
- Cost governance: Monitor capacity, transactions, and egress; shard keys to balance throughput and minimize hot partitions.
- Exceptions: Use Cosmos DB or relational storage for workloads needing rich queries, multi-item transactions, or strict consistency across partitions.

Adopt continuous deployment for platform Cloud Foundry (CF) applications via a GitOps-driven pipeline that promotes immutable artifacts across environments with zero-downtime releases. Source-of-truth is the application repository containing code, CF manifests, and environment overlays (vars files) per org/space/foundation. Commits to main trigger the pipeline to build and sign an artifact, run unit/integration/security tests, and, on success, deploy automatically to non-prod and to production after policy gates. Deployments use CF rolling or blue-green strategies with route mapping to ensure zero downtime; canary is achieved by weighted routes or controlled instance scaling. Rollbacks are executed by reinstating the previously signed artifact and switching routes.

Pipelines are implemented in Concourse or GitHub Actions using CF CLI/API, with multi-foundation promotion (dev -> stage -> prod) from the same artifact, not rebuilds. Secrets and credentials are injected at deploy time from Vault/CredHub; no secrets in repos. Compliance gates include SAST/DAST, dependency/license checks, SBOM generation, image signing/verification, change ticket validation where required, and SLO/SLA health checks. Observability is mandatory: logs, metrics, traces, and deployment events are emitted to the platform observability stack and tied to release versions.

Access is least-privilege via service accounts per pipeline/environment. Feature flags manage risky changes without redeploys. Manual approval is only required for production when policy dictates; otherwise, deployments are fully automated. A global kill switch and maintenance freeze mechanism are provided for emergency halts.

## Decision
Implement a centralized custom save handler in service-front to standardize persistence behavior across views and resources. The handler will be provided as a TypeScript module and React hook (useSaveHandler) exposing a single entry point: save(entityOrPatch, { resource, id, mode, strategy, reason, metadata }). It will support both controlled/manual saves and autosave via debounce and coalescing of rapid changes. All saves will be idempotent and retryable with exponential backoff, jitter, and cancellation on navigation/unmount.

Concurrency will be handled via ETag/If-Match headers and a last-write-wins fallback with user-facing conflict prompts. The handler will maintain a local optimistic cache for responsive UI, with automatic rollback on hard failures. Offline/poor-network scenarios will enqueue operations for background sync when enabled; otherwise, the handler will surface clear, actionable errors mapped to user-friendly messages.

Validation will run client-side before network calls and always defer to server validation, merging server field errors into a normalized error format. The handler will support draft vs publish flows (mode: draft|publish) and partial updates by default (PATCH), falling back to PUT when required by resource adapters. Resource-specific behavior (endpoints, serialization, auth scopes) will be injected via pluggable adapters, allowing reuse across domains.

Observability is built-in: structured logs, metrics for latency/success/failure, and trace propagation. Feature flags will gate rollout per route/resource. The handler becomes the single sanctioned path for save operations in service-front, and direct component-level persistence is disallowed.

Adopt a dedicated URL construction layer separate from HTTP request execution to enable consistent, safe, and complete logging. All outbound requests must obtain URLs from a UrlBuilder/RequestFactory that:
- Accepts a route identifier and typed parameters, performs normalization/encoding, and returns an immutable URL value object.
- Produces a parallel LogView containing structured fields (scheme, host, route, path, query keys) with sensitive values redacted, plus the final resolved URL string for debug-level only.
- Emits standardized log events (INFO: route + parameters redacted; DEBUG: full resolved URL) with correlation/request IDs.

HTTP clients (libraries, interceptors, services) are prohibited from constructing or mutating URLs inline. They receive only the immutable URL object for execution and attach the LogView for observability. Linting/code reviews will enforce use of UrlBuilder and disallow ad‑hoc concatenation.

The UrlBuilder centralizes:
- Encoding, normalization, and default parameter application.
- Redaction rules for secrets/PII in path and query.
- Template handling for dynamic routes and feature flags.
- Sampling controls to constrain DEBUG full-URL logging in production.

This decision improves traceability, reduces data leakage risk, and makes URL creation deterministic and testable. It enables consistent, structured logging across services without coupling logging concerns to transport layers.

Adopt continuous knowledge crunching as a core engineering practice to evolve the domain model collaboratively with domain experts and delivery teams. We will institutionalize recurring, time-boxed collaborative modeling sessions (e.g., event storming, example mapping, and specification-by-example) at project inception, before/after major releases, and at least every two weeks for active domains. Each session will produce actionable artifacts: updated ubiquitous language/glossary, refined domain model diagrams, clarified bounded contexts, identified aggregates/invariants, and example-based specifications.

Establish a “domain stewardship” role within each bounded context responsible for curating the living glossary, ensuring model/code alignment, and coordinating sessions with subject-matter experts and stakeholders. All changes to domain behavior must reference outcomes from knowledge-crunching sessions and be reflected in docs-as-code repositories (versioned alongside the code). Updates to the domain model are considered part of the Definition of Done: code, tests, and documentation must reflect the agreed language, invariants, and scenarios.

Introduce discovery spikes to test uncertain domain concepts rapidly; promote/retire concepts based on validated learning. Encode domain insights as executable specifications (acceptance tests) and contract/property-based tests to guard invariants. Maintain a lightweight decision log linking domain insights to ADRs.

Tooling will support collaborative whiteboarding, model repositories, and automated checks ensuring glossary and model drift is flagged in PRs. Participation from engineering, product, and domain experts is mandatory; schedules and outputs are transparently published to sustain shared understanding and continuous learning.

## Decision
We will upgrade the product’s primary UI typography to the new version of our corporate typeface and standardize on the variable WOFF2 build, self-hosted. The font will be version-pinned and distributed via our asset pipeline with immutable cache-busting (content hashes) and long-lived caching headers. We will enable font-display: swap to avoid FOIT, preload the primary variable font with rel=preload for critical weights/styles, and subset character sets by locale where appropriate to reduce payload, while maintaining a full-unicode build for markets requiring extended coverage.

Fallback stacks will be explicitly defined and tested (system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, Noto Sans, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif). We will retain the previous font version in the bundle for one release behind a feature flag to enable safe, gradual rollout (10% → 50% → 100%) with real-user monitoring of CLS, LCP, and rendering defects. A one-click rollback path will disable the new font via configuration.

Accessibility and internationalization are mandatory gates: contrast and readability checks, hinting/legibility on low-DPI displays, screen reader symbol compatibility, RTL shaping, and language coverage verification. Cross-browser/OS rendering (Windows ClearType, macOS, Android, iOS) will be validated on target devices.

Licensing will be reviewed and documented; self-hosting is chosen over CDN for privacy, availability, and CSP simplicity. Documentation will include usage tokens (weights, optical sizes), do/don’t guidance, and migration steps. Success is measured by neutral-or-better performance metrics and no increase in typography-related support issues.

Testing-only capabilities will be isolated from production artifacts and activated exclusively in non-production builds/environments.

- Code location: test helpers, fakes, fixtures, and seeders live under /tests and /test-support (or language-idiomatic test packages). No test-specific logic resides in production packages/namespaces.
- Substitution: production code exposes interfaces/ports; tests supply fakes/mocks via dependency injection. Any helper that must be shared is kept generic, side-effect free, and production-safe; test-specific variants stay in test scope.
- Runtime hooks: test control endpoints, backdoors, or toggles are provided only in non-prod deployments behind a build-time feature (e.g., compile-time flag) and environment guard. They are namespaced (e.g., /_test/*) and excluded from production builds/bundles.
- Frontend/mobile: test selectors use data-test attributes. Debug menus, sandbox switches, and stubs exist only in debug/staging builds and are stripped from release builds.
- Data: test data generation and database seeding execute via test-only scripts piped through non-prod configs; production data is never mutated by test seeders.
- Feature flags: flags are first-class configuration. Tests override flag state via injected providers; no hardcoded “test” branches in domain logic.
- Observability: additional probes for test assertions are enabled only in non-prod via configuration.
- Governance: CI enforces that production artifacts exclude test packages and test endpoints (build-time checks, bundle analyzers). Static analysis blocks references from production code to test namespaces.

This ensures testability without contaminating production logic, minimizes attack surface, and keeps builds/environment behavior unambiguous.

Implement optimistic, incremental local aggregation for summaries and analytics upon purchase creation. When a new purchase is committed to the local store, emit a PurchaseRecorded domain event and update local summary/analytics aggregates in the same transactional boundary to keep UI/read models immediately consistent (offline-first). The UI reads exclusively from these local aggregates.

Persist the purchase and an outbox event atomically. A background sync processes the outbox to upsert the purchase to the server. Use idempotent identifiers (purchaseId) and versioning to avoid duplicates. On server acknowledgment or conflict response, reconcile by applying server-authoritative changes as deltas to local aggregates; if divergence is detected, trigger a targeted re-aggregation for affected periods/categories, with a fallback to full re-aggregation during low-usage windows.

Aggregation is incremental: maintain rolling totals, counts, and category/time-bucket metrics; avoid scanning full history. Guard with numeric precision policies and caps on aggregate cardinality (e.g., bounded category set and time buckets). All computations use only local data; do not transmit raw analytics externally beyond purchase sync.

Provide eventual-consistency guarantees: local views update instantly; server sync may lag but will converge. All operations are idempotent and retry-safe. Telemetry records latency, failure, and drift metrics to monitor recalculation and reconciliation health.

## Decision

Establish clear ETL logic boundaries across CDH with a layered data architecture (Raw/Bronze → Staging/Silver → Curated/Gold):

- Extract/Ingress (Raw/Bronze): Land source data to HDFS via NiFi/Kafka/Sqoop with no business transformations. Allow only transport concerns: encryption, compression, basic schema normalization, partitioning, PII tokenization/redaction as mandated by policy, and lightweight filters for row scoping. No joins, aggregations, or cross-domain derivations. Preserve original fidelity (immutable, append-only).

- Transform (Staging/Silver): Implement all conformance and data quality logic in Spark on CDH: typing, standardization, deduplication, CDC handling, SCD management, surrogate keying, reference data enrichment, and rule-based validations. Jobs must be deterministic, idempotent, and versioned; UDFs centralized and reviewed. No customer-facing business metrics or report-specific aggregations here.

- Load/Serving (Curated/Gold): Materialize business-ready dimensional models and subject-area marts in Hive/Impala. Compute reusable business metrics and aggregations here. Enforce stable, documented schemas and SLAs for downstream consumers. Prohibit BI/reporting tools from implementing ETL; only semantic calculations allowed.

- Tooling/Orchestration/Governance: Use Airflow/Oozie for orchestration and retries; Hive Metastore for schemas; Atlas for lineage; schema contracts (Avro/JSON) for exchange. Permit limited pushdown (projections/filters) to sources for performance; disallow complex logic in sources and ingestion. All changes follow code review, automated tests, data quality gates, and ADR updates to preserve backward compatibility and lineage.

## Decision

- Aggregate roots govern their own lifetime via explicit factory methods and state transitions; public constructors are disallowed. Creation occurs through domain services/factories that validate invariants and emit AggregateCreated events.
- Child entities/value objects cannot outlive their aggregate root; they are created and destroyed only through root methods. External references to an aggregate are by immutable AggregateId only—no foreign references to internals.
- Aggregates implement a simple lifecycle state machine: Active → Suspended (optional) → Closed. Deletion is soft by default: aggregates transition to Closed with DeletedAt and Status=Closed; all commands except Restore are rejected in Closed. Hard deletion is executed only by a scheduled archival/purge job after a retention period and only when no dependent projections or legal holds exist.
- Optimistic concurrency with version numbers governs all state changes. Idempotency keys are required for commands that may be retried across boundaries; duplicate commands must not resurrect closed aggregates.
- Long-running, multi-aggregate processes (e.g., fulfillment) use sagas/process managers that correlate by AggregateId and drive the transition to Closed when completion criteria are met.
- Transient/ephemeral aggregates have a TTL set at creation; an expiry worker moves them to Closed on timeout. Expired aggregates follow the same archival/purge path.
- Restoration from Closed to Active is allowed only when explicitly modeled and invariant-safe; restoration emits AggregateRestored and bumps version.
- Repositories only rehydrate Active or Closed aggregates; hard-deleted aggregates are non-recoverable. Query models respect Status to exclude Closed by default and include on demand.
- All lifecycle transitions emit domain events for auditing and projections. Archival stores receive a compacted event stream snapshot prior to hard delete.

Adopt an asynchronous background processing architecture built on a durable message queue and stateless worker services.

- Enqueue jobs via a transactional outbox pattern to ensure atomic write-with-publish and at-least-once delivery. Use CDC or a relay to move outbox records to the queue.
- Workers consume messages using visibility timeouts/leases and heartbeats. Handlers must be idempotent, keyed by a deterministic idempotency key persisted in a dedup store.
- Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter, capped attempts, and route poison messages to a dead-letter queue with automated quarantine and manual reprocessing controls.
- Support prioritization and isolation using separate queues (e.g., high/standard/low) and per-tenant queues or tags for multi-tenancy and rate limits.
- For scheduled/recurring jobs, use a scheduler service that persists schedules in a database and materializes due jobs into the queue; prevent duplicate triggers via leases.
- Define SLAs by job class with timeouts, cancellation, and checkpointing for long-running work. Store large payloads in object storage and pass references, not blobs.
- Provide observability: structured logs with correlation ids, metrics (queue depth, age, throughput, success/error rates, retry counts), traces, and a job history store.
- Enable horizontal scaling with containerized workers and autoscaling driven by queue depth and lag; support graceful shutdown with in-flight drain and visibility extension.
- Enforce security: encryption in transit/at rest, least-privilege IAM for queue/object storage access, PII minimization in payloads, and sealed secrets.
- Offer operational controls: admin UI/CLI for pause/resume, replay, cancel, and priority boosts; feature flags for incremental rollout; backpressure/admission control at producers based on queue health.

This decision standardizes background work on a resilient, observable, horizontally scalable pipeline with clear correctness guarantees (at-least-once delivery and application-level exactly-once via idempotency).

## Decision

Adopt AWS ECS with the Fargate launch type as the default host type for running containerized workloads. All stateless services, scheduled tasks, and event-driven workers will run on ECS Fargate using awsvpc networking in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer where applicable. We will use ECS Capacity Providers with a default mix of FARGATE (on-demand) and FARGATE_SPOT for cost-optimized, fault-tolerant scheduling; production, latency-sensitive services will default to on-demand with optional burst to Spot, while nonproduction and asynchronous workloads can prefer Spot.

Images will be stored in ECR; task execution and task IAM roles will follow least-privilege. Secrets will be sourced from AWS Secrets Manager and/or SSM Parameter Store. Service autoscaling will be configured via target tracking on CPU/memory and via custom metrics (e.g., SQS queue depth) where appropriate. Observability will use CloudWatch metrics/logs, Container Insights, FireLens for log routing, and AWS X-Ray for tracing. Health checks and blue/green deployments will be managed via ECS with CodeDeploy or rolling updates.

Ephemeral storage and task sizes will be explicitly configured per workload; tasks requiring elevated privileges, custom kernels, GPUs, host networking, or specialized storage are out of scope for Fargate and will be handled by exception using ECS EC2 launch type or a specialized compute service. Network access will be restricted via security groups, NACLs, and VPC endpoints to minimize egress; ALBs/NLBs will front external/internal traffic as needed.

We will standardize on the latest supported Fargate platform version, apply service quotas monitoring, and implement cost guardrails (Spot utilization policies, budget alerts). Migration will be phased service-by-service, with rollback to prior launch type if SLOs regress.

We will maintain Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as Markdown files in version control under docs/adr at the repository root. In a monorepo, cross-cutting ADRs reside at the root (docs/adr) and service-/package-specific ADRs live under each component’s docs/adr directory; numbering is local to each directory.

File naming: zero-padded sequential numbers followed by a short kebab-case slug, e.g., 0001-adopt-adr.md. One decision per file. Use adr-tools–compatible format and template with required sections: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives, Date, Authors, Tags, Links. Include optional YAML front matter for Tags/Scope/Owners.

Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted | Rejected | Deprecated. Superseded indicates replacement and must link both ways. Accepted ADRs are immutable; changes require a new ADR that deprecates or supersedes prior ones.

Indexing: maintain docs/adr/README.md as a curated index, grouped by status and scope, linking to each ADR. Each ADR must link related ADRs and external references.

Process: new ADRs are proposed via pull request, reviewed by the architecture group, and merged when status becomes Accepted/Rejected. CI enforces naming, required sections, valid status transitions, and bidirectional links on supersession. Editing Accepted ADRs is blocked except to add Superseded metadata via a new ADR.

Scope and discoverability: use Tags/Scope (e.g., “security,” “data,” “payments-service,” “frontend”) to aid search. Prefer repository over external wiki; mirror or publish read-only docs if needed, but the repo is the source of truth.

Number assignment is first-come within a PR; conflicts are resolved during merge by renumbering in the smallest affected directory. Dates use UTC ISO-8601. All ADRs must be in English and pass markdown linting.

We will adopt a standardized, automated release notes process for the Wikibase Extension based on curated change fragments and deterministic assembly at release time.

- Source of truth: A RELEASE-NOTES.md file in the repository root contains versioned sections. An “Unreleased” section is generated from change fragments and is finalized at tag cut.
- Change fragments: Every user-visible change requires a fragment file placed under docs/release-notes/fragments/, named <phab-or-pr>-<short-slug>.(feature|fix|security|perf|deprecation|removal|breaking|maintenance).md. Fragments are short, imperative, link to the task/PR, and avoid internal jargon.
- Categories and order: Release notes are grouped in the following order: Breaking changes, Removals, Deprecations, Security, Features, Performance, Fixes, Maintenance/Docs. Within a category, entries are sorted by fragment filename to ensure stable output.
- Tooling: We use a towncrier-like generator (script provided under tools/release-notes) to validate and assemble RELEASE-NOTES.md. The generator runs in CI to ensure fragments exist for labeled changes, that formatting is correct, and that the Unreleased section is consistent.
- Contributor workflow: PRs labeled release-notes-required must include a fragment; CI enforces this. Trivial/internal changes use the release-notes-none label. Reviewers are accountable for categorization and wording.
- Branching: Each supported branch maintains its own RELEASE-NOTES.md. Backports must include or cherry-pick appropriate fragments; the generator supports branch-specific assembly.
- Release procedure: At release, the Release Manager runs the generator with the new version, which: finalizes the Unreleased section under the new version header with date, resets Unreleased, updates extension.json version metadata, and opens a PR. After merge, we tag and publish notes to GitHub Releases and mediawiki.org.
- Security handling: Security-related fragments are kept private until coordinated disclosure; placeholders are included post-release as appropriate.
- Localization: Release notes remain English-only; user-facing UI changes must still include i18n notes where applicable.

Adopt a clear separation of concerns by splitting the current CI/CD workflow into two distinct pipelines:

- Build Pipeline (CI): Triggered on code changes. Performs checkout, dependency caching, unit/integration tests, static analysis, SCA, vulnerability scans, license checks, and artifact build (e.g., container image/binary). Generates SBOM, signs artifacts and images, embeds provenance (SLSA-compatible), and publishes immutable, versioned artifacts to the artifact registry. No environment credentials are available in this pipeline.

- Deployment Pipeline (CD): Triggered by a release event, tag, or manual/automated promotion using the immutable artifact version. Executes environment-specific deployment steps (Dev → Test → Staging → Prod) with policy gates, change approvals, and audit logging. Applies configuration-as-code and GitOps where applicable; fetches secrets from a vault; supports progressive strategies (canary/blue-green) and automated rollback to a prior artifact version. Enforces idempotent, parameterized deployments.

Access control and compliance: Enforce least-privilege by isolating permissions (build: source and registry; deploy: cluster/cloud targets only). Require signed artifacts, verify signatures at deploy time, and retain full traceability from commit to environment. Capture metrics, logs, and DORA indicators per pipeline.

Migration: Introduce versioned release artifacts and promotion workflows, update branch/tag policies, and deprecate direct-from-branch deployments. Success is measured by reduced lead time to production, improved change fail rate, reproducibility, and auditability.

## Decision

Adopt basepath as the primary aggregation key for traffic and engagement metrics, replacing Content Item identifiers. All collection, storage, and reporting pipelines will normalize incoming requests to a canonical basepath and attribute metrics to that basepath.

Scope:
- Applies to page views, API hits, latency, errors, conversions, search/referrals, and cache metrics.
- Non-content routes (assets, utilities) are excluded by filter rules; only routable, user-facing basepaths are tracked.

Canonicalization:
- Lowercase path; strip querystrings, fragments, trailing slashes; collapse multiple slashes; decode percent-encoding.
- Remove locale and A/B variant tokens from the path; store locale/variant as dimensions.
- Resolve internal rewrites but not external redirects; record redirect hops as a dimension.

Data model:
- Primary key: basepath.
- Dimensions: timestamp, locale, variant, device, referrer, status_code, content_id (nullable), format, app.
- Maintain a basepath_aliases table to group historical paths (migrations/renames) for optional roll-up.

APIs and dashboards:
- Provide v2 endpoints /metrics/by-basepath with filtering on dimensions and alias roll-up.
- Retain content_id as an optional drill-down dimension; deprecate /by-content-item after a 90-day overlap.
- Dashboards default to basepath; content item views pivot via dimension.

Storage and indexing:
- Partition by date; index on (basepath, date). Materialize daily aggregates by basepath and by (basepath, locale).
- Backfill last 180 days from raw logs with canonicalization rules.

Behavior on content moves:
- Metrics remain with their originating basepath; alias groups enable aggregated views across moves.
- When two items share a basepath over time, both are represented under the same basepath with distinct time ranges.

Rollout:
- Ship behind a feature flag, dual-write for 30 days, validate parity, then switch read paths and begin deprecation.

We will maintain the master documentation as the single source of truth in the root README.md of the repository.

- Scope: The README will provide the canonical overview, architecture summary, how-to-get-started, support matrix, contribution guidelines pointer, and an index (table of contents) linking to deeper documents in /docs, /examples, and code-level docs. No other document shall duplicate canonical content; deeper details live in modular files and are referenced from the README.

- Structure: The README will be organized for first-time and returning users: Purpose, Quickstart, Architecture at a glance, Key workflows, Configuration, Operations (build/test/release), Troubleshooting, Security/Compliance notes, and Links to detailed docs. It will include version badges and compatibility notes.

- Change control: All substantive documentation changes must update the README when they affect canonical information. Updates follow the same PR review process as code, with required reviewers for architecture and security sections.

- Size and readability: Keep the README concise (aim < ~500 lines). Move verbose content to /docs and link from the README. Use consistent headings, anchors, and a generated TOC.

- Tooling: Enforce markdown linting and link checking in CI. Optionally generate a docs site (e.g., GitHub Pages) from /docs; the README remains master and is embedded as the homepage.

- Versioning: Tag README changes with releases; include per-release “What changed” links. Maintain per-branch READMEs aligned to that branch’s state.

- Ownership: The tech lead is accountable; all contributors are responsible.

## Decision
Adopt a multi-tenant, multi-site architecture using a single deployable codebase with site isolation enforced at the data, configuration, and caching layers. Sites will be resolved by hostname (Host header) via a tenant-resolution middleware that attaches a site context to each request. Site metadata (domain(s), branding, feature flags, limits) will be stored in a central configuration service/table and cached per site.

Data isolation will be achieved with per-site database schemas (or separate databases where regulatory or performance needs require), with all queries scoped by site_id via the ORM and enforced by row-level security where supported. Cross-site data access will be prohibited except through explicit, audited service interfaces. Background jobs, queues, and scheduled tasks will be site-aware and include site context.

Static assets and themes will be site-specific, loaded via a theming layer with inheritance from a common base. CDN configuration will support per-site domains, with cache keys namespaced by site_id to prevent leakage. Rate limits and feature flags will be evaluated per site.

Provisioning of new sites will be automated through an API/CLI that creates configuration, database schema, secrets, DNS/CDN entries, and default content. Observability will tag logs, metrics, and traces with site_id; error budgets and alerts can be scoped per site. Administrative tooling will support both global operations and site-scoped roles.

CI/CD will build once and deploy once; runtime configuration selects active sites. This approach minimizes operational overhead while enabling strong isolation, tailored experiences, and scalable growth in the number of sites.

Adopt AWS SAM CLI as the standard tool to build, run, and debug AWS Lambda functions locally across all services in this repository. All developers will use sam build and sam local (start-api, start-lambda, invoke) to emulate Lambda runtimes via Docker, ensuring high parity with deployed environments. Docker Desktop (or compatible engine) is a prerequisite; SAM CLI and template metadata (runtime, layers, env vars) are the single source of truth for local execution.

We will:
- Standardize local invocation via sam local with event fixtures committed to the repo.
- Expose debugging ports per runtime (e.g., Node.js, Python) through SAM configuration for step-through debugging in IDEs.
- Manage configuration and secrets via environment variables and per-stage parameter files; no secrets will be committed.
- Use AWS sandbox accounts for integration against managed services when feasible; optional LocalStack may be used for isolated development but is not required nor supported in CI.
- Pin SAM CLI and Docker engine minimum versions and enforce via devcontainer/pre-commit checks to reduce “works on my machine” issues.
- Provide make/npm/yarn tasks that wrap common SAM commands to unify workflows (build, start, test, clean).
- Exclude performance/load testing from local SAM usage; such tests run in sandbox environments. IAM policy evaluation and service limits are validated in cloud only.

CI will not execute Lambdas via sam local; instead, unit tests run in-language, with integration tests executed against sandbox AWS. Templates will include necessary Metadata and Globals to keep local and deployed configurations aligned.

## Decision
We will support direct, first-class usage of the system without project-specific wrapper scripts by providing stable, documented entry points and configurations. The primary interfaces will be:
- A single, versioned CLI binary with subcommands for all tasks (build, test, lint, migrate, run).
- A public programmatic API for automation and integrations.
- A declarative configuration file (e.g., tool.config.*) plus environment variables and flags, eliminating reliance on shell logic.

Wrapper scripts will be deprecated and removed after a two-release grace period. All documentation, examples, and CI templates will demonstrate direct CLI/API usage. We will ensure cross-platform parity (Linux/macOS/Windows) by avoiding shell-specific features, providing prebuilt binaries/containers, and validating commands in CI across OSes.

Dependency and environment management will be handled via:
- Explicit version pinning (lockfiles) and reproducible installs.
- PATH-based discovery with clear installation steps (package managers, archives, container image).
- Optional, non-required convenience targets (e.g., Makefile/Taskfile) that call the CLI verbatim.

UX improvements will include self-documenting commands (help/manpages), consistent exit codes, structured output (JSON) for tooling, and actionable error messages that do not assume wrappers. Backward compatibility shims (thin no-op wrappers) will be provided during the deprecation window with warnings.

Success metrics: zero wrapper usage in official artifacts, green cross-OS CI using direct CLI, and user migration completed within two releases.

Adopt Terraform as the standard IaC tool across all AWS accounts, with strict environment and account isolation per stack. Each stack (account/region/scope) is defined in its own directory; we will not use Terraform workspaces for environment separation. State is isolated per stack and stored in an S3 backend within the target AWS account, with DynamoDB table locking in the same account. Cross-account central state storage is not used. Provider and module versions are pinned.

Authentication and authorization use AWS IAM Role assumption:
- Developers: AWS SSO to assume environment-specific, least-privilege roles.
- CI/CD: OIDC-based role assumption into target accounts; production applies are restricted to CI only.

A mono-repo holds stack definitions under env/account/region folders and consumes reusable, versioned modules from a separate modules repository. Cross-account dependencies are minimized; when unavoidable, read-only terraform_remote_state is permitted with explicit IAM policies, but event-driven or API contracts are preferred.

Plans and applies run via CI pipelines that:
- Validate, format, and lint.
- Generate and store plan artifacts for review.
- Require approvals for privileged environments.
- Enforce drift detection on a schedule for critical stacks.

Naming, tagging, and account/OU mappings follow standardized conventions. Secrets are sourced from OIDC-provided short-lived creds and SSM/Secrets Manager; no long-lived static credentials in code or state. Destructive changes require explicit confirmation gates.

This approach provides clear blast-radius boundaries, least-privilege access, auditable changes, and scalable multi-account governance while keeping state ownership within each account.

Implement a VPC with both public and private subnets across at least two Availability Zones to separate internet-facing and internal resources, improve resilience, and control egress. Create two public subnets (per AZ) for an Internet Gateway–facing Application Load Balancer, bastion/SSM endpoints as needed, and one NAT Gateway per AZ. Create at least two private subnet tiers per AZ: “app” for compute (ECS/EKS/EC2/Lambda in VPC) and “data” for databases, caches, and internal services. Route tables will direct public subnets to the IGW and private subnets to their co-located NAT Gateway for outbound internet access; data subnets will not initiate outbound internet unless explicitly required. Prefer interface and gateway VPC Endpoints (S3, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager, SSM, CloudWatch, ECR, KMS) to reduce NAT costs and improve security.

No inbound traffic reaches private subnets directly; ingress is only via ALB/NLB in public subnets or via SSM Session Manager. Bastion hosts are used only if SSM is unavailable. Security Groups enforce least privilege between tiers; NACLs remain stateless and conservative. Enable VPC Flow Logs and DNS hostnames; use Route 53 private hosted zones for internal resolution.

Adopt dual-stack IPv4 with optional IPv6; if IPv6 is enabled, attach an egress-only IGW for private subnets and maintain the same ingress model. Use separate subnets and route tables per AZ to avoid cross-AZ dependencies. Tag all resources and apply SCPs/guardrails. This topology is the default for all environments, with right-sizing (e.g., single NAT in non-prod) allowed where cost justifies and risk is acceptable.

## Decision

Establish a Common Records Layer as a standalone, versioned artifact that defines all cross-service data contracts (request/response DTOs, event payloads, canonical domain value objects) using Protocol Buffers as the source of truth. Language-specific models are generated from the .proto schemas for each runtime (e.g., JVM, Node, Python), ensuring consistent serialization, validation metadata, and documentation.

Scope:
- Mandatory for inter-service APIs, eventing, and shared canonical models.
- Excludes service-internal persistence models and business logic.

Governance and versioning:
- Semantic versioning with strict backward compatibility guarantees for minor releases; breaking changes require a major version.
- Deprecation policy with minimum two minor versions of overlap before removal.
- Schema evolution rules: only additive fields (optional), no renames/removals without version bump, reserved tags to prevent reuse, oneof for mutually exclusive fields.
- Ownership by the Platform Architecture team; changes via lightweight RFC and automated compatibility checks.

Usage constraints:
- Records are immutable value types; no business behavior.
- Services must not extend or fork generated classes; compose via adapters if needed.
- Namespacing by bounded context; PII fields explicitly tagged for masking/retention.
- No dependencies from Common Records to service code; only leaf dependencies (e.g., validation annotations) permitted.

Tooling and delivery:
- Central repo with codegen pipeline, linting, and schema registry publishing.
- Artifacts published per language runtime.
- On-the-wire default is Protobuf; external integrations may use JSON via generated adapters.

Adopt Electron as the framework for our cross-platform desktop application targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux. The application will be implemented as a web UI running in Chromium with a secure, sandboxed renderer and a minimal Node.js-enabled main process. Node integration will be disabled in renderers; all privileged operations will be exposed via contextBridge and IPC with strict, schema-validated message contracts.

We will package and distribute using electron-builder, with platform-native installers (NSIS for Windows, DMG/PKG for macOS, AppImage for Linux) and differential auto-updates enabled via a signed update server. All binaries will be code-signed and notarized on macOS. Security hardening includes sandboxed renderers, CSP, ASAR integrity, allowlist of IPC channels, dependency auditing, and regular Chromium/Electron patch cadence alignment.

Performance targets: cold start ≤ 2.5s on mid-tier hardware, steady-state memory ≤ 500MB, and smoothness ≥ 60fps for primary views. Native capabilities (e.g., OS keychain, tray, file system watchers) will be accessed through isolated modules; any performance-critical native code will use Node-API bindings (prefer Rust/Go with C-ABI) to preserve ABI stability.

The app will support offline-first operation with a local SQLite database accessed via a controlled preload API. Observability will include opt-in telemetry, crash reporting, and structured logs with PII scrubbing. CI/CD will produce reproducible builds, SBOMs, and signed artifacts.

This decision commits us to Electron for the desktop surface area for the next major version, with periodic reevaluation against alternatives if performance, security, or maintenance costs exceed defined thresholds.

Adopt a TypeScript-first, cloud-native stack:
- Frontend: React with Next.js (SSR/SSG), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and React Query; component library with Radix UI; Playwright for E2E tests.
- Mobile: React Native with Expo for shared TypeScript models and UI patterns.
- Backend: Node.js with NestJS (TypeScript), REST APIs with OpenAPI and internal gRPC for service-to-service calls; input validation via Zod/class-validator; background jobs with BullMQ.
- Data: PostgreSQL (managed, e.g., AWS RDS) with Prisma ORM; Redis (managed, e.g., ElastiCache) for caching, queues, and rate limiting; S3-compatible object storage for assets; optional OpenSearch for full-text/search features.
- Architecture: Modular monorepo (Turborepo) with shared libraries and strict API boundaries; containerized services via Docker; deploy to Kubernetes (AWS EKS) with Helm charts; API Gateway + CloudFront for edge caching; WebSocket/SSE via API Gateway or Socket.IO as needed.
- AuthN/Z: OpenID Connect (Cognito/Auth0/Keycloak), JWT access tokens with short TTL, refresh tokens, and RBAC/ABAC enforced in backend.
- Observability: OpenTelemetry tracing, Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards, and centralized logs (CloudWatch/ELK); feature flags via LaunchDarkly/OpenFeature.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions with ephemeral preview environments, automated testing (Jest/Playwright), linting/formatting, SCA/DAST, IaC scans; infrastructure via Terraform.
- Quality and reliability: Migrations via Prisma, blue/green or canary deployments with progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts), database backups and PITR, and SLOs with alerts.

## Decision
We will standardize on RSpec request specs as the primary approach for testing controller behavior and HTTP endpoints. Effective immediately:
- All new endpoints must be covered by request specs that exercise the full Rails request stack (routing, middleware, authentication/authorization, params parsing, content negotiation, and error handling).
- Existing controller specs are deprecated. They may be touched only for urgent fixes; otherwise, convert them opportunistically when related code is changed, with the goal of eliminating controller specs within two release cycles.
- For APIs, request specs will validate status codes, response bodies, headers, caching directives, and side effects. For HTML endpoints, they will validate redirects, flash, headers, and rendered content where applicable (system specs remain responsible for browser-level behavior).
- Avoid stubbing controller internals in request specs. Prefer stubbing external services at the HTTP boundary (e.g., WebMock/VCR) and isolating domain units with unit specs. Keep business logic in POROs/Service objects covered by fast unit tests.
- Provide shared helpers for authentication, JSON parsing, schema validation, and common assertions. Update generators/templates to create request specs by default.
- CI will track migration progress by flagging new controller specs and reporting coverage parity. Owners will prioritize converting high-value/fragile areas first (auth flows, error handling, pagination, content negotiation).
- Exceptions: Extremely complex before_action logic may retain targeted unit tests on extracted modules; do not reintroduce controller specs for this purpose. Legacy controller specs may be temporarily skipped if a faithful request-spec replacement exists.

This decision aligns tests with Rails’ supported surface, increases confidence in real request behavior, reduces brittle internal coupling, and clarifies test boundaries between request/integration, unit, and system layers.

## Decision
We will implement grant-wise expenditure extraction via an ELT pipeline into the analytics warehouse, standardizing raw financial transactions into a canonical star schema and publishing a materialized “grant_expenditure” aggregate for consumption.

- Source ingestion: Incremental loads from the ERP/general ledger and ancillary systems (procurement, payroll, expenses) using change data capture where available; scheduled batch otherwise.
- Canonical model: FactExpenditure (immutable, ledger-like rows for postings, reversals, adjustments) with dimensions Grant, Project/Program, Cost Center, Vendor, Account, Currency, and Period. Grant and Cost Center will use SCD Type 2 to preserve history.
- Allocation rules: Shared costs and payroll distributions applied via transparent, versioned rule tables; all derived allocations persisted as separate fact rows linked to the original transaction for auditability.
- Currency handling: Store native amounts and convert to reporting currency at posting-time and period-average FX rates; expose both. FX tables are versioned and time-bound.
- Aggregation: A dbt-managed materialized view/table produces grant-level, periodized expenditure (YTD, ITD, and by funding window), with filters for funder constraints and allowable accounts.
- Performance: Partition/cluster fact by fiscal period and grant_id; incremental transformations; late-arriving adjustments handled via idempotent upserts.
- Data access: Expose via SQL views and a read-only API endpoint; enforce row-level security by organizational unit and grant ownership.
- Quality and lineage: Tests for completeness, reconciliation to GL control totals, and column-level lineage maintained in the transformation repo.
- Cadence: Daily refresh, with on-demand backfill support for month-end close.

We will keep the seed template unopinionated with respect to a specific state management framework. The core template will provide a lightweight, framework-agnostic state boundary (e.g., via an application services layer, context-based adapters, and dependency inversion interfaces) that allows teams to adopt Redux Toolkit, MobX, Zustand, XState, React Query/TanStack Query, or simple React state without friction.

Concretely:
- Core includes no runtime dependency on any state library beyond React itself.
- The template exposes well-defined extension points (e.g., StoreProvider, useAppSelector/useAppDispatch shims, effect/async boundaries) that can be implemented by adapters.
- We ship optional, opt-in example modules (“recipes”) for Redux Toolkit, Zustand, and React Query demonstrating integration, patterns, and testing. These are installable via flags (e.g., --with-redux, --with-zustand, --with-react-query) or added post-init.
