- Documentation focuses on generic patterns (state domains, side-effects, normalization, caching, optimistic updates) with links to library-specific guides in the recipes.
- Linting, CI, codegen, and testing utilities remain neutral and do not assume a specific state library.
- Sample features default to local/component state and context to keep the baseline minimal; complex state is shown only in the optional recipes.
- Migration guidance and adapter templates are provided to switch libraries with minimal surface-area changes.

This decision maximizes flexibility and long-term maintainability, avoids premature lock-in, supports varied team preferences, and keeps the seed suitable for both small apps and enterprise-scale projects while still offering curated, production-ready integrations when desired.

Adopt median-based discretization for gamma values across all pipelines. For any discretization bucket/window, the representative value will be the median of the raw gamma values assigned to that bucket.

Scope:
- Applies to data preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, online scoring, and analytics wherever gamma discretization is performed.
- Effective for both batch and streaming pipelines.

Computation:
- Batch: compute exact median by selecting the k-th order statistic (exclude NaNs). For even counts, use the lower of the two middle values to ensure determinism and value provenance.
- Streaming: compute approximate median using t-digest (compression=100) or equivalent; validate error <1% absolute in shadow metrics.
- Weighted data: use weighted median (same tie-breaking rule).
- Missing/invalid values: excluded from computation; if all invalid, emit null and flag for data quality handling.

Operational details:
- Deterministic outputs guaranteed per bucket given the same inputs and random seeds.
- Minimum sample policy: median is defined for n≥1; no fallback to mean is used.
- Configuration flag median_discretization=true (default) with rollback to mean for emergency only.
- Versioning: increment discretization_version and model/feature schema versions; rebaseline thresholds and golden datasets.
- Monitoring: track bucket counts, median vs mean delta, percentile drift, and downstream metric impact; alert on sustained deltas above configured thresholds.

Consequences:
- Improved robustness to outliers and skew at the cost of slightly higher compute for exact selection and minor approximation error in streaming.

Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as the authoritative, lightweight mechanism to capture and evolve significant technical and product-facing architecture decisions. ADRs will be stored in-repo under docs/adr, committed alongside code, and versioned through normal change control (pull requests with review). We will use a consistent template based on Nygard/MADR, with sections: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, and References. Records will be numbered sequentially starting at 000 using the pattern NNN-descriptive-title.md and remain immutable once “Accepted”; changes will be recorded via superseding ADRs that reference and deprecate predecessors.

ADRs are required for decisions with cross-team impact, long-lived cost, or high reversibility cost (e.g., core frameworks, data models, integration patterns, security posture). Teams may author complementary design docs or RFCs; the ADR summarizes the final decision and links to supporting detail. Status values: Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, Superseded, and Rejected. Each ADR must identify decision drivers, considered options, trade-offs, and consequences (positive and negative).

Ownership: the proposing team authors the ADR; architecture reviewers and impacted stakeholders must approve before “Accepted.” All ADRs must be discoverable via an index (docs/adr/README.md) and tagged/linked in tickets and code where relevant. We will automate linting of format and index updates; adr-tools (or equivalent) is recommended but optional.

This practice is effective immediately for all new qualifying decisions; existing major decisions will be backfilled with ADRs during the next quarter.

We will use Splunk as the authoritative, centralized store for all audit logs across services. Services will emit audit events in a standardized JSON schema via Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC) over TLS 1.2+ with token-based authentication. Delivery will occur through an agent/collector (OpenTelemetry Collector or Fluent Bit) with local disk buffering, batching, and exponential backoff retries to minimize loss during outages. Events are written to dedicated Splunk indexes per environment (e.g., idx_audit_prod, idx_audit_nonprod) with sourcetype=audit:event:v1.

The audit event schema includes: event_id, timestamp (UTC ISO8601), service, environment, tenant_id, user_id (or service principal), session_id, correlation_id/trace_id, action, resource_type, resource_id, outcome (success/failure), reason/error, request_ip, user_agent, and optional attributes. PII is minimized; sensitive fields are irreversibly hashed or masked at source/collector according to data classification rules. No secrets or payloads are logged.

Access to audit indexes is restricted via Splunk RBAC; only designated roles may search/export. Data integrity is enforced by disabling event editing/deletion and enabling index-time integrity controls. Retention is 400 days online; for longer retention, events are archived to object storage and restorable on demand. Time sync (NTP) is mandatory for all emitters. Operational dashboards and alerts are implemented in Splunk; schema evolution follows versioned sourcetype and backward-compatible changes.

## Decision

Adopt Continuous Delivery (CD) as the default release methodology for all services to enable frequent, reliable, and reversible releases.

- Development model: Trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches and mandatory PR checks.
- Pipeline as code: Each service defines a single build-and-release pipeline in-repo. Pipelines are versioned and reusable via templates.
- Build once, promote: Create a single immutable artifact per commit (container image and SBOM), signed and promoted through environments.
- Environments: dev → staging → production. Automated promotion on passing quality gates; production requires either risk-based automatic approval (low risk/canary) or lightweight human approval (high risk).
- Quality gates: Unit, integration, contract, and e2e tests; SAST/DAST/Dependency/IaC scans; license compliance; performance smoke; vulnerability and policy checks. Gates are mandatory and blocking.
- Deployment strategy: Progressive delivery (canary by default; blue/green as fallback). Use feature flags for runtime enablement and safe exposure; flags are short-lived and audited.
- GitOps for delivery: Desired state stored in Git; controllers reconcile environments from Git to ensure drift detection and auditable change history.
- Observability and rollback: Every release is monitored with health checks, SLO/error-budget guardrails, and automatic rollback on regression. Rollback is instant by promoting the last good artifact; database changes follow expand-contract migrations with automated checks.
- Secrets and config: Managed via centralized secret store; configuration is externalized, environment-specific, and encrypted in transit/at rest.
- Compliance and audit: All pipeline events, approvals, artifacts, test results, and deployments are logged and retained per policy; attestations (provenance, SBOM, signatures) are produced and verified.
- Targets: Lead time for changes ≤ 1 day, deployment frequency daily or better, change failure rate < 10%, MTTR < 1 hour.
- Scope and exceptions: CD is mandatory for all services; exceptions require architectural review and documented compensating controls.

Adopt Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 for all externally consumed artifacts: public libraries, service APIs (REST/GraphQL endpoints and versions), CLI/tools, event/message schemas, and configuration surfaces. Internal modules may change without SemVer guarantees unless explicitly published.

- Version format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Git tags use vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
- Increments:
  - MAJOR: any backwards-incompatible change to public API or observable contract (including endpoint removals/behavioral changes, breaking schema changes, CLI flag removals/renames, destructive DB changes without compatibility).
  - MINOR: backwards-compatible features or additive changes (new endpoints/fields, optional flags).
  - PATCH: backwards-compatible fixes and internal improvements (bug fixes, performance, security) without API changes.
- Pre-releases: -alpha.N, -beta.N, -rc.N. Build metadata: +build.<id>. Pre-releases are not for production.
- Public API definition includes: request/response schemas, error codes, auth flows, idempotency/ordering guarantees, event payloads, CLI interfaces, and configuration keys.
- Deprecation: mark as deprecated in a MINOR with clear warning and migration guidance; remove no sooner than the next MAJOR after at least one stable MINOR cycle of deprecation.
- Release process: conventional commits with “BREAKING CHANGE:” to signal MAJOR. CI/CD computes next version (e.g., semantic-release), generates changelog (Keep a Changelog), creates signed git tag, and publishes artifacts. Container images are tagged with: latest, MAJOR, MAJOR.MINOR, and full MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
- Branching: main produces releases. Pre-releases from release branches. Critical fixes may produce PATCH releases from hotfix branches.
- Database: MINOR/PATCH require backwards-compatible migrations (expand-and-contract). Destructive changes require MAJOR with migration plan.
- Communication: each release includes release notes and explicit migration steps for any deprecations or breaking changes.

We will use RFC 9562 UUIDv7 as the canonical object identifier for all persistent domain aggregates, records, events, and public API resources.

- Scope: UUIDv7 is the sole surrogate key for new entities across services and databases. Natural keys remain as secondary unique constraints where needed.
- Generation: IDs are generated application-side at creation using a vetted library and a cryptographically secure RNG for the randomized bits. Time source uses the system clock with monotonic sequencing to prevent collisions during same-tick generation.
- Storage/transport: Persist as native 16-byte UUID (e.g., PostgreSQL uuid). Expose as lowercase hyphenated strings in APIs. Comparisons are case-insensitive; canonical form is lowercase.
- Ordering: UUIDv7’s time-ordered property enables efficient index locality and default “by created_at” pagination without relying on database sequences. Time-ordering is a convenience only and not used for authorization or business logic.
- Immutability/reuse: Identifiers are immutable, never reassigned, and not recycled.
- Client interaction: Clients may generate provisional UUIDv7s for optimistic UX; the server remains the source of truth and will reject collisions.
- Security/privacy: We will not use incremental or guessable IDs. UUIDv7 contains no sensitive data; do not encode business semantics in IDs.
- Backward compatibility: Existing UUIDv4 identifiers remain valid; new entities adopt UUIDv7. Mixed-mode is supported indefinitely.
- Idempotency and external keys: Idempotency keys are separate from object IDs. Externally supplied identifiers are mapped to internal UUIDv7s via reference tables.
- Migration and tooling: Schema defaults and ORMs will be configured to generate UUIDv7 by default; database sequences are prohibited for identifiers.

We will inject all external, request-scoped, and environment-dependent parameters as explicit arguments to presenter entry points and router invocations rather than accessing globals, singletons, or service locators.

- Presenters and routers will expose methods that accept immutable parameter objects (DTOs/value objects) containing only the data they require (e.g., user identity, locale, feature flags, correlation ID, AB variants, request timeouts).
- The composition root (or controller layer) is responsible for assembling, validating, and supplying these arguments. Routers that orchestrate flows must thread these arguments through to downstream presenters without re-fetching them.
- Direct reads from global configuration, environment variables, thread-local context, or process-wide singletons within presenters/routers are disallowed. Where necessary, provide thin adapter layers at the boundary to map legacy sources into the new parameter objects during a deprecation period.
- Parameter objects must be:
  - Immutable and serializable.
  - Schema-validated at creation, with clear defaults where appropriate.
  - Minimally scoped (principle of least privilege; no secrets unless required).
  - Versioned to allow non-breaking evolution.
- Error handling: missing/invalid parameters fail fast with typed errors surfaced at the composition root; presenters/routers remain pure and side-effect free.
- Observability: correlation/request IDs and sampling hints are propagated via arguments.
- Performance: use lightweight value objects; avoid per-call container lookups; cache-free within presenters to maintain determinism.
- Testing: unit tests construct parameter objects directly, improving determinism and coverage.

This decision increases testability, predictability, and security while clarifying data flow and removing hidden coupling to runtime context.

## Decision
Adopt Terraform as the primary Infrastructure as Code tool for provisioning, updating, and destroying cloud and platform resources. Standardize on HCL-based Terraform configurations organized into reusable modules with semantic versioning and strict provider and module version pinning. Use a remote backend with state locking and encryption for Terraform state (e.g., object storage + lock table) and enforce state isolation per environment and per workspace. Structure repositories to separate foundational/platform modules from environment/application stacks, with clear inputs/outputs and minimal cross-module coupling. Integrate Terraform execution into CI/CD with plan/apply separation, mandatory peer review of plans, and drift detection. Enforce policy-as-code gates (e.g., OPA/Conftest or Sentinel) and static analysis (fmt/validate/tflint/checkov) in pipelines. Manage secrets via native cloud secret managers and inject them at apply-time rather than committing to code or state where feasible. Prefer immutable infrastructure patterns and idempotent changes, using feature flags and blue/green or canary strategies where applicable. Document standards for naming, tagging, and resource lifecycle, and maintain a curated internal module registry. Limit direct console changes; require reconciliation through Terraform. Provide migration guidance for existing infrastructure, including import procedures and phased adoption to minimize disruption.

Deploy the Pact Broker as a containerized service on AWS using ECS Fargate in a private subnet, fronted by an Application Load Balancer with HTTPS termination via ACM and a Route53-managed DNS record. Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ) as the persistence layer. Store all sensitive configuration (database credentials, broker secrets, webhook credentials) in AWS Secrets Manager and inject them at runtime via task definitions. Place services in dedicated VPC subnets with security groups enforcing least privilege (ALB to ECS only over HTTP, ECS to RDS only over PostgreSQL port).

Build and push container images to Amazon ECR from CI. Deploy via blue/green ECS deployments with automatic rollback based on health checks. Use CloudWatch Logs for application logs and CloudWatch metrics/alarms for service health, latency, and error rates. Enable ALB access logs to S3. Schedule automated RDS backups and snapshots, with point-in-time recovery enabled and cross-Region snapshot copy for DR. Perform nightly broker data exports to S3 for additional backup/archival.

Configure Pact Broker authentication with OAuth2/OIDC (Cognito or enterprise IdP via ALB OIDC) and per-tenant/team read/write permissions via broker configuration. Enable webhook execution with outbound internet egress via NAT. Restrict webhook targets to approved domains via allowlist.

Adopt infrastructure-as-code (Terraform or AWS CDK) for all resources and configuration, including networking, IAM, ECS, RDS, and monitoring. Tag all resources for ownership and cost allocation. Define nonprod and prod environments with separate VPCs, RDS instances, and ECS services. Apply zero-downtime database migrations during deployments.

We will provision a dedicated Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) for OPG Metrics in each environment (dev, staging, production) to isolate network, security, and cost boundaries from other workloads.

- Each environment receives its own non-overlapping CIDR (e.g., 10.60.0.0/16, 10.61.0.0/16, 10.62.0.0/16) with segregated private subnets across at least three AZs for high availability.
- No public subnets and no public IPs. Outbound internet access, where required, is via NAT gateways with egress allowlists. Prefer VPC endpoints (Gateway/Interface) for AWS services (S3, CloudWatch, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, KMS, STS, ECR, SSM).
- Ingress is private-only: from approved producer services via VPC peering/Transit Gateway or AWS PrivateLink. Public entry is only allowed through a controlled edge (e.g., shared WAF/ALB) terminating into the VPC privately.
- Administrative access uses SSM Session Manager via VPC endpoints; no bastion hosts or SSH from the internet.
- Service-to-service connectivity with other OPG systems uses Transit Gateway or PrivateLink; VPC peering allowed where appropriate, avoiding transitive routing. Route tables are least-privilege.
- DNS uses private hosted zones and split-horizon where needed, with Route 53 Resolver endpoints for cross-VPC resolution.
- Centralized observability (metrics/logs/traces) exports via endpoints/PrivateLink; no open egress for telemetry.
- All resources are tagged for ownership, environment, and cost allocation; quotas and guardrails enforced via SCPs/IAM.
- Disaster recovery leverages multi-AZ within the VPC and cross-Region replication where required by RTO/RPO.

This decision establishes strict blast-radius containment, predictable networking, and clear operational boundaries for OPG Metrics while enabling controlled integration with the wider OPG estate.

We will deprecate and remove the chi-squared test option across the product. Effective next minor release, “chi_squared” will be marked deprecated with clear warnings; in the subsequent major release it will be removed from all public APIs, configuration schemas, CLI flags, and UI controls. Where a default is required, we will standardize on likelihood-ratio (G-test) for large-sample categorical independence and Fisher’s exact test for small or sparse contingency tables, selected automatically based on cell counts; users may also explicitly choose among supported tests.

Implementation details:
- Configuration: values of “chi_squared” will trigger a deprecation warning for one release; thereafter they will be rejected with a validation error. Migration guidance and an automated config fixer will rewrite to “g_test” or “fisher_exact” as appropriate.
- API/Schema: remove enum members, update OpenAPI/JSON Schema, and bump versions accordingly.
- Runtime: any legacy model artifacts or pipelines referencing chi-squared will map to G-test during the deprecation window with a warning; after removal, loading will fail fast with a clear error and remediation steps.
- Documentation: update user guides, examples, and tutorials; add a migration section noting potential differences in p-values and decision thresholds.
- Telemetry/Support: instrument usage to monitor remaining adoption and inform outreach.

This change reduces maintenance burden, removes a source of misuse on sparse data, and consolidates validation on more robust, well-behaved alternatives.

Adopt a role-based access control (RBAC) model augmented with attribute-based constraints (ABAC) to enforce least-privilege access across all services. Implement a centralized authorization service that manages roles, permissions, and policies; services will perform authorization via policy evaluation using signed, short-lived JWTs issued by our IdP (OIDC/OAuth2), containing tenant, user, roles, and scoped permissions. Authorization decisions are enforced at the API gateway for coarse-grained checks and within services for fine-grained, resource-level checks (e.g., ownership, tenant, data sensitivity). Default posture is deny-by-default; roles are minimal and task-oriented; privileged operations require step-up MFA and break-glass workflows. Multi-tenant isolation is enforced by mandatory tenant scoping in tokens and queries. All permission changes follow a dual-control approval workflow and are versioned; periodic access recertification is required for high-risk roles. Every access decision and administrative change is audit-logged immutably with actor, scope, resource, and correlation IDs. Caching of authorization results is allowed with strict TTLs and revocation on role/permission changes. Service-to-service access uses mTLS plus service identities with dedicated machine roles. Separation of duties is encoded in policy to prevent conflicting role combinations. This decision balances simplicity of RBAC with ABAC flexibility, supports compliance, and centralizes policy governance while allowing service-level granularity.

Adopt Redux as the application’s predictable, centralized state container, implemented with Redux Toolkit (RTK) and React-Redux. Use RTK “slices” for domain-focused state, createAsyncThunk for async workflows, and RTK’s built-in Immer for immutable updates. Co-locate slices with their features in a feature-based folder structure; expose selectors (memoized with Reselect where needed) as the primary read API.

For server state, use RTK Query to handle data fetching, caching, invalidation, and background refetching. Normalize relational client state with createEntityAdapter to ensure performant updates and rendering. Enable Redux DevTools in non-production and enforce serializable state and action constraints.

Middleware: use RTK defaults (thunk + serializable checks) and add minimal custom middleware for cross-cutting concerns (e.g., analytics). Avoid global state for purely local UI concerns; favor component state for ephemeral UI and use Redux only for shared, cross-cutting, or workflow-critical data. Persist only necessary subsets of state using redux-persist (or equivalent) with explicit whitelists/blacklists.

TypeScript is mandatory: strongly type slices, thunks, selectors, and store; export RootState and AppDispatch from a single store module. Provide a thin store wrapper for testing and storybook; unit test reducers, selectors, and thunks with mocked services.

Migration: introduce Redux incrementally, starting with authentication/session and other cross-cutting domains, then refactor existing prop-drilling and ad-hoc contexts. Performance: rely on useSelector with narrow selectors, co-locate connect points near leaf components, and leverage RTK Query’s cache to minimize re-renders. This decision standardizes state management, improves debuggability, and supports scalability.

We will standardize on a single canonical identifier (ID/URI) per domain entity and introduce a first-class aliasing layer to preserve backward compatibility without propagating ambiguity.

- Canonical-only inside: All internal references, storage keys, foreign keys, and events must use canonical IDs/URIs exclusively.
- Alias ingestion at edges: User input, legacy IDs/slugs, locale/case/diacritic variants, and migrated identifiers are accepted at system boundaries and resolved to canonical before business logic executes.
- Alias registry: Persist aliases in a dedicated, normalized store (alias value, canonical_id, alias_type, source/provenance, created_by, status, validity window). Enforce global uniqueness on alias value and referential integrity to canonical entities.
- HTTP/API behavior: Expose and document canonical resource URLs. Serve 301/308 redirects from alias URLs to canonical. APIs accept aliases but always return canonical identifiers in responses, links, and webhooks.
- Governance: New aliases require a change record with justification and expiry/deprecation plan. Telemetry will track alias usage; low-traffic aliases are candidates for deprecation. Hard-delete only after deprecation window and monitoring.
- Normalization and security: Normalize whitespace, case, and diacritics consistently. Reserve and block sensitive/impersonating aliases; validate ownership for user-generated aliases.
- Performance: Maintain an LRU cache of alias→canonical mappings with write-through invalidation on updates; batch-resolve for high-throughput paths.
- Migration: During data migrations, emit aliases for former IDs and mark as deprecated with redirects.
- Testing/CI: Contract tests ensure aliases resolve and responses are canonical; lint rules reject internal use of aliases.

This decision prevents internal alias proliferation while ensuring stable, backward-compatible external interfaces.

We will adopt Luxon (v3) as the single standard library for date/time handling across all JavaScript/TypeScript services and clients. All new date/time logic must use Luxon’s DateTime, Duration, and Interval types; existing usages of Moment.js, date-fns, Day.js, and ad-hoc utilities are deprecated and must not be introduced in new code.

Internal canonical representation will be UTC. All storage and inter-service communication will use ISO 8601 strings with explicit offset (toISO) or epoch milliseconds where appropriate; no locale-formatted strings will be persisted or transmitted. Parsing must use explicit constructors (e.g., fromISO, fromMillis, fromObject) with an explicitly specified zone when not UTC.

User-facing presentation will respect user-configured locale and IANA time zone; when unavailable, the system time zone and default locale are used. Time zone handling will rely on the platform Intl API; environments lacking full Intl/TimeZone data must include the recommended polyfill.

A thin date adapter module will wrap Luxon usage (construction, formatting, parsing, serialization, timezone lookup) to centralize patterns, enforce conventions, and simplify a potential future migration to Temporal. The adapter will expose only approved operations and formats.

Code owners will block new dependencies on non-Luxon date libraries. Build targets will use ESM to enable tree-shaking, and lint rules will enforce the above conventions.

## Decision
Embed dynamic content directly within the app using an in-app WebView (WKWebView/WebView) that renders pre-approved, versioned HTML/CSS sourced from a headless CMS, with a secure offline cache and bundled fallback assets. Content will not open in an external browser by default; all experiences remain in-app for continuity, accessibility, and analytics.

Key elements:
- Content source: Managed via headless CMS delivering HTML (or Markdown transformed to HTML server-side) with strict templates and components.
- Security: Strict Content Security Policy, domain allowlisting, no inline scripts, no third-party JS, sanitized HTML, and disabled arbitrary navigation. Only app-provided JS bridge for limited, auditable actions.
- Offline and resilience: Content is versioned and cached locally with integrity checks; critical content is also bundled at build time for zero-day availability. Cache invalidation is controlled via ETags and semantic versioning.
- UX consistency: Shared design system via CSS tokens to match native UI; typography, spacing, and theming aligned with platform.
- Telemetry and A/B: In-app analytics and feature flags govern content variants; experiments configured in CMS/flag service without app releases.
- Accessibility and performance: WCAG-compliant templates, reduced motion support, lazy-loading of media, and prefetching for common paths.
- Fallbacks: If CMS unreachable or integrity checks fail, render bundled content; on critical failure, provide minimal native message with retry.

## Decision

We will deliver a frontend-only application with no project-owned backend services. The product will be implemented as a client-side SPA/MPA deployed as static assets to a CDN with global edge caching. No SSR/SSG, custom APIs, BFF layer, webhooks, schedulers, or server-side business logic will be introduced under this scope.

All data access will occur directly from the browser to third-party or existing organization-managed APIs over HTTPS. These APIs must:
- Support CORS for our origins and granular OAuth2/OIDC (Authorization Code with PKCE) or other user-scoped token flows.
- Avoid reliance on server-held secrets; no confidential credentials will be embedded in the client.
- Provide rate limiting and abuse protections suitable for public client access.

Application state is managed client-side; durable user state leverages backend APIs, with local persistence limited to browser storage for non-sensitive, cacheable data. Secrets, privileged operations, and any flows requiring request signing remain out of scope until a backend is introduced.

Security and reliability will be enforced via CSP, SRI, dependency pinning, integrity checks, and privacy-preserving telemetry that does not require proxying. Releases use content-hashed assets and immutable caching via CI/CD to the CDN.

Edge/serverless capabilities are restricted to static asset delivery and cannot host custom logic for this product. Any need for server processing, secret management, or privileged integrations will trigger a new ADR to revisit this decision.

## Decision

Adopt Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as the primary infrastructure platform for deploying and operating containerized workloads across all environments.

- Platform mode: GKE Standard for production and performance-sensitive services; GKE Autopilot for development, test, and ephemeral environments.
- Cluster topology: Regional private clusters per environment (e.g., us-central1, europe-west1) with multi-zonal node pools for high availability. Separate clusters per environment (dev/stage/prod) and per regulatory boundary.
- Networking: VPC-native clusters with dedicated VPCs per environment, private control plane and nodes (no public IPs), Cloud NAT for egress, Ingress via GKE Gateway/HTTP(S) Load Balancer, and internal L7 for east-west where required. DNS via Cloud DNS; service discovery via Kubernetes services.
- Identity and security: Workload Identity for pod-to-GCP auth; least-privilege IAM; Binary Authorization for image provenance; Shielded/COS images; secrets via Secret Manager + CSI driver; network policies enforced; Pod Security Standards (baseline/restricted); regular CIS benchmark scans.
- Supply chain: Container images stored in Artifact Registry; builds via Cloud Build; deployment via GitOps (Argo CD) and Helm. Enforce signed images (Sigstore/COSIGN) and vulnerability scanning.
- Scalability and cost: Cluster autoscaler and HPA/VPA enabled; separate node pools for workload classes; use spot/preemptible nodes for non-critical workloads; resource quotas and requests/limits mandatory.
- Observability: Cloud Logging/Monitoring, GKE managed metrics, distributed tracing (Cloud Trace/OpenTelemetry), error reporting; SLOs defined per service with alerting via Cloud Monitoring.
- Resilience and DR: Regional clusters provide zone failure tolerance; backup/restore via Velero for cluster state and scheduled backups for persistent volumes; cross-region failover playbooks.
- IaC and governance: All infrastructure managed via Terraform; policies enforced with Policy Controller (OPA/Gatekeeper); standardized base images and Helm charts.

This decision centralizes orchestration on a managed Kubernetes service to accelerate delivery while meeting security, reliability, and compliance requirements. Configuration will be iterated via ADRs as needs evolve.

We will operate dedicated Kubernetes Ingress Controllers per product team, per cluster and environment. Each team receives its own NGINX Ingress Controller deployed via a separate Helm release in a team-scoped namespace, with a unique ingressClassName. The controller is fronted by a Service of type LoadBalancer with a dedicated public or private IP (per environment), enabling independent scaling, configuration, and maintenance windows without cross-team impact.

DNS and TLS are managed per controller: ExternalDNS is scoped to the controller’s ingress class for record management, and cert-manager issues certificates via a shared ClusterIssuer, with the option for team-specific Issuers where required (e.g., mutual TLS, custom CAs). NetworkPolicies, WAF/rate-limiting, custom annotations, and NGINX configuration snippets are controlled by the owning team and do not affect other teams.

Operational guardrails apply to each controller: resource requests/limits, HPA, PodDisruptionBudgets, liveness/readiness probes, and per-team dashboards/alerts. RBAC restricts teams to their controller and related namespaces. Blue/green and canary strategies are enabled within each team’s boundary.

Default: all net-new internet- or partner-facing workloads use a dedicated controller. Exception: small, low-risk internal services may use a shared controller upon approval, with an upgrade path to dedicated. This decision prioritizes isolation, security, performance tuning, and change autonomy, accepting the additional cost of extra LoadBalancers and operational overhead. Future migration to Gateway API will be evaluated, but does not change this per-team isolation model.

We will standardize on using Service Manager (sm) to provision and run all supported versions of assets-frontend within Build Jenkins. Each CI execution will start the required assets-frontend versions via sm-managed profiles with pinned versions and deterministic ports, perform health checks, execute builds/tests against them, and then tear them down cleanly.

Concretely:
- Define and maintain one sm profile per supported assets-frontend version (e.g., af_v2, af_v3, af_v4) with explicit version pins, env vars, and port mappings.
- In Jenkins, use a matrix/parallel stage to invoke sm --start <profile> --clean with a bounded startup timeout and health endpoint verification before running tests.
- Consume prebuilt artifacts where available; otherwise allow sm to handle build steps; no bespoke install scripts in Jenkins.
- Reserve non-overlapping port ranges per profile to enable concurrent runs; export these via Jenkins env for downstream tests.
- On completion or failure, always run sm --stop --clean to release ports and processes.
- Cache package managers (npm/yarn) at the Jenkins node level only if not provided by sm; otherwise rely solely on sm.
- Source the versions and profiles from a centrally managed sm-config repository; changes are reviewed and versioned.
- Fail fast if any profile fails to start or health checks do not pass within the SLA; mark the pipeline red.

This decision replaces ad-hoc scripts and per-job setup with a single, declarative, and auditable orchestration mechanism for all assets-frontend versions in CI.

## Decision
Adopt a single, unified external API path prefix for all client-facing HTTP endpoints exposed via the API Gateway:

- Standard prefix: /api
- Versioning: mandatory major version segment in the path, e.g., /api/v1/...; breaking changes increment the major version and create a new route tree (/api/v2/...). Minor/patch changes remain within the same major.
- No service- or team-specific path segments (e.g., /users, /orders) will appear before /api or between /api and /v{major}; internal routing to microservices is handled by the gateway.
- Environment segregation uses hostnames (e.g., api.dev.example.com, api.example.com), not path prefixes.
- GraphQL endpoint (if applicable): /api/v{major}/graphql. WebSocket upgrades use the same prefix.
- File upload/download, pagination, and filtering all live under the same versioned routes.
- Public vs. private APIs differentiated by authentication/authorization scopes, not by path. Truly internal, operator-facing endpoints are excluded from /api and placed under /_infra (e.g., /_infra/healthz, /_infra/metrics) or kept non-routed.
- Webhook receivers may be hosted under /webhooks/... (unversioned) when required by third parties; emitted webhooks reference /api/v{major} resources.

Gateway and tooling requirements:
- Configure routing, rate limiting, and observability rules to match on ^/api/v[0-9]+/.
- Generate and publish documentation from the /api/v{major} schema.
- Provide 308 redirects and Sunset/Deprecation headers for legacy prefixes; support a compatibility window of two release cycles.

This decision removes path fragmentation, simplifies client integration, and enables clear, parallel major-version lifecycles.

Adopt client-side response routing using a typed envelope and a centralized dispatch mechanism. All server responses will include a discriminated envelope {type, action, status, payload, correlationId, sequence} that is validated on receipt. The client routes responses based on the type field via a registry of feature-specific handlers. Handlers are registered lazily with the feature module (code-split) and are pure, idempotent functions that update a normalized global store (e.g., Redux/RTK or equivalent) and emit UI-level events as needed.

Side effects (follow-up requests, toasts, navigation) are executed in middleware (e.g., RTK Query, thunks, sagas/epics) to keep handlers deterministic. Ordering is enforced per correlationId/sequence; out-of-order or duplicate responses are deduplicated. Errors are routed to a default error handler with standardized parsing, retry semantics, and user-facing notifications; unhandled types fall back to a no-op logger to avoid hard failures.

Routing occurs independently of view components; components subscribe to store slices/selectors and remain unaware of transport details. Feature modules declare their response contracts and register handlers at load time via a typed map (response type → handler), enabling compile-time checks and safe dead-code elimination. Telemetry is captured at the router boundary (latency, failure rates, handler duration) with correlationId propagation.

This decision centralizes response handling on the client for resilience to API evolution, enables offline/optimistic flows, reduces UI coupling, and supports progressive delivery via lazy handler registration without blocking the render pipeline.

Adopt an automated release-candidate (RC) artifact workflow triggered by the creation of a release branch. When a branch matching release/x.y or release/x.y.z is created, CI will build, test, and publish immutable RC artifacts with semantic prerelease versions (x.y.z-rc.0), incrementing on subsequent commits to the release branch (x.y.z-rc.1, rc.2, …). Artifacts include binaries, containers, packages, and SBOMs/signatures, published to the staging registries/repositories with provenance metadata. RC builds will be gated by the same mandatory checks as main (unit/integration tests, security scans, license checks) plus release-specific validations (migration dry-runs, upgrade/downgrade tests, backward-compat checks). Promotion to GA will be a no-rebuild operation: the exact RC artifact is promoted by tag (x.y.z) after approval, ensuring bit-for-bit parity; if fixes are needed, new commits on the release branch produce the next RC. The workflow is initiated automatically on branch creation and on new commits; it can also be manually triggered (workflow_dispatch) for reruns without incrementing the rc counter unless content changes. Artifacts are retained per policy (e.g., last 5 RCs) and are clearly labeled “pre-release.” Security and compliance: artifacts are signed, SBOMs attached, attestations stored; staging registries are read-restricted; promotion requires protected environment approvals. Scope covers all supported platforms and package formats. Teams may opt out only via an approved exception. This decision replaces ad-hoc/manual RC creation and standardizes the path from branch cut to RC availability and final release.

We will eliminate long‑lived AWS access keys and adopt short‑lived, role‑based credentials across all environments.

- Workforce access: Use AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS SSO) as the single entry point with enforced MFA and least‑privilege permission sets. Session duration max 8–12 hours.
- Applications and runtime: Use IAM roles rather than static keys. For compute, use instance profiles (EC2), task roles (ECS), and IRSA (EKS). Lambda functions use execution roles. No application stores AWS keys.
- CI/CD and automation: Use OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation (e.g., GitHub Actions/Azure DevOps) to assume purpose‑built roles without storing secrets. Self‑hosted runners use instance/task roles.
- Cross‑account access: Use role assumption with external IDs and scoped trust policies. Prefer resource‑based policies where applicable.
- Secrets management: Store non‑AWS secrets in AWS Secrets Manager/SSM Parameter Store with KMS encryption. Do not commit secrets to VCS.
- Policy enforcement: Organization SCPs deny iam:CreateAccessKey for workforce users and block inline/admin policies. Config rules and detective controls alert on any access keys created or used.
- Break‑glass: A time‑boxed, highly privileged role requires secondary approval and is logged; no persistent keys are issued.
- Monitoring and audit: CloudTrail, Access Analyzer, and GuardDuty enabled org‑wide; all role assumptions and credential usage are logged to a centralized account with alerts on anomalies.

This decision standardizes secure, auditable, least‑privilege, short‑lived credentials and removes static key sprawl.

We will use releases.wikimedia.org as the single, authoritative host for all official release tarballs of this project. Effective with the next tagged release:
- All release artifacts (source tarballs, vendor bundles if applicable) will be published under releases.wikimedia.org/<project>/<version>/ with immutable files once published.
- Each release will include SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.asc, plus detached GPG signatures for every tarball using the Wikimedia Release Engineering signing key.
- Only tagged, GA releases and security point releases are hosted; nightly, CI, or snapshot builds are excluded.
- Publication is automated via the Release Engineering pipeline; manual uploads are prohibited except in documented emergency procedures.
- Retention policy: all supported releases retained; historical, unsupported releases retained for archival integrity unless legal/security requirements mandate removal.
- Backwards compatibility: existing distribution channels (e.g., GitHub/GitLab “release archives”, package registries) will no longer host tarballs. They will reference releases.wikimedia.org and, where possible, provide links or redirects. A deprecation window of one release cycle will be observed.
- Consumers and downstream packagers must fetch from releases.wikimedia.org and verify checksums/signatures.
- Directory structure, file naming, and metadata follow MediaWiki/RelEng conventions to support mirroring and caching. No executable install scripts are served.
- Access control, monitoring, and incident response follow the platform’s standard policies. Availability expectations inherit releases.wikimedia.org SLAs, with mirrors encouraged but not authoritative.

We will prioritize familiar, widely adopted, and organization-supported tools to minimize delivery risk, improve developer productivity, and simplify operations. The baseline stack is:

- Language/Runtime: TypeScript (Node.js LTS) for services; Python 3 LTS for data/automation; Bash for ops scripts.
- Frameworks: NestJS/Express (backend), React with TypeScript (frontend).
- Data: PostgreSQL (primary OLTP), Redis (caching/queues).
- Messaging/Async: Kafka (event streaming) or SQS/SNS where managed equivalents are available.
- Packaging/Runtime: Docker containers; Kubernetes (managed: EKS/GKE/AKS) for orchestration.
- Cloud/Infra: AWS as primary; Terraform for IaC; Helm for K8s deployments.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions; GitHub for SCM; Renovate/Dependabot for dependencies.
- Observability: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/Grafana, Loki/ELK, and CloudWatch for managed integrations.
- AuthN/Z: OIDC/OAuth2 via the existing IdP (e.g., Azure AD/Okta).
- Testing: Jest/Playwright; pytest for Python.

Constraints and governance:

- Prefer LTS releases and managed services. Avoid introducing new languages, runtimes, or core platforms without an approved RFC.
- New tools require: problem statement, alternatives considered, risk/ops assessment, ownership plan, and a time-bounded pilot; Architecture sign-off is mandatory.
- Reuse existing patterns, templates, and modules before adopting new libraries.
- Esoteric or single-maintainer tools are prohibited for critical paths.
- Security, compliance, and SRE onboarding are required before production use of any new tool.
- Where gaps exist, extend the approved stack first (plugins/add-ons) before adding categories.

Transition:

- Replace nonstandard tools opportunistically during scheduled maintenance/refactors.
- Migrations must include rollback plans and documentation aligned with our engineering playbooks.

We will open selected repositories to the public under a phased open-source program to increase transparency, collaboration, and adoption.

Scope
- Open-source the core SDKs, CLIs, reference services, and example apps.
- Keep proprietary integrations, internal tooling, and data-model migrations private.
- Split mixed repositories where needed to isolate public modules.

Licensing and IP
- Apply Apache-2.0 license by default; note exceptions per repo.
- Complete legal provenance review and third-party license compliance.
- Add NOTICE files and SPDX headers.

Preparation
- Remove secrets, credentials, and tenant data; rotate affected keys.
- Rewrite history as needed; run secret scans and SCA/SAST before publishing.
- Normalize repo structure with README, LICENSE, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY, and CHANGELOG.

Governance
- Use a public GitHub organization with protected branches and required reviews.
- Establish MAINTAINERS and CODEOWNERS; adopt DCO for contributions.
- Define semantic versioning and release cadence; publish roadmap and RFC process.

Security and Quality
- Provide coordinated vulnerability disclosure and private reporting channel.
- Generate SBOMs and provenance attestations in CI; sign releases.
- Maintain backward compatibility guarantees and deprecation policy.

Operations
- Migrate CI to public runners where appropriate; keep sensitive jobs internal.
- Track issues publicly; mirror internal work items when necessary.
- Document support tiers and SLAs for community vs. commercial users.

Timeline
- Execute in three waves over two quarters, starting with libraries, then services, then tooling.

We will maintain the product wiki in a dedicated repository and consume it from the main code repository as a Git submodule.

- Location: add the submodule at /docs/wiki in the main repo, pointing to repo <ORG>/<PROJECT>-wiki on branch main.
- Versioning: the submodule will be pinned to explicit commits; releases will update the submodule to the corresponding tagged commit to align docs with released code.
- Workflow:
  - Contributors making documentation changes propose PRs to the wiki repo.
  - When a docs change needs to accompany code, the code PR will include a submodule pointer update to the intended wiki commit.
  - Release managers must bump the submodule pointer to the release tag and include it in the release PR.
- Bootstrap: cloning the main repo requires --recurse-submodules or running scripts/bootstrap (which runs git submodule init && git submodule update --remote as appropriate).
- CI/CD:
  - Validate that the submodule pointer is not dirty and references an existing commit on the allowed branch.
  - For release builds, fail if the submodule is not pointing at a tagged wiki commit matching the release.
  - Build and publish the documentation site by reading from /docs/wiki; preview environments include the submodule contents.
- Access control: the wiki repo has its own review policy; write access is scoped to docs maintainers. The main repo only tracks the pointer.
- Developer experience: editors and IDEs reference the submodule path for local preview. Pre-commit hooks warn on detached or uninitialized submodules.
- Dependency policy: no nested submodules within the wiki. Large binaries are managed via LFS in the wiki repo if needed.

We will standardize on named exports and a single public barrel per module/package to enforce a clear, stable, and tree-shakeable API surface.

- All source modules use named exports only; default exports are prohibited.
- Each package exposes a single public entry point via src/index.ts that re-exports the supported API; no deep or path-internal imports are allowed by consumers.
- package.json will define an explicit exports map with subpath entries only for documented surface areas. We will publish dual ESM and CJS entry points ("exports" with module and require conditions) and type declarations via "types".
- Internal files are private by default (not listed in exports) and may change without notice.
- Side-effectful modules are avoided; where necessary, they are isolated and marked in package.json sideEffects to preserve correct bundling.
- Tree-shaking is a requirement; all public APIs must be re-exported as live bindings to preserve correctness under bundlers.
- Breaking changes to the exported surface require a major version; deprecations are staged with codemods where feasible.
- Linting rules (e.g., no-default-export, no-restricted-imports) and CI checks will enforce no deep imports and no default exports.
- Documentation will include a single “how to import” section per package, reflecting the exports map, with examples for ESM and CJS.
- Transitional support: existing default exports will be re-exposed as named exports and flagged deprecated for one minor release before removal.

Implement “special pages” via a declarative SpecialPageRegistry that maps explicit route patterns to dedicated handlers/components, with per-route metadata controlling auth, caching, SSR/SSG mode, and SEO. Special routes take precedence over CMS/content routes and wildcards to avoid collisions and ensure predictable behavior.

Each special page is a self-contained module (or package) exposing:
- route definition (exact path or pattern, i18n variants)
- handler/controller (server) and/or view/component (client)
- capabilities metadata: requiresAuth, cachePolicy (CDN, surrogate, no-store), renderMode (SSR, SSG, ISR), sitemap/robots flags, rate limits, feature flags

Rendering strategy:
- SSR for data-dependent or personalized pages (e.g., /search, /settings).
- SSG/ISR for stable pages (e.g., /help, /about, legal) with incremental revalidation hooks.
- Non-HTML machine endpoints (e.g., /sitemap.xml, /status, /robots.txt) served via lightweight server handlers.

Extensibility is achieved by allowing internal modules or plugins to register entries with the SpecialPageRegistry at startup. The router composes the registry into high-priority routes before mounting generic/CMS routes. Route conflicts are detected at build/startup and fail fast.

Cross-cutting concerns are enforced centrally using registry metadata:
- Auth/authorization guards and CSRF/session checks
- Caching headers and surrogate keys
- Localization (path prefixes, locale negotiation)
- Observability (structured logs, traces, page-level metrics)
- A/B and feature flags
- Security headers and content policies

Testing requirements:
- Contract tests for each registered route (auth, cache, SEO tags)
- Snapshot/render tests for SSR/SSG outputs
- Performance budgets for SSR handlers

Deployment:
- Build system emits static assets for SSG pages and registers SSR handlers.
- CDN rules honor cachePolicy from metadata.

This approach yields clarity, safety, and incremental addition of special pages without entangling them with CMS or generic routing.

Adopt ISO 8601 as the sole canonical representation of dates and date-times across all systems and interfaces.

- API contracts: All request/response payloads must use ISO 8601 date formats. Use YYYY-MM-DD for dates and RFC 3339-compliant timestamps (e.g., 2026-01-23T14:30:00Z). Include timezone as “Z” (UTC) or explicit numeric offset; omit ambiguous local times.
- Storage: Persist timestamps in UTC using database-native time types with timezone (e.g., TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE) where available; otherwise store normalized ISO 8601 strings with “Z”.
- Internal services: Normalize all incoming date/time inputs to UTC upon ingestion; propagate and compute in UTC internally.
- Logging/audit: Emit ISO 8601 UTC timestamps with millisecond precision and “Z”.
- Validation: Reject non-ISO or locale-specific formats. Allow parsing of ISO 8601 with offsets but normalize to UTC. Require zero-padded fields and 24-hour clock.
- Precision: Support up to millisecond precision (e.g., .123). Higher precision may be truncated or rounded per subsystem policy but must remain valid ISO 8601.
- UI: Display formats may be localized for users, but any data interchange (APIs, exports, imports, integrations, webhooks, config) must remain ISO 8601. Inputs from UI are converted to UTC ISO 8601 before persistence.
- Backward compatibility: For legacy integrations, accept previous formats only at adapter boundaries and transform to ISO 8601; no new non-ISO formats permitted.

## Decision
Adopt a progressive delivery strategy on Kubernetes with the following standards:
- Default deployment method: rolling updates for low-risk, stateless services.
- High-risk, user-facing changes: canary releases with automated progressive traffic shifting and guardrails (error rate, latency, saturation) enforced via Argo Rollouts/Flagger and service mesh traffic management.
- Zero-downtime cutovers for critical/stateful components: blue-green deployments reserved for major version upgrades or breaking changes, with explicit readiness and data backfill validation before switch.
- Database changes: expand-and-contract migrations, gated behind feature flags; no destructive changes without confirmed cutover and backout plan. Deploy app changes before schema contraction.
- Environments and promotion: dev → staging → production; all releases pass automated build, security scans, integration tests, and smoke tests. Production rollouts proceed regionally/phased.
- CI/CD and control: GitOps with Argo CD; all changes declared in versioned IaC (Terraform/Helm). Promotion is pull-request driven with mandatory reviews and change approvals.
- Observability and release gates: SLO-based canary analysis using metrics, logs, and traces; rollouts auto-halt and auto-rollback on policy breaches. Feature flags control exposure and enable instant disablement.
- Rollback strategy: immediate rollback to previous ReplicaSet/version or blue environment; database rollbacks rely on feature reversion and reversible migrations.
- Availability and maintenance: deploy during low-traffic windows when possible; no global DNS flips without prior regional validation.
This strategy balances safety, speed, and operability while providing deterministic rollback and auditable change control.

We will enforce a stateless application-tier architecture. All business state must be externalized to managed state stores; no in-memory or sticky-session state is permitted in services or functions. Durable state (source of truth) will be persisted in the primary relational database; ephemeral/derived state (caching, rate limits, feature flags) will use a distributed cache. Long-running workflow state will be managed via a durable orchestration mechanism (e.g., workflow engine) rather than ad hoc timers or background threads.

Clients are the only allowed holders of local UI state; any server-observable state must be persisted or recoverable on the server side. All mutating operations must be idempotent and accept idempotency keys to support retries. State transitions will be modeled explicitly with versioned domain events; outbox pattern is required for reliable publication. Read models may be denormalized but must be rebuildable from the source of truth.

Inter-service calls must be stateless and retry-safe; no affinity routing. Authentication is token-based; session data is stored server-side only when required by compliance, using centralized stores. Configuration and secrets are treated as state and managed via the configuration service and secret manager with versioning and rollback.

Observability of state is mandatory: every state change is traceable with correlation IDs, audit logs, and metrics. Data residency and retention requirements are enforced at the store level via policies. This requirement is gate-checked in design reviews and CI to prevent introduction of stateful service logic.

We will harden Sprout’s pre-request lifecycle and traffic gating to prevent user-impacting failures before it can accept requests:

- Introduce an explicit startup phase with deterministic self-checks (config load/validation, schema migrations if any, critical dependency reachability, certificate/key presence, ports binding).
- Expose separate endpoints/signals: liveness (process health) and readiness (end-to-end ability to serve). Readiness remains false until all startup checks pass.
- Integrate with orchestration and load balancing: use startupProbe, livenessProbe, and readinessProbe; only register instance in service discovery and attach to the load balancer once ready; enable outlier detection to eject unhealthy instances automatically.
- Implement fail-fast with controlled degradation: if a non-critical dependency is unavailable, start in drain mode (readiness=false, no traffic) instead of crashing; for critical dependencies, apply bounded exponential backoff during init with a max wall-clock timeout before failing the pod/VM and alerting.
- Make initialization idempotent and retryable; cache validated immutable configuration locally to allow cold start without the config server when safe.
- Provide a maintenance “safe mode” flag to bring Sprout up for diagnostics (no traffic, debug enabled) without participating in routing.
- Emit structured startup telemetry (per-check status, timings, failure reasons) and wire alerts on repeated init failures or prolonged unready states.
- Update deployment policy: rolling updates gated on readiness; canary new builds behind traffic shadowing where possible; automatic rollback on readiness regression.

This decision ensures Sprout never accepts traffic until it is truly ready, avoids crash loops due to transient dependencies, and improves observability and operability of pre-request failures.

## Decision
We will update the threebot deployer flist to a new, reproducible, and security-hardened build with pinned dependencies and immutable references, while preserving backward compatibility for existing deployments.

- Build: Create a new flist derived from the latest stable base image with minimal footprint; pin all system and Python/package dependencies; remove deprecated/unused tooling; enable multi-arch support where applicable.
- Versioning and immutability: Publish the flist under a semver tag and immutable digest; deployment manifests will reference the digest only. Retain the previous stable version (n-1) for rollback; deprecate older versions with a scheduled EOL.
- Signing and provenance: Sign the flist and publish SBOM; store build metadata (git SHA, dependency locks) to ensure reproducibility and auditability.
- Security and compliance: Integrate vulnerability scanning (e.g., Trivy) and policy gates in CI; fail builds on high/critical CVEs; apply minimal runtime capabilities and read-only root where feasible.
- CI/CD: Introduce a deterministic build pipeline that produces, scans, signs, and publishes the flist to the registry; releases occur on tagged commits only; no nightly rebuilds without code or dependency changes.
- Backward compatibility: Preserve external interfaces and deployment parameters; migrate runtime configuration to environment variables with defaults matching current behavior; data remains persisted outside the flist.
- Rollout: Use a staged rollout (canary <10%, then progressive) and monitor health metrics; provide a one-click rollback to the previous digest.
- Documentation: Update deployment references, changelog, and migration notes; communicate timeline and EOL for superseded flists.

We will adopt explicit version-based directories and paths for all public-facing artifacts (APIs, docs, UI bundles, CLIs), using semantic versioning.

- Path scheme:
  - Major versioned root: /v{MAJOR}/… is the canonical public path.
  - Optional minor/patch pinning: /v{MAJOR}.{MINOR}/… and /v{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH}/… are supported for consumers requiring stricter pinning.
  - Unversioned paths are disallowed for public consumption; internal use may reference “/current” only during build.

- Directory layout in repos and build artifacts:
  - /dist/v{MAJOR}/, /dist/v{MAJOR}.{MINOR}/, /dist/v{MAJOR}.{MINOR}.{PATCH}/ produced per release.
  - A “latest” pointer per major (symlink or manifest) maps to the highest MINOR.PATCH for that MAJOR; not publicly exposed as a stable URL.

- API routing:
  - Gateways route requests strictly by prefix (/v1/, /v2/). No implicit upgrades across majors.
  - Minor/patch releases must be backward compatible within a major. Breaking changes require a new major.

- Deprecation and EOL:
  - Support window per major is defined; new deployments default to the highest supported major.
  - Deprecation headers and scheduled removal communicated; 301 redirects permitted only within a major.

- Build and deployment:
  - CI tags releases with semver and publishes to versioned directories.
  - CDN caching keyed by full version; cache-busting via patch increments.
  - Infrastructure-as-code parametrizes MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH to avoid manual path edits.

- Observability:
  - Logs and metrics include resolved version from the path.
  - Error budgets and SLOs tracked per major.

This decision ensures deterministic consumption, safe evolution, and parallel support of versions without path conflicts.

Adopt ECMAScript Modules (ESM) as the default module system across the codebase.

- Scope: All application code and new libraries target ESM. Minimum Node.js runtime is 18+. Browsers are targeted via bundlers that support ESM.
- Packaging:
  - Applications: ESM-only.
  - Published libraries: dual publish with ESM as primary and CJS fallback via conditional exports.
  - package.json: set "type": "module", define "exports" with "import" (ESM) and "require" (CJS) conditions, include "types" for TypeScript.
- File conventions: Use .js/.ts under "type":"module". Use .cjs only where CJS interop is unavoidable. Avoid default exports in libraries; prefer named exports.
- TypeScript: Set "module": "ESNext" and "moduleResolution": "node16" or "bundler". Emit ESM. Preserve JSX/TS as needed for bundlers.
- Interop:
  - Use import/export and dynamic import() exclusively.
  - For CJS-only dependencies, use createRequire from module.
  - Replace __dirname/__filename with dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)).
  - Import JSON via import assertions (assert { type: "json" }).
- Runtime features: Allow top-level await in applications; avoid it in library public APIs to preserve compatibility.
- Tooling:
  - Testing: Prefer Node test runner or Vitest; configure Jest for ESM only if necessary.
  - Linting: ESLint with sourceType: "module".
  - Bundling/SSR: Ensure Vite/Webpack/Rollup are configured for ESM inputs and tree-shaking.
- Migration: Convert modules incrementally; keep .cjs shims where required during transition; update imports, build, and CI. Deprecate CJS-only entry points after one major release cycle.

We will introduce stable, tool-resolved aliases for our source and data packages and mandate their use across all runtime targets and tooling.

- Define two top-level logical packages: src (application code) and data (datasets, schemas, fixtures, generated artifacts). Expose them via canonical import aliases (for example, @src/... and @data/...) rather than relative or project-root–relative paths.
- Configure the build and runtime to resolve these aliases consistently (compiler/transpiler path mapping, bundler/module resolver, test runner, and REPL/CLI). The canonical paths are the single source of truth; relative imports into src or data are prohibited.
- Version the data package independently. Treat schemas and generated data contracts as API: changes require semantic versioning and changelogs. Data is read-only at runtime; mutations occur only in build/generation steps.
- Provide editors/IDEs with alias awareness (language server config). Add lint rules to forbid deep relative imports that cross package boundaries.
- Ensure cross-environment parity: server, client, worker, and scripting environments must resolve the same aliases. CI validates resolution and import hygiene.
- Supply thin adapter modules for legacy paths and deprecate them with a defined sunset period.
- Document the alias conventions and update project templates. New modules must be published under the aliasified packages.

## Decision
We will decouple event production from state mutation by adopting an event-intent architecture backed by a single source of truth state store (reactive, immutable). UI/event listeners will be thin: they capture user/system events, derive intents/commands, and dispatch them to the domain layer. State changes will occur exclusively via reducers/use-cases reacting to these intents.

Key rules:
- State ownership: A centralized store holds application state. Components consume state via selectors and never mutate it directly.
- Listener purity: Event listeners must avoid side effects and not read captured/stale state. When state is needed to compute an intent, it must be read via current selectors at handling time, not captured in closures.
- Lifecycle and cleanup: Listeners are registered on mount/initialization and removed on unmount/teardown. No anonymous inline listeners that cannot be removed. Stable references (or controller objects) are required.
- Performance: Prefer event delegation on high-churn DOM trees. Apply standardized debounce/throttle utilities for high-frequency events. Batch state updates to minimize re-renders.
- Concurrency and ordering: Intents are queued and processed serially within the store to ensure deterministic state transitions. Long-running effects are executed via an effects layer with cancellation support.
- Error handling and telemetry: All listener-to-intent dispatches are observable. Failures in effects must not mutate state; they dispatch error intents. Instrument dispatch rates and handler latencies.
- Memory safety: Avoid listeners inside loops without cleanup; use WeakRef/AbortController where supported. Static analysis/lint rules enforce registration/cleanup patterns.
- Testing: Listeners are unit-tested as mapping functions (event → intent). Reducers/use-cases are tested separately (intent → state).

This decision standardizes event handling, prevents stale state bugs and leaks, and ensures predictable, testable state evolution.

We will decommission Spring Cloud Netflix components and adopt Spring Cloud Kubernetes to align the microservices platform with Kubernetes-native capabilities.

- Service discovery: Retire Eureka; use Kubernetes Services and DNS for discovery. Clients will rely on service names and Spring Cloud Kubernetes Discovery where needed.
- Client-side load balancing: Remove Ribbon; adopt Spring Cloud LoadBalancer backed by Kubernetes endpoints and rely on kube-proxy/IPVS for distribution.
- API gateway/routing: Replace Zuul with Kubernetes Ingress (NGINX or Envoy) or a managed API gateway; consolidate routing, TLS termination, and rate limiting at the ingress layer.
- Resilience: Replace Hystrix with Resilience4j integrated via Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker.
- Configuration: Use Spring Cloud Kubernetes Config to externalize configuration via ConfigMaps and Secrets with reload support (Config Watcher) for selected services.
- Leadership/coordination: Use Spring Cloud Kubernetes Leader Election where required.
- Observability: Standardize on Kubernetes-native telemetry (Prometheus scraping, OpenTelemetry traces, Grafana dashboards) and Spring Boot actuators.
- Security: Manage secrets via Kubernetes Secrets or external KMS; enforce mTLS and policy via ingress or service mesh if adopted later.
- Deployment model: Containerize all services and run them on Kubernetes; remove Eureka server and Netflix infra services from the runtime and CI/CD pipelines.
- Backward compatibility: Provide a transitional profile supporting both discovery modes during rollout; cut over service-by-service with canary releases and blue/green strategies.
- Deliverables: Updated dependencies, configuration, Helm/manifest changes, operational runbooks, and deprecation of Netflix OSS artifacts.

## Decision

Adopt the cloud provider’s managed secrets service as the single source of truth for all infrastructure and application secrets (AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store with KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP Secret Manager), with encryption at rest via customer-managed keys and TLS in transit. Disallow hardcoded or long-lived secrets in source code, container images, AMIs, config files, or Terraform variables/state.

Access to secrets will be granted via least-privilege identities and short-lived, federated credentials:
- Workloads use instance profiles/managed identities or OIDC/IAM Roles for Service Accounts (Kubernetes) to fetch secrets at runtime.
- CI/CD pipelines use OIDC-based federation to assume narrowly scoped roles; no secrets are stored in the CI system.
- Human access is SSO-based and logged; break-glass access is controlled, time-bound, and audited.

Rotation will be automated where supported (database credentials, API keys) using native rotation features or automation (Lambdas/Functions/Cloud Run Jobs). All access and rotation events are audited via cloud logs and KMS key usage logs, with alerts on anomalies.

For Kubernetes, the External Secrets Operator will synchronize from the secrets manager to namespace-scoped Kubernetes Secrets; pods access secrets via service-account-bound identities. For VMs and serverless, secrets are fetched at startup/runtime via the provider SDK/sidecars; bootstrap secrets are minimized and fetched just-in-time.

Terraform will reference secrets via data sources and will not store secret values in state; the state backend is encrypted and access-controlled. Local development uses CLI-based retrieval to ephemeral .env files ignored by VCS; secret scanning is enforced in repos and pipelines.

A phased migration will replace existing embedded secrets with references to the managed store, rotate/revoke legacy credentials, and enable continuous monitoring and compliance reporting. This approach centralizes control, enforces least privilege, enables automated rotation, and reduces secret sprawl and leakage risk.

## Decision

We will treat attributes as unique keys within a given scope and prohibit repeated attributes in authoring and persisted representations.

- Data model: Attributes are represented as a map/dictionary keyed by attribute name, enforcing uniqueness at compile/runtime.
- Validation: Schema and ingestion layers will reject payloads/documents containing duplicate attribute names for the same entity/element. In strict mode this is a hard error; in compatibility mode the last occurrence wins and a structured warning is emitted.
- Parsing/serialization: Parsers normalize to a single value per attribute. If duplicates are encountered in compatibility mode, only the final occurrence (right-most) is retained; serialization will never output duplicates.
- API behavior: Write operations that attempt to set the same attribute multiple times in a single request are invalid. Read operations guarantee a single deterministic value per attribute.
- Tooling and governance: Linters and CI checks enforce uniqueness pre-merge. Schemas/specs explicitly mark attributes as non-repeatable; where multiplicity is required, a collection-valued attribute (list/set) must be defined instead of repeating the same scalar attribute.
- Backward compatibility: A temporary feature flag enables compatibility mode for legacy producers for one deprecation cycle, with metrics and logging to identify offenders.
- Observability: Duplicate detections are counted and surfaced via dashboards and alerts to drive remediation.

This decision eliminates ambiguity, improves determinism and security, and simplifies caching, diffing, and change detection by ensuring one authoritative value per attribute.

## Decision

Adopt a standardized, measurable quality-level framework for all software assets (services, libraries, CLIs, data pipelines) with four tiers:

- L0 Experimental: no guarantees; not for critical paths.
- L1 Bronze (Beta): basic reliability and docs; suitable for limited internal use.
- L2 Silver (Production-Ready): meets core production criteria.
- L3 Gold (Mission-Critical): highest rigor for critical paths and external exposure.

Each level requires meeting explicit, auditable criteria across these dimensions:
- Reliability/SLOs: L1 none; L2 ≥99.9% availability with error budgets; L3 ≥99.95% (or domain-specific), documented SLOs and incident response.
- Performance: defined P95/P99 latency and throughput per API; load test evidence for L2/L3.
- Security: no open High/Critical vulns; secrets management; static/dynamic scans; threat model (L2+) and pen test/sign-off (L3).
- Testing: unit/integration/e2e; code coverage targets (e.g., L1 ≥60%, L2 ≥75%, L3 ≥85%) and mutation testing (L3 where applicable).
- Observability: structured logs, metrics, traces; SLO-based alerts; runbooks; on-call rotations (L2+/L3).
- Reliability engineering: graceful degradation, circuit breakers, retries, timeouts, chaos/resilience tests (L3).
- Data/Schema: versioning, backward compatibility policy; migrations with rollbacks.
- Compliance/Privacy: DSR handling, data classification, retention; DPIA where needed (L2+/L3).
- Documentation: architecture, APIs, ADRs, SLOs, runbooks, onboarding guides.
- Operability: blue/green or canary deploys (L2+), rollback procedures, capacity planning.

Governance:
- Each component declares target level; CI/CD quality gates enforce criteria.
- Promotion requires evidence via standardized checklist and automated reports; exceptions need risk acceptance by product + architecture.
- Levels and criteria reviewed quarterly; status visible on a centralized dashboard. Components below L2 cannot join critical paths or external SLAs.

We will ship a single top-level executable with hierarchical subcommands as the primary CLI interface. The root command provides global concerns (help, version, auth/context, logging, output format), while subcommands implement discrete operations.

- Binary: a single entrypoint (e.g., acme).
- Structure: acme <subcommand> [subcommand] [flags]; prefer verb-noun where it improves readability and aligns with domain (e.g., acme project create, acme project list, acme deploy run).
- Global flags: defined at the root and inherited (e.g., --config, --profile, --output=json|yaml|text, --quiet, --verbose, --no-color, --timeout).
- Subcommand flags: local to subcommand; no overlap with globals.
- Consistency: POSIX-style short/long flags; kebab-case names; predictable pluralization; stable ordering; machine-readable output via --output.
- Discoverability: built-in help for every node (acme help, acme <cmd> --help); examples and flag defaults shown; top-level synopsis summarized.
- Completion: first-class shell completion (bash/zsh/fish/pwsh) and man pages generated from command metadata.
- Extensibility: plugin model via acme-<name> executables on PATH that appear as subcommands; isolated versioning; namespaced to avoid collisions.
- Backward compatibility: semantic versioning of CLI; additive changes favored; deprecations announced with warnings and grace periods; aliases may be added but not removed without deprecation.
- Exit codes: non-zero on failures; distinct codes for common error classes; no mixed stdout/stderr (human-readable to stdout; errors to stderr).
- Non-interactive by default; interactive prompts gated behind explicit flags or TTY detection; all prompts overridable via flags/env.
- Configuration precedence: flags > environment > config file.

We will implement application search using PostgreSQL’s native capabilities rather than introducing an external search engine. Specifically:
- Full-text search will use tsvector/tsquery with a materialized tsvector column per searchable entity, maintained via BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE triggers. We will apply language-specific dictionaries (default: english; fallback: simple) and the unaccent extension for diacritics-insensitive search.
- Relevance ranking will use ts_rank_cd with weighted document sections (A/B/C/D) to prioritize titles, tags, and key fields. Queries will use websearch_to_tsquery for user-friendly syntax; plainto_tsquery for simple terms.
- Indexing will use GIN on the tsvector column and pg_trgm (gin_trgm_ops) indexes on selected text fields to support prefix and fuzzy search (e.g., autocomplete, tolerant matching). Autocomplete will use trigram-based similarity with configurable thresholds; exact matches remain indexed via FTS.
- Multilingual content will be supported by storing language code per record and generating tsvector with the appropriate configuration; where uncertain, “simple” will be used.
- Operationally, we will add the necessary extensions (unaccent, pg_trgm), columns, triggers, and indexes via migrations. We will monitor index bloat and vacuum/analyze; reindex concurrently as needed. Backups and RLS policies remain unchanged.
- Constraints: no cross-document aggregations/faceting beyond SQL capabilities; horizontal scaling is bounded by the primary database. If query volume, latency (>P95 150 ms), or corpus size (>10M docs) exceed targets, or if advanced features (e.g., complex facets, synonyms at scale) become required, we will revisit adopting a dedicated search engine (e.g., OpenSearch).

We will standardize on Luigi as the workflow orchestration framework for all batch extract/transform/load (ETL) pipelines in the data platform. Luigi will be used to define tasks, dependencies, and idempotent outputs (Targets), and to manage execution ordering, retries, and backfills. This decision applies to batch, file- and database-oriented workflows; streaming or event-driven pipelines are out of scope.

Implementation:
- Define each ETL step as a Luigi Task with explicit Targets (e.g., S3/GCS files, tables, checkpoints) to guarantee idempotency and incremental recomputation.
- Use the Luigi Central Scheduler for dependency resolution and task state; deploy scheduler as a managed service with persistent storage.
- Execute workers in Kubernetes as CronJobs for scheduled workflows and as Jobs for ad-hoc/backfill runs; package tasks as Docker images.
- Manage configuration via environment-specific config files and secrets managers; avoid hard-coding credentials.
