- Correlation, idempotency, and trace identifiers are distinct from entity IDs and follow their own schemes.
- No encoding of domain meaning or timestamps beyond the inherent properties of UUIDv7.

Migration:
- Existing records with heterogeneous ID formats will be migrated to the canonical type and representation; dual-read/dual-write may be used during transition.
- Public documentation and API contracts will specify the canonical format and validation rules.

We will require every externally exposed API operation to declare and enforce its version explicitly, with no implicit or global default. For HTTP/REST endpoints, the major version is part of the URL path (/v{major}), and the operation’s precise semantic version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is also declared in the contract (OpenAPI) via an operation-level extension and emitted in responses via the X-API-Version header. Requests must include a versioned path; unversioned calls will be rejected by the API gateway. Minor and patch updates are backward compatible within the same major version; breaking changes require a new major version path. Each operation can evolve independently; introducing a breaking change to one operation does not force a new major for the entire API surface.

The API gateway will route by major version and support side-by-side deployment of versions. Deprecation is managed per operation with a published policy: introduce new version, mark prior version as Deprecated via response headers and documentation, maintain for the deprecation window, then sunset with clear error messaging. SDKs and clients must pin to a specific major version and may opt-in to minor/patch within that major.

Internal service-to-service contracts follow the same rule (per-operation versioning) using RPC method options or headers; service registries will treat versions as distinct routes. Documentation, monitoring, and alerting are version-aware, and CI/CD pipelines validate that operations are explicitly versioned and that backward compatibility guarantees are met within a major version.

## Decision
- Centralize application configuration in a dedicated private Git repository with per-environment directories and strict branch protections; all changes require pull requests and code-owner review.
- Grant machine access using short‑lived, least‑privileged credentials via Git provider OIDC/JWT federation (no long‑lived PATs or static deploy keys). CI/CD pipelines obtain time‑boxed read scopes to the specific repo/paths needed.
- Deny direct write access from workloads and pipelines to the configuration repo; only humans via SSO and approved PRs can modify configuration.
- Runtime services do not clone the repo directly in-cluster. Configuration is resolved at build/deploy time: 
  - Non-secret config is vendored into artifacts per environment or mounted via a config delivery layer (e.g., artifact registry or config service) sourced from the repo at deploy time. 
  - Secret values are not stored in the repo; only references/templates are. Secrets are materialized from the enterprise secret manager (e.g., Vault/SSM/Key Vault) during deploy/runtime.
- Enforce path-based authorization to limit each pipeline/service to its environment scope (e.g., prod vs non-prod) and read-only permissions.
- Enable comprehensive auditability: PR history, required checks, signed commits, protected tags/releases, and Git provider audit logs. Periodically reconcile actual permissions against policy.
- Implement automated credential hygiene: minimum scopes, short expirations, rotation policies, and revocation on job completion; block self-hosted runners from exfiltrating tokens.
- Provide a documented escalation path for temporary elevated access with time-bound approvals and automatic rollback.
- Integrate policy-as-code (e.g., OPA) in CI to validate config schema, drift, and environment constraints before merge and before deploy.

We will adopt NestJS (TypeScript) as the primary backend framework for all new services and for incremental modernization of existing Node.js services. NestJS will be used to build HTTP (REST) and GraphQL APIs, background workers, and (when needed) microservices, standardizing on its modular architecture, dependency injection, and decorators for consistency and speed of development.

Key selections and conventions:
- Runtime/platform: Node.js LTS (aligned with NestJS support matrix).
- HTTP server: Fastify adapter for improved throughput and lower overhead.
- API styles: REST (default) with OpenAPI via @nestjs/swagger; GraphQL via @nestjs/graphql (code-first) where schema evolution benefits apply.
- Data access: Prefer Prisma for relational stores; TypeORM permitted for legacy alignment; repository pattern abstracted behind application services.
- Validation/serialization: class-validator and class-transformer with whitelisting, transform, and strict DTO usage at boundaries.
- AuthN/Z: Passport strategies (JWT as default), role/permission guards, and CSRF where applicable.
- Configuration and secrets: @nestjs/config with schema validation; environment-based config and centralized secrets management.
- Caching and sessions: cache-manager with Redis; short-lived HTTP caching where appropriate.
- Messaging and async: BullMQ for jobs/queues; Nest microservices (e.g., NATS/Kafka) for inter-service messaging when required.
- Observability: Pino logger, structured request logging, global exception filters, metrics and tracing via OpenTelemetry, health checks via @nestjs/terminus.
- Testing: Jest with unit tests on providers, e2e tests on modules via testing module; Testcontainers for integration with infra deps.
- Project structure: domain-centric modules, clear layering (controllers -> services -> repositories), shared libraries for cross-cutting concerns, strict ESLint/Prettier rules.
- Deployment: containerized services with graceful shutdown hooks and readiness/liveness probes.

This decision establishes NestJS as the standardized backend foundation to maximize developer productivity, maintainability, and operational reliability.

Adopt a conditional naming convention that uses product prefixes only when needed to disambiguate artifacts across products or shared environments. Within a single product boundary, prefer clean, prefix-free names; introduce a product prefix when an artifact is visible outside that boundary or risks collision (e.g., shared repositories/registries, mono-repos, cloud resources, CI/CD artifacts, SDKs/libraries, containers, queues/topics).

Define and maintain a canonical registry of product prefixes (2–5 lowercase letters, kebab-case with hyphen separator). Standard pattern: <prefix>-<domain>-<component> (kebab-case). Language-specific adaptations are allowed (e.g., package namespaces) while preserving the prefix. Avoid prefixes in user-facing product/UX labels and marketing names.

Scope of enforcement: source repositories, build artifacts, container images, package names, cloud resource names, CI/CD pipelines, monitoring/alerting entities, and shared storage buckets/topics. Do not retroactively rename existing assets unless there is an active collision or compliance need; when renaming, provide deprecation windows, redirects/aliases, and migration guides.

Governance: Architecture group owns the prefix registry and approves additions through a lightweight proposal. Automation: provide linters/policies and CI checks to validate names in affected systems. This decision balances clarity and discoverability in cross-product contexts while minimizing verbosity within product-specific contexts.

## Decision
Proceed with a timeboxed experiment to introduce an xUnit-specific build target (“xunit:test”) in the CI/CD pipeline to evaluate whether dedicated xUnit execution improves test reliability, performance, and reporting over the current approach.

We will:
- Add an explicit xUnit target in the build system (e.g., Nuke/Cake/GitHub Actions) that invokes the xunit.runner (preferably via deterministic, pinned versions using .NET local tools or a locked NuGet package).
- Enable parallelization with sensible defaults and the ability to override at the suite/trait level.
- Produce machine-consumable test results (xUnit XML) and publish them as CI artifacts; integrate with the platform’s test reporting if available.
- Integrate coverage collection using coverlet (collector or console) and publish coverage in Cobertura/LCOV formats.
- Support cross-platform execution (Windows/Linux/macOS) and ensure compatibility with Dockerized runners.
- Keep the existing “dotnet test” path as a fallback target to de-risk the change.

Scope:
- Apply to projects already on xUnit; do not migrate non-xUnit test projects during the experiment.
- Run on all PRs and main branch; mark the xUnit target as required status checks only after stability is verified.

Success criteria (over two iterations):
- Deterministic, non-flaky runs with <1% intermittent failures not attributable to code.
- No increase in total test time; target equal or faster execution versus baseline.
- Reliable publishing of results and coverage in CI with actionable failure output.
- Developer ergonomics maintained or improved (local parity with CI via the same target).

If criteria are not met, revert to the prior test execution approach and document findings; otherwise, adopt the xUnit target as the standard test execution path.

We will add an explicit AdvanceToEnd capability to workflow instances that deterministically progresses a workflow from its current state to a terminal state without further human interaction. This will be exposed as a privileged API/command (AdvanceToEnd) that runs as a background, resumable job. The job repeatedly evaluates the workflow’s transition rules and executes only idempotent, side-effect-safe steps, committing after each transition checkpoint until a terminal state is reached or a guard condition halts progress.

Key aspects:
- Deterministic progression: uses the same transition engine/path resolution as normal execution, honoring guards and invariants. No new “shortcuts”; only permitted transitions are traversed.
- Side-effect handling: steps are executed via idempotent handlers; external effects must be either (a) no-op/dry-run during advance, or (b) executed exactly-once via outbox pattern. Steps marked “manual” or “non-idempotent” are skipped with reasons recorded; the run halts if such steps are mandatory.
- Checkpointing and resumability: each applied transition is persisted with a progress index and replay cursor to allow safe retries and crash recovery.
- Authorization and audit: operation limited to admin/system roles; every transition, skip, and stop reason is logged with correlation IDs.
- Safety guards: maximum step count/timebox per invocation; circuit-breakers on repeated failures; read-your-writes consistency on state reads.
- Observability: metrics for steps advanced, duration, skips, failures; detailed run report available to callers.
- API surface: POST /workflows/{id}:advanceToEnd with options {dryRun, maxSteps, executeExternalEffects}; returns runId and summary; GET to poll status.
- Data model: add fields progressCursor, terminalReason, lastAdvanceRunId; tag steps with idempotency and manual flags.

This approach provides a controlled, auditable fast-forward to terminal state while preserving correctness, safety, and operability.

## Decision

Adopt Trunk-Based Development with protected main and short‑lived topic branches.

- main is the single integration branch and must remain green and releasable at all times.
- All work occurs on short‑lived branches created from main:
  - Branch prefixes: feature/<slug>, fix/<slug>, chore/<slug>, docs/<slug>, refactor/<slug>, spike/<slug>.
- Integration is via Pull Requests with:
  - Required CI checks (build, tests, lint, security).
  - At least one reviewer (two for risky changes or code owners).
  - No direct pushes to main.
- Merge strategy:
  - Squash merge to maintain a linear, readable history; contributors rebase locally to keep branches up to date.
  - Fast‑forward merges to main are disabled; merge commits are disallowed.
- Incomplete or risky work is gated behind feature flags; long‑running branches are prohibited.
- Releases:
  - Semantic version tags (vX.Y.Z) are applied to main for deployments.
  - Optional release/X.Y branches may be created for stabilization of major/minor lines when needed; only fixes and release hardening allowed.
  - Hotfixes use hotfix/<slug> from the relevant release branch or tag; changes are back‑merged to main and other supported release branches.
- No environment or per‑team branches; promotion through environments is tag/commit based.
- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits to enable automated changelogs and versioning.
- Large/cross‑cutting changes use incremental PRs behind flags to preserve flow and reduce risk.

All application services, background workers, and user-facing components shall be stateless by default. Components must not rely on in-memory, local disk, or process-affine state for correctness across requests or restarts. Any state required for processing must be externalized to managed infrastructure (e.g., relational/NoSQL databases, object storage, message queues/streams, distributed caches) and accessed via well-defined interfaces.

Implications and rules:
- No server-side sessions; authentication is stateless (e.g., JWT or opaque token with centralized introspection). Request context is derived from tokens/headers on each call.
- Idempotency is mandatory for externally visible write operations; use idempotency keys and optimistic concurrency controls (ETags/version columns).
- Retries and horizontal scaling must be safe without affinity. Do not require sticky sessions or instance pinning.
- Ephemeral filesystem only for transient data; never for durability. Configuration via environment/centralized config; no runtime mutation persisted locally.
- In-process caches are allowed only as best-effort, disposable read-through caches with bounded size/TTL and feature flags; correctness must not depend on cache warmth.
- Long-running workflows and cross-service consistency use durable patterns (outbox/inbox, sagas, event sourcing where appropriate). Avoid distributed locks; if unavoidable, use managed primitives with timeouts.
- Streaming/stateful dataflow exceptions (e.g., Flink, Kafka Streams) are allowed when the framework externalizes/checkpoints state and provides recovery semantics.

Exceptions require an explicit ADR, performance justification, and sign-off from architecture and SRE, including resilience tests demonstrating safe scale-out, restart, and failover. Observability must include correlation IDs and replay-safe logging to support retries and deduplication. Components must tolerate being stopped at any time without data loss or user-visible inconsistency.

We will standardize editor selection via explicit environment variables with a clear precedence and safe invocation. The application will resolve the editor command in this order:
1) CLI flag: --editor
2) APP_EDITOR (application-specific)
3) APP_VISUAL (application-specific, intended for GUI editors)
4) VISUAL (conventional)
5) EDITOR (conventional)
6) Platform defaults (Windows: notepad; macOS: open -t; Linux/Unix: nano or vi, in that order if available)

When performing operations specific to VCS integrations, we will prefer tool-specific variables if present (e.g., GIT_EDITOR, HGEDITOR, SVN_EDITOR) before falling back to the global chain above.

Invocation will avoid shell interpretation by default: commands are parsed using POSIX-like shlex (Windows: CreateProcess argument rules) and executed without an intermediate shell to reduce injection risk. If a shell is explicitly required, users must wrap the command via the CLI flag (--editor "sh -lc '...'" ) and accept the associated risks.

Behavioral constraints:
- Non-interactive contexts (no TTY or CI=true) will not spawn an editor; the operation must receive content via flags/stdin or use --no-edit.
- If the resolved editor is not found or fails to start, we fail fast with a clear diagnostic and guidance to set APP_EDITOR.
- We will document the variables and precedence, recommend APP_EDITOR/APP_VISUAL for reproducibility, and provide examples per OS.
- Telemetry (if enabled) records which tier of precedence was used, not the command content.

We will create a utility class only when a cohesive set of stateless, side-effect-free functions does not fit naturally within an existing domain model or service and when reuse spans multiple bounded contexts or layers. Utility classes must:
- Encapsulate cross-cutting, low-level concerns (e.g., string/date/number formatting, pure transformations, lightweight adapters) with no hidden state, I/O, network, or persistence.
- Group only highly cohesive operations around a single technical concern; if cohesion drifts or responsibilities grow, split or retire the class.
- Expose pure functions with clear inputs/outputs; avoid global configuration, caching, or thread-local dependencies.
- Be language-idiomatic: prefer free functions/extension methods/modules where supported; if the language lacks these, use a final/static class or equivalent.
- Live in a dedicated utilities/ folder with subpackages by concern (e.g., text/, time/), not in domain packages. Names must reflect the concern (e.g., DateParsing), not generic “Utils/Helpers.”
- Be covered by unit tests with deterministic, property-based checks where feasible.
- Be treated as stable APIs: backward compatibility is required once adopted across modules; breaking changes require deprecation and migration notes.

We will not use utility classes to bypass proper design: domain logic stays in domain services/entities; integration logic stays in adapters. Before adding a utility class, architects will assess alternatives (refactoring to a domain/service, leveraging library features) and approve via lightweight review.

We will not include runnable example applications, templates, or sample projects in the v1.0 distribution artifacts (packages, containers, binaries) or official releases. Examples will be maintained in a separate public repository marked “experimental,” versioned independently, and excluded from all publish/build pipelines. The primary docs will provide minimal quick-start snippets and API references only; no end-to-end samples will be shipped with the product.

Operationalization:
- Exclude examples via packaging rules (.npmignore/.gitignore, build filters) and CI/CD checks that fail a release if example content is detected in artifacts.
- Document this policy in the README and release notes; link to the separate examples repo with clear caveats (non-API-stable, subject to change).
- Internal examples remain for development and testing but are not published.

Revisit criteria to begin shipping curated examples:
- API stability: no breaking changes across two consecutive minor releases or one LTS milestone.
- Documentation maturity: task-focused guides covering top 5 user journeys with validated usability tests.
- Quality gate: example projects have >90% unit coverage for example-specific code, integration tests in CI across supported platforms.
- Security and compliance: third-party dependencies in examples pass vulnerability and license checks; provenance/SBOM available.
- Ownership: named maintainers, update SLAs aligned with product releases, and clear deprecation/versioning policy.

Timeline and governance:
- Reevaluate at v1.2 or by Q3 2026, whichever comes first, via an ADR review.
- Any exceptions require architecture approval and a signed maintenance plan.

User experience mitigation:
- Provide concise, copy-pasteable snippets for common tasks in docs.
- Offer sandbox links (e.g., Codesandbox/StackBlitz) pointing to the experimental repo for those who opt in.

This decision reduces maintenance burden and user confusion during early stabilization while keeping a path to ship high-quality, supported examples later.

Adopt Google Cloud Firestore (Native mode) as the authoritative, low-latency, managed datastore for subscription platform metadata (e.g., products, plans, entitlements, offers, billing cycles, regional pricing) across all providers (Stripe, Apple, Google Play). Model data with a provider-centric hierarchy for efficient lookups and evolution:
- Collection providers/{providerId}/products/{productId}
- Subcollections: plans, prices, entitlements, offers, features, regionalOverrides
- Cross-provider lookup collection: catalogs/{env}/products/{normalizedSku}
- A change-log collection for immutable audit/versioning

Consistency and concurrency:
- Use document-level optimistic concurrency (update with precondition on updateTime).
- Transactions for multi-document invariants within a single provider.
- Store canonical version field; clients must pass If-Match semantics.

Data freshness and sync:
- Ingest and reconcile via event-driven pipelines (Pub/Sub + Cloud Functions/Cloud Run) triggered by provider webhooks and scheduled backfills.
- Maintain source-of-truth attribution and lastSyncedAt per document; prefer provider timestamps when available.
- Implement idempotent upserts keyed by provider resource IDs.

Security and governance:
- Access via service accounts with least-privilege IAM; no client-SDK writes.
- Enforce Firebase Security Rules for read segmentation by tenant/environment.
- Encrypt with CMEK where required; enable PITR and daily exports to GCS.
- Pseudonymize/remove user-identifying fields; metadata only.

Performance and cost:
- Use composite indexes only for required queries; cap document size < 256 KB.
- Denormalize hot read fields; avoid deep nesting beyond two levels.
- Multi-region (nam5/eu) for availability; cache read-most data at edge (Cloud CDN/Redis) with short TTLs.

Operations and lifecycle:
- Schema versioning per document; blue/green rollouts guarded by feature flags.
- TTL policies for stale change-log entries; retention 180 days.
- Provide migration tooling to seed from existing sources and verify parity.

We will adopt github.com/stretchr/testify as the standard assertion and (where needed) mocking library for all Go tests.

- Scope: All new Go tests will use testify/assert and testify/require alongside the standard testing package. Existing tests may be migrated opportunistically during maintenance.
- Assertions: Use assert for non-fatal checks; use require for preconditions and critical invariants to fail fast and reduce cascade failures.
- Mocking: Use testify/mock only for well-defined external dependencies (e.g., network, storage, third-party services). Prefer interface-driven design to enable mocking. Avoid overspecifying interactions; verify only behaviors relevant to the test. Reset mocks between tests.
- Exclusions: Do not adopt testify/suite to keep tests idiomatic, table-driven, and parallelizable with the standard testing package.
- Style: Maintain table-driven tests and subtests (t.Run). Keep tests deterministic, avoid global state, and prefer helpers over suites. Use clear failure messages for readability.
- Versioning: Pin to the latest stable v1.x release via Go modules; allow minor/patch updates automatically, review majors explicitly.
- Tooling/CI: No CI changes required. go test remains the entry point. Coverage and race detection workflows stay unchanged.
- Performance: Minimal overhead; acceptable for unit and integration tests.
- Risks/Mitigations: Limit reliance on mock-specific features to avoid brittleness; when behavior is complex, prefer fakes or in-memory implementations.
- Rollout: Effective immediately for new code. Document patterns in the testing guidelines and add lint examples. Migrate legacy assertions incrementally when files are touched.

We will implement a process-local, thread-safe, bounded in-memory cache for PropertyInfoStore using Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Memory (IMemoryCache) with stampede protection and predictable keys.

- Cache scope: per-process, per-AppDomain. No cross-process distribution. Types are immutable at runtime; no active invalidation is required beyond eviction policies.
- Keying: composite key of (DeclaringType, BindingFlags/options, IncludeNonPublic, InheritanceTraversalMode, NameComparer). For typed/generic scenarios, use the constructed generic type (e.g., typeof(List<int>)) to ensure correctness. Keys are value-tuples hashed deterministically.
- Value: an immutable, precomputed PropertyMap/descriptor set containing resolved PropertyInfo/Accessors and normalized name index. Values are safe to share across threads.
- Concurrency and stampede control: cache population guarded via Lazy<T> per key within the cache factory, ensuring single computation per miss.
- Eviction and lifetime:
  - Size-limited IMemoryCache with size per entry proportional to property count (1 + N properties).
  - Sliding expiration: 30 minutes; Absolute expiration: 24 hours.
  - Size limit configurable; default tuned to keep hot types (e.g., 5–10k entries or ~50–100 MB depending on profile).
- Warm path: optional pre-warm for known hot types at startup hooks to reduce first-hit latency.
- Metrics/observability: expose counters for hits/misses, insertions, evictions, and compute latency; add optional tracing tags with the key summary.
- API shape: IPropertyInfoStore with CacheAwarePropertyInfoStore decorator layering over a ReflectionPropertyInfoStore. The decorator is responsible for key creation, lookup, Lazy-wrapped value construction, and cache sizing.
- Failure modes: on factory exceptions, do not cache failures; propagate error to caller. On memory pressure, rely on IMemoryCache eviction; operations remain functional with increased reflection cost.
- Versioning/compatibility: cache key includes behavior-affecting options; any future option that changes resolution semantics must be added to the key. Binary compatibility maintained via interface; configuration provided via options class.
- Thread-safety: all public methods are safe for concurrent use; underlying cached values are immutable; no locks beyond Lazy per-key initialization.

## Decision

Adopt Algolia as the primary search platform, replacing Elasticsearch for user-facing search across all products and environments.

- Scope: All interactive, end-user search (site/app search, autocomplete, typo tolerance, faceting, synonyms, geo). Internal analytics/search pipelines that require document-level aggregations remain on the data platform.
- Deployment: Use Algolia multi-cluster (Premium) with replication to required regions. Configure per-environment indices (prod/stage/dev) with namespacing.
- Indexing: Build near-real-time incremental indexing via webhooks/event bus; nightly full reindex as a safety net. Use Algolia’s partial updates and atomic reindexing with index aliases for zero-downtime swaps.
- Relevancy: Centralize ranking strategy using custom ranking attributes, synonyms, rules, and A/B testing in Algolia. Product and content teams own tuning via Algolia dashboard with guardrails in code.
- Features: Enable query suggestions, typo tolerance, highlighting/snippets, faceting, filtering, and personalization where privacy policies allow.
- Security & Compliance: Restrict data to necessary fields; use secured API keys with per-user filters; enforce GDPR/CCPA data minimization and regional data hosting as required. Rotate keys via secrets manager.
- Observability: Use Algolia analytics, usage limits, and SLA monitoring; export logs/metrics to central observability. Alert on quota, errors, latency.
- Cost Control: Implement index size guards, attribute whitelists, and rate limiting; quarterly cost/relevancy reviews.
- Rollout: Phase by domain/page type behind feature flags; maintain read-only Elasticsearch for 60 days as fallback. Decommission ES clusters post cutover and data retention validation.
- Ownership: Search platform owned by the Web Platform team; SRE manages credentials/monitoring; Data team supports enrichment pipelines.

## Decision
Adopt a declarative, versioned workflow capability based on an open-source orchestration engine (Netflix Conductor) to enable safe, auditable custom workflows without allowing arbitrary user-supplied code execution.

- Workflow definitions will be authored in a constrained JSON DSL and stored in Git with code review, schema validation, and automated linting. Definitions compile directly to Conductor workflows.
- Only approved task types are allowed in the DSL: service call (HTTP/gRPC), message publish/consume, timers/waits, retries/timeouts, branching (switch), parallel/map, compensation/saga steps, and human-approval gates. Arbitrary scripts are prohibited. Custom behaviors must be implemented as vetted worker services registered as task executors.
- Execution is centralized in a managed Conductor cluster with durable state, idempotency, and exactly-once task semantics; all steps are asynchronous and retriable. Long-running workflows are supported.
- Workflow definitions are immutable and versioned. New versions are deployed alongside existing ones; routing of new executions to versions is controlled via configuration. Migration tools will support draining/continuing in-flight executions when compatible.
- Security and governance: RBAC on create/update/execute; per-tenant quotas and rate limits; input/output schemas with PII tagging; secrets injected via vault references; allow-list of endpoints; audit logs for all changes and runs.
- Observability: end-to-end tracing, metrics, and structured logs for each step; run-level and task-level dashboards. A dry-run/simulation mode validates data flow and policies before activation.
- Developer experience: SDKs to register workers, a minimal visual designer backed by the JSON DSL, and a library of reusable workflow templates. This feature will roll out behind feature flags per tenant.

We will support explicit links between ADRs using stable numeric IDs and markdown relative links to ensure navigability, traceability, and toolability.

- Identifier and filename: each ADR keeps its immutable 4-digit ID and slug (e.g., 0009-support-links-between-adrs-inside-an-adrs.md). IDs never change; titles/slugs may change, but filenames do not.
- Link format: links use markdown relative paths with optional section anchors (e.g., ./0003-deploy-strategy.md#decision). No absolute URLs within the repo.
- Cross-ADR relationships: every ADR must include structured metadata fields when applicable: Supersedes, Superseded by, Amends, Amended by, Depends on, Related to. Values are ADR IDs (with optional inline links). When setting one side, the reciprocal side must be added in the counterpart ADR.
- Backlinks/indexing: we will auto-generate a backlinks section and an ADR index to show inbound/outbound links using a documentation job.
- Validation: CI will enforce that all ADR links resolve, reciprocal links exist for symmetric relationships, and anchors (#context, #decision, #status) are valid. Broken links fail the build.
- Section anchors: section headings are standardized (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, References) to provide stable anchors.
- Status transitions: on supersede, update Status accordingly and add Supersedes/Superseded by links on both ADRs; content remains intact.
- External references: allowed in References, but not used for internal ADR cross-linking.
- Tooling: provide a dev script/ADR linter to insert/update relationships and regenerate backlinks and the index.

We will standardize on Playwright as the default end-to-end (e2e) testing framework and provide a minimal, opinionated tooling layer to make common e2e scenarios easy by default. This includes:

- A single “blessed” path: Playwright test runner with TypeScript, cross-browser support (Chromium default), built-in tracing, and parallelization. We will not support Selenium/WebDriver. Existing Cypress suites may remain but are deprecated for new work.
- Simple commands: `npm run e2e` (headless smoke), `npm run e2e:ui` (headed with inspector), and `npm run e2e:trace` (record/replay traces).
- Deterministic data and isolation: database seed/reset utilities, idempotent fixtures, and stable data contracts. All UI elements under test expose data-testids.
- Network control: MSW-based stubbing for local e2e and contract-like flows, with an environment flag to switch between stubbed and real backends.
- Environment provisioning: a Dockerized test runner image and a “test harness” compose file that boots app + dependencies with seeded data. Ephemeral preview environments run the same harness.
- CI policy: PRs run smoke e2e on Chromium only; main branch runs full cross-browser nightly. Flaky test quarantine is enforced; failure artifacts (video, screenshots, traces) are retained.
- Scaffolding: template tests, fixtures, and utilities for auth, navigation, accessibility checks (axe), and file uploads. Documentation covers patterns, anti-patterns, and performance tips.
- Governance: e2e remains at the top of the test pyramid; teams must prefer unit/integration tests where feasible. New e2e tests require stable identifiers and deterministic setup to be accepted.

This decision optimizes for simplicity, speed, and reliability while providing a clear, maintainable path for e2e coverage.

## Decision

Adopt standardized build automation and code coverage across all repositories and services, enforced via CI.

- Build: Use the ecosystem’s de facto build tools per language:
  - Java/Kotlin: Gradle (Kotlin DSL) with dependency locking
  - JavaScript/TypeScript: pnpm with workspaces; build via npm scripts and tsup/tsc
  - Python: Poetry for builds and dependency management
  - .NET: dotnet CLI with centralized Directory.Build.props
- Tests: Execute unit tests on every push/PR; run integration/e2e tests on main and nightly.
- Coverage: Collect and report line, branch, and condition coverage using:
  - Java/Kotlin: JaCoCo
  - JS/TS: Istanbul (nyc)
  - Python: coverage.py
  - .NET: Coverlet
- Thresholds and gating:
  - Minimum project thresholds: 80% line, 70% branch coverage.
  - PRs must not reduce module-level coverage; builds fail if thresholds are not met.
  - Generated code, migrations, and vendored/third-party code are excluded by convention (centralized exclude patterns).
- CI/CD integration:
  - Standard GitHub Actions workflows (or equivalent in CI) provide build, test, coverage, and caching.
  - Coverage reports uploaded to a central dashboard (SonarQube or Codecov) with PR annotations.
  - Status checks required before merge; badges displayed in READMEs.
- Developer workflow:
  - Pre-commit hooks run fast unit tests and local coverage diffs.
  - Monorepo aware: only affected packages/services are built/tested using change detection.
  - Deterministic builds via lockfiles and reproducible flags; remote caching where supported.
- Governance:
  - A central “engineering-infra” repo defines reusable CI templates and enforces policy via branch protections.
  - Teams may raise justified exceptions via ADRs; temporary waivers auto-expire within one release.
  - Thresholds may ratchet up by 5% per quarter until target (e.g., 90%/80%) is met.
- Reporting and observability:
  - Coverage trends tracked over time; flaky test quarantine and alerting.
  - Artifacts (coverage HTML, test results) retained for 14 days.

This decision ensures consistent quality, faster feedback, and measurable test health, while allowing language-appropriate tooling and controlled exceptions.

Adopt collaborative Event Storming for domain discovery and use domain events as the primary integration mechanism within our Rails monolith. Model bounded contexts from Event Storming as Rails engines; interactions between engines occur via published domain events, not direct cross-engine calls. Implement event publishing and subscription with RailsEventStore, persisting events in PostgreSQL. Events are immutable, append-only, and published only on successful transaction commit (outbox pattern). Delivery is at-least-once; all consumers must be idempotent. Use Sidekiq for asynchronous dispatch and retries with exponential backoff.

Maintain a clear taxonomy of events:
- Internal events (engine-private) are package-private.
- Public domain events (cross-engine/externally consumed) are versioned and documented.

Define and enforce event contracts:
- JSON schema stored in-repo with CI validation.
- Event versioning via additive changes and upcasters; breaking changes require new event names/versions.
- Correlation and causation IDs included for tracing; timestamps in UTC; tenant and actor metadata included where applicable.

Persistence remains CRUD-first (ActiveRecord) for read/write models; we do not adopt full event sourcing for aggregates by default. Event-sourced aggregates may be introduced selectively where auditing, temporal queries, or complex invariants justify it, gated by an explicit ADR. Projections (read models) are built from events for cross-context views and external integrations.

Operational concerns:
- Central event catalog and ownership metadata.
- Observability via logs and metrics for publish/handle latency, failure rates, and dead-letter queues.
- Backfills and replays are controlled operations with safeguards against duplicate side effects.
- Security review for PII in payloads; prefer references over embedding sensitive data.

Governance:
- Naming conventions, retention policies, and SLAs for public events.
- Changes to public event contracts require review by affected teams.

This decision enables scalable, decoupled evolution of the monolith, preserves transactional integrity, and prepares for future extraction of services without upfront complexity of full event sourcing.

We will not adopt a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) for application runtime or deployment. Instead, we will run containerized workloads on a portable, self-managed platform (Kubernetes on IaaS) with infrastructure provisioned via IaC. We will leverage cloud-managed building blocks where they do not create runtime lock-in (e.g., managed databases, object storage, CDN, secrets management), but avoid opinionated PaaS layers that constrain runtime, networking, scaling models, or CI/CD integration.

This decision prioritizes portability, fine-grained control over performance and cost, compliance-driven network/security controls, and predictable multi-environment parity. We will build a minimal internal platform layer (golden base images, standardized Helm charts, service templates, SSO, observability, policy-as-code, and paved-path CI/CD) to deliver PaaS-like developer experience without sacrificing control. Autoscaling, blue/green and canary releases, and runtime policies will be implemented via Kubernetes-native tooling (e.g., HPA, service mesh, GitOps).

Where a managed service is adopted, we will abstract via open interfaces (e.g., CNCF APIs, 12-factor configs, backing services via well-defined contracts) to preserve portability. This decision will be revisited if operational burden or time-to-market proves materially worse than a PaaS alternative, or if compliance constraints are eased such that a PaaS can meet our control and portability requirements.

We will persist asynchronous message examples in distinct, purpose-specific fields instead of a single shared “example” blob. For each async message definition, we will store separate examples for each direction and component:
- Direction: outbound (produced) and inbound (consumed)
- Component: payload, headers, and key (where applicable)
- Variant: success and error

Schema (canonical model and storage) will introduce nullable fields:
- outbound_payload_example, outbound_headers_example, outbound_key_example
- inbound_payload_example, inbound_headers_example, inbound_key_example
- outbound_error_example, inbound_error_example

All examples are stored as JSON serialized text, UTF-8, with a per-field size cap (e.g., 64KB). Binary examples must be base64-encoded. PII-sensitive values must be pre-redacted by producers; storage enforces redaction patterns where configured.

APIs will expose these fields explicitly and deprecate the legacy combined example field. Read-path will remain backward compatible by mapping the legacy field to outbound_payload_example when present; write-path to the legacy field is disabled in new API versions. UI and docs will display and edit examples per field, clarifying direction and component.

Validation will ensure examples conform to the referenced schemas (when provided) and are structurally independent across fields. Indexing is not applied to example fields beyond existence flags. Versioning of examples follows the message version; examples are not independently versioned.

## Decision

Adopt a dedicated JPEG 2000 ingest pipeline that (1) preserves the original bitstream, (2) validates and extracts technical metadata, and (3) normalizes to standard internal derivatives for access.

- Accept .jp2, .j2k, and .jpx containers. Store the original object losslessly and immutably as the preservation master.
- Use OpenJPEG (opj_decompress) as the default decoder for validation and transcoding due to permissive licensing and broad platform support; optionally enable Kakadu as a pluggable decoder for environments requiring maximum performance, gated by license availability.
- Perform format validation and characterization with JHOVE (jp2k module) and Apache Tika; extract technical metadata (dimensions, bit depth, color space, ICC profile, compression layers, tiles, resolution levels) with ExifTool and OpenJPEG probes; persist as sidecar JSON aligned to our preservation metadata schema.
- Normalize for access to pyramidal TIFF (lossless, Deflate/LZW) as the standard derivative; also generate web derivatives (JPEG/PNG) and thumbnails. Preserve embedded ICC profiles; convert to sRGB only for access derivatives when profiles are missing or unsupported.
- Support 8/16-bit, gray/RGB, and tiled/untiled codestreams; reject or quarantine files with broken boxes, unsupported multi-component transforms, or malformed profiles, with actionable error codes.
- Implement a containerized, stateless worker that streams from object storage (range requests), uses tile/strip windowed decode to cap memory, and parallelizes per-asset ingestion within configured concurrency limits.
- Record full provenance (tool versions, command lines, checksums pre/post) and ensure idempotency so re-runs do not duplicate artifacts.
- Provide toggles to retain JP2 as delivery format for IIIF deployments; otherwise serve from pyramidal TIFF.

## Decision
- Containerize all application components (services, jobs, CLI tools) using Docker to ensure environment parity across development, CI, staging, and production.
- Standardize on multi-stage Dockerfiles per service with pinned base images (Alpine or distroless where feasible) to produce minimal, reproducible, non-root runtime images.
- Use Docker Compose for local development and integration testing to orchestrate services, networks, and volumes; define dev/test overrides for hot-reload and debug tooling.
- Build images with Docker BuildKit, leveraging deterministic builds, layer caching, and SBOM generation; enforce image scanning (vuln and license) in CI.
- Publish images to a centralized container registry with immutable, content-addressable tags (git SHA) and human-readable version tags (semver); prohibit :latest in deployments.
- Enforce least-privilege runtime: non-root users, read-only root filesystem where possible, minimal capabilities, healthchecks, and resource constraints (CPU/memory) defined per container.
- Externalize configuration via environment variables and secrets providers; mount secrets as files where required; never bake secrets into images.
- Define network boundaries via dedicated Docker networks per environment; expose only necessary ports; inter-service communication via service names.
- Persist state using named volumes and/or managed external services; treat containers as stateless/ephemeral.
- Introduce consistent observability hooks: structured logs to stdout/stderr, OpenTelemetry instrumentation, and health/metrics endpoints; centralize logs/metrics in CI and higher environments.
- Gate image promotion through CI/CD pipelines: build → test → scan → sign → push → deploy; only signed images are eligible for staging/production.
- Maintain backward-compatible interfaces to enable independent service releases; support blue/green or rolling updates where orchestrator allows.
- For production orchestration, prefer Kubernetes (or managed equivalent) consuming the same images; this ADR focuses on Dockerization, with a separate ADR covering cluster operations.
- Document per-service Dockerfile guidelines and Compose templates; enforce via linters and CI checks to prevent drift and ensure repeatability.

## Decision

We will decommission and remove the unused Skylight performance monitoring integration from the application and its delivery pipeline. Specifically:
- Remove the skylight gem from the Gemfile and regenerate Gemfile.lock.
- Delete Skylight configuration and initialization (e.g., config/skylight.yml, config/initializers/skylight.rb) and any related middleware or rake tasks.
- Remove environment variables and secrets (e.g., SKYLIGHT_AUTHENTICATION) from all environments and CI/CD.
- Eliminate any Skylight-related deployment hooks, add-ons, or buildpacks.
- Update operational runbooks and developer documentation to reflect the removal and the current observability toolchain.
- Verify there are no code paths conditionally referencing Skylight; replace with no-ops where necessary.

Rationale: Skylight is not actively used and provides no current operational value. Its removal decreases runtime and build-time dependencies, reduces attack surface and secret sprawl, simplifies configuration, and may eliminate licensing costs. There is no expected user-visible impact.

Mitigation and validation:
- Ensure alternative observability remains in place (existing logs/metrics/APM).
- Monitor baseline app performance and error rates post-removal.
- Retain historical Skylight data/export (if needed) before deprovisioning.
- Provide a simple rollback path by retaining the prior configuration in version control should re-enablement be required.

Adopt Vue 3 as the primary front-end framework for all user-facing web applications. Use the Composition API and Single-File Components with TypeScript as mandatory. Standardize the toolchain on Vite for build/dev, pnpm for package management, ESLint + Prettier for linting/formatting, and commitlint + husky for conventional commits.

- State management: Pinia as the default global store.
- Routing: Vue Router with route-based code splitting.
- HTTP: Axios with interceptors; generate API clients from OpenAPI where available.
- Styling: Tailwind CSS with PostCSS; component-scoped CSS for exceptions.
- UI components: Adopt Headless UI (Vue) and Radix Primitives where applicable; teams may add a design-system layer via Storybook-driven components.
- Internationalization: vue-i18n.
- Accessibility: Enforce WCAG AA via eslint-plugin-vuejs-accessibility and automated checks in CI.
- Testing: Vitest + Vue Test Utils for unit tests; Playwright for E2E; Cypress allowed for legacy suites.
- Documentation: Storybook for components and VitePress for developer docs.
- Performance: Enable script setup, defineProps/defineEmits, and Vite’s dynamic import for lazy loading; monitor with Web Vitals in CI.
- SSR/SSG: Default to SPA; use Nuxt 3 for products requiring SSR/SSG or advanced routing/meta management, sharing components via a common internal package.
- Packaging: Internal reusable components published as versioned packages (npm workspace), following semantic versioning.
- Security: Dependabot (or Renovate) for dependency updates; Content Security Policy compatible build; sanitize user input and enforce CSP nonces.
- CI/CD: Run type checks, lint, unit, and E2E tests on PRs; produce versioned artifacts; deploy static assets to CDN behind the main domain.

This decision establishes Vue as the consistent front-end foundation, improving developer productivity, coherence, and maintainability across projects while allowing SSR via Nuxt where necessary.

We will use Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL (Core/SQL) API as our primary data store. This API provides native JSON document support, rich SQL-like querying, transactional batch operations within a partition, change feed, TTL, unique keys, and the best feature coverage, tooling, and Azure integration compared to other Cosmos DB APIs.

Key choices:
- Data model: JSON documents with flexible schema and denormalized aggregates for read-optimized access patterns.
- Containers and partitioning: Per-bounded context containers. Partition key = tenantId for multi-tenant data; where hot-spot risk exists, use composite identifiers (e.g., tenantId+bucket) or operational partitions (e.g., orderId for order items). Enforce unique keys as needed.
- Consistency: Account-level Session consistency for read-your-writes with low latency; clients propagate session tokens for critical read-after-write paths.
- Throughput: Autoscale RU on primary containers; dedicated throughput per container for isolation; shared throughput only for small reference data.
- Indexing: Consistent indexing with selective path exclusion for large/unqueried fields; define composite indexes to accelerate common filters/sorts; enable TTL where appropriate.
- Change feed: Used to drive projections, cache invalidation, and downstream integration. Consider analytical store/Synapse Link for BI without impacting transactional RU.
- Geo-redundancy: Multi-region reads with a single write region, automatic failover enabled; regions colocated with primary user bases.
- SDK and features: Use the official Cosmos DB SDK for our language/runtime, enabling optimistic concurrency (ETags), transactional batches within a partition, and minimal use of stored procedures/triggers (kept within partition boundaries).

We explicitly do not use MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, or Table APIs to avoid compatibility gaps, driver constraints, and reduced feature parity relative to the NoSQL (Core) API.

## Decision
We will structure the application so that the vast majority of logic is framework-agnostic and testable outside the browser, reserving browser-based testing for a small set of critical end-to-end flows and cross-browser rendering checks.

- Domain and application logic will reside in pure, side-effect-free modules (TypeScript), shared across client and server when applicable. These modules will be covered primarily by fast unit tests running in Node.
- UI components will be kept thin; state management and side effects will be isolated behind ports/adapters. Direct use of browser APIs (e.g., DOM, Storage, Clipboard) will be wrapped in small adapters with contract tests and feature detection.
- Data access will be abstracted via an API client layer with schema/contract tests (e.g., OpenAPI/GraphQL). Network interactions in non-browser tests will be mocked (e.g., MSW) to avoid reliance on real browsers.
- Rendering logic will favor SSR/SSG and hydration where feasible to reduce client-only code and to enable server-side testability.
- Testing strategy will follow a strict test pyramid:
  - 70–80% unit tests (Node/Vitest/Jest).
  - 15–25% component/integration tests using jsdom and testing-library.
  - ≤5–10% browser E2E smoke/regression tests (Playwright/Cypress) covering only critical user journeys and cross-browser issues.
- Static analysis and type safety (TypeScript, ESLint, type-aware lint rules) will be mandatory to catch issues before runtime.
- Governance and guardrails:
  - Lint rules to prohibit direct browser API access outside adapters.
  - CI gates enforcing coverage thresholds per layer and limits on new E2E tests.
  - Architectural review for changes that introduce browser-only logic.
  - Bundle size budgets to discourage unnecessary client complexity.

This decision optimizes test speed, reliability, and maintainability by concentrating tests where they are fastest and most deterministic, while keeping a minimal, high-value browser test surface for end-to-end assurance.

## Decision

Adopt PostgreSQL 16 as the primary OLTP database, provisioned as a managed service (e.g., AWS RDS/Aurora PostgreSQL or GCP Cloud SQL) to ensure high availability, automated maintenance, and operational efficiency.

- Data model: Relational, schema-first with explicit constraints and indexes. Use strong consistency and ACID transactions for core business operations.
- Multi-tenancy: Single database with row-level multi-tenancy using tenant_id and PostgreSQL Row Level Security (RLS) where applicable. For isolated tenants with strict compliance, support optional separate schemas or databases.
- Availability and resilience: Enable Multi-AZ/zone HA with automated failover. Maintain at least one read replica for read-heavy workloads and zero-downtime maintenance. Configure cross-region read replica for disaster recovery.
- Scalability: Scale vertically first; horizontally via read replicas. Use connection pooling (PgBouncer) to protect against connection storms. Employ table partitioning (time- or tenant-based) for large/high-churn tables; defer sharding until justified by load.
- Migrations: Enforce versioned, repeatable migrations via Flyway or Liquibase. Integrate migrations into CI/CD with automated checks and rollback procedures.
- Performance: Establish indexing standards (covering indexes, partial indexes where beneficial). Enable pg_stat_statements and slow query logging. Regularly review query plans and vacuum/analyze settings. Use prepared statements and parameterized queries.
- Security: Encrypt data at rest and in transit. Manage credentials via a secrets manager with rotation. Apply least-privilege IAM/roles, RLS, and native auditing. Restrict network access via private subnets and security groups. Enable logical decoding only when explicitly needed.
- Backups and recovery: Enable automated daily snapshots and point-in-time recovery with minimum 35-day retention (environment-specific). Perform quarterly restore drills and document RTO/RPO targets.
- Observability: Centralize metrics (CPU, IOPS, connections, replication lag), logs, and alerts (e.g., disk growth, deadlocks, replication issues). Track capacity and growth forecasts.
- Data lifecycle and compliance: Define retention and archival policies (e.g., tiered storage, partition detach/archival). Implement data deletion processes to meet privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR).
- Usage patterns: OLTP and operational reporting via read replicas only; offload heavy analytics to a separate warehouse/lakehouse pipeline.
- Version and maintenance policy: Stay within N-1 minor versions; schedule maintenance windows; validate extensions (pgcrypto, pg_trgm, PostGIS as needed) per environment.

We will standardize on tsmon for running TypeScript during local development and watch-mode workflows, replacing ts-node across all packages. This decision applies to developer-facing commands (e.g., dev servers, CLIs, scripts) but does not change production execution, which remains “compile with tsc and run with node.”

Primary drivers:
- Faster cold starts and reloads compared to ts-node-based flows, improving developer feedback cycles.
- More reliable file watching and restart behavior in larger workspaces/monorepos.
- Simpler configuration and fewer flags to support ESM/CJS, tsconfig paths, and source maps out of the box.
- Reduced flakiness seen with ts-node + nodemon combinations, especially around transient type errors and partial rebuilds.

Scope and implementation:
- Replace package.json scripts that use ts-node (or ts-node/register) with tsmon equivalents (e.g., dev, start:dev, local tooling).
- Remove ts-node and dependent wrappers from dependencies; add tsmon.
- Ensure source maps remain enabled for debugging; preserve Node --inspect and environment variable passthrough.
- CI will not rely on tsmon; tests and tools in CI should run against compiled JS (tsc) for determinism.

Risks and mitigations:
- Potential incompatibility with custom ts-node transformers or runtime transpile hooks: retire or replace with build-time transforms; provide a fallback script using precompiled output.
- Watcher performance on very large codebases: tune include/exclude globs; document opt-in to prebuild + node for edge cases.
- Developer environment variance: provide a bootstrap script to pin tsmon version and verify Node compatibility.

Rollout:
- Migrate scripts per package, update developer docs, and run a 1-sprint bake-in with a rollback path to ts-node if blocking issues arise.

We will adopt Scala as the primary programming language for backend services and data-processing components on the JVM.

- Version and platform: Use Scala 3 (current LTS line) for all new development, targeting JDK 21 LTS. Existing Scala 2.13 codebases will be maintained and incrementally migrated to Scala 3 when feasible.
- Build and tooling: Standardize on sbt, with enforced scalafmt and scalafix configurations across repositories. CI will compile with -Xfatal-warnings and a consistent, vetted set of compiler options.
- Interoperability: Java interoperability is first-class. Teams may consume mature Java libraries where appropriate, encapsulating interop boundaries to preserve idiomatic Scala APIs.
- Language subset and style: Prefer immutable data, expression-oriented design, and referentially transparent functions. Use given/using and extension methods judiciously; avoid macros and implicit tricks unless justified and reviewed. Favor readability and maintainability over cleverness.
- Concurrency and effects: Adopt a structured-concurrency, effect-safe approach consistent across services. Selection of a single effects/concurrency library will be standardized in a separate ADR; until then, avoid mixing paradigms within a codebase.
- Packaging and distribution: Target JVM applications and libraries; Scala.js/Scala Native are out of scope unless approved by separate ADRs.
- Backward compatibility: Public library APIs must follow semantic versioning with MiMa (or equivalent) checks where applicable.
- Governance: A language working group will curate compiler flags, lint rules, and approved libraries; deviations require ADRs.

We will adopt GitHub as the primary identity provider for user and workload authentication across our products and internal tooling. Authentication will use GitHub OAuth 2.0/OIDC with PKCE, state, and nonce. We will request minimal scopes: read:user, user:email, and read:org to obtain verified email, profile, and organization/team membership. Authorization will be derived from GitHub org/team membership mapped to application roles; no roles are stored in tokens. We will implement just-in-time provisioning on first login and deprovision by denying access when membership is absent; a daily sync job will reconcile role mappings and handle revocation promptly. For enterprises, we support GitHub Enterprise Cloud with SSO-enforced organizations and enterprise-managed users.

For non-interactive workloads, we will use GitHub OIDC federation to obtain short-lived cloud credentials; no long-lived secrets are stored. For CLI and headless clients, we will support the device authorization grant.

Security measures: use rotating refresh tokens, short-lived access tokens, strict redirect URI allowlists, token binding to client, and encrypted at-rest token storage; we will not request write scopes. We will cache membership for up to 5 minutes to mitigate rate limits and provide graceful degradation; access decisions always re-validate on critical operations. A break-glass local admin account will exist for continuity during GitHub outages and will be audited and rotated.

Compliance and privacy: we will store only the GitHub user ID, login, verified email(s), and team/organization identifiers necessary for authorization, retaining audit logs per policy. This decision centralizes identity, simplifies developer onboarding, leverages existing org governance, and aligns with our security posture without introducing a separate IdP.

## Decision
Adopt a modular, feature-first directory structure within a single monorepo to improve scalability, discoverability, and ownership boundaries.

Top-level layout:
- /apps: Deployable applications (e.g., web, api, worker), each self-contained.
- /packages: Shared libraries (domain, UI components, utilities), versioned via workspace tooling.
- /infra: Infrastructure-as-code (e.g., Terraform, CDK) and deployment manifests.
- /config: Environment-specific configuration templates and schema.
- /scripts: Operational and developer scripts (idempotent, cross-platform where possible).
- /tools: Build, codegen, and custom CLI tooling.
- /docs: Architecture and developer documentation.
- /ci: CI/CD pipeline definitions and templates.

Application/package layout:
- /src
  - /features/<feature-name>/{ui, domain, data}
  - /shared: Cross-feature primitives (adapters, utils, types)
  - /app: Composition root (routing, DI, bootstrapping)
  - /assets, /styles (if applicable)
- Tests co-located next to code as *.spec|test.* and integration tests under /tests.
- Public API exposed only via package-level index.ts; deep imports are disallowed.

Conventions and constraints:
- Kebab-case for directories; files kebab-case; classes/types PascalCase.
- Avoid barrel files within features; one barrel only at package root.
- Enforce boundaries via lint rules (e.g., no feature-to-feature imports except through shared/public API).
- Environment config loaded via /config with strict schema validation; no env-specific branches in code.
- README.md in each app/package describing purpose, public API, and ownership.

Tooling:
- Use workspace manager (e.g., pnpm) and an orchestrator (e.g., Turborepo/Nx) to cache, build, and test by scope.
- Codeowners map to top-level directories to clarify ownership.

A migration plan will incrementally reshape existing modules to this structure without breaking public APIs.

We will implement the web application as a single-page app using client-side rendering, bootstrapped with Create React App (CRA). The initial HTML will be a minimal shell; rendering and routing occur entirely in the browser. No server-side rendering (SSR) or static site generation (SSG) are in scope for this iteration.

Key decisions:
- Stack: React 18 via CRA, React Router for client routing, Fetch/Axios for API calls.
- Build/deploy: CRA build (Webpack/Babel) producing static assets deployed to a CDN behind edge caching; environment-specific configs via CRA env vars.
- Performance: code splitting with dynamic imports and React.lazy/Suspense, tree-shaking, image/font optimization, HTTP/2 with asset compression, optional service worker via CRA’s Workbox for offline/asset caching.
- UX/Resilience: skeletons/placeholders for perceived performance, robust error boundaries, retry/backoff for network requests.
- SEO/Sharing: SPA-friendly metadata via react-helmet-async, sitemap/robots hosted statically; no hard SEO guarantees. If SEO-critical pages emerge, consider targeted prerendering as a stopgap or revisit SSR/SSG.
- Observability: web vitals collection, client logging, feature flags for progressive rollouts.
- Testing: Jest and React Testing Library for unit/integration; Cypress/Playwright for E2E.

This decision optimizes for developer velocity, static hosting simplicity, and dynamic client interactions. We will revisit if requirements demand first-paint SEO, faster time-to-content on slow networks, or server-rendered personalization.

## Decision

Replace the current file storage subsystem with an S3-compatible object storage backend. Access to storage will be mediated through a versioned StorageProvider interface to decouple application code from vendor specifics. We will support AWS S3 in production and a compatible provider (e.g., MinIO) for local/test environments.

Key behaviors:
- All new writes are directed to object storage with server-side encryption (SSE-S3/KMS), bucket-level policies enforcing least-privilege IAM, and object versioning enabled.
- Read access uses presigned URLs for client downloads; server-side streaming remains available for internal services.
- Lifecycle policies manage retention, archival (Glacier/Deep Archive), and deletion; legal hold support where required.
- Cross-region replication enabled for DR; eventual consistency mitigated via read-after-write checks for critical paths.
- CDN integration for public assets; cache-control headers and ETag support maintained.

Migration approach:
- Introduce dual-write for a limited period; backfill historical objects via parallel migration jobs with integrity verification (ETag/MD5 and size checks).
- Read-through fallback: on cache miss in object storage, fetch from legacy store once, then promote to object storage.
- Feature flag controls cutover per service/tenant; canary rollout with progressive ramp-up and monitored error budgets.
- Clear rollback plan by disabling dual-write and reverting read path to legacy storage if SLOs regress.

Operational considerations:
- Observability via metrics (latency, error rate, throughput), structured audit logs, and object-level access logging.
- Cost guardrails through storage class transitions and per-tenant quotas.
- Decommission legacy storage after successful migration and retention window.

We will implement a lightweight, explicit finite state machine (FSM) in the domain layer as the single source of truth for submission lifecycle, rather than adopting an external workflow engine. The FSM will be deterministic, event-driven, and persist both current state and an immutable audit trail of transitions.

Canonical states:
- Draft
- Submitted
- InReview
- ChangesRequested
- Resubmitted
- Approved
- Rejected
- Withdrawn
- Expired

Allowed transitions (non-exhaustive):
- Draft → Submitted (author)
- Submitted → InReview (system/triage)
- InReview → Approved | Rejected (reviewer)
- InReview → ChangesRequested (reviewer)
- ChangesRequested → Resubmitted (author)
- Any non-terminal → Withdrawn (author, if policy allows)
- Submitted/InReview → Expired (system via SLA timeout)

Transitions are driven by commands, validated by guards (role, policy, data completeness, integrity checks) and are idempotent. Side effects (notifications, indexing, scoring) are executed via domain events emitted on successful transitions to decouple processing and ensure reliability. Concurrency is controlled via optimistic locking on the submission aggregate; conflicting updates will be retried with command revalidation. Time-based transitions (e.g., Expired) are triggered by a scheduler emitting commands, not by background mutation, to retain auditability.

The FSM will be defined by a declarative transition table (configuration) and enforced by a domain service to centralize rules and facilitate evolution without schema changes. Every transition writes an append-only audit record with actor, timestamp, prior/new state, and correlation ID.

APIs expose commands (not raw state setting). Read models include current state plus derived status labels for UX. Backward-incompatible state changes require a versioned transition map and migration scripts. Terminal states (Approved, Rejected, Withdrawn, Expired) are immutable except for administrative overrides logged under a privileged policy.

Adopt native Web Components (Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, HTML Templates) as the UI composition model across the application and standardize on Lit for authoring components. Do not use Polymer; existing Polymer elements will be incrementally migrated to Lit-based components or replaced with native implementations.

Components will:
- Be shipped as ES modules, framework-agnostic, and consumable across microfrontends.
- Encapsulate styles via Shadow DOM; expose theme hooks via CSS Custom Properties and parts.
- Define narrow public APIs via attributes/properties, events, and slots; no global singletons.
- Avoid runtime polyfills beyond a minimal webcomponents loader for legacy browsers; official browser matrix will require evergreen browsers.

Tooling and conventions:
- Use TypeScript, open-wc/lit analyzers, and Storybook for documentation and visual tests.
- Test with Web Test Runner and Playwright; accessibility checks with axe.
- Publish versioned packages to the internal registry with semver and changelogs.
- Enforce linting and SSR-safety guidelines; no DOM access before connectedCallback.

Integration:
- Framework wrappers (React/Vue/Angular) are thin adapters; web components remain the source of truth.
- Design tokens drive theming; tokens are distributed as CSS and JSON.

Governance:
- A component review board approves new primitives, enforces reuse, and monitors migration off Polymer until decommissioned.

We will index localized content per locale using one index per language/region (e.g., content_en, content_fr-CA), all governed by a shared index template. Each published locale of a content item becomes an independent document sharing a stable contentId and carrying a locale attribute; versioning keys are (contentId, locale, version).

Language-appropriate analyzers, stemmers, and stopwords will be applied per index to maximize relevance and avoid cross-locale tokenization conflicts. Non-localized attributes (IDs, timestamps, numeric facets) are duplicated in each locale document; filterable fields get keyword subfields to ensure exact matches across locales. Search-as-you-type fields are locale-aware with ICU normalization; diacritics-insensitive matching is enabled where appropriate.

Applications query the locale-specific index through an alias (content_active_<locale>) to decouple callers from physical indices. Fallback is handled by a deterministic chain (e.g., fr-CA → fr → en) via multi-search against multiple locale indices with result merging and boosting for exact-locale matches; cross-locale mixing in a single query is avoided unless explicitly using fallback.

Publishing flows index or update only the affected locale document; unpublishing or deletion removes that locale’s document and leaves others intact. Reindexing uses the shared template to roll out analyzer or mapping changes uniformly. This design is chosen to preserve per-language relevance, simplify operational concerns, reduce document bloat compared to multi-locale documents, and allow independent lifecycle and permissions per locale while supporting predictable fallback behavior.

## Decision
We will encrypt and authenticate all non-opaque cookie values that contain sensitive data. The application will use authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM or equivalent AEAD via a vetted library) with a unique random nonce per issuance. Cookie metadata (name, domain, path, expiry, SameSite) will be included as additional authenticated data to bind integrity to context. Encrypted payloads will be base64url-encoded.

Key management will use envelope encryption: a per-environment primary data-encryption key (DEK) held in application memory, wrapped by a KMS-managed key (KEK). We will maintain a key ring with key identifiers to support seamless rotation. Encryption uses the current primary DEK; decryption attempts all active DEKs. DEKs rotate at least every 90 days or on incident response; KEKs follow cloud/KMS policy. Operational runbooks will cover rotation and emergency revoke/rollover.

For migration, the system will accept legacy plaintext cookies for a limited window and reissue encrypted versions on the next response; after the window, legacy cookies are rejected. On decryption or authentication failure, cookies are treated as absent and re-authentication or session re-issuance is triggered.

We will set Secure and HttpOnly on all cookies and enforce SameSite=Lax by default (Strict where feasible). Cookies will not store long-term secrets; prefer opaque session IDs with server-side state. Size budgets will be enforced (<3 KB total per domain). Metrics will track encryption/decryption counts and failures; no sensitive values or keys are logged.

We will expose immutable state via public final fields only for simple, self-contained, immutable data carriers, while retaining accessor methods for domains requiring encapsulation or future evolution.

- Scope: Allow public final fields for:
  - Pure value objects with no invariants beyond construction-time validation.
  - Internal DTOs, event payloads, and performance-critical hot paths.
  - Classes declared final, with all fields final and immutable (primitives, Strings, other immutable types, unmodifiable collections).

- Exclusions: Continue to use accessors for:
  - Public domain models exposed to external clients (API stability).
  - Entities requiring backward-compatible evolution, lazy computation, or derived invariants.
  - Any class needing field-level access control, validation on read, or binary compatibility guarantees.

- Preferences:
  - Prefer Java Records for new value types; otherwise, use final classes with public final fields.
  - Collections must be defensively copied and wrapped unmodifiable at construction.

- Constraints:
  - No setters, no reflection-based mutation, no serialization frameworks that bypass final safety.
  - Thread-safety must be guaranteed by safe publication (fully constructed before exposure).
  - Field renames are API-breaking; versioning policy applies for externally visible types.

- Enforcement:
  - Coding guidelines and static analysis checks.
  - Code reviews verify immutability invariants and correct scoping (internal vs external).

We will make the ETL pipeline re-entrant and safe to re-run without changing final state beyond intended effects.

- Adopt idempotent, deterministic stages:
  - Extract: read-only, checkpointed by immutable offsets/watermarks (e.g., event offsets, incremental timestamps). Inputs are snapshotted and content-address addressed; re-reads produce identical records.
  - Transform: pure, deterministic functions with versioned configs; no external side effects.
  - Load: upsert/merge semantics keyed by stable business keys; soft-deletes via tombstones; change detection via record hashes to avoid redundant writes.

- Implement exactly-once or effective-once delivery:
  - Use transactional sinks (e.g., MERGE in warehouse/Delta/BigQuery/Snowflake) within atomic batches.
  - Where only at-least-once is available, deduplicate using idempotency keys and unique constraints.

- Introduce re-entrancy mechanics:
  - Run-scoped idempotency key (run_id + partition) persisted in a runs ledger; each target table tracks last successful watermark per partition.
  - Stage-and-swap pattern: write to staging tables/paths, validate, then atomic swap/merge to production.
  - Manifest-driven processing: explicit lists of input files/offset ranges ensure deterministic replays.

- Support backfills and partial retries:
  - Partition by natural time (e.g., ingestion_date) and source partitions; enable selective reprocessing by partition with overwrite-safe merges.
  - Maintain transform version in targets to allow parallel old/new logic and safe replays.

- Robust failure handling and observability:
  - Checkpoint after atomic batch commits; never mid-batch.
  - Dead-letter queues for irrecoverable records; reprocessing honors idempotency keys.
  - End-to-end lineage, metrics, and alerts ensure reruns are verifiable.

- External side effects:
  - All outbound calls use idempotency keys; side effects are deferred until after durable write or recorded in an outbox consumed idempotently.

This decision ensures retries, restarts, and backfills are safe, deterministic, and do not duplicate, omit, or corrupt data.

Pottery shards will be represented as UTF-8 Markdown text files (.md) and serve as the canonical content format across authoring, storage, review, and publishing workflows.

- Markdown dialect: CommonMark with a minimal set of GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) extensions (tables, strikethrough, task lists, fenced code blocks, autolink literals).
- Metadata: Optional YAML front matter at the top of each shard for structured fields (id, title, slug, version, locale, authors, created/updated timestamps, tags, relationships, status). The body follows as Markdown.
- Structure and conventions: Enforce a single H1 as the shard title, hierarchical headings (H2+), stable anchor IDs derived from headings, and canonical LF newlines. Admonitions use standardized fenced syntax. No binary data inline.
- HTML policy: Disallow raw HTML by default; allow a whitelisted subset only when explicitly enabled. All output is sanitized during rendering.
- Assets and links: Reference images and attachments via relative paths within the repository. External links must use HTTPS. Internal cross-links use stable slugs/anchors.
- Parsing and rendering: A single, versioned Markdown toolchain produces HTML and other targets (PDF, DOCX) via AST. Linting and schema checks validate front matter and content rules in CI.
- Internationalization: One shard per locale (e.g., filename.lang.md) with shared IDs in front matter.
- Versioning and migrations: Changes tracked via VCS; breaking format changes are versioned in front matter with migration scripts provided.

We will not support Python 2.7. The baseline runtime for this project is Python 3.9+ and we will use Python 3–only language features, standard library APIs, and dependencies that have dropped Python 2.7 compatibility. We will not maintain shims (e.g., six/future), conditional imports, or backports for Python 2.7, and we will not run CI or publish wheels targeting Python 2.7. Packaging metadata will enforce this via python_requires=">=3.9".

For users constrained to Python 2.7 environments, integration should occur across a process boundary (e.g., REST/gRPC/CLI) so clients can remain on 2.7 while the service/library runs on Python 3. Alternatively, use containerized deployment or a separate microservice to isolate the Python 3 runtime. We will provide migration guidance and examples for consuming the API from Python 2.7 where feasible, but no runtime compatibility guarantees.

This decision enables use of modern typing, asyncio, performance improvements, security patches, and current third‑party libraries, and reduces maintenance burden and risk. Any incoming contributions must adhere to the Python 3.9+ policy; requests to reintroduce Python 2.7 support will be declined.

We will use Angular Material as the primary inspiration for our component library’s design language, component taxonomy, interaction patterns, accessibility standards, and theming model, without taking a runtime dependency on Angular or Angular Material. Specifically:
- Component scope and behavior: We will align our component set and default behaviors with Angular Material’s mature, accessibility-first patterns (focus management, keyboard interaction, ARIA usage), using it as the reference benchmark for parity and UX quality.
- Theming and tokens: We will adopt a Material-like design token system (color roles, elevation, typography scale, density, shape, motion) and support both light/dark and high-contrast modes, with first-class CSS variable/theming APIs inspired by Angular Material’s configuration capabilities.
- API ergonomics: We will mirror the clarity and composability of Angular Material’s APIs where applicable, while keeping framework-agnostic, tree-shakeable, and aligned with our platform architecture. Naming may be similar when it improves discoverability, but we will avoid one-to-one duplication that could cause confusion with Angular-specific concepts.
