- Centralize connector configuration and secret management.

Non‑goals:
- No business/domain logic or data transformation.
- Not a long‑running sync/ETL platform.

Security and compliance:
- Pizzly network access limited to private cluster; ingress via API gateway only.
- Authentication/authorization enforced via gateway service accounts and mTLS between BFF and Pizzly.
- Secrets supplied via our secret manager; tokens encrypted at rest with KMS; periodic key rotation.
- Audit logging of OAuth events and token operations; align with SOC2 controls.

Operations and observability:
- Export structured logs and metrics to our observability stack; include correlation/trace IDs.
- Configure retries with backoff and connector‑specific rate‑limit handling.
- Health/readiness probes and automated rollouts via GitOps.

Rollout and migration:
- Phase out custom OAuth handlers per integration; dual‑run then cutover.
- Provide connector parity list and fallback path to legacy handlers if blocking defects arise.

SLOs and support:
- 99.9% monthly availability; <250 ms p50 proxy overhead; <2 min mean token refresh latency.
- Versioning and change control for connector configs via code review.

Enable AWS VPC Flow Logs for all production and staging VPCs to capture ALL traffic (ACCEPT and REJECT) at the VPC level by default, with targeted overrides at subnet/ENI level for high-volume or sensitive workloads. Use Flow Logs version 5 with 1-minute aggregation and an explicit field set including vpc-id, subnet-id, interface-id, src/dst addr and ports, protocol, packets, bytes, action, log-status, tcp-flags, flow-direction, traffic-path, region, and az-id.

Publish logs to:
- CloudWatch Logs (encrypted) with 14-day retention for rapid triage and alerting via metric filters.
- S3 (encrypted, partitioned by region/account/vpc/date) with 180-day retention and lifecycle to Glacier for 1 year, enabling Athena/Glue queries and SIEM ingestion via Kinesis Data Firehose.

Apply IAM least-privilege roles for log delivery and read-only analytics; enable KMS CMKs for both destinations. Enforce tagging (environment, owner, data-classification) and per-account, per-region deployment via infrastructure-as-code. Non-production developer sandboxes are opt-in with 7-day retention to control cost; explicitly exclude ephemeral test VPCs unless required by compliance.

Integrate alerts for anomalous patterns (e.g., sudden REJECT spikes, egress to unauthorized CIDRs) with incident management. Feed logs to GuardDuty and network analytics dashboards. Maintain data residency by keeping logs in-region; cross-region replication only where mandated.

The Network Security team owns operations and review; quarterly validation will assess coverage, retention, cost, and field set completeness, adjusting filters and scope as needed. Limitations (no payload content, some AWS-managed traffic omissions) are accepted and supplemented by other telemetry where required.

Adopt a first-run, early-startup experiment framework that assigns cohorts deterministically without blocking the critical path and applies treatments only after the first frame is rendered. On initial launch, a built-in, versioned experiment manifest (shipped with the build) is used for eligibility and assignment; remote configuration is fetched asynchronously and takes effect on subsequent launches. Assignments are derived from a stable, privacy-preserving hash of a device/user-scoped seed and experiment ID to ensure deterministic, auditable cohorts. The FirstRunExperimentCoordinator initializes during early startup, evaluates eligibility in-memory under a strict time budget (e.g., ≤20 ms) with a hard fail-fast; if the budget is exceeded or data is unavailable, control is assumed. No network calls or synchronous heavy I/O are permitted on the hot path; assignments are persisted asynchronously after startup completion for reproducibility.

Treatments impacting startup must be guarded by feature flags and executed in safe hooks (post-first-frame or background) with a defined performance budget and rollback path. A global kill switch and per-experiment allow/deny lists are enforced via remote config. Experiments must be idempotent, side-effect aware, and tagged with ownership, hypothesis, metrics, and end date. Telemetry respects user privacy/consent; until consent is granted, only necessary, non-identifying counters are recorded, and experiments requiring PII are disabled. The system guarantees that first-run user experience is never degraded by experiments: if any preconditions fail, defaults are used, and assignments are cached for stability across sessions until the experiment ends or is explicitly reset by config.

We will document all significant architectural decisions as Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) to create a durable, searchable, and auditable decision history.

- Storage and format: ADRs will be Markdown files stored in the repository at docs/adr/, numbered sequentially (e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md) and dated.
- Template: Based on Michael Nygard’s format, each ADR will include Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives Considered, and References.
- Status workflow: proposed → accepted/rejected → superseded/deprecated. Accepted ADRs are immutable; changes occur via a new ADR that references and supersedes the prior one. Only clerical fixes are edited in place.
- Scope: Any decision with lasting impact on architecture, cross-cutting concerns, data models, integrations, security, compliance, SLAs/SLOs, or significant cost/risk.
- Process: Authors open a PR with the ADR; reviewers include the architecture group and relevant stakeholders. Acceptance requires architectural sign-off. ADRs must be linked from related epics, RFCs, and design docs.
- Tooling: We will use lightweight automation (e.g., adr-tools or repo scripts) to initialize, number, and link ADRs; CI will validate filename pattern, required sections, and status transitions.
- Visibility: ADRs are discoverable via an index (docs/adr/README.md) and referenced in onboarding and release notes when applicable.

Adopt GlusterFS as the distributed storage layer for shared, POSIX-compliant persistent storage across services. Deploy a minimum 3-node cluster on dedicated storage nodes with anti-affinity across failure domains, 10/25GbE networking, and SSD/NVMe for bricks and metadata. Create distributed-replicated volumes with replica 3 (or replica 2 with arbiter) to balance availability and capacity; use arbiter volumes where capacity efficiency and split-brain avoidance are priorities. Enable quorum, self-heal daemon, and split-brain detection; enforce client and server quorum policies.

Access will be via the Gluster CSI driver for Kubernetes workloads and native FUSE client for VMs/hosts; NFS-Ganesha may be enabled for legacy clients where needed. GlusterFS will serve shared files, artifacts, media, and application uploads; it will not be used for latency-sensitive databases or message queues, which require dedicated storage. Performance tuning will follow workload profiles: enable sharding for large files, set appropriate write-behind/read-ahead, disable quick-read for DB-like patterns, and size caches conservatively. Backups will snapshot at the brick filesystem layer and/or replicate to object storage; disaster recovery will use geo-replication for critical volumes.

Operationally, standardize on a vetted GlusterFS LTS version, automate provisioning via Ansible/Terraform, and monitor with Prometheus exporters for brick, heal, and quorum health. Upgrades will be rolling with prechecks for heal backlog. Security will enforce TLS for intra-cluster traffic and client auth. Revisit this decision if sustained p99 latency exceeds SLOs, scale requirements surpass practical rebalance times, or if a managed, cloud-native alternative meets requirements with lower TCO.

## Decision
Adopt CQRS with Event Sourcing as a strategic pattern for domains where strong auditability, complex state transitions, high write concurrency, and multiple heterogeneous read models are required; use conventional CRUD with transactional consistency elsewhere. The system will be partitioned by bounded contexts. Within selected contexts:

- Write side: Aggregate roots enforce invariants, emit immutable domain events as the source of truth, with optimistic concurrency and idempotent command handling. Event versioning and schema evolution are mandatory (backward-compatible changes, upcasters as needed).
- Read side: One or more denormalized materialized projections per use case, updated asynchronously from the event stream. Projections are disposable and rebuildable; snapshotting will be applied to long-lived aggregates to optimize rehydration.
- Messaging and delivery: Events are persisted before publication using the outbox pattern; a durable broker ensures at-least-once delivery. Consumers are idempotent. Sagas/process managers coordinate cross-aggregate workflows.
- Consistency model: Eventual consistency is accepted across read models; critical user flows expose command acceptance and projection freshness explicitly. Compensations are modeled as events rather than distributed transactions.
- Data governance: Events avoid sensitive PII where possible; when unavoidable, apply field-level encryption and data minimization. Redaction/forget-me processes are handled via cryptographic erasure or derived store purges; original event mutation is avoided.
- Operations: Support replay-safe projections, blue/green projection deployments, and backfills with rate limiting. Observability includes event lag, projection health, and dead-letter queues. Backup/restore at the event store level is authoritative.
- Tooling: Use a managed event store or log with first-class event streams and snapshots; choose frameworks that support aggregates, sagas, and upcasting. Standardize event naming, metadata, and correlation/causation IDs.
- Adoption guardrails: Apply CQRS+ES only when the above benefits outweigh complexity. A lightweight decision checklist must be satisfied before opting in; otherwise, default to CRUD.

We will adopt RabbitMQ as the central message broker and implement a publish–subscribe pattern for cross-service communication.

- Exchanges and routing: Use topic exchanges as the default for domain events with semantic routing keys (e.g., <domain>.<aggregate>.<event>.<version>). Use fanout exchanges for broad broadcasts and direct exchanges for command routing when needed. Consumers bind their own durable queues with appropriate binding keys.
- Durability and delivery: Enable persistent messages, durable exchanges/queues, consumer acknowledgments, and publisher confirms. Use dead-letter exchanges (DLX) with retry/backoff policies (e.g., limited retries with exponential delays) and a poison-message quarantine.
- Queue types and HA: Use quorum queues for high availability and data safety; avoid classic mirrored queues for new workloads. Size clusters for expected throughput; enable lazy queues where appropriate to reduce memory pressure.
- Exactly-once semantics: Design for at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers. For producer consistency, implement the outbox pattern and transactional publishing. Use message keys and deduplication windows where necessary.
- Schema and versioning: Standardize on JSON with explicit schemas initially; support backward-compatible evolution via versioned event names and additive fields. Consider Avro/Schema Registry if stricter contracts are required later.
- Security and isolation: Enforce TLS in transit, per-environment virtual hosts, least-privilege users, and per-queue/exchange permissions.
- Observability: Emit metrics (publish/consume rates, acks/nacks, DLX counts, queue depth, confirms latency), traces with correlation/causation IDs, and structured logs. Set SLOs and alerts based on lag and DLX rates.
- Operations: Provide IaC-managed RabbitMQ provisioning, automated topology creation, and blue/green compatible configuration. Use managed RabbitMQ or a Kubernetes cluster with persistent volumes and rolling upgrades.
- Client libraries: Use officially supported clients; wrap with a shared library for connection management, retries, and standardized headers.

## Decision

Adopt a managed, headless CMS for all non-transactional content pages (marketing, blog, docs, FAQs, landing pages), while keeping product/transactional UI content in-application. Integrate via a CMS-agnostic adapter exposing typed domain models, backed by the provider’s GraphQL/REST APIs. Render content via SSR/SSG where applicable, with CDN/edge caching and ETag/Surrogate-Control headers. Use webhooks to trigger cache purges and incremental rebuilds on publish/unpublish.

Enable draft/preview flows through a preview API and environment-based routing. Manage SEO (titles, meta, open graph, canonical, slugs), redirects, and scheduling in the CMS. Store and serve media via the CMS’s DAM with on-the-fly image transforms and responsive variants.

Implement i18n and localization within the CMS (locale-aware models and fallbacks) and map to app locales. Establish role-based access, editorial workflows, versioning, and audit logs in the CMS. Separate dev/stage/prod spaces/projects and enforce content model governance via code-reviewed migrations/schemas.

Provide resilience with a read-through cache and stale-while-revalidate; on CMS outages, serve stale content. Nightly exports and on-publish snapshots provide backup and portability. Secure with least-privilege tokens, secret management, network restrictions, and request signing for webhooks.

Adopt a cost-capped plan aligned to expected entries, assets, locales, and API throughput. Maintain an exit strategy by keeping the adapter interface stable, models portable (JSON exports), and templates/view logic CMS-agnostic, enabling provider swap or self-hosted alternative with minimal downstream impact.

We will implement A/B testing at the routing layer using Rails route constraints to deterministically direct traffic to variant-specific controllers/actions based on an experiment assignment stored in a signed, expiring cookie. Variant assignment will be generated on first request using a stable hashing strategy (seeded by user_id when available, else a random UUID persisted in the cookie) to honor experiment allocation ratios, ensure stickiness across sessions/devices where possible, and remain consistent across clustered deployments.

Routes will define variant-specific endpoints behind a single public path, e.g., get "/signup", to: "signup_v1#new", constraints: VariantConstraint[:signup_redesign, :control] and corresponding :treatment mapping, falling back to control when assignment is unknown, user is ineligible, or the experiment is disabled. Experiments will be gated and remotely configurable via our feature flag system (Flipper), allowing percentage rollouts, cohort targeting, geo/device filters, and instant kill switches without deploys.

All variant resolution, cookie management, and bot filtering will be encapsulated in a small, tested Rack middleware and a reusable Route Constraint class to avoid duplication and to keep controllers unaware of experiment logic. We will instrument assignments and outcomes with consistent experiment/variant tags to our analytics pipeline, enforce mutual exclusivity across overlapping experiments on the same route, exclude crawlers and internal traffic, and provide an emergency bypass param for QA. On experiment end, routes will be simplified to the winning variant and legacy code removed promptly.

Adopt npm scripts as the primary interface for all development, build, test, and CI tasks, with Gulp used selectively for file-processing pipelines that benefit from streaming and incremental work (e.g., asset compilation, transforms, watch-based builds). All Gulp tasks will be invoked exclusively through npm scripts to ensure a single, consistent entry point and to maintain cross-platform compatibility.

Key points:
- Task execution is standardized via npm run <task>; CI uses npm ci and npm run <pipeline>.
- Prefer native CLI tooling directly in npm scripts (e.g., eslint, jest, tsc) and simple shell-free composition (npm-run-all, cross-env) for portability.
- Use Gulp only where it provides clear value (chained transforms, caching, watch, parallelization) and keep Gulpfiles minimal, typed when appropriate, and colocated per package.
- Pin tool versions in package.json; use local binaries (npx) only via npm scripts; no global Gulp installation.
- Provide canonical scripts: build, build:watch, test, lint, format, clean, dev, start, release. Gulp-backed tasks are exposed as build:assets, build:assets:watch, etc.
- Ensure reproducibility and isolation: Node LTS, lockfile committed, deterministic CI.
- Deprecate alternative task runners (e.g., Grunt, ad hoc shell scripts). Prefer replacing Gulp usage with native tool supports over time if complexity decreases.

This decision establishes npm scripts as the orchestration layer and Gulp as an implementation detail for complex pipelines, improving developer ergonomics, portability, and CI consistency while minimizing tooling surface area.

We will integrate the Advance Passenger Information (API) functionality into the main service as an internal module, retiring the standalone service. The integration will preserve a clear bounded context via a dedicated package and internal façade, maintaining the existing external API contract and message schemas to avoid client impact. A feature flag will control activation, enabling dark/shadow traffic and gradual rollout with canary releases.

Data handling will follow current PII policies: encryption in transit and at rest, least-privilege access, audit logging, and data minimization. Any required schema changes will be applied via backward-compatible migrations; if a separate database exists, we will migrate data with idempotent jobs and dual-write/verify during transition. Performance budgets and SLOs for the main service will be updated; load/perf tests must pass before full cutover.

Observability will include dedicated metrics, structured logs, distributed traces, and health checks for the new module. Security and privacy reviews are mandatory pre-GA. Failure domains will be contained using circuit breakers and timeouts to protect core flows.

After two successful release cycles in production under the feature flag, we will decommission the old service, remove cross-service calls, and archive its infrastructure and runbooks. Ownership transfers to the main service team; versioning and documentation will be updated accordingly.

We will treat Aleph circrequests with a status of “Denied” as non-actionable operational records that are not imported or surfaced as active requests in the operational system or patron-facing UI. Instead, we will persist a normalized, read-only audit record to the analytics/audit datastore capturing: Aleph request ID, patron ID, bib/item identifiers, request type, timestamps (requested/denied), denial operator, and denial reason (mapped to a controlled vocabulary; missing values mapped to “unspecified,” malformed to “invalid”).

During migration, denied circrequests will not create holds/requests in the target fulfillment domain. We will backfill the past 13 months of denied entries to analytics for reporting and trend analysis; older records will be omitted. For ongoing ingestion, denied entries received via ETL or API will be stored only in the audit store and excluded by default from staff APIs and dashboards, with an explicit includeDenied=true filter for staff reporting endpoints.

Access to denied-request details is restricted to staff with the CirculationManager (or higher) role; patrons will never see denied entries. Denied entries will be retained for 13 months, after which patron identifiers will be pseudonymized to satisfy privacy requirements while preserving aggregate reporting utility.

We will enforce idempotent ingestion using a composite key (request_id, patron_id, item_id, status_date), and reject duplicates. Observability will include counters and breakdowns by reason, branch, and operator (e.g., metric circrequests_denied_total and labels reason, library, source). This decision ensures operational clarity (no dead requests), preserves auditability and reporting needs, and upholds privacy and access controls without polluting active circulation workflows.

## Decision
We will prohibit default exports in application and library code and require named exports for all modules.

- Scope: All new and existing TypeScript/JavaScript modules in this codebase. Public packages we publish will expose only named exports.
- Enforcement: 
  - ESLint: enable import/no-default-export = error; disable import/prefer-default-export. 
  - TS/IDE: configure auto-imports to prefer named exports.
- Patterns:
  - Export functions, classes, constants, and types via named exports.
  - Use explicit named re-exports (export { Foo } from './foo') or export * from './foo' where appropriate; avoid default re-exports.
  - Organize public APIs via index.ts “barrel” files with named exports only.
- Migration:
  - Replace default exports with named equivalents and update all import sites.
  - Use codemods where available; batch changes per package to minimize churn.
  - For published packages, treat the change as breaking (major version bump) if it alters import syntax for consumers.
- Exceptions (allow default exports only when required by external contracts):
  - Framework-mandated signatures (e.g., legacy Next.js pages, certain Storybook/webpack plugin hooks, or toolchains that require default).
  - Third-party interop where the external API only provides a default export and cannot be consumed via named export.
  - Document each exception in-code with a comment and eslint-disable-next-line import/no-default-export.
- Bundling/Tree-shaking:
  - Ensure modules are side-effect free where possible; set sideEffects: false appropriately.
  - Prefer named exports to maximize static analysis and dead-code elimination.

This policy is effective immediately for new code; existing code will be migrated incrementally with lint autofix and targeted PRs.

We will keep a single Git repository as the canonical source of truth and distribute to other version control hosts via automated, read-only mirrors. On every push to default and release branches, and on signed, versioned tags (SemVer), CI/CD will:

- Build, test, and produce reproducible, signed source and binary artifacts (including checksums and SBOM).
- Publish artifacts to our artifact repository and language/package registries as applicable.
- Push-mirror the Git repository (including branches and tags) to designated hosts (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) as read-only mirrors.

Mirrors will have issues and pull requests disabled or clearly configured to redirect contributors to the canonical repository. Only the canonical repository accepts changes; mirrors are for distribution and discovery. We will not maintain native mirrors in non-Git VCS. For non-Git consumers, we will publish versioned tarballs/ZIP archives with signatures.

Security and integrity:

- All release tags are cryptographically signed; artifacts are signed (GPG or Sigstore) and accompanied by checksums.
- CI uses least-privilege credentials for publishing and mirroring; secrets are stored in the platform’s secret manager.
- Provenance metadata is generated for supply-chain verification.

Operational details:

- Mirroring is fast-forward where possible; force-push is restricted to release managers and mirrored with safety checks.
- Mirror sync is event-driven (on push/tag) with periodic reconciliation jobs.
- Repository packaging metadata and manifests are maintained in-repo to enable deterministic builds.

This approach centralizes governance, ensures consistent packaging across ecosystems, broadens distribution via familiar hosts, and reduces operational complexity by avoiding multi-writer or multi-VCS workflows.

Adopt a dedicated Download File Manager (DFM) component responsible for orchestrating all file downloads across the system. The DFM will expose an internal API/SDK for request submission and status querying, and emit domain events for progress, completion, and failure. It will maintain a durable, prioritized queue with per-tenant quotas and rate limits, and execute downloads via a worker pool with bounded concurrency.

Downloads will support resumability using HTTP Range requests and chunked transfer, with checkpointing metadata persisted to durable storage. Integrity will be enforced via checksum/etag verification; optional server-side or pluggable client-provided hashes are supported. Retries will use exponential backoff with jitter and failure classification; idempotency keys will prevent duplicate work.

Storage will be abstracted behind a pluggable interface (local, object storage), with encryption at rest and configurable retention policies; temporary artifacts will be garbage-collected on a schedule. Security controls include allowlist-based egress, signed URL support, and per-request credentials scoping.

Observability will include structured logs, metrics (queue depth, throughput, latency, error rates), and traces. Configuration will be dynamic and centrally managed (limits, timeouts, chunk sizes). The DFM will be stateless in compute, horizontally scalable, and deployable independently.

We will implement the “visittkort” as an independent, framework-agnostic UI library to enable reuse across apps and channels without code duplication. The library will be delivered as a Web Component (Custom Element) built with TypeScript and Lit, exposing a stable, documented API and minimal peer dependencies.

Key decisions:
- Packaging and distribution: Publish as @org/visittkort on npm with ESM-first output, CJS fallback, type definitions, and proper “exports” map. CDN compatibility via jsDelivr/UNPKG. Versioning follows SemVer with automated changelogs and release notes.
- Styling and theming: Encapsulate styles via Shadow DOM; expose customization via CSS custom properties and design tokens. Provide a small set of slots for content extensibility. No global CSS dependencies.
- Accessibility and i18n: Meet WCAG 2.1 AA; include ARIA roles/labels; ensure keyboard and screen reader support. Support localization via attributes/properties; avoid hardcoded text.
- Performance and footprint: Tree-shakeable build with strict size budget. No heavyweight dependencies; Lit as the only runtime helper.
- SSR/prerendering: Provide a lightweight server-side render/prerender helper to emit static HTML with attribute hydration for progressive enhancement.
- API surface: Typed properties/attributes, events for interaction hooks, and safe defaults. Publish Custom Elements Manifest and TypeScript types.
- Quality and DX: Storybook-based docs and live examples; unit and visual regression tests; CI validating lint, type, a11y checks. Backward compatibility guaranteed with deprecation policy and migration notes.

We will standardize on Ubuntu 18.04 LTS (Bionic) as the baseline operating system across production servers, build agents, and container base images to ensure consistency, reproducibility, and compatibility with current dependencies.

- Scope:
  - All Linux servers, VM images (e.g., AMIs), and Kubernetes nodes will run Ubuntu 18.04.
  - Container images will use ubuntu:18.04 or ubuntu:bionic as the base unless an explicit exception is granted.
  - CI/CD runners and golden images will be built from Ubuntu 18.04 minimal images.

- Version pinning and updates:
  - Pin to the “bionic” series with explicit package versions where reproducibility is required.
  - Enable and subscribe to Ubuntu Pro/ESM for security updates and critical fixes.
  - Prohibit upgrading core libraries beyond bionic repositories; backports allowed only via approved PPA or vendor repositories after security review.

- Architecture and kernels:
  - Primary architecture: x86_64. Any ARM usage requires prior approval and validation on 18.04.
  - Use the GA kernel unless a hardware enablement (HWE) kernel is explicitly approved for required drivers.

- Operationalization:
  - Provide hardened baseline via configuration management (CIS-aligned).
  - Maintain a single golden image and a single base container image, rebuilt weekly with security patches.
  - Enforce with CI policy checks that block non-18.04 base images.

- Exceptions and lifecycle:
  - Exceptions require architecture review and documented risk acceptance.
  - Establish a migration plan to the next LTS and a deprecation timeline aligned with Ubuntu 18.04 ESM end-of-life.

## Decision
Implement a standardized, pluggable Status Reporter interface for all portals and supporting services, with a single source of truth in a central Status Service.

- Define a Status Reporter contract exposing health, readiness, and dependency checks, returning normalized states: OK, DEGRADED, OUTAGE, and UNKNOWN, with optional telemetry (latency, error rates), version, and build metadata.
- Provide two integration modes:
  - Pull: Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoints and lightweight /healthz, /readyz HTTP endpoints for infrastructure probes and SLO tracking.
  - Push: Authenticated gRPC/HTTP webhook to the Status Service for near-real-time updates, including heartbeats and change events.
- Standardize payload schema (JSON/gRPC) with:
  - Service identity (name, environment, region), correlation/trace IDs, incident link, and timestamp.
  - Dependency breakdown with per-dependency state and impact.
  - Severity, user impact summary, and remediation hint fields.
- Enforce bounded update cadence (default heartbeat 30s, change events immediate), idempotency, retries with exponential backoff, and circuit breaking to avoid thundering herds.
- Secure reporters with mTLS between services and the Status Service; require signed tokens for push; limit public endpoints to read-only health.
- Expose a consolidated API and UI from the Status Service for consumers (portal banner, status page, alerting) and publish events to our messaging bus for automation.
- Provide SDKs and a conformance test suite; deprecate ad-hoc pings and bespoke status pages over two releases with an adapter for legacy services.

We will standardize on SDL2 as the cross-platform abstraction for windowing, display management, input mapping, and 2D rendering to reliably support multiple screen resolutions, aspect ratios, and DPI settings across all target platforms.

- Rendering and scaling:
  - Use SDL_Renderer with a fixed logical resolution via SDL_RenderSetLogicalSize to decouple game coordinates from physical pixels.
  - Enable high-quality scaling using SDL_HINT_RENDER_SCALE_QUALITY set per-platform (linear default; nearest for pixel-art modes).
  - Default to letterboxing to preserve aspect ratio; allow configurable modes: letterbox, extend (pillar/letter), and safe-crop.
  - Support high-DPI by enabling SDL_WINDOW_ALLOW_HIGHDPI and resolving drawable size via SDL_GL_GetDrawableSize/SDL_GetRendererOutputSize.

- Display modes and resizing:
  - On startup, enumerate SDL display modes and select the closest supported fullscreen mode; provide borderless-windowed as default.
  - Handle runtime window resizes; recompute viewport/letterbox and update input mapping without changing logical size.
  - Enable VSync by default; allow override for benchmarking.

- Input and UI:
  - Map input coordinates through SDL’s logical size transform to remain resolution-agnostic.
  - Implement UI/layout with relative anchors and constraints against the logical coordinate system; define safe areas for notches/cutouts.

- Assets and quality:
  - Ship assets authored for the logical resolution; support multi-LOD textures where needed.
  - Provide per-platform overrides for texture filtering and font rasterization.

- Abstraction and testing:
  - Encapsulate SDL usage behind a DisplayService to allow future renderer swaps.
  - Establish automated tests across representative resolutions/aspect ratios (4:3, 16:9, 21:9, portrait) and DPI classes.

Adopt a hexagonal (ports-and-adapters) architecture as the primary structural pattern to decouple domain logic from delivery and infrastructure. Define clear module boundaries: domain, application (use cases), inbound adapters (HTTP/CLI/Messaging), and outbound adapters (databases, external services). All communication crosses via explicit interfaces (ports) owned by the domain/application layers. Enforce dependency direction: adapters depend inward; domain depends on no framework.

Within modules, standardize use of structural design patterns:
- Facade to expose cohesive entry points per bounded context and per adapter.
- Adapter to integrate external systems and legacy libraries to domain ports.
- Composite for hierarchical domain aggregates where uniform operations are required.
- Decorator for orthogonal cross-cutting concerns (caching, metrics, retries) around ports and repositories.
- Proxy for lazy-loading or remote-resource access where network boundaries must be abstracted.
- Bridge when multiple orthogonal dimensions of variation exist (e.g., storage backend vs. serialization).
- Flyweight only in memory-critical hotspots, gated by profiling.

Use a DI container to bind ports to adapters and to compose decorators/proxies. Forbid cyclic dependencies and direct adapter-to-adapter calls. Provide code templates and linting rules to enforce boundaries and naming (Port, Adapter, Facade, Decorator). Tests target ports with contract tests for adapters and in-memory doubles for domain. This decision is mandatory for new services and applied incrementally to existing code during refactors.

We will implement application-scoped Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) using FusionAuth as the authoritative source of user roles, while keeping fine-grained permissions in our applications.

- Define roles per application in FusionAuth; assign users to roles via application registrations. Roles will be the only authorization construct stored in FusionAuth. Groups may be used for admin workflows but not for runtime authorization.
- Maintain a versioned, code-owned permission matrix in each service mapping roles to permissions. Authorization decisions are enforced in application/services based on this mapping; no runtime calls to FusionAuth are required for authorization.
- Propagate roles (and, when needed, organization/tenant identifiers) in JWT access tokens. Use FusionAuth lambdas to shape JWT claims (e.g., roles, tenant, org) and to minimize token size while preserving required context.
- Adopt short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation to reduce risk and ensure timely revocation. Token TTLs will be tuned per application sensitivity.
- Manage roles and registrations via FusionAuth Admin UI for routine operations and via FusionAuth APIs for automation. All role definitions and assignments critical to production will be managed through Infrastructure-as-Code and audited change workflows.
- Separate environments/tenants in FusionAuth; roles are not shared across tenants. Cross-tenant access is not supported.
- For service-to-service interactions, prefer OAuth2 client credentials with explicit scopes; map scopes to internal permissions similarly to roles. Do not overload user roles for machine identities.
- Deprovisioning is enforced by removing registrations/roles in FusionAuth; downstream access is naturally revoked on token expiry. Emergency revocations will invalidate refresh tokens and, when necessary, rotate signing keys.
- Backward compatibility will be maintained by supporting legacy role names during a migration window via JWT claim transformation in lambdas.

Adopt Locust as the primary tool for load and performance testing of our HTTP and WebSocket services. Test scenarios will be authored in Python, enabling reuse of our existing libraries, domain models, and fixtures. We will run Locust in headless mode in CI for smoke/perf gates and in distributed mode (multiple workers) for larger tests in ephemeral or staging environments, orchestrated via Docker/Kubernetes. Metrics and results will be exported to Prometheus (via Pushgateway) and/or InfluxDB with Grafana dashboards; pass/fail thresholds will be enforced in CI.

Scope:
- Use Locust for API-level throughput/latency testing, soak tests, and user-journey modeling at protocol level.
- Store test code alongside services; version tests with the service; pin Locust and plugin versions.

Constraints and guardrails:
- Each worker is single-threaded; scale via multiple processes/pods. Avoid CPU-bound Python in user code; keep client think-time realistic.
- For protocols Locust does not natively support (gRPC, MQTT) or for browser-level benchmarks, prefer k6/Gatling or Playwright-based suites.
- Large-scale tests will run against production-like environments with synthetic data and isolated tenants.

Operationalization:
- Provide a shared Locust base library, fixtures, and common auth/client utilities.
- Standardize test data management and environment configuration via environment variables and secrets.
- Automate reports and trend baselines; fail builds on regression beyond agreed SLO/SLA thresholds.

This decision may be revisited if protocol coverage, scale needs, or team composition change materially.

We will process long-running, resource-intensive, or non-critical operations asynchronously via a dedicated background worker service consuming tasks from a durable queue. The web/API layer will enqueue jobs and return immediately; no request will block on work exceeding the synchronous SLA.

Implementation:
- Separate worker deployment (container/pod) with its own autoscaling, lifecycle hooks, and graceful shutdown handling.
- Durable message queue with at-least-once delivery semantics; tasks must be idempotent and accept duplicates via idempotency keys or natural keys. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter and a capped maximum; failed tasks land in a dead-letter queue for triage.
- Priority queues (high/default/low) and a scheduled/delayed queue for time-based execution; concurrency and per-queue rate limits are configurable.
- Task contracts define strict input schemas, maximum runtime, and cancellation semantics; jobs exceeding limits are terminated and retried according to policy.
- Observability: structured logs with correlation/job IDs, metrics (enqueue/dequeue rates, lag, success/failure, runtime), traces across enqueue→execute, and alerting on backlog thresholds and DLQ growth.
- Data consistency: where tasks are triggered by DB writes, use the outbox pattern (transactional write + relay) to avoid lost or duplicated work; when not feasible, use best-effort enqueue with reconciliation jobs.
- Security: only trusted services may enqueue; payloads exclude PII where possible, are minimal and validated; encryption in transit and server-side at rest for the queue; secrets managed via the platform’s secret store.
- API for task status and progress via job IDs; SLAs documented per task class.
- Backward compatibility: versioned task handlers to allow zero-downtime deploys.

This decision enables independent scaling, improved reliability, and predictable latency for the synchronous path while providing robust controls for background execution.

We will implement two dedicated, null-safe comparators for the Observation domain entity to serve distinct business needs: deduplication and deterministic ordering.

1) ObservationIdentityComparator
- Purpose: logical equivalence for deduplication/merging.
- Keys (in order): subjectId → code/system → category → effectiveInstant/period start → deviceId → specimenId → bodySite → method → qualifiers/dimensions (e.g., unit system/code for quantitative values).
- Ignores transient/volatile fields (id/UUID, createdAt, updatedAt, provenance, notes, performer) and presentation-only formatting.
- Normalizes: code systems to lowercase, trims strings, canonicalizes units (UCUM where available), and flattens effectiveDateTime/effectivePeriod to an instant (period start).
- Outcome: two observations compare equal (compare == 0) when they represent the same clinical measurement instance regardless of persistence identifiers.

2) ObservationSortComparator
- Purpose: stable, deterministic ordering for lists/feeds.
- Order (descending recency first): effectiveInstant (nulls last) → clinicalPriority (e.g., critical > high > normal; nulls lowest) → category → code → subjectId → value presence (with quantities sorted by value then unit; strings lexicographically; booleans true before false) → deviceId → tie-breaker by persistent id to ensure total order.
- Stable across runs and independent of locale; uses English/ASCII collation and numeric comparison for quantities.

Implementation notes
- Provided as immutable, reusable strategies (e.g., Java Comparator<Observation> or equivalent), exposed via ObservationComparators.identity() and ObservationComparators.sorting().
- Unit and code normalization delegated to shared Terminology/Units services where available; fall back to raw values if normalization fails.
- Documented null-handling, transitivity guarantees, and that neither comparator defines equals/hashCode semantics on Observation.
- Backward compatible: no changes to Observation schema; solely adds utilities and usage guidelines in services and UIs.

## Decision

All code and infrastructure changes must be proposed, reviewed, validated, and merged via pull requests (PRs) to the default branch. Direct commits to protected branches are prohibited.

- Branching and protections:
  - Default branch is protected; requires PR with status checks passing.
  - At least 1 approval for low-risk repos; 2 approvals for core, security, or production-impacting changes.
  - Code Owners enforce mandatory reviewers for owned paths.
  - Require up-to-date branch before merge; auto-merge enabled when checks pass.

- Review and quality gates:
  - CI must run on every PR: build, unit/integration tests, linting, security scans, license checks.
  - PRs must include linked issue/work item, meaningful title, and a template-driven description (scope, rationale, testing, risk).
  - Squash merge is the default strategy; rebase allowed for libraries; merge commits disabled.
  - Small, incremental PRs are preferred; large PRs require prior design discussion and clear test evidence.

- Workflow and SLAs:
  - Draft PRs encouraged for early feedback; convert to Ready for Review when complete.
  - Review SLA: initial response within 1 business day; authors address feedback within 2 business days.
  - Use labels for priority, risk, breaking change, and release notes.

- Security and compliance:
  - Require signed commits and verified identities.
  - Enforce DCO/CLA where applicable.
  - Secrets scanning and SAST must block merges on critical findings.

- Exceptions:
  - Emergency hotfixes may use a streamlined PR path with on-call approval; postmortem PR to follow.
  - Generated or vendored code may have adapted review rules but must still merge via PR.

- Tooling:
  - Standard PR templates, CODEOWNERS, branch rules, and CI pipelines are maintained as code in the repo.
  - Bots may auto-assign reviewers, suggest owners, and enforce policy.

Adopt a versioned, immutable Launch Config model with controlled, event-driven propagation. All changes produce a new, immutable version stored in a central configuration service backed by Git for auditability. Clients do not mutate configs in place; they resolve and cache the latest compatible version.

Propagation is asynchronous via a message bus topic (launch-config.updated) carrying config ID, semantic version, scope, and effectiveAt timestamp. Services subscribe and pull the referenced version from the config service, validating signature and schema before activating. The default rollout is staged: sandbox → canary → partial → full per environment, with optional effectiveAt scheduling and an emergency override. We target 95th percentile propagation within 5 minutes; clients must tolerate eventual consistency and support graceful fallback to the last-known-good version.

Compatibility policy: additive changes only for minor/patch versions; breaking changes require a new major version, dual-publish, and client support for version ranges. Schemas are enforced via CI/CD validation, policy checks, and mandatory approval gates. Feature flags within the config are used for fine-grained toggles during rollout.

Reliability: retries with exponential backoff, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues, and alerts on propagation failures. If validation or activation fails, clients retain the previous version and report health signals. Rollback is achieved by promoting a prior version and re-emitting the update event; no destructive edits occur.

Security and governance: configs are signed, access-controlled, and fully audited (who/what/when). This approach ensures safe, traceable, and timely propagation with predictable blast radius and rapid recovery.

## Decision

Adopt a consistent, human- and machine-friendly naming convention for all katas across code, directories, and documentation.

- Canonical kata identifier: KATA-<zero-padded id>-<slug>-<difficulty>-v<major>
  - Example: KATA-005-bowling-game-beginner-v1
- Slug rules:
  - Lowercase kebab-case ASCII only (a–z, 0–9, -)
  - Concise, domain-relevant terms (max ~5 words), no stopwords if unnecessary
  - Stable once published; only corrected for clear errors via deprecation notice
- Difficulty vocabulary: beginner | intermediate | advanced (fixed set)
- Versioning:
  - Major versions only in the canonical name (v1, v2, …) for breaking changes to requirements
  - Minor/patch changes are tracked in repository tags/releases but do not change the directory name
- Directory layout:
  - /katas/KATA-<id>-<slug>-<difficulty>-v<major>/<language>/
  - Language folder names: lowercase (e.g., java, kotlin, python, js, ts, csharp)
- File/project names within language implementations follow that language’s idioms but must include the kata slug in README and package metadata
- Git tags/releases:
  - kata/KATA-<id>/v<major.minor.patch>
- Prohibited:
  - Spaces, underscores, special characters, diacritics
  - Renaming published canonical paths except via deprecation + redirect README
- Metadata (README front matter or manifest):
  - id, slug, difficulty, domain tags, source/attribution, created date (ISO-8601), current version

This convention ensures discoverability, stability, and automated tooling compatibility across the kata catalog.

## Decision

We will decouple Monitoring Forwarders from any specific storage technology by introducing a storage-agnostic delivery contract and pluggable sink adapters.

- Define a stable Telemetry Envelope schema (events, metrics, logs, traces) with explicit versioning and backward-compatible evolution.
- Implement a Forwarder OutputPort interface that abstracts delivery (enqueue, batch, flush, health, backpressure) with context propagation (trace, tenant, auth).
- Provide sink adapters as plugins:
  - Asynchronous broker adapters (e.g., Kafka, SQS, Pub/Sub) as the preferred path for scale and durability.
  - Direct write adapters (e.g., Elasticsearch, ClickHouse, Timeseries DB) for low-latency scenarios, still behind the same interface.
- Default deployment uses a broker-based path: forwarders publish envelopes to a message bus; independent Storage Writers (separate services) consume and persist to chosen backends. Multiple writers can be configured for fan-out.
- Maintain at-least-once delivery with idempotency keys, retry with exponential backoff, dead-letter queues, and bounded on-disk buffering for transient outages.
- Support runtime selection and multi-sink routing via configuration (and feature flags), enabling progressive migration and A/B validation. Direct storage coupling in legacy forwarders will be deprecated behind the new interface.
- Adopt OpenTelemetry semantic conventions and resource attributes to maximize interoperability; include per-tenant quotas and rate limiting in the output layer.
- Enforce security and compliance: encryption in transit, optional envelope encryption at rest in the broker, signed envelopes for integrity, and tenancy-aware isolation.
- Provide operational introspection: metrics, health endpoints, sink lag, drop rates, schema mismatch alerts, and end-to-end traceability.
- Backward compatibility: introduce shims that adapt legacy payloads to the envelope schema, with a staged deprecation timeline.

Success is measured by the ability to add or change storage backends without forwarder code changes, zero-downtime migrations, and maintained SLOs for ingestion latency and durability.

Adopt a shared Generic Startup Library to standardize service and CLI bootstrapping across the portfolio. The library will be published as an internal versioned package and will provide opinionated, secure-by-default wiring for configuration loading (hierarchical env/secret stores), dependency injection, structured logging, distributed tracing/metrics, health/ready/startup probes, HTTP pipeline hardening (CORS, compression, rate limiting, security headers), feature flags, and graceful shutdown. It will expose extension points via composable modules and opt-in/opt-out flags, allowing services to override defaults and register custom middleware, handlers, and integrations without forking.

Scope:
- Mandatory for all new services; recommended migration path for existing services as part of active iterations.
- First-class support for our primary runtime(s) and transport patterns (HTTP, messaging, background workers).
- Built-in integrations for our standard platform components (observability, secrets, service discovery), guarded behind interfaces to permit stubbing in tests.

Non-goals:
- Business logic scaffolding or persistence abstractions beyond minimal wiring.
- Breaking application behavior; all defaults can be explicitly overridden.

Quality and governance:
- Semantic versioning with documented upgrade guides; LTS branches for major versions.
- Backward-compatible defaults; breaking changes only in majors with deprecation notices.
- Extensive examples, templates, and lint rules to enforce baseline usage.
- Security baselines enabled by default; configuration validation and startup fail-fast on misconfiguration.

Rollout:
- Provide migration kit and automated codemods where possible.
- CI conformity checks to ensure adoption and consistent configuration across services.

We will standardize the production runtime to depend exclusively on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) managed services and primitives. All compute will run on Cloud Run and/or GKE; data storage will use Cloud SQL/Spanner/BigQuery; messaging and streaming will use Pub/Sub; object storage will use Cloud Storage; secrets will use Secret Manager; networking will use GCP VPC, Cloud Load Balancing, and Cloud NAT; observability will use Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring, and Cloud Trace; container images will be hosted in Artifact Registry; IAM will use GCP IAM with Workload Identity (no long‑lived keys).

No AWS/Azure/on‑prem runtimes, SDKs, or managed services will be part of the production execution path. Third‑party SaaS in the critical path requires explicit approval; otherwise, only GCP services are permitted. CI/CD may run on any platform but will deploy only to GCP. For local/dev/test, we will prefer official GCP emulators (e.g., Pub/Sub, Datastore), and any non‑GCP stubs must be fully replaceable by GCP services in production.

We will maintain cloud‑agnostic interfaces at the application boundary to preserve a migration path, but the default implementations will target GCP only. Infrastructure will be provisioned with Terraform using GCP providers and secured via per‑service accounts, organization policies, CMEK where required, and regional multi‑AZ deployments with cross‑region DR within GCP. Exceptions to this decision require an architecture review and documented risk acceptance.

## Decision
We will eliminate mutable, process-wide configuration and singletons. Configuration will be explicit, scoped, and injected.

- Each service/module defines a typed, immutable Config object capturing only what it needs. Configs are constructed at the composition root (app startup) and provided via dependency injection or explicit parameters—never via global accessors.
- Runtime values are sourced from layered providers with clear precedence: code defaults < environment files < environment variables/secret manager < CLI flags < in-memory test overrides. Libraries must accept options objects and must not read environment or files directly.
- Secrets and credentials are resolved via the centralized secret manager; no secrets in code, repos, or environment files in non-local environments.
- Request- or tenant-scoped settings (e.g., locale, feature entitlements) are passed via an explicit request context and propagated through call chains; no thread-locals or implicit globals.
- Configuration is immutable after construction. Where live reload is required, a configuration provider publishes change events and consumers reinitialize safely behind feature-flagged, zero-downtime mechanisms; otherwise, changes require restart.
- We will deprecate and remove GlobalConfig and similar patterns. Transitional adapters will wrap legacy consumers, and static analysis rules will block new imports of global config.
- Tests supply configuration fixtures explicitly; test helpers provide factories for minimal valid configs.

## Decision
All reusable components will be published as versioned, immutable artifacts to organization-managed registries, with automated, policy-enforced release workflows.

- Distribution: 
  - JavaScript/TypeScript libraries to the internal npm-compatible registry.
  - JVM artifacts to the internal Maven-compatible repository.
  - .NET packages to the internal NuGet feed.
  - Python packages to the internal PyPI.
  - Container images to the internal OCI registry.
  - Design tokens/assets to the CDN-backed asset repository.

- Versioning and compatibility:
  - Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is mandatory.
  - Backwards compatibility is required for all MINOR/PATCH releases; breaking changes only in MAJOR releases with migration guides.

- Release governance:
  - CI-driven release pipelines with automated linting, tests, security scans, license checks, SBOM generation, and artifact signing (provenance attestations).
  - Conventional Commits drive automated changelog generation and version bumps.
  - Release channels: canary, beta, stable; pre-releases are clearly tagged.
  - Artifacts are immutable; re-publishing the same version is forbidden.

- Access and discoverability:
  - Components are private-by-default; public publishing requires security/legal approval.
  - Ownership, support SLA, lifecycle status, and deprecation policy are declared in component metadata.
  - All published components are indexed in the internal developer catalog with usage docs and examples.

- Deprecation and lifecycle:
  - Deprecations announced with at least one MINOR cycle notice; supported window and EOL date documented.
  - Security fixes may be backported per severity and SLA.

- Operational policies:
  - Retention rules keep latest N majors and LTS lines.
  - Reproducible builds (locked dependencies) are required.
  - Consumers pin compatible versions (~ or ^ as appropriate) and receive automated update notifications.

We will model phosphorylation (and corresponding dephosphorylation) as linear mass-action kinetics per site/state, using pseudo–first-order rates:
- d[S_P]/dt = k_phos · S_U − k_dephos · S_P
- k_phos and k_dephos are apparent first-order rate constants calibrated from data or derived from enzyme parameters under the assumption of non-saturating conditions and approximately constant active enzyme.

Implementation details:
- Generate one forward (phos) and one reverse (dephos) reaction per phosphorylation site/state.
- Ensure mutual exclusivity of states (e.g., S_U + S_P = S_total for single-site models; use independent terms per site for multi-site).
- Support per-site, context-specific rate constants; allow time-/condition-dependent modulation via provided signals (e.g., k_phos = f(signal)).
- Provide optional temperature dependence (e.g., Arrhenius/Q10) applied to k values.
- Default solver integration uses linear propensity functions; stochastic and deterministic backends consume identical rate definitions.

Guardrails and fallbacks:
- Apply linear kinetics by default; if enzyme saturation or strong enzyme dynamics are explicitly modeled, allow an opt-in mode to promote to bilinear mass action with explicit kinase species (v = k · [Kinase] · S_U) while maintaining the same interface.
- Document validity assumptions at model boundaries and flag configurations that violate pseudo–first-order conditions.

Adopt snapshot testing to capture and verify stable, renderable outputs (UI component trees, serialized API contracts, config generation, templated content) where full value-based assertions are impractical. Store human-reviewable “golden” snapshots in-repo alongside tests to enable peer-reviewed diffs in pull requests. Use snapshots as a supplement, not a replacement, for behavior-focused assertions; critical logic must retain explicit assertions.

Tooling:
- Frontend: Jest + React Testing Library + Storybook snapshots for visual states; image snapshots via jest-image-snapshot only for explicitly approved flows.
- Backend: Jest/Vitest/Mocha with deterministic serializers for API payloads and codegen outputs.

Determinism:
- Normalize and mask non-deterministic fields (timestamps, IDs, ordering).
- Enforce stable sorting and locale.
- Provide custom serializers for noisy objects; exclude platform-specific values.

Governance:
- Any snapshot update requires human review of diffs; “update snapshots” is not allowed to pass CI without reviewer approval.
- CI will fail on missing/changed snapshots; large snapshot diffs (>500 lines) require a second reviewer.
- Snapshots >2KB should be split or replaced with targeted assertions; binary/image snapshots limited to essential cases.

Organization:
- One snapshot per test case/state; descriptive names reflecting user-visible behavior.
- Co-locate snapshots with tests; version-control all snapshots.
- Tag snapshots with semantic intent; breaking visual/API changes require a CHANGELOG entry.

Lifecycle:
- Review and prune obsolete snapshots quarterly.
- Prohibit snapshots for unstable or experimental components until stabilized.
- Prefer contract tests for public APIs; snapshot tests focus on private/internal render trees.

Adopt APS as the authoritative benchmark framework for performance, scalability, and resource-efficiency evaluation across all services and libraries. APS will be the single source for baseline definitions, test scenarios, datasets, and result reporting, and will be integrated into CI/CD as a mandatory gate for release candidates and critical merges.

Key elements of this decision:
- Scope: All performance-sensitive components (APIs, batch jobs, data pipelines, SDKs). New components must define APS suites before production rollout; existing components must onboard within two release cycles.
- Metrics and SLAs: Standardize on latency percentiles, throughput, error rates, tail latencies, startup time, memory/CPU/IO footprints, and cost-per-transaction. SLAs encoded as versioned APS profiles per service tier.
- Reproducibility: Fixed, versioned datasets and workload models; pinned runtime/toolchain; containerized runners; environment descriptors (CPU/memory limits) committed to repo.
- CI/CD integration: Nightly trending runs and per-PR smoke benchmarks; hard gates on SLA regressions beyond defined budget; soft alerts for early warnings with owner acknowledgment required.
- Result management: Centralized results store with immutable run metadata, provenance, and trend dashboards; automated regression detection with issue auto-filing to owning teams.
- Governance: Performance Working Group maintains shared APS modules, profiles, and datasets; any SLA/profile change requires PR review and traceable approval.
- Extensibility: Support custom probes and domain-specific workloads via plugin interface without forking core APS; cross-language runners where applicable.
- Cost control: Scheduled execution windows and tiered test depths (smoke, standard, exhaustive) to balance signal and spend.
- Security and compliance: Sanitize datasets; enforce secrets-free configs; restrict benchmark environments to non-production, isolated networks.

This decision deprecates ad-hoc benchmarking and disparate scripts. Success is measured by reproducible baselines, faster regression detection, and clear performance ownership tied to APS gates and reports.

Adopt TypeScript as the primary language for all new application and library code, with a gradual migration path for existing JavaScript. Use TypeScript ≥5.x with "strict": true across all projects. Establish a shared base tsconfig (tsconfig.base.json) consumed by packages/apps, with NodeNext module resolution, target ES2022, sourceMap true, incremental true, skipLibCheck true, and path aliases managed via compilerOptions.paths (with corresponding tooling resolution).

For build performance, use tsc --noEmit for type checking and swc/esbuild for transpilation/bundling; include source maps in all build outputs. For Node services, require Node 18+; for web, target evergreen browsers. React code will use .tsx with JSX set to react-jsx. Maintain type-safe boundaries at API/IO using typed clients and generated types (e.g., OpenAPI/GraphQL codegen) where applicable.

Enforce linting and formatting via ESLint + @typescript-eslint and Prettier, with CI gates for type-check and lint. Disallow implicit any and ban the use of // @ts-ignore except with justification. Provide .d.ts declaration outputs for any published packages; expose stable, well-documented types as part of public APIs.

Permit existing JavaScript during migration using allowJs and checkJs for selected modules, with prioritized conversion to .ts/.tsx. Small, one-off scripts may remain JavaScript if kept outside product code and CI-enforced folders.

Developer ergonomics: enable editor tooling via tsconfig references, maintain fast feedback with project references and incremental builds, and document common patterns (enums vs unions, branded types, utility types) in a shared guide.

## Decision

We will deprecate and remove DynamicServiceLocator across all codebases in favor of explicit dependency injection and well-defined composition roots.

- Effective immediately: no new usages are allowed. A linter rule and CI check will block new references.
- Replacement approach:
  - Use constructor injection via the standard DI container (AppContainer) at composition roots.
  - For dynamic/plugin resolution, use a typed Registry + Factory pattern keyed by capability identifiers, backed by configuration and module metadata; discovery occurs at startup, not at call sites.
  - Cross-module access must occur via explicit interfaces defined in the domain boundary modules and registered in the container.
- Migration path:
  - vNext: annotate DynamicServiceLocator as @Deprecated and emit runtime warnings on first use; provide codemods and recipes to replace calls with injected dependencies or registry lookups.
  - vNext+1: ship a compatibility shim behind feature flag serviceLocator.enabled (default: false). Teams may opt-in temporarily while migrating.
  - vNext+2: remove DynamicServiceLocator and the flag; breaking change documented in release notes.
- Backward compatibility and risk mitigation:
  - Maintain behavior parity in the shim; add tracing around lookups to identify remaining call sites.
  - Provide sample modules, test helpers, and container-scoped lifetimes to avoid regressions and circular dependencies.
  - Performance SLOs will be validated; expected improvements: reduced reflection, faster cold start, deterministic wiring.
- Ownership and support:
  - Platform team owns the deprecation, tooling, and documentation; each service team owns migration in their code.
  - Exceptions require Architecture Council approval and are time-boxed to vNext+1 only.
